title: Psalms

stories.title: 🌳 Psalms 1
summaryBullets: Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, or set foot on the path of sinners, or sit in the seat of mockers. (1:1).
But his delight is in the Law of the LORD, and on His law he meditates day and night. (1:2).
He is like a tree planted by streams of water, yielding its fruit in season, whose leaf does not wither, and who prospers in all he does. (1:3).
Not so the wicked! For they are like chaff driven off by the wind. (1:4).
Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous. (1:5).
For the LORD guards the path of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish. (1:6).
crossRefs: Joshua 1:8: The same charge in almost the same words, spoken to Joshua as he takes command after Moses dies. What this psalm describes as a way of life was first an order given to a man about to invade Canaan.
Jeremiah 17:7-8: Jeremiah takes the same tree by water and presses it further than the psalm does: it does not fear when the heat comes and keeps producing fruit through a year of drought.
Psalm 92:12-14: The tree image again, this time planted in the house of the LORD, and the point is old age. The righteous still bear fruit when they are old, healthy and green.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַשְׁרֵי (ʾashrei); Greek (LXX): μακάριος (makarios)
translationNotes.note: Exclamation of happiness or fortunate status; plural of intensity in Hebrew.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תּוֹרָה (torah), Greek: νόμος (nomos), Aramaic: אורייתא (orayta)
translationNotes.note: Instruction/teaching; not only legal codes but God’s revealed instruction.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֹץ (mots), Greek (LXX): χνοῦς (chnous), Aramaic: מוץ (mots)
translationNotes.note: Light husks blown off grain; image of instability and worthlessness.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הָגָה (hagah)
translationNotes.note: The verb means to mutter, growl, or murmur out loud. It is used of a lion growling over its kill (Isaiah 31:4) and of a man moaning like a dove (Isaiah 38:14). Meditation in verse 2 is not silent reflection; it is saying the words half aloud, over and over, day and night.

stories.keyTakeaway: Those who delight in the LORD’s law are stable and fruitful; the wicked are blown away and perish.

stories.title: 👑 Psalms 2
summaryBullets: Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain? (2:1).
The kings of the earth take their stand and the rulers gather together, against the LORD and against His Anointed One: (2:2).
“Let us break Their chains and cast away Their cords.” (2:3).
The One enthroned in heaven laughs; the Lord taunts them. (2:4).
Then He rebukes them in His anger, and terrifies them in His fury: (2:5).
“I have installed My King on Zion, upon My holy mountain.” (2:6).
I will proclaim the decree spoken to Me by the LORD: “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father. (2:7).
Ask Me, and I will make the nations Your inheritance, the ends of the earth Your possession. (2:8).
You will break them with an iron scepter; You will shatter them like pottery.” (2:9).
Therefore be wise, O kings; be admonished, O judges of the earth. (2:10).
Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling. (2:11).
Kiss the Son, lest He be angry and you perish in your rebellion, when His wrath ignites in an instant. Blessed are all who take refuge in Him. (2:12).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 7:12-14: The promise this psalm is built on. God tells David that his own descendant will build the house and hold the throne forever, and says of him, I will be his Father and he will be My son.

Acts 4:25-26: Peter and John and the believers pray these opening lines back to God after the Sanhedrin bans them from preaching, and they name Herod and Pontius Pilate as the kings and rulers who took their stand.
Revelation 2:26-27: Jesus hands the iron scepter of verse 9 to the one at Thyatira who overcomes, promising him authority over the nations and the same shattering of pottery.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָשִׁיחַ (mashiach), Greek: χριστός (christos), Aramaic: משיחא (meshicha)
translationNotes.note: The LORD’s chosen, consecrated king.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נַשְּׁקוּ־בַר (nashqu-bar); Greek (LXX): δράξασθε παιδείας (draksasthe paideias)
translationNotes.note: Textual issue: Hebrew MT reads “kiss the son (bar [Aram.])”; LXX reads “embrace discipline.” Both express submission.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֵׁבֶט בַּרְזֶל (shevet barzel); Greek: ῥάβδος σιδηρᾶ (rhabdos sidēra)
translationNotes.note: Symbol of firm royal rule.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּכְלִי יוֹצֵר תְּנַפְּצֵם (kikhli yotser tenappetsem)
translationNotes.note: A fired clay jar cannot be mended, so breaking one served as a formal act of cancellation. Jeremiah smashed a potter's jar in the Valley of Hinnom in front of the elders and priests as a sign that Jerusalem would be broken past repair (Jeremiah 19:1-11). The image in verse 9 is not damage; it is ruin that cannot be undone.

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD establishes His anointed King on Zion and warns the nations to submit to His rule.

stories.title: 🛡️ Psalms 3
summaryBullets: O LORD, how my foes have increased! How many rise up against me! (3:1).
Many say of me, “God will not deliver him.” Selah (3:2).
But You, O LORD, are a shield around me, my glory, and the One who lifts my head. (3:3).
To the LORD I cry aloud, and He answers me from His holy mountain. Selah (3:4).
I lie down and sleep; I wake again, for the LORD sustains me. (3:5).
I will not fear the myriads set against me on every side. (3:6).
Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God! Strike all my enemies on the jaw; break the teeth of the wicked. (3:7).
Salvation belongs to the LORD; may Your blessing be on Your people. Selah (3:8).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 15:13-14: The occasion the heading names. A messenger tells David that the hearts of Israel have gone over to Absalom, and David orders everyone out of Jerusalem on foot that same hour.
2 Samuel 16:5-8: On that flight Shimei throws stones and shouts that the LORD has paid David back and handed the kingdom to his son, which is the taunt of verse 2 with a name attached to it.
Psalm 4:8: The companion line from the next psalm. Here David sleeps and wakes because the LORD sustains him; there he lies down in peace because the LORD alone makes him dwell in safety.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֶלָה (selah); Greek (LXX): διάψαλμα (diapsalma)
translationNotes.note: Musical/structural marker in Psalms; exact function unspecified.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָגֵן (magen); Greek: θυρεός (thyreos)
translationNotes.note: Protective image for God’s defense.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַר קָדְשׁוֹ (har qodsho); Greek: ὄρος τὸ ἅγιον αὐτοῦ
translationNotes.note: Zion/Jerusalem as the site of God’s presence.

translationNotes.term: When he fled from his son Absalom
translationNotes.note: The account runs through 2 Samuel 15-18. David left Jerusalem on foot, crossed the Kidron Valley, and went up the Mount of Olives barefoot with his head covered, weeping as he climbed (2 Samuel 15:23, 30). Ahithophel asked Absalom for twelve thousand men to set out after him that same night (2 Samuel 17:1). That is the night behind verse 5, 'I lie down and sleep.'

stories.keyTakeaway: Surrounded by enemies, the psalmist sleeps and wakes in safety because the LORD sustains and saves.
stories.superscription: A Psalm of David, when he fled from his son Absalom.

stories.title: 🌙 Psalms 4
summaryBullets: Answer me when I call, O God of my righteousness! You have relieved my distress; show me grace and hear my prayer. (4:1).
How long, O men, will my honor be maligned? How long will you love vanity and seek after lies? Selah (4:2).
Know that the LORD has set apart the godly for Himself; the LORD hears when I call to Him. (4:3).
Be angry, yet do not sin; on your bed, search your heart and be still. Selah (4:4).
Offer the sacrifices of the righteous and trust in the LORD. (4:5).
Many ask, “Who can show us the good?” Shine the light of Your face upon us, O LORD. (4:6).
You have filled my heart with more joy than when grain and new wine abound. (4:7).
I will lie down and sleep in peace, for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety. (4:8).
crossRefs: Ephesians 4:26: Paul opens his instruction on anger by quoting verse 4 word for word, then sets his own limit on it: do not let the sun set upon your anger.
Numbers 6:24-26: The blessing David is asking for at verse 6. A shining face is the second of the three lines Aaron and his sons were told to speak over Israel.
Psalm 3:5: The matching line from the psalm before it. There David wakes because the LORD sustains him; here he lies down because the LORD alone keeps him safe.

translationNotes.term: Be angry and do not sin
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רִגְזוּ וְאַל־תֶּחֱטָאוּ (rigzu veʾal techetaʾu); Greek (LXX): ὀργίζεσθε καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε
translationNotes.note: Exhortation to self-control; cited in the New Testament.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זִבְחֵי־צֶדֶק (zivkhei-tsedeq); Greek: θυσίας δικαιοσύνης
translationNotes.note: Sacrifices offered properly, in integrity.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לַמְנַצֵּחַ (lamnatstseach) - Greek (LXX): εἰς τὸ τέλος (eis to telos)
translationNotes.note: This heading stands over fifty-five psalms and over Habakkuk's prayer (Habakkuk 3:19). The root means to oversee, and it is the same word used of the Levites who supervised the workmen on the temple (Ezra 3:8-9; 1 Chronicles 23:4). It marks a psalm handed to the man in charge of the temple music. The Greek translators read the root differently and rendered it 'to the end.'

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בִּנְגִינוֹת (binginot)
translationNotes.note: From the verb nagan, to pluck a string, the same verb used of David playing before Saul (1 Samuel 16:16-23). The strings meant are the kinnor, a hand-held lyre, and the nevel, a larger and deeper harp. The direction fixes this psalm as sung music with accompaniment rather than a spoken prayer.

stories.keyTakeaway: At night, the psalmist urges truth and trust, then sleeps in peace under the LORD’s care.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🙏 Psalms 5
summaryBullets: Give ear to my words, O LORD; consider my groaning. (5:1).
Attend to the sound of my cry, my King and my God, for to You I pray. (5:2).
In the morning, O LORD, You hear my voice; at daybreak I lay my plea before You and wait in expectation. (5:3).
For You are not a God who delights in wickedness; no evil can dwell with You. (5:4).
The boastful cannot stand in Your presence; You hate all workers of iniquity. (5:5).
You destroy those who tell lies; the LORD abhors the man of bloodshed and deceit. (5:6).
But I will enter Your house by the abundance of Your loving devotion; in reverence I will bow down toward Your holy temple. (5:7).
Lead me, O LORD, in Your righteousness because of my enemies; make straight Your way before me. (5:8).
For not a word they speak can be trusted; destruction lies within them. Their throats are open graves; their tongues practice deceit. (5:9).
Declare them guilty, O God; let them fall by their own devices. Drive them out for their many transgressions, for they have rebelled against You. (5:10).
But let all who take refuge in You rejoice; let them ever shout for joy. May You shelter them, that those who love Your name may rejoice in You. (5:11).
For surely You, O LORD, bless the righteous; You surround them with the shield of Your favor. (5:12).
crossRefs: Romans 3:13: Paul builds his case that no one is righteous out of a chain of Old Testament lines, and the first of them is verse 9 here: their throats are open graves, their tongues practice deceit.
1 Kings 8:29-30: Solomon dedicates the temple by asking God to keep His eyes on that place and hear whoever prays toward it, which is exactly the posture of verse 7, bowing toward the holy temple.
Habakkuk 1:13: The same claim as verses 4 and 5, that God cannot tolerate wrongdoing, turned into a prophet's complaint that He tolerates the faithless anyway.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (ḥesed), Greek (LXX): ἔλεος (eleos), Aramaic: חסדא (ḥasda)
translationNotes.note: Covenant kindness; basis for approach to worship (v. 7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חָסָה (ḥasah), Greek: καταφεύγω, Aramaic: חסא
translationNotes.note: To seek shelter or protection in God.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶל־הַנְּחִילוֹת (el-hannechilot)
translationNotes.note: The word appears in no other heading and nowhere else in Scripture, so its sense is not certain. Translators connect it to chalil, the reed pipe played by the prophets Saul met on the road (1 Samuel 10:5) and by the crowd at Solomon's coronation (1 Kings 1:40). Wind instruments are otherwise rare in the Psalms, which run to strings and percussion.

translationNotes.term: I lay my plea before You
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָרַךְ (arak)
translationNotes.note: The verb means to set out in order. It is the word for arranging the wood on the altar and laying the cut pieces of the offering on top of it (Leviticus 1:7-8). Verse 3 pairs it with daybreak, the hour of the daily burnt offering that opened worship at the sanctuary (Exodus 29:38-39; Numbers 28:3-4). The English 'lay before' hides a sacrificial verb.

stories.keyTakeaway: At daybreak the psalmist seeks guidance; the LORD rejects deceit and shelters those who take refuge in Him.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster, to be accompanied by flutes. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 😢 Psalms 6
summaryBullets: O LORD, do not rebuke me in Your anger or discipline me in Your wrath. (6:1).
Be merciful to me, O LORD, for I am frail; heal me, O LORD, for my bones are in agony. (6:2).
My soul is deeply distressed. How long, O LORD, how long? (6:3).
Turn, O LORD, and deliver my soul; save me because of Your loving devotion. (6:4).
For there is no mention of You in death; who can praise You from Sheol? (6:5).
I am weary from groaning; all night I flood my bed with weeping and drench my couch with tears. (6:6).
My eyes fail from grief; they grow dim because of all my foes. (6:7).
Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for the LORD has heard my weeping. (6:8).
The LORD has heard my cry for mercy; the LORD accepts my prayer. (6:9).
All my enemies will be ashamed and dismayed; they will turn back in sudden disgrace. (6:10).
crossRefs: Psalm 30:9: David makes the identical argument there. Dust cannot praise God or proclaim His faithfulness, so there is nothing gained for God in letting him die.
Isaiah 38:18-19: Hezekiah, told he will die, prays the same way. Sheol cannot thank God; only the living can, and fathers tell their children about His faithfulness.
Luke 13:27: Jesus shuts the door on those who claim to have eaten and drunk with Him using the line of verse 8, telling all who work evil to depart from Him.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רָפָא (rapha), Greek: ἰάομαι (iaomai), Aramaic: אסי (asa)
translationNotes.note: To restore to health.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
translationNotes.note: The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַל־הַשְּׁמִינִית (al-hasheminit)
translationNotes.note: The word means 'on the eighth.' It heads Psalms 6 and 12 and turns up once in the record of David's musicians, where the lyres are set 'according to Sheminith' while the harps are set 'according to Alamoth' (1 Chronicles 15:20-21). The pairing points to a register or tuning rather than a melody, most likely the lower voices against the higher. The precise meaning is not recoverable.

Psalm 6 stands first in a group of seven read together as prayers of repentance: 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, and 143. Cassiodorus set them out as a group in his commentary on the Psalms in the sixth century AD, and Christian worship has used them as a set ever since. Nothing in the Hebrew text marks them off; the grouping is a later reading order, not a feature of the book.

stories.keyTakeaway: In weakness and grief, the psalmist pleads for mercy and affirms that the LORD has heard.

headings.text: Do Not Rebuke Me in Your Anger

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments, according to Sheminith. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: ⚖️ Psalms 7
summaryBullets: O LORD my God, I take refuge in You; save me and deliver me from all my pursuers, (7:1).
or they will shred my soul like a lion and tear me to pieces with no one to rescue me. (7:2).
O LORD my God, if I have done this, if injustice is on my hands, (7:3).
if I have rewarded my ally with evil, if I have plundered my foe without cause, (7:4).
then may my enemy pursue me and overtake me; may he trample me to the ground and leave my honor in the dust. Selah (7:5).
Arise, O LORD, in Your anger; rise up against the fury of my enemies. Awake, my God, and ordain judgment. (7:6).
Let the assembled peoples gather around You; take Your seat over them on high. (7:7).
The LORD judges the peoples; vindicate me, O LORD, according to my righteousness and integrity. (7:8).
Put an end to the evil of the wicked, but establish the righteous, O righteous God who searches hearts and minds. (7:9).
My shield is with God, who saves the upright in heart. (7:10).
God is a righteous judge and a God who feels indignation each day. (7:11).
If one does not repent, God will sharpen His sword; He has bent and strung His bow. (7:12).
He has prepared His deadly weapons; He ordains His arrows with fire. (7:13).
Behold, the wicked man travails with evil; he conceives trouble and births falsehood. (7:14).
He has dug a hole and hollowed it out; he has fallen into a pit of his own making. (7:15).
His trouble recoils on himself, and his violence falls on his own head. (7:16).
I will thank the LORD for His righteousness and sing praise to the name of the LORD Most High. (7:17).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 32:35: The ground under the whole prayer. Vengeance belongs to God and He repays in due time, which is why David asks the judge to rise instead of striking Cush himself.

1 Samuel 24:12: In the cave at En-gedi, holding a piece of Saul's robe, David says the same sentence out loud: let the LORD judge between us and take vengeance, but my own hand will never be against you.
Psalm 9:7-8: The answer to the request at verse 7 that God take His seat over the assembled peoples. The throne is already established for judgment and He governs the peoples with equity.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁגָּיוֹן (shiggayon); Greek (LXX): ᾠδή (ōdē, general ‘song’)
translationNotes.note: Musical/poetic term in the heading; precise meaning uncertain.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁפַט (shafat), Greek: κρίνω (krinō), Aramaic: דן (dan)
translationNotes.note: Render a decision; administer justice.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כּוּשׁ בֶּן־יְמִינִי (Kush ben-yemini)
translationNotes.note: Cush is named here and nowhere else in Scripture. What the heading does supply is his tribe, Benjamin, which was Saul's tribe (1 Samuel 9:1-2). Benjamites keep turning on David: Shimei son of Gera cursed him and threw stones from the hillside during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 16:5-8), and Sheba son of Bichri raised a rebellion immediately after it (2 Samuel 20:1-2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בּוֹר (bor) - שַׁחַת (shachat)
translationNotes.note: Neither word means a natural hollow. A bor is a cut cistern, plastered inside and narrow at the mouth; a shachat is a pit dug and then covered over to take large game or a predator, and Ezekiel uses it of the pit that caught a lion (Ezekiel 19:4, 8). Both took hand labour to make. Verse 15 pictures a man doing that digging and then dropping into it himself.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalmist appeals to the LORD’s just judgment, expecting the wicked’s schemes to rebound on themselves.
stories.superscription: A Shiggaion of David, which he sang to the LORD concerning the words of Cush, a Benjamite.

stories.title: 🌌 Psalms 8
summaryBullets: O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is Your name in all the earth! You have set Your glory above the heavens. (8:1).
From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise on account of Your adversaries, to silence the enemy and avenger. (8:2).
When I behold Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, the moon and the stars, which You have set in place — (8:3).
what is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him? (8:4).
You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor. (8:5).
You made him ruler of the works of Your hands; You have placed everything under his feet: (8:6).
all sheep and oxen, and even the beasts of the field, (8:7).
the birds of the air and the fish of the sea, all that swim the paths of the seas. (8:8).
O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is Your name in all the earth! (8:9).
crossRefs: Genesis 1:26-28: The mandate this psalm is restating. Man is made in God's image and told to rule the fish of the sea and the birds of the air, the same two categories the psalm lists at verse 8.
Hebrews 2:6-8: The writer quotes verses 4 through 6 and then presses on the gap in them. God left nothing outside man's control, yet at present we do not see everything subject to him.

Matthew 21:15-16: When the chief priests are indignant at children shouting in the temple courts, Jesus answers them with verse 2, that God has ordained praise from the mouths of children and infants.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֶּן־אָדָם (ben-adam), Greek: υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου, Aramaic: בר אנש (bar enash)
translationNotes.note: Hebrew idiom meaning “human being.”

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תְּעַטְּרֵהוּ (teʿattrehu); Greek: ἐστεφάνωσας (estephanōsas)
translationNotes.note: To encircle with honor; give distinction.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַל־הַגִּתִּית (al-haggittit) - Greek (LXX): ὑπὲρ τῶν ληνῶν (hyper ton lenon)
translationNotes.note: The term heads three psalms: 8, 81, and 84. It can be read from Gath, the Philistine city where David lived among Achish's men for sixteen months (1 Samuel 27:2-7), or from gat, a winepress. The Greek translators took the second and rendered it 'for the winepresses,' which would tie the psalm to the autumn vintage. Which reading is right is not settled.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְהוָה אֲדֹנֵינוּ (YHWH Adoneinu)
translationNotes.note: Two different Hebrew words stand behind the two English ones. LORD in small capitals renders the four letters yod, he, waw, he, the personal name given to Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:15), which occurs about 6,800 times in the Hebrew Bible. Lord in ordinary type renders adon, 'master,' here with 'our' attached. Verses 1 and 9 put the name and the title side by side, and only the small capitals tell you so.

translationNotes.term: A little lower than the angels
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֵאֱלֹהִים (me'elohim) - Greek (LXX): παρ' ἀγγέλους (par' angelous)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew word in verse 5 is elohim, the ordinary word for God, so the line reads 'a little lower than God.' The Greek translators rendered it 'than angels,' and Hebrews 2:7 quotes that Greek form. English versions divide accordingly, printing 'angels,' 'God,' or 'heavenly beings.' The difference lies in which text a version follows, not in a disagreement among the Hebrew manuscripts.

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD’s majesty is displayed in creation, and humanity is granted honor and rule within it.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. According to Gittith. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🎶 Psalms 9
summaryBullets: I will give thanks to the LORD with all my heart; I will recount all Your wonders. (9:1).
I will be glad and rejoice in You; I will sing praise to Your name, O Most High. (9:2).
When my enemies retreat, they stumble and perish before You. (9:3).
For You have upheld my just cause; You sit on Your throne judging righteously. (9:4).
You have rebuked the nations; You have destroyed the wicked; You have erased their name forever and ever. (9:5).
The enemy has come to eternal ruin, and You have uprooted their cities; the very memory of them has vanished. (9:6).
But the LORD abides forever; He has established His throne for judgment. (9:7).
He judges the world with justice; He governs the people with equity. (9:8).
The LORD is a refuge for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble. (9:9).
Those who know Your name trust in You, for You, O LORD, have not forsaken those who seek You. (9:10).
Sing praises to the LORD, who dwells in Zion; proclaim His deeds among the nations. (9:11).
For the Avenger of bloodshed remembers; He does not ignore the cry of the afflicted. (9:12).
Be merciful to me, O LORD; see how my enemies afflict me! Lift me up from the gates of death, (9:13).
that I may declare all Your praises — that within the gates of Daughter Zion I may rejoice in Your salvation. (9:14).
The nations have fallen into a pit of their making; their feet are caught in the net they have hidden. (9:15).
The LORD is known by the justice He brings; the wicked are ensnared by the work of their hands. Higgaion Selah (9:16).
The wicked will return to Sheol— all the nations who forget God. (9:17).
For the needy will not always be forgotten; nor the hope of the oppressed forever dashed. (9:18).
Rise up, O LORD, do not let man prevail; let the nations be judged in Your presence. (9:19).
Lay terror upon them, O LORD; let the nations know they are but men. Selah (9:20).
crossRefs: Psalm 10:1: The next psalm carries no heading of its own and picks this one up where it stops. Here the LORD is a stronghold in times of trouble; there the complaint is that He hides in times of trouble.
Psalm 7:8-9: The same court seen from the other side. There David asks the God who searches hearts to vindicate him; here he thanks the LORD for having already upheld his just cause.
Psalm 96:10: The announcement carried to the nations, that the LORD reigns and will judge the peoples with equity, which is what verse 8 here says He already does.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִשְׂגָּב (misgav); Greek: καταφυγή (katafygē)
translationNotes.note: High, secure place of refuge (vv. 9-10).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֶאֱבַדְתָּ שְׁמָם (heʾevedaʿta shemam); Greek: ἀπώλεσας τὸ ὄνομα
translationNotes.note: Erase memory/reputation; judgment on nations (v. 5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
translationNotes.note: The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַל־מוּת לַבֵּן (al-mut labben)
translationNotes.note: The words can be divided several ways, and the phrase appears in no other heading and in no narrative, so nothing fixes its sense. It is best taken as the name of a known melody, in the way 'The Doe of the Dawn' heads Psalm 22 and 'Do Not Destroy' heads Psalms 57 through 59. The Greek translators divided the letters differently and read 'concerning the hidden things of the son.'

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הִגָּיוֹן (higgayon)
translationNotes.note: Verse 16 is the only place this word stands beside Selah. It comes from hagah, to murmur or sound low, and it appears again in Psalm 92:3, where English versions render it as the sounding of the lyre, and in Lamentations 3:62 of an enemy's muttering. A low instrumental passage fits all three. Like Selah it is a direction to the musicians, not part of the sentence.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalmist praises the LORD’s enduring rule and asks Him to act against oppressing nations.

headings.text: I Will Give Thanks to the Lord

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. To the tune of “The Death of the Son.” A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🙌 Psalms 10
summaryBullets: Why, O LORD, do You stand far off? Why do You hide in times of trouble? (10:1).
In pride the wicked pursue the needy; let them be caught in the schemes they devise. (10:2).
For the wicked man boasts in the cravings of his heart; he blesses the greedy and reviles the LORD. (10:3).
In his pride the wicked man does not seek Him; in all his schemes there is no God. (10:4).
He is secure in his ways at all times; Your lofty judgments are far from him; he sneers at all his foes. (10:5).
He says to himself, “I will not be moved; from age to age I am free of distress.” (10:6).
His mouth is full of cursing, deceit, and violence; trouble and malice are under his tongue. (10:7).
He lies in wait near the villages; in ambush he slays the innocent; his eyes watch in stealth for the helpless. (10:8).
He lies in wait like a lion in a thicket; he lurks to seize the oppressed; he catches the lowly in his net. (10:9).
They are crushed and beaten down; the helpless fall prey to his strength. (10:10).
He says to himself, “God has forgotten; He hides His face and never sees.” (10:11).
Arise, O LORD! Lift up Your hand, O God! Do not forget the helpless. (10:12).
Why has the wicked man renounced God? He says to himself, “You will never call me to account.” (10:13).
But You have regarded trouble and grief; You see to repay it by Your hand. The victim entrusts himself to You; You are the helper of the fatherless. (10:14).
Break the arm of the wicked and evildoer; call him to account for his wickedness until none is left to be found. (10:15).
The LORD is King forever and ever; the nations perish from His land. (10:16).
You have heard, O LORD, the desire of the humble; You will strengthen their hearts. You will incline Your ear, (10:17).
to vindicate the fatherless and oppressed, that the men of the earth may strike terror no more. (10:18).
crossRefs: Proverbs 15:3: The flat answer to what the wicked man tells himself at verse 11. God has not forgotten and does not hide His face; His eyes are in every place, observing evil and good.
Exodus 22:22-24: The law standing behind the plea of verse 18. Mistreat a widow or an orphan and God says He will surely hear their cry, and His anger will be kindled.
Psalm 9:19-20: The prayer this psalm keeps repeating at verse 12. Rise up, do not let man prevail, and let the nations learn that they are only men.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָנִי / דַּךְ / עָשׁוּק (ʿani / dakh / ashuq), Greek (LXX): πτωχός / ταπεινός, Aramaic: מסכן / ענו
translationNotes.note: Terms for poor, crushed, or exploited persons in the psalm.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יָתוֹם (yatom), Greek: ὀρφανός (orphanos), Aramaic: יתום (yatom)
translationNotes.note: Child without a father; object of God’s protection.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קוּמָה (qumah), Greek: ἀνάστα (anasta), Aramaic: קום (qum)
translationNotes.note: Call for God to take visible action.

Psalm 10 carries no heading, and the two psalms together work down the Hebrew alphabet, a new letter generally opening every second verse. Psalm 9 runs from aleph to kaph; Psalm 10 picks up at lamed in verse 1 and closes with qoph, resh, shin and taw in verses 12 to 18, with the middle letters absent. The Greek and Latin versions count the two as a single Psalm 9, which is why their numbering runs one behind the Hebrew for most of the rest of the book. The two systems line up again at Psalm 148.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalmist describes the wicked crushing the poor and calls on the LORD, who sees and defends the afflicted.

stories.title: 🏰 Psalms 11
summaryBullets: In the LORD I take refuge. How then can you say to me: “Flee like a bird to your mountain! (11:1).
For behold, the wicked bend their bows. They set their arrow on the string to shoot from the shadows at the upright in heart. (11:2).
If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (11:3).
The LORD is in His holy temple; the LORD is on His heavenly throne. His eyes are watching closely; they examine the sons of men. (11:4).
The LORD tests the righteous and the wicked; His soul hates the lover of violence. (11:5).
On the wicked He will rain down fiery coals and sulfur; a scorching wind will be their portion. (11:6).
For the LORD is righteous; He loves justice. The upright will see His face. (11:7).
crossRefs: Habakkuk 2:20: The same sentence about the holy temple, used there to silence the whole earth after the prophet's complaint. Here it steadies a man being told to run for the mountains.
Psalm 7:9: The identical claim, that God searches hearts and minds, which is what the watching eyes of verse 4 are doing when they examine the sons of men.
Psalm 27:4: The other side of verse 7. Here the upright will see God's face; there David asks for one thing only, to gaze on the beauty of the LORD in His temple.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַשָּׁתוֹת (hashshatot), Greek (LXX): θεμέλια, Aramaic: אשיותא (ashyuta)
translationNotes.note: Figurative for social/moral order (v. 3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פָּנָיו (panav), Greek: τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ, Aramaic: אפוהי
translationNotes.note: Idiom for direct favor/presence (v. 7).

translationNotes.term: Flee like a bird to your mountain
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַר (har) - צִפּוֹר (tsippor)
translationNotes.note: The Judean hill country is limestone cut with caves and crags, and it is where hunted men actually went. David hid in the Wilderness of Ziph and in the strongholds at En-gedi (1 Samuel 23:14; 24:1-3), and he told Saul he was being chased 'as one hunts a partridge in the mountains' (1 Samuel 26:20). Verse 1 quotes the ordinary advice of the period and refuses it.

translationNotes.term: Fiery coals and sulfur, a scorching wind
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גָּפְרִית (gophrit) - רוּחַ זִלְעָפוֹת (ruach zil'aphot)
translationNotes.note: Gophrit is sulfur, and fire with sulfur names what fell on Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24). The scorching wind is the desert wind out of the east, called the qadim: it withered the grain in Pharaoh's dream (Genesis 41:6) and beat on Jonah's head until he wanted to die (Jonah 4:8). Both halves of verse 6 name things the first readers had seen for themselves.

stories.keyTakeaway: When foundations shake, the psalmist declares the LORD reigns from heaven, tests the righteous, and the upright will behold His face.

headings.text: In the Lord I Take Refuge

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. Of David.

stories.title: 🗣️ Psalms 12
summaryBullets: Help, O LORD, for the godly are no more; the faithful have vanished from among men. (12:1).
They lie to one another; they speak with flattering lips and a double heart. (12:2).
May the LORD cut off all flattering lips and every boastful tongue. (12:3).
They say, “With our tongues we will prevail. We own our lips— who can be our master?” (12:4).
“For the cause of the oppressed and for the groaning of the needy, I will now arise,” says the LORD. “I will bring safety to him who yearns.” (12:5).
The words of the LORD are flawless, like silver refined in a furnace, like gold purified sevenfold. (12:6).
You, O LORD, will keep us; You will forever guard us from this generation. (12:7).
The wicked wander freely, and vileness is exalted among men. (12:8).
crossRefs: Proverbs 30:5: The same verdict on God's speech as verse 6, with the reason attached. Every word of God is flawless, and He is a shield to those who take refuge in Him.
Psalm 119:140: The same test applied to God's promise. It is completely pure, which is what silver refined in a furnace and gold purified sevenfold means at verse 6.
Romans 3:13-14: Paul's catalogue of what human mouths do, open graves and deceitful tongues and mouths full of cursing, is the world verses 2 through 4 are describing.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׂפַת חֲלָקוֹת (sefat ḥalaqot), Greek (LXX): χείλη δόλια, Aramaic: שפוות מחליקתא
translationNotes.note: Smooth/insincere speech (vv. 2-3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צְרוּפָה (tzerufah), Greek: πεπυρωμένος, Aramaic: מצרפא
translationNotes.note: Smelted/refined metal imagery for tested speech (v. 6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הוֹשִׁיעָה (hoshi'ah) - Greek: ὡσαννά (hosanna)
translationNotes.note: The psalm opens on a one-word imperative: save. Attach the particle na to it, as Psalm 118:25 does, and it becomes hoshi'ah-na, which the Gospel writers carry into Greek without translating it as the crowds shout it at the entry into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:9; Mark 11:9-10). Hosanna is a cry for rescue, not a word of praise.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּלֵב וָלֵב (belev valev)
translationNotes.note: Verse 2 reads, word for word, 'with a heart and a heart.' The same phrase appears in 1 Chronicles 12:33, where the men of Zebulun come to David 'not with a heart and a heart,' meaning undivided. English has to supply 'double' or 'deceitful' because the Hebrew simply counts the organ twice and leaves you to draw the conclusion.

stories.keyTakeaway: Amid deceitful speech, the LORD promises to arise for the needy and His refined words stand pure and protective.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. According to Sheminith. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: ⏳ Psalms 13
summaryBullets: How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me? (13:1).
How long must I wrestle in my soul, with sorrow in my heart each day? How long will my enemy dominate me? (13:2).
Consider me and respond, O LORD my God. Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death, (13:3).
lest my enemy say, “I have overcome him,” and my foes rejoice when I fall. (13:4).
But I have trusted in Your loving devotion; my heart will rejoice in Your salvation. (13:5).
I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me. (13:6).
crossRefs: Habakkuk 1:2: The prophet opens his book with the same two words, how long, asking why God does not hear when he cries out about violence.
Psalm 27:9: The same request word for word, that God not hide His face, set beside the memory that He has already been the helper of the man praying.
Psalm 31:16: The reverse of verse 1. Instead of a hidden face David asks for a shining one, and asks to be saved by God's loving devotion.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (ḥesed), Greek (LXX): ἔλεος (eleos), Aramaic: חסדא (ḥasda)
translationNotes.note: Covenant kindness (v. 5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁנַת הַמָּוֶת (shenat ha-mavet); Greek: ὕπνον θανάτου
translationNotes.note: Poetic for dying (v. 3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַד־אָנָה (ad-anah)
translationNotes.note: The phrase opens four lines running across verses 1 and 2, and the English keeps the repetition. Hebrew laments are built in three movements: complaint, then petition, then a vow to praise. Psalm 13 runs all three inside six verses, turning at verse 5 and ending in song, which makes it the shortest complete example of the form in the book.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הָאִירָה עֵינַי (ha'irah einai)
translationNotes.note: Bright eyes meant strength and dull eyes meant a man at the end of himself. Jonathan, faint after a day of fighting without food, ate honey and 'his eyes brightened' (1 Samuel 14:27-29), and Ezra uses the same idiom for relief granted in captivity (Ezra 9:8). Verse 3 pairs it with 'lest I sleep in death,' so the request is for life, not for insight.

stories.keyTakeaway: After repeated “How long?” the psalmist asks for life and ends with trust, joy, and song.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🚫 Psalms 14
summaryBullets: The fool says in his heart, “There is no God.” They are corrupt; their acts are vile. There is no one who does good. (14:1).
The LORD looks down from heaven upon the sons of men to see if any understand, if any seek God. (14:2).
All have turned away, they have together become corrupt; there is no one who does good, not even one. (14:3).
Will the workers of iniquity never learn? They devour my people like bread; they refuse to call upon the LORD. (14:4).
There they are, overwhelmed with dread, for God is in the company of the righteous. (14:5).
You sinners frustrate the plans of the oppressed, yet the LORD is their shelter. (14:6).
Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion! When the LORD restores His captive people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad! (14:7).
crossRefs: Romans 3:10-12: Paul opens his case that no one is righteous by quoting verses 1 through 3 almost intact: no one who understands, no one who seeks God, no one who does good, not even one.
Psalm 53:1-3: The same psalm again with the divine name swapped. Here it is the LORD who looks down from heaven; there it is God, and the change runs through the whole piece.
Isaiah 59:7-8: The same portrait filled out. Feet swift to shed innocent blood, ruin and destruction in their wake, and the way of peace never known.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נָבָל (naval), Greek (LXX): ἄφρων (aphrōn), Aramaic: נבל
translationNotes.note: Moral-spiritual dullness, not mere lack of intelligence (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְשִׁיב שְׁבוּת (yeshiv shevut); Greek: ἐπιστρέψει αἰχμαλωσίαν
translationNotes.note: Idiomatic for reversing captivity or circumstances (v. 7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְהוָה (YHWH) - אֱלֹהִים (Elohim)
translationNotes.note: Psalm 53 is this psalm again with differences. The clearest is the divine name: Psalm 14 uses LORD, the personal name, four times, and Psalm 53 uses God throughout. The same preference runs across Psalms 42 to 83, which favour Elohim, while Psalms 1 to 41 favour the name. Psalm 70 repeats Psalm 40:13-17 with the same substitution.

translationNotes.term: There is no one who does good
translationNotes.note: Paul quotes verses 1 to 3 in Romans 3:10-12 to open a chain of Old Testament citations, following the Greek wording. Some Greek copies of Psalm 14 carry the rest of that chain, drawn from Psalms 5, 140, 10 and 36 and from Isaiah 59, inserted after verse 3. The Hebrew does not have those lines, and English versions follow the Hebrew, which is why a Latin or Greek psalter of this psalm looks longer.

stories.keyTakeaway: A universal indictment of human corruption is stated, yet the psalm ends with a wish for Zion’s salvation and restoration.

headings.text: The Fool Says There Is No God

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. Of David.

stories.title: ⛺ Psalms 15
summaryBullets: O LORD, who may abide in Your tent? Who may dwell on Your holy mountain? (15:1).
He who walks with integrity and practices righteousness, who speaks the truth from his heart, (15:2).
who has no slander on his tongue, who does no harm to his neighbor, who casts no scorn on his friend, (15:3).
who despises the vile but honors those who fear the LORD, who does not revise a costly oath, (15:4).
who lends his money without interest and refuses a bribe against the innocent. He who does these things will never be shaken. (15:5).
crossRefs: Psalm 24:3-4: The same question asked at the same gate, who may ascend the hill of the LORD, answered there in one line about clean hands and a pure heart rather than the list given here.
Exodus 22:25: The law behind verse 5. Lend money to one of My people who is poor and you may not act as a creditor toward him or charge him interest.
Leviticus 25:35-37: The same ban spelled out further. No interest and no profit from a destitute countryman, not on silver lent to him and not on food sold to him.
Isaiah 33:14-16: Isaiah asks who can dwell with a consuming fire and answers with the same kind of list: refusing gain from extortion, taking no bribe, shutting the eyes against evil.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גוּר (gur), Greek (LXX): παροικέω, Aramaic: אגור
translationNotes.note: To reside as a temporary guest (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֶשֶׁךְ (neshekh), Greek: τόκος (tokos), Aramaic: נשכא (nashka)
translationNotes.note: “Bite”; profit on loans among kin is banned here (v. 5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֹהֶל (ohel)
translationNotes.note: A literal tent. David pitched one on Zion for the ark and set Levites before it (2 Samuel 6:17; 1 Chronicles 16:1, 37), while the tabernacle itself stood first at Shiloh and later at Gibeon (Joshua 18:1; 1 Chronicles 16:39). Verse 1 asks who may be a guest in that tent, and a host in the ancient Near East owed his guest protection while he was under the cloth.

translationNotes.term: Does not revise a costly oath
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נִשְׁבַּע לְהָרַע וְלֹא יָמִר (nishba lehara velo yamir)
translationNotes.note: Word for word: he swears to his own hurt and does not change it. An oath in Israel was enforceable, not a courtesy. Numbers 30:2 forbids a man to break his word once he has bound himself, and Leviticus 5:4 makes even a rash oath a matter requiring a guilt offering. Verse 4 sets the standard at keeping the one that turned out to cost you money.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm lists conduct required to dwell with the LORD: integrity, truthful speech, just dealings, and refusal of bribes or usury.

headings.text: Who May Dwell on Your Holy Mountain?

stories.superscription: A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🛟 Psalms 16
summaryBullets: Preserve me, O God, for in You I take refuge. (16:1).
I said to the LORD, “You are my Lord; apart from You I have no good thing.” (16:2).
As for the saints in the land, they are the excellence in whom all my delight resides. (16:3).
Sorrows will multiply to those who chase other gods. I will not pour out their libations of blood, or speak their names with my lips. (16:4).
The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; You have made my lot secure. (16:5).
The lines of my boundary have fallen in pleasant places; surely my inheritance is delightful. (16:6).
I will bless the LORD who counsels me; even at night my conscience instructs me. (16:7).
I have set the LORD always before me. Because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken. (16:8).
Therefore my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices; my body also will dwell securely. (16:9).
For You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay. (16:10).
You have made known to me the path of life; You will fill me with joy in Your presence, with eternal pleasures at Your right hand. (16:11).
crossRefs: Acts 2:25-28: Peter quotes verses 8 through 11 in the first sermon after Pentecost, then points at David's tomb a few streets away and argues that David, who is buried and did decay, was speaking about someone else.

Acts 13:35: Paul makes the same argument in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch from the single line about the Holy One not seeing decay, adding that David served his own generation, died, and did see decay.

Psalm 73:26: Asaph reaches the same conclusion by a longer road. Flesh and heart fail, but God is the portion forever, and portion is the word this psalm uses at verse 5 for an inherited share of land.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִכְתָּם (miktam); Greek (LXX): στηλογραφία (inscription?)
translationNotes.note: Heading term; exact meaning uncertain.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
translationNotes.note: The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶבֶל (chevel) - גּוֹרָל (goral)
translationNotes.note: A chevel is the measuring cord used to survey land, and by extension the parcel it measured off. Canaan was divided by lot and written down in a survey (Joshua 17:5; 18:6-10), so a man's chevel was the field his family drew. Verse 5 then calls the LORD Himself the portion and the cup, which is exactly what the law says of the Levites, who drew no land at all (Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 10:9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁחַת (shachat) - Greek (LXX): διαφθορά (diaphthora)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew word carries both the pit and the rotting that happens in it. The Greek translators chose 'corruption,' and Peter at Pentecost and Paul at Antioch both quote verse 10 in that form and build on it (Acts 2:25-31; 13:35-37). Peter's argument rests on a fact his hearers could check: David's tomb was still standing in Jerusalem while he spoke.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalmist takes refuge in the LORD, rejects other gods, and declares confidence in preservation from Sheol and the path of life.
stories.superscription: A Miktam of David.

stories.title: 🕊️ Psalms 17
summaryBullets: Hear, O LORD, my righteous plea; listen to my cry. Give ear to my prayer— it comes from lips free of deceit. (17:1).
May my vindication come from Your presence; may Your eyes see what is right. (17:2).
You have tried my heart; You have visited me in the night. You have tested me and found no evil; I have resolved not to sin with my mouth. (17:3).
As for the deeds of men — by the word of Your lips I have avoided the ways of the violent. (17:4).
My steps have held to Your paths; my feet have not slipped. (17:5).
I call on You, O God, for You will answer me. Incline Your ear to me; hear my words. (17:6).
Show the wonders of Your loving devotion, You who save by Your right hand those who seek refuge from their foes. (17:7).
Keep me as the apple of Your eye; hide me in the shadow of Your wings (17:8).
from the wicked who assail me, from my mortal enemies who surround me. (17:9).
They have closed their callous hearts; their mouths speak with arrogance. (17:10).
They have tracked us down, and now surround us; their eyes are set to cast us to the ground, (17:11).
like a lion greedy for prey, like a young lion lurking in ambush. (17:12).
Arise, O LORD, confront them! Bring them to their knees; deliver me from the wicked by Your sword, (17:13).

from such men, O LORD, by Your hand— from men of the world whose portion is in this life. May You fill the bellies of Your treasured ones and satisfy their sons, so they leave their abundance to their children. (17:14).
As for me, I will behold Your face in righteousness; when I awake, I will be satisfied in Your presence. (17:15).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 32:10: The source of the phrase at verse 8. Moses says God guarded Israel in the howling wilderness as the apple of His eye, so David is asking to be kept the way the whole nation was kept.
Psalm 36:7: The other half of verse 8, the shadow of God's wings, an image of a bird sheltering its young and of the wings the cherubim stretch over the ark.
Psalm 11:7: The same ending. The upright will see God's face, which is what David expects at verse 15 when he awakes and is satisfied in God's presence.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אִישׁוֹן (ishon), Greek (LXX): κόρη ὀφθαλμοῦ, Aramaic: בת עינא
translationNotes.note: Pupil; idiom for precious protection (v. 8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אָקִיץ (aqitz); Greek: ἐξεγερθῶ
translationNotes.note: Rousing from sleep; poetic for renewed consciousness (v. 15).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּצֵל כְּנָפֶיךָ (betsel kenafekha)
translationNotes.note: The wings are carved ones. Two cherubim of gold stood over the ark with their wings spread across the atonement cover (Exodus 25:20), and Solomon's pair in the inner sanctuary stood ten cubits high with wings that met in the middle of the room (1 Kings 6:23-27). Asking for the shadow of the wings asks for the space directly above the ark. Ruth 2:12 uses the same words of taking refuge under God's wings.

translationNotes.term: Like a lion greedy for prey
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַרְיֵה (aryeh) - כְּפִיר (kephir)
translationNotes.note: Lions still lived in the land. They came up out of the thickets along the Jordan (Jeremiah 49:19), one killed a man on the road from Bethel (1 Kings 13:24), and they took sheep from David's flock until he went after them bare-handed (1 Samuel 17:34-35). Verse 12 uses two words, the full-grown aryeh and the kephir, a young lion already hunting on its own.

stories.keyTakeaway: Seeking vindication, the psalmist asks for protection as the apple of God’s eye and expects to behold God’s face.
stories.superscription: A prayer of David.

stories.title: 🗻 Psalms 18
summaryBullets: I love You, O LORD, my strength. (18:1).
The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer. My God is my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold. (18:2).
I will call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised; so shall I be saved from my enemies. (18:3).
The cords of death encompassed me; the torrents of chaos overwhelmed me. (18:4).
The cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me. (18:5).
In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried to my God for help. From His temple He heard my voice, and my cry for His help reached His ears. (18:6).
Then the earth shook and quaked, and the foundations of the mountains trembled; they were shaken because He burned with anger. (18:7).
Smoke rose from His nostrils, and consuming fire came from His mouth; glowing coals blazed forth. (18:8).
He parted the heavens and came down with dark clouds beneath His feet. (18:9).
He mounted a cherub and flew; He soared on the wings of the wind. (18:10).
He made darkness His hiding place, and storm clouds a canopy around Him. (18:11).
From the brightness of His presence His clouds advanced — hailstones and coals of fire. (18:12).
The LORD thundered from heaven; the voice of the Most High resounded — hailstones and coals of fire. (18:13).
He shot His arrows and scattered the foes; He hurled lightning and routed them. (18:14).
The channels of the sea appeared, and the foundations of the world were exposed, at Your rebuke, O LORD, at the blast of the breath of Your nostrils. (18:15).
He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters. (18:16).
He rescued me from my powerful enemy, from foes too mighty for me. (18:17).
They confronted me in my day of calamity, but the LORD was my support. (18:18).
He brought me out into the open; He rescued me because He delighted in me. (18:19).
The LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness; He has repaid me according to the cleanness of my hands. (18:20).
For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God. (18:21).
For all His ordinances are before me; I have not disregarded His statutes. (18:22).
And I have been blameless before Him and kept myself from iniquity. (18:23).
So the LORD has repaid me according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands in His sight. (18:24).
To the faithful You show Yourself faithful, to the blameless You show Yourself blameless; (18:25).
to the pure You show Yourself pure, but to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd. (18:26).
For You save an afflicted people, but You humble those with haughty eyes. (18:27).
For You, O LORD, light my lamp; my God lights up my darkness. (18:28).
For in You I can charge an army, and with my God I can scale a wall. (18:29).
As for God, His way is perfect; the word of the LORD is flawless. He is a shield to all who take refuge in Him. (18:30).
For who is God besides the LORD? And who is the Rock except our God? (18:31).
It is God who arms me with strength and makes my way clear. (18:32).
He makes my feet like those of a deer and stations me upon the heights. (18:33).
He trains my hands for battle; my arms can bend a bow of bronze. (18:34).
You have given me Your shield of salvation; Your right hand upholds me, and Your gentleness exalts me. (18:35).
You broaden the path beneath me so that my ankles do not give way. (18:36).
I pursued my enemies and overtook them; I did not turn back until they were consumed. (18:37).
I crushed them so they could not rise; they have fallen under my feet. (18:38).
You have armed me with strength for battle; You have subdued my foes beneath me. (18:39).
You have made my enemies retreat before me; I destroyed those who hated me. (18:40).
They cried for help, but there was no one to save them — to the LORD, but He did not answer. (18:41).
I ground them as dust in the face of the wind; I trampled them like mud in the streets. (18:42).
You have delivered me from the strife of the people; You have made me the head of nations; a people I had not known shall serve me. (18:43).
When they hear me, they obey me; foreigners cower before me. (18:44).
Foreigners lose heart and come trembling from their strongholds. (18:45).
The LORD lives, and blessed be my Rock! And may the God of my salvation be exalted— (18:46).
the God who avenges me and subdues nations beneath me, (18:47).
who delivers me from my enemies. You exalt me above my foes; You rescue me from violent men. (18:48).
Therefore I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing praises to Your name. (18:49).
Great salvation He brings to His king. He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever. (18:50).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 22:1-4: The same song recorded a second time inside the history, introduced by the narrator on the day the LORD delivered David from all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.
Exodus 19:18: The one line the theophany of verses 7 through 15 is built out of. Sinai was wrapped in smoke because the LORD came down on it in fire, and the whole mountain quaked violently.
Psalm 144:1-2: The same stack of titles, rock and fortress and deliverer and shield, with the line about God training David's hands for war that stands at verse 34 here.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַיִם רַבִּים (mayim rabbim); Greek: ὕδατα πολλὰ
translationNotes.note: Poetic danger/death imagery (v. 16).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְשִׁיחוֹ (meshicho); Greek: χριστῷ αὐτοῦ
translationNotes.note: Refers to the king (v. 50).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
translationNotes.note: The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

This psalm stands twice in Scripture. The second copy is 2 Samuel 22, placed near the end of David's life with the same heading, that the LORD delivered him from all his enemies and from Saul. The two run nearly word for word with small differences throughout, and the opening line here, 'I love You, O LORD, my strength,' is not in the Samuel text, which begins at what is verse 2 here.

translationNotes.term: Feet like those of a deer
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַיָּלוֹת (ayyalot)
translationNotes.note: The animal is the deer of the hill country, and the point is its footing. Its hooves take bare rock at an angle that puts a man on his back. Verse 33 pairs the image with being stationed on the heights, and the heights are the ridge lines that decide who holds the country. Habakkuk 3:19 closes the prophet's psalm with the same two lines.

stories.keyTakeaway: David recounts dramatic deliverance, victory over enemies, and God’s steadfast love to His anointed.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. Of David the servant of the LORD, who sang this song to the LORD on the day the LORD had delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul. He said:

stories.title: 🌞 Psalms 19
summaryBullets: The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands. (19:1).
Day after day they pour forth speech; night after night they reveal knowledge. (19:2).
Without speech or language, without a sound to be heard, (19:3).
their voice has gone out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world. In the heavens He has pitched a tent for the sun. (19:4).
Like a bridegroom emerging from his chamber, like a champion rejoicing to run his course, (19:5).
it rises at one end of the heavens and runs its circuit to the other; nothing is deprived of its warmth. (19:6).
The Law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul; the testimony of the LORD is trustworthy, making wise the simple. (19:7).
The precepts of the LORD are right, bringing joy to the heart; the commandments of the LORD are radiant, giving light to the eyes. (19:8).
The fear of the LORD is pure, enduring forever; the judgments of the LORD are true, being altogether righteous. (19:9).
They are more precious than gold, than much pure gold; they are sweeter than honey, than honey from the comb. (19:10).
By them indeed Your servant is warned; in keeping them is great reward. (19:11).
Who can discern his own errors? Cleanse me from my hidden faults. (19:12).
Keep Your servant also from willful sins; may they not rule over me. Then I will be blameless and cleansed of great transgression. (19:13).
May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be pleasing in Your sight, O LORD, my Rock and my Redeemer. (19:14).
crossRefs: Romans 10:18: Paul answers whether Israel ever heard by quoting verse 4, that their voice has gone out into all the earth, turning the reach of the heavens into the reach of the preaching.

Psalm 119:7-14: The long treatment of the same subject. The words piled up here, law and testimony and precepts and commandments, become the spine of an acrostic running the whole Hebrew alphabet eight times.
James 3:2: The concern of verses 12 through 14 restated. A man who never stumbles in what he says is a perfect man, able to control his whole body.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְסַפְּרִים (mesapperim); Greek (LXX): διηγοῦνται
translationNotes.note: To recount or tell (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פִּקּוּדִים / מִשְׁפָּטִים (piqqudim / mishpatim); Greek: προσταγμάτα / κρίματα
translationNotes.note: Divine directives and judgments (vv. 8-9).

Hebrew poetry does not rhyme sounds; it pairs lines. The second line restates the first in other words, sharpens it, or turns against it. Verses 7 to 9 run six pairs in one fixed frame: a name for the law, a quality, then what it does, six times over. Robert Lowth, Professor of Poetry at Oxford, described the pattern and named it in lectures published in 1753, and English Bibles have set the Psalms in poetic lines ever since.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קַו (qav) - Greek (LXX): φθόγγος (phthongos)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew word in verse 4 is qav, a measuring line, the cord stretched out to mark a boundary (Isaiah 34:17; Jeremiah 31:39). The Greek translators put a sound where the Hebrew has a line and read 'their voice,' and that is the form Paul quotes in Romans 10:18. English versions follow the Greek here because the matching line says 'their words.'

stories.keyTakeaway: Creation proclaims God’s glory and the LORD’s instruction is perfect and sweet, guiding speech and heart.

headings.text: The Heavens Declare the Glory of God

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🪖 Psalms 20
summaryBullets: May the LORD answer you in the day of trouble; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you. (20:1).
May He send you help from the sanctuary and sustain you from Zion. (20:2).
May He remember all your gifts and look favorably on your burnt offerings. Selah (20:3).
May He give you the desires of your heart and make all your plans succeed. (20:4).
May we shout for joy at your victory and raise a banner in the name of our God. May the LORD grant all your petitions. (20:5).
Now I know that the LORD saves His anointed; He answers him from His holy heaven with the saving power of His right hand. (20:6).
Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God. (20:7).
They collapse and fall, but we rise up and stand firm. (20:8).
O LORD, save the king. Answer us on the day we call. (20:9).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 13:5-7: What chariots and horsemen actually did to Israel. Three thousand Philistine chariots at Michmash drove the men into caves and cisterns and across the Jordan, with Saul's troops quaking at Gilgal.
Psalm 33:16-17: The same verdict stated flat. No king is saved by a vast army and a horse is a vain hope for salvation, which is what verse 7 here sets against the name of the LORD.
Proverbs 21:31: The proverb version, which leaves the preparation in place and moves the outcome. The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but victory belongs to the LORD.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הוֹשִׁיעָה יְהוָה הַמֶּלֶךְ (hoshiʿah YHWH ha-melekh); Greek (LXX): κύριε, σῶσον τὸν βασιλέα
translationNotes.note: Liturgical acclamation for royal deliverance (v. 9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֵׁם יְהוָה (shem YHWH); Greek: ὄνομα κυρίου
translationNotes.note: Invoked as covenant identity/power (v. 7).

translationNotes.term: Your gifts and your burnt offerings
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִנְחָה (minchah) - עוֹלָה (olah)
translationNotes.note: Two named offerings, not general piety. The minchah is the grain offering of fine flour with oil and frankincense, a handful burned and the rest going to the priests (Leviticus 2:1-3). The olah is the whole burnt offering, killed, skinned, cut up and burned entire so that nothing comes back to the giver (Leviticus 1:3-9). The Hebrew of verse 3 asks God to count the olah as fat, meaning to accept it as a full one.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רֶכֶב (rekhev) - סוּס (sus)
translationNotes.note: The chariot was the armoured strike weapon of the age, and Israel went without it for most of its history. The law forbade the king to multiply horses (Deuteronomy 17:16); David hamstrung the chariot horses he took from Hadadezer, keeping only enough for a hundred chariots (2 Samuel 8:4); Solomon reversed that and stabled fourteen hundred chariots (1 Kings 10:26). Verse 7 is a statement about equipment the enemy had and Israel did not.

stories.keyTakeaway: A communal prayer asks the LORD to give victory to the king, contrasting trust in chariots with trust in the LORD’s name.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 👑 Psalms 21
summaryBullets: O LORD, the king rejoices in Your strength. How greatly he exults in Your salvation! (21:1).
You have granted his heart’s desire and have not withheld the request of his lips. Selah (21:2).
For You welcomed him with rich blessings; You placed on his head a crown of pure gold. (21:3).
He asked You for life, and You granted it— length of days, forever and ever. (21:4).
Great is his glory in Your salvation; You bestow on him splendor and majesty. (21:5).
For You grant him blessings forever; You cheer him with joy in Your presence. (21:6).
For the king trusts in the LORD; through the loving devotion of the Most High, he will not be shaken. (21:7).
Your hand will apprehend all Your enemies; Your right hand will seize those who hate You. (21:8).
You will place them in a fiery furnace at the time of Your appearing. In His wrath the LORD will engulf them, and the fire will consume them. (21:9).
You will wipe their descendants from the earth, and their offspring from the sons of men. (21:10).
Though they intend You harm, the schemes they devise will not prevail. (21:11).
For You will put them to flight when Your bow is trained upon them. (21:12).
Be exalted, O LORD, in Your strength; we will sing and praise Your power. (21:13).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 7:12-16: The grant behind verse 4, where the king asks for life and is given length of days forever. God told David his house and his throne would be established forever.

Psalm 20:4-6: The prayer this psalm answers. There the congregation asks God to give the king the desires of his heart; here it reports that He granted them and did not withhold the request of his lips.
Psalm 72:1-4: What the crowned king of verse 3 is for. Justice for the afflicted, salvation for the children of the needy, and the oppressor crushed.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲטֶרֶת פָּז (ʿateret paz), Greek (LXX): στέφανον ἐκ λίθου τιμίου, Aramaic: כליל דדהבא
translationNotes.note: Royal insignia of divine blessing (v. 3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רוּם (rum), Greek: ὑψόω, Aramaic: רום
translationNotes.note: To be lifted high (v. 13).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תַּנּוּר (tannur)
translationNotes.note: The word is the household bread oven: a clay dome or a clay-lined pit, heated with brushwood until the walls glow, then wiped out and used for baking. Every village had them, and Leviticus 2:4 and Hosea 7:4-7 both take the reader inside one. Verse 9 puts the enemy in that oven. It is a kitchen image, not a foundry.

translationNotes.term: Length of days, forever and ever
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֹרֶךְ יָמִים (orekh yamim)
translationNotes.note: Court language for a long reign. Bathsheba answers David with 'May my lord King David live forever' (1 Kings 1:31), and Nehemiah greets Artaxerxes the same way (Nehemiah 2:3). The formula was spoken to a man standing in the room, so verse 4 is using the ordinary language of the throne room and not a statement about the king's own death.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm praises God for granting the king victory, life, and glory while consuming enemies.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🕊️ Psalms 22
summaryBullets: My God, my God, why have You forsaken me? Why are You so far from saving me, so far from my words of groaning? (22:1).
I cry out by day, O my God, but You do not answer, and by night, but I have no rest. (22:2).
Yet You are holy, enthroned on the praises of Israel. (22:3).
In You our fathers trusted; they trusted and You delivered them. (22:4).
They cried out to You and were set free; they trusted in You and were not disappointed. (22:5).
But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by men and despised by the people. (22:6).
All who see me mock me; they sneer and shake their heads: (22:7).
“He trusts in the LORD, let the LORD deliver him; let the LORD rescue him, since He delights in him.” (22:8).
Yet You brought me forth from the womb; You made me secure at my mother’s breast. (22:9).
From birth I was cast upon You; from my mother’s womb You have been my God. (22:10).
Be not far from me, for trouble is near and there is no one to help. (22:11).
Many bulls surround me; strong bulls of Bashan encircle me. (22:12).
They open their jaws against me like lions that roar and maul. (22:13).
I am poured out like water, and all my bones are disjointed. My heart is like wax; it melts away within me. (22:14).
My strength is dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue sticks to the roof of my mouth. You lay me in the dust of death. (22:15).
For dogs surround me; a band of evil men encircles me; they have pierced my hands and feet. (22:16).
I can count all my bones; they stare and gloat over me. (22:17).
They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing. (22:18).
But You, O LORD, be not far off; O my Strength, come quickly to help me. (22:19).
Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of wild dogs. (22:20).
Save me from the mouth of the lion; at the horns of the wild oxen You have answered me! (22:21).
I will proclaim Your name to my brothers; I will praise You in the assembly. (22:22).
You who fear the LORD, praise Him! All descendants of Jacob, honor Him! All offspring of Israel, revere Him! (22:23).
For He has not despised or detested the torment of the afflicted. He has not hidden His face from him, but has attended to his cry for help. (22:24).
My praise for You resounds in the great assembly; I will fulfill my vows before those who fear You. (22:25).
The poor will eat and be satisfied; those who seek the LORD will praise Him. May your hearts live forever! (22:26).
All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the LORD. All the families of the nations will bow down before Him. (22:27).
For dominion belongs to the LORD and He rules over the nations. (22:28).
All the rich of the earth will feast and worship; all who go down to the dust will kneel before Him— even those unable to preserve their lives. (22:29).
Posterity will serve Him; they will declare the Lord to a new generation. (22:30).
They will come and proclaim His righteousness to a people yet unborn — all that He has done. (22:31).
crossRefs: Matthew 27:46: About the ninth hour Jesus cries out verse 1 from the cross in Aramaic, Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani, and bystanders standing there mishear it as a call for Elijah.
John 19:24: The soldiers split the garments four ways and cast lots for the seamless tunic rather than tear it, and John names verse 18 as the Scripture that was being fulfilled.
Hebrews 2:12: The turn at verse 22, where the sufferer begins proclaiming God's name to his brothers, is quoted as the reason Jesus is not ashamed to call believers His brothers.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָזַב (ʿazav), Greek (LXX): ἐγκαταλείπω, Aramaic: שבק
translationNotes.note: To abandon or leave (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew (variant): כָּאֲרִי (kaʾari, 'like a lion') vs. כָּרוּ (karu, 'they pierced'), Greek: ὤρυξαν, Aramaic: כארי
translationNotes.note: Textual variant at v. 16 about hands and feet.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַיֶּלֶת הַשַּׁחַר (ayyelet hashachar)
translationNotes.note: The heading names the tune the psalm was sung to, the way 'Do Not Destroy' heads Psalms 57 through 59 and 'Lilies' heads Psalms 45 and 69. The words themselves mean the hind of the morning. No song by that name survives, so the melody is gone and only the label is left; the phrase is not part of the psalm and says nothing about its subject.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַבִּירֵי בָשָׁן (abbirei Bashan)
translationNotes.note: Bashan is the high plateau east of the Sea of Galilee, well watered and given over to grazing; today it is the Golan and the Hauran. Its cattle were proverbial for size, so much so that Amos calls the rich women of Samaria 'cows of Bashan' to their faces (Amos 4:1; see also Deuteronomy 32:14; Ezekiel 39:18). Verse 12 names the largest animals anyone in Israel had stood next to.

translationNotes.term: My God, my God, why have You forsaken Me
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵלִי אֵלִי לָמָה עֲזַבְתָּנִי (Eli Eli lamah azavtani) - Greek: ελωι ελωι λεμα σαβαχθανι (eloi eloi lema sabachthani)
translationNotes.note: Jesus speaks this line from the cross and the Gospel writers keep the sound of it before giving the meaning: Matthew 27:46 has 'Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani' and Mark 15:34 has 'Eloi, Eloi.' Sabachthani is Aramaic, the everyday speech of first-century Judea, where the psalm's Hebrew has azavtani. The bystanders mishear Eli as a call for Elijah (Matthew 27:47), which only works in the Semitic wording, not in Greek or English.

translationNotes.term: they cast lots for my clothing
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גּוֹרָל (goral), a lot
translationNotes.note: Casting lots meant shaking marked stones or sticks out of a fold of cloth or a vessel and reading the result, and Israel used it for serious decisions: dividing the land among the tribes (Numbers 26:55), finding Achan (Joshua 7:14), the sailors identifying Jonah (Jonah 1:7), choosing which priest burned the incense (Luke 1:9), and replacing Judas (Acts 1:26). Proverbs 16:33 says the lot is cast into the lap but its decision is from the LORD. Psalm 22:18 puts the practice in the hands of men stripping a dying man, and John 19:23-24 reports Roman soldiers doing it at the cross.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm moves from agonized lament over abandonment and mockery to universal praise of the LORD’s deliverance.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. To the tune of “The Doe of the Dawn.” A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🌿 Psalms 23
summaryBullets: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. (23:1).
He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters. (23:2).
He restores my soul; He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name. (23:3).
Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me. (23:4).
You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies. You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows. (23:5).
Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever. (23:6).
crossRefs: John 10:11: Jesus takes the title this psalm gives to the LORD and adds what it costs. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.
Ezekiel 34:11-16: God announces He will do the shepherding Himself because Israel's leaders would not, searching for the scattered flock, making them lie down in good pasture, binding up the broken.
Revelation 7:17: The last appearance of this psalm in Scripture, where the Lamb at the center of the throne shepherds His people and leads them to springs of living water.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צַלְמָוֶת (tsalmavet), Greek: σκιά θανάτου, Aramaic: טולמותא
translationNotes.note: Deep darkness or death-shade (v. 4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דִּשֵּׁנְתָּ (dishanta, 'make fat/enrich'), Greek: ἔλιπας (anointed), Aramaic: משחת
translationNotes.note: Oil as sign of honor and blessing (v. 5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֵׁבֶט (shevet) - מִשְׁעֶנֶת (mish'enet)
translationNotes.note: Two separate objects. The shevet is a short heavy club of hard wood carried against predators and thieves, the same word used for a tribal rod and a king's scepter. The mish'enet is the long walking staff a man leans on, from the verb 'to lean.' David used the first when a lion and a bear came for his flock (1 Samuel 17:34-35); the second is what got him up and down the hills.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְאוֹת דֶּשֶׁא (ne'ot deshe) - מֵי מְנֻחוֹת (mei menuchot)
translationNotes.note: Deshe is the new grass that comes up after the winter rains and is gone by early summer, so the pasture is a season and not a meadow. 'Quiet waters' reads literally 'waters of rest,' meaning still water, which in Judea meant a well or a cistern more often than a stream. Watering a flock was work: Jacob rolled the stone off the well mouth for Rachel's sheep (Genesis 29:2-10) and Moses had to drive shepherds away from the well in Midian (Exodus 2:16-17).

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalmist depicts the LORD as shepherd who provides, guides, protects, and hosts forever.
stories.superscription: A Psalm of David.

stories.title: ⛰️ Psalms 24
summaryBullets: The earth is the LORD’s, and the fullness thereof, the world and all who dwell therein. (24:1).
For He has founded it upon the seas and established it upon the waters. (24:2).
Who may ascend the hill of the LORD? Who may stand in His holy place? (24:3).
He who has clean hands and a pure heart, who does not lift up his soul to an idol or swear deceitfully. (24:4).
He will receive blessing from the LORD and vindication from the God of his salvation. (24:5).
Such is the generation of those who seek Him, who seek Your face, O God of Jacob. Selah (24:6).
Lift up your heads, O gates! Be lifted up, O ancient doors, that the King of Glory may enter! (24:7).
Who is this King of Glory? The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle. (24:8).
Lift up your heads, O gates! Be lifted up, O ancient doors, that the King of Glory may enter! (24:9).
Who is He, this King of Glory? The LORD of Hosts — He is the King of Glory. Selah (24:10).
crossRefs: Exodus 19:10-15: What approaching the mountain cost the first time. Two days of consecration, clothes washed, a boundary set around it, and death for anyone who so much as touched its base.
