Psalm 15:1-2: The same question in nearly the same words, who may dwell on God's holy mountain, answered there with a list of what the man does rather than the state of his hands and heart.
Isaiah 33:14-16: The question asked from the other side. Who can dwell with a consuming fire, answered with clean conduct, refused bribes, and eyes shut tight against evil.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְקִי כַפַּיִם וּבַר לֵבָב (naqi kappayim u-var levav); Greek: καθαρὸς χεῖρας καὶ καθαρὸς καρδίας
translationNotes.note: Idioms for outward deeds and inward integrity (v. 4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֶלֶךְ הַכָּבוֹד (melekh hakkavod), Greek: βασιλεὺς τῆς δόξης, Aramaic: מלכא דיקרא
translationNotes.note: Title for the LORD as victorious King (vv. 7-10).

translationNotes.term: Lift up your heads, O gates
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁעָרִים (she'arim) - פִּתְחֵי עוֹלָם (pitchei olam)
translationNotes.note: A city gate of this period was a building, not a doorway: paired towers, a passage with two or three chambers along each side, and heavy timber doors plated with bronze that dropped behind a bar. Samson pulled the doors of Gaza's gate out with both posts and the bar and carried the whole assembly uphill (Judges 16:3). Verses 7 and 9 address that structure and tell it to raise its head.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת (YHWH Tseva'ot) - Greek: κύριος σαβαώθ (kyrios sabaoth)
translationNotes.note: Tseva'ot is the plural of an army in the field, so the title reads 'the LORD of armies.' It enters the record at Shiloh, where the ark stood (1 Samuel 1:3), and it attaches to the ark itself in the phrase 'the LORD of Hosts, who is enthroned between the cherubim' (1 Samuel 4:4; 2 Samuel 6:2). The Greek left the word untranslated, which is why Romans 9:29 and James 5:4 still print Sabaoth.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm declares the LORD as Creator, demands purity for His presence, and proclaims Him King of glory entering in.
stories.superscription: A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🙏 Psalms 25
summaryBullets: To You, O LORD, I lift up my soul; (25:1).
in You, my God, I trust. Do not let me be put to shame; do not let my enemies exult over me. (25:2).
Surely none who wait for You will be put to shame; but those who engage in treachery without cause will be disgraced. (25:3).
Show me Your ways, O LORD; teach me Your paths. (25:4).
Guide me in Your truth and teach me, for You are the God of my salvation; all day long I wait for You. (25:5).
Remember, O LORD, Your compassion and loving devotion, for they are from age to age. (25:6).
Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my rebellious acts; remember me according to Your loving devotion, because of Your goodness, O LORD. (25:7).
Good and upright is the LORD; therefore He shows sinners the way. (25:8).
He guides the humble in what is right and teaches them His way. (25:9).
All the LORD’s ways are loving and faithful to those who keep His covenant and His decrees. (25:10).
For the sake of Your name, O LORD, forgive my iniquity, for it is great. (25:11).
Who is the man who fears the LORD? He will instruct him in the path chosen for him. (25:12).
His soul will dwell in prosperity, and his descendants will inherit the land. (25:13).
The LORD confides in those who fear Him, and reveals His covenant to them. (25:14).
My eyes are always on the LORD, for He will free my feet from the mesh. (25:15).
Turn to me and be gracious, for I am lonely and afflicted. (25:16).
The troubles of my heart increase; free me from my distress. (25:17).
Consider my affliction and trouble, and take away all my sins. (25:18).
Consider my enemies, for they are many, and they hate me with vicious hatred. (25:19).
Guard my soul and deliver me; let me not be put to shame, for I take refuge in You. (25:20).
May integrity and uprightness preserve me, because I wait for You. (25:21).
Redeem Israel, O God, from all its distress. (25:22).
crossRefs: Psalm 34:15-18: The same assurance in a psalm built on the same alphabet pattern. The LORD's eyes are on the righteous, His ears are inclined to their cry, and He is near the brokenhearted.
Lamentations 3:25-26: Written over the ruins of Jerusalem, the same conclusion as verses 3 and 5. The LORD is good to those who wait for Him, and it is good to wait quietly for His salvation.
James 1:5: The New Testament form of the request at verses 4 and 5. Ask God for wisdom and He gives generously to all without finding fault.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵלֶיךָ יְהוָה נַפְשִׁי אֶשָּׂא (elekha YHWH nafshi essa); Greek: πρὸς σὲ, κύριε, τὴν ψυχήν μου ἦρα
translationNotes.note: Expression of dependence and prayer (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פָּדָה (padah), Greek: λυτρόω, Aramaic: פרק
translationNotes.note: Deliver, buy back, rescue (v. 22).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: א ב ג (aleph, beth, gimel)
translationNotes.note: In Hebrew the verses start down the alphabet, roughly one letter each, and no translation can show it. The sequence here is not exact: no verse begins with waw, and verse 22 begins with pe, one letter past the end, standing outside the pattern. Psalm 34 has both of those same features, and in both psalms the extra final verse opens with the verb padah, to redeem. Psalms 9 and 10, 37, 111, 112, 119 and 145 are the other alphabetic psalms.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רֶשֶׁת (reshet)
translationNotes.note: A net, and specifically the fowler's net: a mesh pegged flat on the ground over bait and pulled shut on the bird. Proverbs 1:17 mocks spreading one in sight of the birds, Hosea 7:12 has God throwing one over Ephraim like a bird, and Psalm 91:3 names the trade outright as the snare of the fowler. Verse 15 puts the feet in it, so the picture is a man caught in a trap another man set.

stories.keyTakeaway: In an acrostic prayer the psalmist lifts his soul to the LORD, asking to be shown His paths, forgiven the sins of his youth, and guarded from treacherous enemies; he declares that the LORD guides the humble and confides in those who fear Him, and asks God to redeem Israel from all its distress.

headings.text: To You I Lift Up My Soul

stories.superscription: Of David.

stories.title: ⚖️ Psalms 26
summaryBullets: Vindicate me, O LORD! For I have walked with integrity; I have trusted in the LORD without wavering. (26:1).
Test me, O LORD, and try me; examine my heart and mind. (26:2).
For Your loving devotion is before my eyes, and I have walked in Your truth. (26:3).
I do not sit with deceitful men, nor keep company with hypocrites. (26:4).
I hate the mob of evildoers, and refuse to sit with the wicked. (26:5).
I wash my hands in innocence that I may go about Your altar, O LORD, (26:6).
to raise my voice in thanksgiving and declare all Your wonderful works. (26:7).
O LORD, I love the house where You dwell, the place where Your glory resides. (26:8).
Do not take my soul away with sinners, or my life with men of bloodshed, (26:9).
in whose hands are wicked schemes, whose right hands are full of bribes. (26:10).
But I will walk with integrity; redeem me and be merciful to me. (26:11).
My feet stand on level ground; in the congregations I will bless the LORD. (26:12).
crossRefs: Psalm 1:1: The same three refusals in the same order, not walking in the counsel of the wicked, not standing on the path of sinners, not sitting with mockers, which verses 4 and 5 here claim as a record.
Psalm 24:3-6: The hand-washing of verse 6 is the requirement stated there, clean hands and a pure heart for anyone who would stand in God's holy place.
Proverbs 11:20: The verdict this prayer appeals to. The perverse in heart are an abomination to the LORD, but the blameless in their walk are His delight.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁפַט (shafat, 'judge'), Greek: κρῖναι, Aramaic: דון
translationNotes.note: Here means to judge favorably (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶרְחַץ בְּנִקָּיוֹן (erkhatz b’niqqayon); Greek: νίψομαι ἐν ἀκακίᾳ
translationNotes.note: Ceremonial gesture symbolizing purity (v. 6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כְּלָיוֹת (kelayot) - לֵב (lev)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew of verse 2 reads 'test my kidneys and my heart.' Hebrew locates the deepest and least visible thoughts in the kidneys, the organs buried furthest inside the body, and the will and reasoning in the heart. English has no equivalent, so versions print 'mind' or 'inmost being.' The two verbs beside them, tsaraf and bachan, are metalworkers' words for assaying silver.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִזְבֵּחַ (mizbeach)
translationNotes.note: The altar of burnt offering stood in the open courtyard, five cubits square and three high, with a horn projecting at each corner (Exodus 27:1-2), and it was reached by a ramp because the law forbade steps (Exodus 20:26). Verse 6 pictures a man circling it, and verse 6 pairs that with washing, which is what the bronze basin standing between the tent and the altar was for (Exodus 30:17-21).

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalmist appeals for vindication, distancing from sinners, and affirming love for God’s house.
stories.superscription: Of David.

stories.title: 💡 Psalms 27
summaryBullets: The LORD is my light and my salvation— whom shall I fear? The LORD is the stronghold of my life— whom shall I dread? (27:1).
When the wicked came upon me to devour my flesh, my enemies and foes stumbled and fell. (27:2).
Though an army encamps around me, my heart will not fear; though a war breaks out against me, I will keep my trust. (27:3).
One thing I have asked of the LORD; this is what I desire: to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze on the beauty of the LORD and seek Him in His temple. (27:4).
For in the day of trouble He will hide me in His shelter; He will conceal me under the cover of His tent; He will set me high upon a rock. (27:5).
Then my head will be held high above my enemies around me. At His tabernacle I will offer sacrifices with shouts of joy; I will sing and make music to the LORD. (27:6).
Hear, O LORD, my voice when I call; be merciful and answer me. (27:7).
My heart said, “Seek His face.” Your face, O LORD, I will seek. (27:8).
Hide not Your face from me, nor turn away Your servant in anger. You have been my helper; do not leave me or forsake me, O God of my salvation. (27:9).
Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me. (27:10).
Teach me Your way, O LORD, and lead me on a level path, because of my oppressors. (27:11).
Do not hand me over to the will of my foes, for false witnesses rise up against me, breathing out violence. (27:12).
Still I am certain to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living. (27:13).
Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous. Wait patiently for the LORD! (27:14).
crossRefs: John 8:12: Jesus takes the first title of verse 1 for Himself. I am the light of the world, and whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness.
Psalm 23:6: The same wish stated as a certainty rather than a request. Here David asks to dwell in the house of the LORD all his days; there he says outright that he will.
Isaiah 40:31: What the command at verse 14 leads to. Those who wait upon the LORD renew their strength, mount up with wings like eagles, and run without growing weary.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אוֹר (or), Greek: φῶς (phōs), Aramaic: נהורא
translationNotes.note: Symbol for guidance and salvation (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קַוֵּה (qavveh), Greek: ὑπόμεινον, Aramaic: קוי
translationNotes.note: To hope, expect, look eagerly (v. 14).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֵיכָל (heikhal)
translationNotes.note: The word means a large hall or a palace and it does not by itself mean Solomon's building. It is used of the tent shrine at Shiloh, where Eli sat by the doorpost and where the boy Samuel slept near the ark (1 Samuel 1:9; 3:3), generations before any stone temple existed. Verse 4 asks for residence and a clear view, the access a household member has, not a visitor's.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵדֵי־שֶׁקֶר (edei-sheqer)
translationNotes.note: A capital charge in Israel required two or three witnesses, and a single accuser could not convict (Deuteronomy 19:15). The law's answer to perjury was to do to the false witness what he intended for his target (Deuteronomy 19:16-21). Jezebel used exactly two hired men to have Naboth stoned for his vineyard (1 Kings 21:10-13), so verse 12 names a live danger with a known procedure behind it.

stories.keyTakeaway: With the LORD as his light, salvation, and stronghold, the psalmist fears no encamped army; he asks one thing, to dwell in the LORD’s house and gaze on His beauty, pleads for God not to hide His face when false witnesses rise, and waits for the LORD in courage, certain to see His goodness in the land of the living.
stories.superscription: Of David.

stories.title: 📯 Psalms 28
summaryBullets: To You, O LORD, I call; be not deaf to me, O my Rock. For if You remain silent, I will be like those descending to the Pit. (28:1).
Hear my cry for mercy when I call to You for help, when I lift up my hands toward Your holy sanctuary. (28:2).
Do not drag me away with the wicked, and with the workers of iniquity, who speak peace to their neighbors while malice is in their hearts. (28:3).
Repay them according to their deeds and for their works of evil. Repay them for what their hands have done; bring back on them what they deserve. (28:4).
Since they show no regard for the works of the LORD or what His hands have done, He will tear them down and never rebuild them. (28:5).
Blessed be the LORD, for He has heard my cry for mercy. (28:6).
The LORD is my strength and my shield; my heart trusts in Him, and I am helped. Therefore my heart rejoices, and I give thanks to Him with my song. (28:7).
The LORD is the strength of His people, a stronghold of salvation for His anointed. (28:8).
Save Your people and bless Your inheritance; shepherd them and carry them forever. (28:9).
crossRefs: Psalm 18:2: The title David uses at verse 1, my Rock, laid out there at full length as rock and fortress and deliverer and shield and horn of salvation.
Jeremiah 17:10: The principle behind the request at verse 4. God searches the heart and examines the mind in order to repay a man according to his way and what his deeds deserve.
Psalm 80:1: The same closing image as verse 9, God as the shepherd of Israel who leads Joseph like a flock and sits enthroned between the cherubim.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צוּר (tsur), Greek: πέτρα (petra), Aramaic: כיפא (kepha)
translationNotes.note: Metaphor for stability and protection (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רָעָה (raʿah), Greek: ποιμαίνω, Aramaic: רעי
translationNotes.note: To tend a flock, care for (v. 9).

translationNotes.term: I lift up my hands toward Your holy sanctuary
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דְּבִיר (devir)
translationNotes.note: Devir is the innermost room, the windowless cube at the back where the ark stood. Prayer was made facing it: Solomon spread out his hands toward heaven at the dedication and told Israel to pray toward this house (1 Kings 8:22, 29-30), and Daniel kept windows open toward Jerusalem and knelt three times a day (Daniel 6:10). Raised open hands were the standing posture, not folded ones.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נָשָׂא (nasa)
translationNotes.note: The verb is to lift and carry a load. Isaiah puts the same picture in full: the shepherd gathers the lambs in his arms and carries them against his chest (Isaiah 40:11), and Moses says God carried Israel through the wilderness as a man carries his son (Deuteronomy 1:31). Verse 9 asks for the treatment given to an animal that cannot keep up.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalmist pleads for deliverance from the wicked and blesses the LORD for being his strength and shepherd.
stories.superscription: Of David.

stories.title: ⚡ Psalms 29
summaryBullets: Ascribe to the LORD, O heavenly beings, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength. (29:1).
Ascribe to the LORD the glory due His name; worship the LORD in the splendor of His holiness. (29:2).
The voice of the LORD is over the waters; the God of glory thunders; the LORD is heard over many waters. (29:3).
The voice of the LORD is powerful; the voice of the LORD is majestic. (29:4).
The voice of the LORD breaks the cedars; the LORD shatters the cedars of Lebanon. (29:5).
He makes Lebanon skip like a calf, and Sirion like a young wild ox. (29:6).
The voice of the LORD strikes with flames of fire. (29:7).
The voice of the LORD shakes the wilderness; the LORD shakes the Wilderness of Kadesh. (29:8).
The voice of the LORD twists the oaks and strips the forests bare. And in His temple all cry, “Glory!” (29:9).
The LORD sits enthroned over the flood; the LORD is enthroned as King forever. (29:10).
The LORD gives His people strength; the LORD blesses His people with peace. (29:11).
crossRefs: Exodus 19:16-19: The one occasion when Israel heard this voice for themselves. Thunder over Sinai, the ram's horn growing louder and louder, and God answering Moses in the thunder.
Psalm 93:3-4: The same contest with the waters of verse 3. The seas lift up their pounding waves and the LORD on high is more majestic than all their roar.
Revelation 10:3-4: Thunder that speaks instead of rumbling. Seven thunders sound their voices and John is told to seal up what they said and not write it down.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קוֹל (qol), Greek: φωνή (phōnē), Aramaic: קל (qal)
translationNotes.note: Central motif repeated 7 times in psalm.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַבּוּל (mabbul), Greek: κατακλυσμός, Aramaic: מבולא
translationNotes.note: Word used elsewhere only for Noah’s flood (v. 10).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַרְזֵי הַלְּבָנוֹן (arzei hallevanon)
translationNotes.note: Cedar of Lebanon grows on the mountains north of Israel and was the prestige timber of the ancient world: tall, straight, fragrant and slow to rot. Solomon bought it from Hiram of Tyre, and the logs were floated down the coast in rafts and landed at Joppa (1 Kings 5:6-9; 2 Chronicles 2:16). Verse 5 has the thunder snapping the largest and toughest trees anyone in the region knew.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׂרְיֹן (Siryon)
translationNotes.note: Sirion is Mount Hermon under another name. Deuteronomy 3:9 explains it directly: the Sidonians call Hermon Sirion, and the Amorites call it Senir. Hermon is the highest ground in the region at about 9,200 feet, snow-capped most of the year. Verse 6 has the storm running the length of the country, from Lebanon and Hermon in the north to the wilderness of Kadesh in the south.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm portrays the LORD’s majestic voice in storm theophany, enthroned as King who gives peace.
stories.superscription: A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🎶 Psalms 30
summaryBullets: I will exalt You, O LORD, for You have lifted me up and have not allowed my foes to rejoice over me. (30:1).
O LORD my God, I cried to You for help, and You healed me. (30:2).
O LORD, You pulled me up from Sheol; You spared me from descending into the Pit. (30:3).
Sing to the LORD, O you His saints, and praise His holy name. (30:4).
For His anger is fleeting, but His favor lasts a lifetime. Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning. (30:5).
In prosperity I said, “I will never be shaken.” (30:6).
O LORD, You favored me; You made my mountain stand strong. When You hid Your face, I was dismayed. (30:7).
To You, O LORD, I called, and I begged my Lord for mercy: (30:8).
“What gain is there in my bloodshed, in my descent to the Pit? Will the dust praise You? Will it proclaim Your faithfulness? (30:9).
Hear me, O LORD, and have mercy; O LORD, be my helper.” (30:10).
You turned my mourning into dancing; You peeled off my sackcloth and clothed me with joy, (30:11).
that my heart may sing Your praises and not be silent. O LORD my God, I will give thanks forever. (30:12).
crossRefs: Psalm 116:3-8: The same rescue told again. Ropes of death, the anguish of Sheol, a cry to the LORD, and a soul delivered from death and eyes delivered from tears.
Lamentations 3:22-23: The other place that times mercy to the morning. His mercies never fail and are new every morning, which is the joy that comes in the morning at verse 5.
John 16:20: On the night before He dies Jesus tells the disciples their grief will turn to joy, the same reversal celebrated at verse 11 where mourning becomes dancing.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂק (saq); Greek: σάκκος (sakkos)
translationNotes.note: A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
translationNotes.note: The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

translationNotes.term: For the dedication of the house
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲנֻכַּת הַבַּיִת (chanukkat habbayit)
translationNotes.note: David bought the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite and built an altar there when the plague stopped (2 Samuel 24:18-25), and that floor is where Solomon later built the temple (2 Chronicles 3:1). The heading's word chanukkah is the same one used of the rededication of the altar under Judah Maccabee on the twenty-fifth of Chislev, 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:52-59), the winter feast John 10:22 calls the Feast of Dedication.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָחוֹל (machol)
translationNotes.note: Machol is the circle dance, done to the beat of the hand drum and led by women: Miriam after the sea (Exodus 15:20), Jephthah's daughter at the gate (Judges 11:34), the women who met Saul and David after the Philistine campaign (1 Samuel 18:6). Verse 11 sets it against sackcloth, which was belted on; the Hebrew says God untied the sackcloth, the way you undo a belt.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm thanks the LORD for deliverance from death, turning mourning into joy and restoring life.

headings.text: You Turned My Mourning into Dancing

stories.superscription: A Psalm. A song for the dedication of the temple. Of David.

stories.title: 🛡️ Psalms 31
summaryBullets: In You, O LORD, I have taken refuge; let me never be put to shame; save me by Your righteousness. (31:1).
Incline Your ear to me; come quickly to my rescue. Be my rock of refuge, the stronghold of my deliverance. (31:2).
For You are my rock and my fortress; lead me and guide me for the sake of Your name. (31:3).
You free me from the net laid out for me, for You are my refuge. (31:4).
Into Your hands I commit my spirit; You have redeemed me, O LORD, God of truth. (31:5).
I hate those who cling to worthless idols, but in the LORD I trust. (31:6).
I will be glad and rejoice in Your loving devotion, for You have seen my affliction; You have known the anguish of my soul. (31:7).
You have not delivered me to the enemy; You have set my feet in the open. (31:8).
Be merciful to me, O LORD, for I am in distress; my eyes fail from sorrow, my soul and body as well. (31:9).
For my life is consumed with grief and my years with groaning; my iniquity has drained my strength, and my bones are wasting away. (31:10).
Among all my enemies I am a disgrace, and among my neighbors even more. I am dreaded by my friends — they flee when they see me on the street. (31:11).
I am forgotten like a dead man, out of mind. I am like a broken vessel. (31:12).
For I hear the slander of many; there is terror on every side. They conspire against me and plot to take my life. (31:13).
But I trust in You, O LORD; I say, “You are my God.” (31:14).
My times are in Your hands; deliver me from my enemies and from those who pursue me. (31:15).
Make Your face shine on Your servant; save me by Your loving devotion. (31:16).
O LORD, let me not be ashamed, for I have called on You. Let the wicked be put to shame; let them lie silent in Sheol. (31:17).
May lying lips be silenced — lips that speak with arrogance against the righteous, full of pride and contempt. (31:18).
How great is Your goodness which You have laid up for those who fear You, which You have bestowed before the sons of men on those who take refuge in You! (31:19).
You hide them in the secret place of Your presence from the schemes of men. You conceal them in Your shelter from accusing tongues. (31:20).
Blessed be the LORD, for He has shown me His loving devotion in a city under siege. (31:21).
In my alarm I said, “I am cut off from Your sight!” But You heard my plea for mercy when I called to You for help. (31:22).
Love the LORD, all His saints. The LORD preserves the faithful, but fully repays the arrogant. (31:23).
Be strong and courageous, all you who hope in the LORD. (31:24).
crossRefs: Luke 23:46: Jesus dies with verse 5 on His lips, calling out in a loud voice, Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit, and adding the word Father to what David wrote.
Jeremiah 20:10: The prophet reports the identical phrase from verse 13, terror on every side, and names who is saying it: his own trusted friends, watching for him to fall.
Psalm 27:14: The same closing command that ends this psalm at verse 24, be strong and take courage, spoken twice to anyone waiting on the LORD.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּיָדְךָ אַפְקִיד רוּחִי (beyadkha afkid ruchi), Greek: εἰς χεῖράς σου παραθήσομαι τὸ πνεῦμά μου, Aramaic: בידך אפקיד רוחי
translationNotes.note: Entrust one’s life/breath to God (v. 5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
translationNotes.note: The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עִיר מָצוֹר (ir matsor)
translationNotes.note: Siege was the standard way to take a walled town, and the vocabulary is technical. An attacker threw up a ramp of packed earth against the wall (solelah), ringed the town with a counter-wall so nothing got in or out, and worked battering rams up the ramp. Ezekiel was told to model the whole set-up on a clay brick (Ezekiel 4:1-3), and Nebuchadnezzar ran one against Jerusalem for about eighteen months (2 Kings 25:1-3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּכְלִי אֹבֵד (kikhli oved)
translationNotes.note: Literally 'like a vessel that is gone.' Fired clay could not be mended, so a cracked jar was not repaired, it was discarded; the fragments got reused for scooping coals or dipping water (Isaiah 30:14) and for writing short notes. Verse 12 pairs the image with being forgotten like a dead man, which is what happened to the pot.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalmist entrusts his spirit to God amidst enemies, affirming trust and urging others to take courage.

headings.text: Into Your Hands I Commit My Spirit

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🙏 Psalms 32
summaryBullets: Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered. (32:1).
Blessed is the man whose iniquity the LORD does not count against him, in whose spirit there is no deceit. (32:2).
When I kept silent, my bones became brittle from my groaning all day long. (32:3).
For day and night Your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was drained as in the summer heat. Selah (32:4).
Then I acknowledged my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity. I said, “I will confess my transgressions to the LORD,” and You forgave the guilt of my sin. Selah (32:5).
Therefore let all the godly pray to You while You may be found. Surely when great waters rise, they will not come near. (32:6).
You are my hiding place. You protect me from trouble; You surround me with songs of deliverance. Selah (32:7).
I will instruct you and teach you the way you should go; I will give you counsel and watch over you. (32:8).
Do not be like the horse or mule, which have no understanding; they must be controlled with bit and bridle to make them come to you. (32:9).
Many are the sorrows of the wicked, but loving devotion surrounds him who trusts in the LORD. (32:10).
Be glad in the LORD and rejoice, O righteous ones; shout for joy, all you upright in heart. (32:11).
crossRefs: Romans 4:6-8: Paul quotes verses 1 and 2 to prove that God credits righteousness apart from works, and introduces the quotation as David describing the blessedness of such a man.
Proverbs 28:13: The proverb states as a rule what verses 3 through 5 report as experience. Conceal your sins and you will not prosper; confess and renounce them and you find mercy.
Psalm 51:1-5: The confession itself rather than the relief that follows it. There David asks God to blot out his transgressions and wash him; here he tells what happened when he stopped hiding them.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַשְׁרֵי (ashrei), Greek: μακάριος (makarios), Aramaic: טבוי
translationNotes.note: Expression of happiness or fortune (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כָּסָה (kasah), Greek: ἐπικαλύπτω, Aramaic: כסי
translationNotes.note: Figurative for hiding/removing sin (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַשְׂכִּיל (maskil)
translationNotes.note: Thirteen psalms carry this word in the heading: 32, 42, 44, 45, 52, 53, 54, 55, 74, 78, 88, 89 and 142. The root means to have insight or to give it, and the related verb is used in Psalm 32:8 itself, 'I will instruct you.' Whether the label names a teaching psalm, a skilful composition, or a musical setting is not settled, but the instructional sense fits this psalm's own claim.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חַרְבֹנֵי קַיִץ (charvonei qayits)
translationNotes.note: Verse 4 says his moisture was turned into the droughts of summer. In Judea rain falls between about October and April and then stops completely; nothing falls from June to September, streams die back to stone, and the land dries out until the autumn rains. Qayits also names the summer fruit harvest that comes at the end of that dry stretch. The image is a man dried down to nothing over months, not a hot afternoon.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm proclaims blessedness of forgiveness and exhorts confession, trust, and rejoicing in the LORD.
stories.superscription: Of David. A Maskil.

stories.title: 🎵 Psalms 33
summaryBullets: Rejoice in the LORD, O righteous ones; it is fitting for the upright to praise Him. (33:1).
Praise the LORD with the harp; make music to Him with ten strings. (33:2).
Sing to Him a new song; play skillfully with a shout of joy. (33:3).
For the word of the LORD is upright, and all His work is trustworthy. (33:4).
The LORD loves righteousness and justice; the earth is full of His loving devotion. (33:5).
By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all the stars by the breath of His mouth. (33:6).
He piles up the waters of the sea; He puts the depths into storehouses. (33:7).
Let all the earth fear the LORD; let all the people of the world revere Him. (33:8).
For He spoke, and it came to be; He commanded, and it stood firm. (33:9).
The LORD frustrates the plans of the nations; He thwarts the devices of the peoples. (33:10).
The counsel of the LORD stands forever, the purposes of His heart to all generations. (33:11).
Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD, the people He has chosen as His inheritance! (33:12).
The LORD looks down from heaven; He sees all the sons of men. (33:13).
From His dwelling place He gazes on all who inhabit the earth. (33:14).
He shapes the hearts of each; He considers all their works. (33:15).
No king is saved by his vast army; no warrior is delivered by his great strength. (33:16).
A horse is a vain hope for salvation; even its great strength cannot save. (33:17).
Surely the eyes of the LORD are on those who fear Him, on those whose hope is in His loving devotion (33:18).
to deliver them from death and keep them alive in famine. (33:19).
Our soul waits for the LORD; He is our help and our shield. (33:20).
For our hearts rejoice in Him, since we trust in His holy name. (33:21).
May Your loving devotion rest on us, O LORD, as we put our hope in You. (33:22).
crossRefs: Psalm 19:1: The same testimony from the same witness. The heavens declare the glory of God, which is what verse 6 here says they were made by His word to do.
Hebrews 11:3: Verses 6 and 9 stated as an article of faith. The universe was formed at God's command, so what is seen was not made out of what was visible.
Proverbs 19:21: The proverb form of verses 10 and 11. Many plans are in a man's heart, but the purpose of the LORD is the one that stands.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דָּבָר (davar), Greek: λόγος (logos), Aramaic: מֵימְרָא (memra)
translationNotes.note: Creative command of God (v. 6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּנּוֹר (kinnor) - נֵבֶל (nevel) - עָשׂוֹר (asor)
translationNotes.note: Two different instruments and a count. The kinnor is the hand-held lyre, light enough to carry and play walking; it is what David played for Saul (1 Samuel 16:23). The nevel is the larger, deeper standing harp, and its name is also the word for a leather skin bottle, which suggests a bulging sound box. Asor means 'ten,' a ten-stringed instrument, and it appears only in Psalms 33:2, 92:3 and 144:9.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תְּרוּעָה (teru'ah)
translationNotes.note: Teru'ah is not ordinary shouting. It is the massed blast used to signal: the trumpet blast that moved the camps in the wilderness (Numbers 10:5-6), the shout that brought Jericho's wall down (Joshua 6:5, 20), the war cry of an army going in. Leviticus 23:24 names the first day of the seventh month a day of teru'ah, which is why that feast is called a day of blowing. Verse 3 is asking for volume with intent.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁיר חָדָשׁ (shir chadash)
translationNotes.note: A set phrase, and it marks a song written for a fresh act of deliverance rather than a fresh tune. It appears in Psalms 33:3, 40:3, 96:1, 98:1, 144:9 and 149:1, and Isaiah 42:10 uses it of what the nations will sing. Revelation 5:9 and 14:3 carry the phrase into Greek.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm praises God as Creator and Sovereign whose counsel stands and who preserves those who fear Him.

stories.title: 🦁 Psalms 34
summaryBullets: I will bless the LORD at all times; His praise will always be on my lips. (34:1).
My soul boasts in the LORD; let the oppressed hear and rejoice. (34:2).
Magnify the LORD with me; let us exalt His name together. (34:3).
I sought the LORD, and He answered me; He delivered me from all my fears. (34:4).
Those who look to Him are radiant with joy; their faces shall never be ashamed. (34:5).
This poor man called out, and the LORD heard him; He saved him from all his troubles. (34:6).
The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear Him, and he delivers them. (34:7).
Taste and see that the LORD is good; blessed is the man who takes refuge in Him! (34:8).
Fear the LORD, you His saints, for those who fear Him lack nothing. (34:9).
Young lions go lacking and hungry, but those who seek the LORD lack no good thing. (34:10).
Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the LORD. (34:11).
Who is the man who delights in life, who desires to see good days? (34:12).
Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from deceitful speech. (34:13).
Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it. (34:14).
The eyes of the LORD are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their cry. (34:15).
But the face of the LORD is against those who do evil, to wipe out all memory of them from the earth. (34:16).
The righteous cry out, and the LORD hears; He delivers them from all their troubles. (34:17).
The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit. (34:18).
Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him from them all. (34:19).
He protects all his bones; not one of them will be broken. (34:20).
Evil will slay the wicked, and the haters of the righteous will be condemned. (34:21).
The LORD redeems His servants, and none who take refuge in Him will be condemned. (34:22).
crossRefs: John 19:36: The soldiers break the legs of the two men crucified beside Jesus, find Him already dead, and John names the promise of verse 20 as the Scripture fulfilled: not one of His bones will be broken.
1 Peter 2:3: Peter tells new believers to crave pure spiritual milk now that they have tasted that the Lord is good, which is the invitation David issues at verse 8.
Exodus 23:20: The angel of verse 7 doing the work he was first sent to do, going ahead of Israel to protect them on the road and bring them to the place God prepared.
1 Samuel 21:10-15: The occasion the heading names. David runs from Saul to Achish of Gath, is recognized as the man the songs credit with ten thousands, and escapes by feigning madness at the gate.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: טָעַם (taʿam), Greek: γεύομαι, Aramaic: טעם
translationNotes.note: Metaphor for experiencing personally (v. 8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲבִימֶלֶךְ (Avimelekh)
translationNotes.note: The account is 1 Samuel 21:10-15, where the king of Gath is named Achish. Abimelech, which means 'my father is king,' works as a throne name among Philistine and Philistine-area rulers: Genesis 20:2 and Genesis 26:1 both name an Abimelech at Gerar, two generations apart. In the narrative David scratched marks on the doors of the gate and let saliva run into his beard until Achish threw him out.

translationNotes.term: The angel of the LORD encamps
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חָנָה (chanah)
translationNotes.note: Chanah is military vocabulary: to pitch camp, the word used of armies taking up a position around a town. Jacob met the angels of God at Mahanaim and said, 'This is the camp of God' (Genesis 32:1-2), and Elisha's servant at Dothan saw the hills full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:15-17). Verse 7 posts a guard around a position, and the picture is a perimeter, not a hovering presence.

translationNotes.term: Not one of them will be broken
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא נִשְׁבָּרָה (lo nishbarah)
translationNotes.note: Verse 20 uses the wording of the Passover rule. The lamb had to be eaten whole in one house, and 'you shall not break any of its bones' (Exodus 12:46; repeated for the second-month Passover in Numbers 9:12). John 19:36 cites that rule when the soldiers break the legs of the two men crucified beside Jesus and find Him already dead.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm calls to taste the LORD’s goodness, promising deliverance for the righteous who fear Him.

headings.text: Taste and See That the Lord Is Good

stories.superscription: Of David, when he pretended to be insane before Abimelech, so that the king drove him away.

stories.title: ⚔️ Psalms 35
summaryBullets: Contend with my opponents, O LORD; fight against those who fight against me. (35:1).
Take up Your shield and buckler; arise and come to my aid. (35:2).
Draw the spear and javelin against my pursuers; say to my soul: “I am your salvation.” (35:3).
May those who seek my life be disgraced and put to shame; may those who plan to harm me be driven back and confounded. (35:4).
May they be like chaff in the wind, as the angel of the LORD drives them away. (35:5).
May their path be dark and slick, as the angel of the LORD pursues. (35:6).
For without cause they laid their net for me; without reason they dug a pit for my soul. (35:7).
May ruin befall them by surprise; may the net they hid ensnare them; may they fall into the hazard they created. (35:8).
Then my soul will rejoice in the LORD and exult in His salvation. (35:9).
All my bones will exclaim, “Who is like You, O LORD, who delivers the afflicted from the aggressor, the poor and needy from the robber?” (35:10).
Hostile witnesses come forward; they make charges I know nothing about. (35:11).
They repay me evil for good, to the bereavement of my soul. (35:12).
Yet when they were ill, I put on sackcloth; I humbled myself with fasting, but my prayers returned unanswered. (35:13).
I paced about as for my friend or brother; I was bowed down with grief, like one mourning for his mother. (35:14).
But when I stumbled, they assembled in glee; they gathered together against me. Assailants I did not know slandered me without ceasing. (35:15).
Like godless jesters at a feast, they gnashed their teeth at me. (35:16).
How long, O Lord, will You look on? Rescue my soul from their ravages, my precious life from these lions. (35:17).
Then I will give You thanks in the great assembly; I will praise You among many people. (35:18).
Let not my enemies gloat over me without cause, nor those who hate me without reason wink in malice. (35:19).
For they do not speak peace, but they devise deceitful schemes against those who live quietly in the land. (35:20).
They gape at me and say, “Aha, aha! Our eyes have seen!” (35:21).
O LORD, You have seen it; be not silent. O Lord, be not far from me. (35:22).
Awake and rise to my defense, to my cause, my God and my Lord! (35:23).
Vindicate me by Your righteousness, O LORD my God, and do not let them gloat over me. (35:24).
Let them not say in their hearts, “Aha, just what we wanted!” Let them not say, “We have swallowed him up!” (35:25).
May those who gloat in my distress be ashamed and confounded; may those who exalt themselves over me be clothed in shame and reproach. (35:26).
May those who favor my vindication shout for joy and gladness; may they always say, “Exalted be the LORD who delights in His servant’s well-being.” (35:27).
Then my tongue will proclaim Your righteousness and Your praises all day long. (35:28).
crossRefs: Romans 12:19: Paul forbids believers to avenge themselves and tells them to leave room for God's wrath, which is what David does here by handing the whole case to the LORD rather than lifting a hand.
Psalm 69:4: The same complaint in the same words. Those who hate him without cause outnumber the hairs of his head, which is the charge made at verses 7 and 19 here.
Exodus 23:22: The covenant promise this prayer is calling in at verse 1. Listen to God's voice and He will be an enemy to your enemies and a foe to your foes.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רִיב (riv), Greek: δικάζω, Aramaic: דון
translationNotes.note: Legal term for dispute or lawsuit, here applied to God’s defense (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂק (saq); Greek: σάκκος (sakkos)
translationNotes.note: A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָגֵן (magen) - צִנָּה (tsinnah)
translationNotes.note: Two different shields. The magen is the small round shield strapped to the forearm, carried by archers and light troops. The tsinnah is the full body shield, large enough to cover a man standing, and heavy enough that it was often carried by a separate bearer; Goliath had a man walking in front of him with his (1 Samuel 17:7, 41). Verse 2 asks God to take up both, the light and the heavy.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עִנִּיתִי בַצּוֹם נַפְשִׁי (innithi vatsom nafshi)
translationNotes.note: The wording is the law's own. Leviticus 16:29-31 and 23:27-32 command Israel to 'afflict your souls' on the tenth day of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement, and abstaining from food is what that came to mean. Verse 13 uses the same verb, so David is saying he treated his enemies' sickness as an occasion for the most serious observance in the calendar.

stories.keyTakeaway: David calls the LORD to take up shield and spear against those who fight him without cause; he fasted and mourned when they were ill, yet they repay him evil for good and gather gloating at his stumble, so he pleads for vindication, that his tongue may proclaim God’s righteousness all day long.

headings.text: Contend with My Opponents, O Lord

stories.superscription: Of David.

stories.title: 💧 Psalms 36
summaryBullets: An oracle is in my heart regarding the transgression of the wicked man: There is no fear of God before his eyes. (36:1).
For his eyes are too full of conceit to detect or hate his own sin. (36:2).
The words of his mouth are wicked and deceitful; he has ceased to be wise and well-doing. (36:3).
Even on his bed he plots wickedness; he sets himself on a path that is not good; he fails to reject evil. (36:4).
Your loving devotion, O LORD, reaches to the heavens, Your faithfulness to the clouds. (36:5).
Your righteousness is like the highest mountains; Your judgments are like the deepest sea. O LORD, You preserve man and beast. (36:6).
How precious is Your loving devotion, O God, that the children of men take refuge in the shadow of Your wings! (36:7).
They feast on the abundance of Your house, and You give them drink from Your river of delights. (36:8).
For with You is the fountain of life; in Your light we see light. (36:9).
Extend Your loving devotion to those who know You, and Your righteousness to the upright in heart. (36:10).
Let not the foot of the proud come against me, nor the hand of the wicked drive me away. (36:11).
There the evildoers lie fallen, thrown down and unable to rise. (36:12).
crossRefs: John 1:4-5: The two claims of verse 9, life and light, set side by side in the same order. In Him was life, that life was the light of men, and it shines in the darkness.
Jeremiah 2:13: The fountain of life at verse 9 named as the thing Israel walked away from, digging its own broken cisterns that cannot hold water instead.
Psalm 91:4: The shelter of verse 7 pictured in close-up. He covers you with His feathers, and under His wings you find refuge, with His faithfulness as shield and rampart.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (ḥesed), Greek: ἔλεος (eleos), Aramaic: חסדא
translationNotes.note: Loyal covenant love (v. 5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְאֻם (ne'um)
translationNotes.note: Ne'um is a technical word for a declaration, and it almost always appears in the fixed phrase 'declares the LORD,' stamped on prophetic speech across the Old Testament. Verse 1 uses it of transgression speaking inside the wicked man's heart. English versions print 'oracle,' 'message,' or 'transgression speaks,' depending on how they read the line, because the formula is being used somewhere it does not normally go.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נַחַל עֲדָנֶיךָ (nachal adaneikha)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew word for 'delights' here is the plural of eden. Genesis 2:10 has a river going out of Eden to water the garden, and the psalm uses the same two words, river and Eden, in one phrase. English cannot show it without printing the proper name. The nachal itself is a wadi, a valley stream, which in Judea usually runs only in the wet season.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דֶּשֶׁן (deshen)
translationNotes.note: Deshen is fat, and specifically the rich portion of an offering. Verse 8 is a picture of a meal at the sanctuary: the peace offering was eaten by the worshipper and his household in the presence of the LORD, and had to be finished within a day or two (Leviticus 7:15-16; Deuteronomy 12:5-7). The line describes guests at a table in the courts, not a figure of general plenty.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm contrasts human wickedness with God’s immeasurable love, life, and light.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David, the servant of the LORD.

stories.title: 🌱 Psalms 37
summaryBullets: Do not fret over those who do evil; do not envy those who do wrong. (37:1).
For they wither quickly like grass and wilt like tender plants. (37:2).
Trust in the LORD and do good; dwell in the land and cultivate faithfulness. (37:3).
Delight yourself in the LORD, and He will give you the desires of your heart. (37:4).
Commit your way to the LORD; trust in Him, and He will do it. (37:5).
He will bring forth your righteousness like the dawn, your justice like the noonday sun. (37:6).
Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him; do not fret when men prosper in their ways, when they carry out wicked schemes. (37:7).
Refrain from anger and abandon wrath; do not fret— it can only bring harm. (37:8).
For the evildoers will be cut off, but those who hope in the LORD will inherit the land. (37:9).
Yet a little while, and the wicked will be no more; though you look for them, they will not be found. (37:10).
But the meek will inherit the land and delight in abundant prosperity. (37:11).
The wicked scheme against the righteous and gnash their teeth at them, (37:12).
but the Lord laughs, seeing that their day is coming. (37:13).
The wicked have drawn the sword and bent the bow to bring down the poor and needy, to slay those whose ways are upright. (37:14).
But their swords will pierce their own hearts, and their bows will be broken. (37:15).
Better is the little of the righteous than the abundance of many who are wicked. (37:16).
For the arms of the wicked will be broken, but the LORD upholds the righteous. (37:17).
The LORD knows the days of the blameless, and their inheritance will last forever. (37:18).
In the time of evil they will not be ashamed, and in the days of famine they will be satisfied. (37:19).
But the wicked and enemies of the LORD will perish like the glory of the fields. They will vanish; like smoke they will fade away. (37:20).
The wicked borrow and do not repay, but the righteous are gracious and giving. (37:21).
Surely those He blesses will inherit the land, but the cursed will be destroyed. (37:22).
The steps of a man are ordered by the LORD who takes delight in his journey. (37:23).
Though he falls, he will not be overwhelmed, for the LORD is holding his hand. (37:24).
I once was young and now am old, yet never have I seen the righteous abandoned or their children begging for bread. (37:25).
They are ever generous and quick to lend, and their children are a blessing. (37:26).
Turn away from evil and do good, so that you will abide forever. (37:27).
For the LORD loves justice and will not forsake His saints. They are preserved forever, but the offspring of the wicked will be cut off. (37:28).
The righteous will inherit the land and dwell in it forever. (37:29).
The mouth of the righteous man utters wisdom, and his tongue speaks justice. (37:30).
The law of his God is in his heart; his steps do not falter. (37:31).
Though the wicked lie in wait for the righteous, and seek to slay them, (37:32).
the LORD will not leave them in their power or let them be condemned under judgment. (37:33).
Wait for the LORD and keep His way, and He will raise you up to inherit the land. When the wicked are cut off, you will see it. (37:34).
I have seen a wicked, ruthless man flourishing like a well-rooted native tree, (37:35).
yet he passed away and was no more; though I searched, he could not be found. (37:36).
Consider the blameless and observe the upright, for posterity awaits the man of peace. (37:37).
But the transgressors will all be destroyed; the future of the wicked will be cut off. (37:38).
The salvation of the righteous is from the LORD; He is their stronghold in time of trouble. (37:39).
The LORD helps and delivers them; He rescues and saves them from the wicked, because they take refuge in Him. (37:40).
crossRefs: Matthew 5:5: Jesus takes verse 11 into the Beatitudes almost unchanged. Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth.
Proverbs 3:5-6: The instruction of verses 3 through 5 put as a proverb. Trust in the LORD with all your heart, do not lean on your own understanding, and He will make your paths straight.
Isaiah 41:10: The promise standing behind verse 24, that a man may fall and not be overwhelmed, because God says He will uphold him with His righteous right hand.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חָרָה (charah, 'burn'), Greek: παροξύνω, Aramaic: חרי
translationNotes.note: To be inflamed with anger (v. 1).

Psalm 37 runs the Hebrew alphabet across forty verses, a new letter beginning every second verse instead of every verse. That spacing gives each letter a full pair of lines, which is why the psalm reads as a string of self-contained sayings rather than an argument. Psalms 9 and 10, 25, 34, 111, 112, 119 and 145 are the other alphabetic psalms, each spacing the letters differently.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יִירְשׁוּ־אָרֶץ (yireshu-arets)
translationNotes.note: Land in Israel was not real estate to be traded. It was assigned by family and could not be sold in perpetuity; a sale was really a lease that ran out at the Jubilee, when the field returned to the household that held it (Leviticus 25:23-28). That is why Naboth would not sell his vineyard to Ahab at any price (1 Kings 21:3). The refrain running through verses 9, 11, 22, 29 and 34 is about holding your family's ground, and Jesus quotes verse 11 in Matthew 5:5.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חָצִיר (chatsir)
translationNotes.note: Chatsir is the wild grass that sprouts after the first rains, greens the hills for a few weeks, and is burnt brown by early summer. Nobody in Judea had to be told how fast it went. The same image carries Isaiah 40:6-8 and James 1:10-11, and verse 2 pairs it with a garden herb, which lasts no longer.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm contrasts the short-lived success of evildoers with the secure inheritance of the righteous who trust the LORD.
stories.superscription: Of David.

stories.title: 😔 Psalms 38
summaryBullets: O LORD, do not rebuke me in Your anger or discipline me in Your wrath. (38:1).
For Your arrows have pierced me deeply, and Your hand has pressed down on me. (38:2).
There is no soundness in my body because of Your anger; there is no rest in my bones because of my sin. (38:3).
For my iniquities have overwhelmed me; they are a burden too heavy to bear. (38:4).
My wounds are foul and festering because of my sinful folly. (38:5).
I am bent and brought low; all day long I go about mourning. (38:6).
For my loins are full of burning pain, and no soundness remains in my body. (38:7).
I am numb and badly crushed; I groan in anguish of heart. (38:8).
O Lord, my every desire is before You; my groaning is not hidden from You. (38:9).
My heart pounds, my strength fails, and even the light of my eyes has faded. (38:10).
My beloved and friends shun my disease, and my kinsmen stand at a distance. (38:11).
Those who seek my life lay snares; those who wish me harm speak destruction, plotting deceit all day long. (38:12).
But like a deaf man, I do not hear; and like a mute man, I do not open my mouth. (38:13).
I am like a man who cannot hear, whose mouth offers no reply. (38:14).
I wait for You, O LORD; You will answer, O Lord my God. (38:15).
For I said, “Let them not gloat over me — those who taunt me when my foot slips.” (38:16).
For I am ready to fall, and my pain is ever with me. (38:17).
Yes, I confess my iniquity; I am troubled by my sin. (38:18).
Many are my enemies without cause, and many hate me without reason. (38:19).
Those who repay my good with evil attack me for pursuing the good. (38:20).
Do not forsake me, O LORD; be not far from me, O my God. (38:21).
Come quickly to help me, O Lord my Savior. (38:22).
crossRefs: Isaiah 53:4-5: The same vocabulary of wounds and crushing, turned the other way. Here the body suffers for its own sin; there the servant is pierced for transgressions that are not His.
Psalm 32:3-4: The same ordeal from the other end. Bones brittle from groaning, God's hand heavy day and night, and strength drained as in the summer heat.
Job 19:13-19: The desertion of verse 11 taken further. Brothers removed, kinsmen failed, servants who will not answer, and a wife repelled by his breath.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יָדְךָ נִכְבְּדָה (yadkha nikbedah), Greek: βαρεῖα χείρ σου, Aramaic: ידך תקיפא
translationNotes.note: Image of God’s discipline (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לְהַזְכִּיר (lehazkir)
translationNotes.note: The word heads only two psalms, 38 and 70. It is built on the root behind azkarah, the memorial portion of the grain offering: the priest took a handful of the flour and oil with all the frankincense and burned it on the altar while the rest went to the priests (Leviticus 2:2, 9, 16). The heading most likely assigns the psalm to that moment in the service.

translationNotes.term: My kinsmen stand at a distance
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֶגַע (nega)
translationNotes.note: Verse 11 describes a legal condition, not just unpopularity. A man with an infectious skin condition wore torn clothes, left his hair unbound, covered his upper lip, called out 'Unclean!' and lived alone outside the camp until a priest examined him and declared him clean (Leviticus 13:45-46; 14:1-9). Verses 5 and 7 describe the sores; verse 11 describes the quarantine that followed.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מוֹקֵשׁ (moqesh) - פַּח (pach)
translationNotes.note: Two parts of one device. The pach is the trap itself, a spring-loaded net or clapper hidden on the ground; the moqesh is the bait stick that triggers it when the bird touches it. Amos 3:5 puts both in one line and asks whether a trap springs from the ground when nothing has set it off. Verse 12 has men setting the trigger and waiting.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm laments deep physical, social, and spiritual anguish, pleading for God’s presence and help.

headings.text: Do Not Rebuke Me in Your Anger

stories.superscription: A Psalm of David, for remembrance.

stories.title: 🕰️ Psalms 39
summaryBullets: I said, “I will watch my ways so that I will not sin with my tongue; I will guard my mouth with a muzzle as long as the wicked are present.” (39:1).
I was speechless and still; I remained silent, even from speaking good, and my sorrow was stirred. (39:2).
My heart grew hot within me; as I mused, the fire burned. Then I spoke with my tongue: (39:3).
“Show me, O LORD, my end and the measure of my days. Let me know how fleeting my life is. (39:4).
You, indeed, have made my days as handbreadths, and my lifetime as nothing before You. Truly each man at his best exists as but a breath. Selah (39:5).
Surely every man goes about like a phantom; surely he bustles in vain; he heaps up riches not knowing who will haul them away. (39:6).
And now, O Lord, for what do I wait? My hope is in You. (39:7).
Deliver me from all my transgressions; do not make me the reproach of fools. (39:8).
I have become mute; I do not open my mouth because of what You have done. (39:9).
Remove Your scourge from me; I am perishing by the force of Your hand. (39:10).
You discipline and correct a man for his iniquity, consuming like a moth what he holds dear; surely each man is but a vapor. Selah (39:11).
Hear my prayer, O LORD, and give ear to my cry for help; do not be deaf to my weeping. For I am a foreigner dwelling with You, a stranger like all my fathers. (39:12).
Turn Your gaze away from me, that I may again be cheered before I depart and am no more.” (39:13).
crossRefs: Psalm 90:10-12: Moses asks for the same thing David asks for at verse 4, to be taught to number his days, and puts the count at seventy years, or eighty if we are strong.
James 4:14: The same measure applied to men planning a year ahead. Your life is a mist that appears for a little while and vanishes, which is the breath of verses 5 and 11.
Job 14:1-2: Man born of woman is short of days and full of trouble, coming forth like a flower and passing like a fleeting shadow, which is the phantom of verse 6.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֶבֶל (hevel), Greek: ματαιότης, Aramaic: הבל
translationNotes.note: Vanity, vapor, fleeting (v. 5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְדוּתוּן (Yedutun)
translationNotes.note: Jeduthun was one of the three men David put in charge of the music, with Asaph and Heman. They sounded bronze cymbals and trumpets before the ark, and Jeduthun's sons prophesied with the lyre in giving thanks and praise (1 Chronicles 16:41-42; 25:1-6). His name heads Psalms 39, 62 and 77. The heading names a guild and its leader, not the author of the words.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: טֶפַח (tefach)
translationNotes.note: A handbreadth is the width of the four fingers across the palm, about three inches. Six of them make a cubit, which is why it is the smallest ordinary building measure in Scripture: the rim of the table in the tabernacle was a handbreadth wide (Exodus 25:25), and the bronze Sea was a handbreadth thick (1 Kings 7:26). Verse 5 measures a life with the smallest unit on the rule.

translationNotes.term: A foreigner dwelling with You, a stranger
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֵּר (ger) - תּוֹשָׁב (toshav)
translationNotes.note: Two legal statuses. A ger is a resident alien, protected by law but holding no ancestral land; a toshav is a temporary settler with less standing still. Abraham called himself both when he had to buy a burial plot at Hebron (Genesis 23:4). Leviticus 25:23 turns the pair around on Israel itself: the land is God's, and 'you are but foreigners and sojourners with Me,' which is exactly what verse 12 claims.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm reflects on life’s shortness and asks God for mercy before death.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. For Jeduthun. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🎶 Psalms 40
summaryBullets: I waited patiently for the LORD; He inclined to me and heard my cry. (40:1).
He lifted me up from the pit of despair, out of the miry clay; He set my feet upon a rock, and made my footsteps firm. (40:2).
He put a new song in my mouth, a hymn of praise to our God. Many will see and fear and put their trust in the LORD. (40:3).
Blessed is the man who has made the LORD his trust, who has not turned to the proud, nor to those who lapse into falsehood. (40:4).
Many, O LORD my God, are the wonders You have done, and the plans You have for us — none can compare to You — if I proclaim and declare them, they are more than I can count. (40:5).
Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but my ears You have opened. Burnt offerings and sin offerings You did not require. (40:6).
Then I said, “Here I am, I have come — it is written about me in the scroll: (40:7).
I delight to do Your will, O my God; Your law is within my heart.” (40:8).
I proclaim righteousness in the great assembly; behold, I do not seal my lips, as You, O LORD, do know. (40:9).
I have not covered up Your righteousness in my heart; I have declared Your faithfulness and salvation; I have not concealed Your loving devotion and faithfulness from the great assembly. (40:10).
O LORD, do not withhold Your mercy from me; Your loving devotion and faithfulness will always guard me. (40:11).
For evils without number surround me; my sins have overtaken me, so that I cannot see. They are more than the hairs of my head, and my heart has failed within me. (40:12).
Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me; hurry, O LORD, to help me. (40:13).
May those who seek my life be ashamed and confounded; may those who wish me harm be repelled and humiliated. (40:14).
May those who say to me, “Aha, aha!” be appalled at their own shame. (40:15).
May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You; may those who love Your salvation always say, “The LORD be magnified!” (40:16).
But I am poor and needy; may the Lord think of me. You are my helper and deliverer; O my God, do not delay. (40:17).
crossRefs: Hebrews 10:5-7: The writer quotes verses 6 through 8 as the words of Christ entering the world, following the Greek Old Testament, which renders the opened ears of verse 6 as a body You prepared for Me.
Psalm 27:6: The same vow made at the same place. Sacrifices offered at God's tabernacle with shouts of joy, matching the proclamation in the great assembly at verses 9 and 10.
1 Samuel 15:22: Samuel says to Saul's face what verse 6 says here. God does not delight in burnt offerings the way He delights in obedience to His voice.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בּוֹר (bor), Greek: λάκκος, Aramaic: בורא
translationNotes.note: A cistern-like pit, symbol of danger or death (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אָזְנַיִם כָּרִיתָ לִּי (aznayim karita li, 'dug ears for me'), Greek: σῶμα δὲ κατηρτίσω μοι ('a body prepared for me'), Aramaic: אודני פתח לי
translationNotes.note: Metaphor for readiness to obey; textual variation noted (v. 6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: טִיט הַיָּוֵן (tit hayaven)
translationNotes.note: A cistern was cut into rock, plastered, and fed by runoff; when the water was gone, the bottom held a layer of silt that behaved like wet mortar. Jeremiah was let down by ropes into exactly such a cistern in the courtyard of the guard, and the text says there was no water in it, only mud, and he sank into the mud (Jeremiah 38:6). Verse 2 is describing a man standing in that.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְגִלַּת־סֵפֶר (megillat-sefer)
translationNotes.note: A book in this period was a roll of papyrus or prepared skin, written in columns and wound on rods, read by unrolling with one hand and rolling with the other. Jeremiah 36 shows the whole life of one: dictated to Baruch, read aloud in the temple, read again to the king, then cut column by column with a scribe's knife and thrown into the brazier. Verse 7 refers to a written record, not to a book with pages.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm thanks the LORD for rescue, declares obedience better than sacrifice, and prays for further deliverance.

headings.text: I Waited Patiently for the Lord

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🤝 Psalms 41
summaryBullets: Blessed is the one who cares for the poor; the LORD will deliver him in the day of trouble. (41:1).
The LORD will protect and preserve him; He will bless him in the land and refuse to give him over to the will of his foes. (41:2).
The LORD will sustain him on his bed of illness and restore him from his bed of sickness. (41:3).
I said, “O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me, for I have sinned against You.” (41:4).
My enemies say with malice: “When will he die and be forgotten?” (41:5).
My visitor speaks falsehood; he gathers slander in his heart; he goes out and spreads it abroad. (41:6).
All who hate me whisper against me; they imagine the worst for me: (41:7).
“A vile disease has been poured into him; he will never get up from where he lies!” (41:8).
Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me. (41:9).
But You, O LORD, be gracious to me and raise me up, that I may repay them. (41:10).
By this I know that You delight in me, for my enemy does not triumph over me. (41:11).
In my integrity You uphold me and set me in Your presence forever. (41:12).
Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. Amen and Amen. (41:13).
crossRefs: John 13:18: At the last meal Jesus quotes verse 9 across the table, that the one who shares His bread has lifted up his heel against Him, and says He knows whom He has chosen.
Proverbs 19:17: The blessing of verse 1 stated as an accounting. Kindness to the poor is a loan made to the LORD, and He is the one who repays the lender.
Psalm 37:17-24: The same guarantee at length. The LORD upholds the righteous, they are satisfied in days of famine, and though a man falls he is held by the hand.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַשְׂכִּיל אֶל־דַּל (maskil el-dal); Greek (LXX): συνετός ἐστιν ἐπὶ πτωχόν
translationNotes.note: To act wisely toward the weak or poor (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הִגְדִּיל עָקֵב (higdil aqev); Greek: ἐπῆρεν ἐπ᾽ ἐμὲ πτέρναν
translationNotes.note: Idiomatic for hostile betrayal (v. 9).

translationNotes.term: The five books of the Psalms
translationNotes.note: Verse 13 is not part of the psalm's argument; it is a closing doxology that marks the end of a section. The Psalms are arranged in five books, and each of the first four ends with the same kind of formula: Book I at 41:13, Book II at 72:18-19, Book III at 89:52, Book IV at 106:48. Book V ends with the whole of Psalm 150. Every one of them closes with Amen or Hallelujah, and the divisions are printed in Hebrew manuscripts.

translationNotes.term: The one who shared my bread
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אוֹכֵל לַחְמִי (okhel lachmi)
translationNotes.note: Eating at a man's table put you under an obligation to him; that is why sharing bread and then turning on the host was the sharpest treachery the culture could name. Jesus quotes this verse at the last meal before the arrest, dropping the words 'whom I trusted' and applying the rest to the one dipping in the same dish (John 13:18, 26). Verse 9 is the source of that citation.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm blesses care for the poor, laments betrayal by a close friend, and affirms the LORD’s sustaining presence.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 💧 Psalms 42
summaryBullets: As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God. (42:1).
My soul thirsts for God, the living God. When shall I come and appear in God’s presence? (42:2).
My tears have been my food both day and night, while men ask me all day long, “Where is your God?” (42:3).
These things come to mind as I pour out my soul: how I walked with the multitude, leading the festive procession to the house of God with shouts of joy and praise. (42:4).
Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him for the salvation of His presence. (42:5).
O my God, my soul despairs within me. Therefore I remember You from the land of Jordan and the peaks of Hermon — even from Mount Mizar. (42:6).
Deep calls to deep in the roar of Your waterfalls; all Your breakers and waves have rolled over me. (42:7).
The LORD decrees His loving devotion by day, and at night His song is with me as a prayer to the God of my life. (42:8).
I say to God my Rock, “Why have You forgotten me? Why must I walk in sorrow because of the enemy’s oppression?” (42:9).
Like the crushing of my bones, my enemies taunt me, while they say to me all day long, “Where is your God?” (42:10).
Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God. (42:11).
crossRefs: Psalm 63:1: The same thirst in a literal dry place. There David's body yearns for God in a land without water; here the deer pants for streams and the soul longs for the living God.
Jonah 2:3: The identical line prayed from inside the fish, that all God's breakers and waves swept over him, which stands at verse 7 here.
Psalm 43:5: The third run of the refrain that closes verses 5 and 11. The next psalm carries no heading of its own and ends on exactly these words.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תִּשְׁתּוֹחֲחִי (tishetokhachi); Greek: καταπεφρόνηται ἡ ψυχή μου
translationNotes.note: To be bowed down, depressed (vv. 5, 11).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תְּהוֹם אֶל־תְּהוֹם קוֹרֵא (tehom el-tehom qore); Greek: ἄβυσσος ἄβυσσον ἐπικαλεῖται
translationNotes.note: Poetic for surging waters; overwhelming distress (v. 7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּנֵי־קֹרַח (benei-Qorach)
translationNotes.note: Korah led the revolt against Moses and the ground closed over him (Numbers 16:31-33), but Numbers 26:11 records plainly that his line did not die out. His descendants became Levitical gatekeepers and singers: they guarded the thresholds of the sanctuary (1 Chronicles 9:19; 26:1) and stood up to praise at Jehoshaphat's battle (2 Chronicles 20:19). Eleven psalms carry their name: 42, 44 through 49, 84, 85, 87 and 88.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲפִיקֵי מָיִם (aphiqei mayim)
translationNotes.note: An aphiq is a stream channel, and in this country most of them are wadis that run hard for a few days after rain and then hold nothing but stone for the rest of the year. Job 6:15-20 has caravans turning aside to such a channel and finding it empty, and dying of it. The deer in verse 1 is not standing at a pleasant brook; it is at a dry bed in summer.

translationNotes.term: The land of Jordan and the peaks of Hermon
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶרְמוֹן (Chermon) - מִצְעָר (Mitsar)
translationNotes.note: Real ground, roughly a hundred miles north of Jerusalem. Hermon rises to about 9,200 feet and holds snow; its meltwater feeds the springs at Dan and Banias, which are the headwaters of the Jordan and the source of the falling water in verse 7. Mount Mizar is named nowhere else in Scripture and has not been identified. The psalmist is placing himself as far from the sanctuary as the country allows.

stories.keyTakeaway: Separated and taunted, the psalmist thirsts for God and repeatedly urges his soul to hope in Him.

headings.text: BOOK II As the Deer Pants for the Water

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Maskil of the sons of Korah.

stories.title: 🕯️ Psalms 43
summaryBullets: Vindicate me, O God, and plead my case against an ungodly nation; deliver me from deceitful and unjust men. (43:1).
For You are the God of my refuge. Why have You rejected me? Why must I walk in sorrow because of the enemy’s oppression? (43:2).
Send out Your light and Your truth; let them lead me. Let them bring me to Your holy mountain and to the place where You dwell. (43:3).
Then I will go to the altar of God, to God, my greatest joy. I will praise You with the harp, O God, my God. (43:4).
Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God. (43:5).
crossRefs: Psalm 42:5-11: The psalm this one continues. That psalm carries the refrain twice and this one repeats it a third time, and the complaint about walking in sorrow under the enemy's oppression is word for word the same.
Psalm 27:1: The light this psalm asks God to send out at verse 3, named there as a title rather than a request. The LORD is my light and my salvation.
Psalm 2:6: The holy mountain of verse 3 identified. God says He has installed His King on Zion, upon His holy mountain, which is where the light and truth are meant to lead.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁפְטֵנִי (shafteni, ‘judge me’); Greek: κρῖνόν με
translationNotes.note: Forensic plea for favorable judgment (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אוֹרְךָ וַאֲמִתֶּךָ (orkha va’amittekha); Greek: τὸ φῶς σου καὶ ἡ ἀλήθειά σου
translationNotes.note: Personified guides to God’s dwelling (v. 3).

Psalm 43 has no heading of its own, which is rare in Book II, and it closes with the refrain of Psalm 42 repeated word for word, the same lines that stand at 42:5 and 42:11. A number of Hebrew manuscripts write the two as one psalm. Read together they run three stanzas, each ending in that refrain.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִזְבֵּחַ (mizbeach)
translationNotes.note: The word comes from zavach, to slaughter, so the name of the object says what happened on it. The altar of burnt offering stood outside in the courtyard where anyone bringing an animal could reach it, in front of the sanctuary building. Verse 4 makes reaching that altar the goal of the journey the psalm is asking for, because that is the point past which a layman could not go.

stories.keyTakeaway: Seeking justice and guidance, the psalmist asks for God’s light and truth to bring him to worship.

stories.title: 🛡️ Psalms 44
summaryBullets: We have heard with our ears, O God; our fathers have told us the work You did in their days, in the days of old. (44:1).
With Your hand You drove out the nations and planted our fathers there; You crushed the peoples and cast them out. (44:2).
For it was not by their sword that they took the land; their arm did not bring them victory. It was by Your right hand, Your arm, and the light of Your face, because You favored them. (44:3).
You are my King, O God, who ordains victories for Jacob. (44:4).
Through You we repel our foes; through Your name we trample our enemies. (44:5).
For I do not trust in my bow, nor does my sword save me. (44:6).
For You save us from our enemies; You put those who hate us to shame. (44:7).
In God we have boasted all day long, and Your name we will praise forever. Selah (44:8).
But You have rejected and humbled us; You no longer go forth with our armies. (44:9).
You have made us retreat from the foe, and those who hate us have plundered us. (44:10).
You have given us up as sheep to be devoured; You have scattered us among the nations. (44:11).
You sell Your people for nothing; no profit do You gain from their sale. (44:12).
You have made us a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those around us. (44:13).
You have made us a byword among the nations, a laughingstock among the peoples. (44:14).
All day long my disgrace is before me, and shame has covered my face, (44:15).
at the voice of the scorner and reviler, because of the enemy, bent on revenge. (44:16).
All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten You or betrayed Your covenant. (44:17).
Our hearts have not turned back; our steps have not strayed from Your path. (44:18).
But You have crushed us in the lair of jackals; You have covered us with deepest darkness. (44:19).
If we had forgotten the name of our God or spread out our hands to a foreign god, (44:20).
would not God have discovered, since He knows the secrets of the heart? (44:21).
Yet for Your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered. (44:22).
Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping? Arise! Do not reject us forever. (44:23).
Why do You hide Your face and forget our affliction and oppression? (44:24).
For our soul has sunk to the dust; our bodies cling to the earth. (44:25).
Rise up; be our help! Redeem us on account of Your loving devotion. (44:26).
crossRefs: Romans 8:36: Paul quotes verse 22 while asking what can separate believers from the love of Christ, and answers that in all these things we are more than conquerors.
Joshua 24:12: The claim of verse 3 made by God Himself at Shechem. He drove out the two Amorite kings with the hornet, not by Israel's own sword or bow.

Psalm 60:9-12: The same complaint in nearly the same words, that God has rejected His people and no longer marches out with their armies, except that psalm ends by asking for aid rather than an explanation.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צֹאן טִבְחָה (tson tivchah); Greek: πρόβατα σφαγῆς
translationNotes.note: Image of defenseless victims (v. 22).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פָּדָה (padah), Greek: λύτρωσαι, Aramaic: פרק
translationNotes.note: To buy back/deliver (v. 26).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קוּמָה (qumah) - עוּרָה (urah)
translationNotes.note: These are the words of the ark. Numbers 10:35-36 records the formula Moses spoke every time the ark set out, 'Rise up, O LORD, and may Your enemies be scattered,' and the answering line when it came to rest. Psalm 68 opens with the same sentence. Verses 23 and 26 are calling for the ark to move again, which is a demand that the army take the field with God in front of it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְקוֹם תַּנִּים (meqom tannim)
translationNotes.note: Jackals move into ruins after the people are gone, and Scripture uses them as the standard marker of a site that has been destroyed and left: Jerusalem a haunt of jackals (Jeremiah 9:11), Hazor the same (Jeremiah 49:33), the towers of a fallen city given over to them (Isaiah 34:13). Verse 19 says the nation has been crushed down into that kind of place.
