stories.keyTakeaway: The community laments defeat despite professed loyalty and pleads for God to rise and redeem.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Maskil of the sons of Korah.

stories.title: 💍 Psalms 45
summaryBullets: My heart is stirred by a noble theme as I recite my verses to the king; my tongue is the pen of a skillful writer. (45:1).
You are the most handsome of men; grace has anointed your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever. (45:2).
Strap your sword at your side, O mighty warrior; appear in your majesty and splendor. (45:3).
In your splendor ride forth in victory on behalf of truth and humility and justice; may your right hand show your awesome deeds. (45:4).
Your arrows pierce the hearts of the king’s foes; the nations fall beneath your feet. (45:5).
Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever, and justice is the scepter of Your kingdom. (45:6).
You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you above your companions with the oil of joy. (45:7).
All your garments are fragrant with myrrh and aloes and cassia; from palaces of ivory the harps make you glad. (45:8).
The daughters of kings are among your honored women; the queen stands at your right hand, adorned with the gold of Ophir. (45:9).
Listen, O daughter! Consider and incline your ear: Forget your people and your father’s house, (45:10).
and the king will desire your beauty; bow to him, for he is your lord. (45:11).
The Daughter of Tyre will come with a gift; men of wealth will seek your favor. (45:12).
All glorious is the princess in her chamber; her gown is embroidered with gold. (45:13).
In colorful garments she is led to the king; her virgin companions are brought before you. (45:14).
They are led in with joy and gladness; they enter the palace of the king. (45:15).
Your sons will succeed your fathers; you will make them princes throughout the land. (45:16).
I will commemorate your name through all generations; therefore the nations will praise you forever and ever. (45:17).
crossRefs: Hebrews 1:8-9: The writer quotes verses 6 and 7 and says God speaks them about the Son, so the throne addressed as God endures forever and the anointing above companions belongs to Him.

Song of Songs 3:6-11: The other royal wedding in Scripture. Solomon's carriage comes up from the wilderness escorted by sixty armed men, and he wears the crown his mother set on him on his wedding day.
1 Kings 1:39: What the anointing of verse 7 looked like in practice. Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tabernacle, anointed Solomon, and the ram's horn was blown.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֵׁבֶט מִישׁוֹר (shevet mishor); Greek: ῥάβδος εὐθύτητος
translationNotes.note: Scepter of uprightness (v. 6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְשַׁחֲךָ אֱלֹהִים שֶׁמֶן שָׂשׂוֹן (meshachakha… shemen sason); Greek: ἔχρισέν σε… ἔλαιον ἀγαλλιάσεως
translationNotes.note: Ceremonial consecration with joyful oil (v. 7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֹר (mor); Greek: σμύρνα (smurna)
translationNotes.note: A fragrant gum resin from the Commiphora tree of Arabia and East Africa. Used as a holy anointing-oil ingredient (Exodus 30:23), as perfume, as an embalming spice (John 19:39), and, mixed with wine, as a pain-dulling drink (Mark 15:23). One of the magi's gifts.

translationNotes.term: To the tune of The Lilies
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַל־שֹׁשַׁנִּים (al-shoshannim)
translationNotes.note: A melody title, used again over Psalm 69 and, in a longer form meaning 'the lily of the testimony,' over Psalms 60 and 80. The lily or lotus was a standard decorative motif in Solomon's temple: the capitals on the two bronze pillars were worked in lilies, and the rim of the bronze Sea was shaped like a lily blossom (1 Kings 7:19, 22, 26). The tune itself is lost.

translationNotes.term: The gold of Ophir and palaces of ivory
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אוֹפִיר (Ofir) - שֵׁן (shen)
translationNotes.note: Ophir was the source of the finest gold; Solomon's fleet sailed from Ezion-geber and brought back 420 talents of it (1 Kings 9:26-28), and a Hebrew potsherd dug up at Tell Qasile near the coast records a shipment of 'gold of Ophir' by weight. Ivory was not a building material but an inlay, cut into panels and furniture; Ahab's ivory house drew comment (1 Kings 22:39) and Amos names ivory beds as the mark of the very rich (Amos 3:15; 6:4).

stories.keyTakeaway: A wedding ode praises the king’s beauty, rule, and anointing, and describes the bride’s entrance and future offspring.

headings.text: My Heart Is Stirred by a Noble Theme

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. To the tune of “The Lilies.” A Maskil of the sons of Korah. A love song.

stories.title: 🏔️ Psalms 46
summaryBullets: God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble. (46:1).
Therefore we will not fear, though the earth is transformed and the mountains are toppled into the depths of the seas, (46:2).
though their waters roar and foam and the mountains quake in the surge. Selah (46:3).
There is a river whose streams delight the city of God, the holy place where the Most High dwells. (46:4).
God is within her; she will not be moved. God will help her when morning dawns. (46:5).
Nations rage, kingdoms crumble; the earth melts when He lifts His voice. (46:6).
The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. Selah (46:7).
Come, see the works of the LORD, who brings devastation upon the earth. (46:8).
He makes wars to cease throughout the earth; He breaks the bow and shatters the spear; He burns the shields in the fire. (46:9).
“Be still and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted over the earth.” (46:10).
The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. Selah (46:11).
crossRefs: Psalm 48:1-8: The companion piece about the same city. There the kings assemble, look at Zion, and flee in terror, which is what nations raging and kingdoms crumbling means at verse 6.
Isaiah 2:4: The disarming of verse 9 pictured as reforging rather than burning. Swords become plowshares, spears become pruning hooks, and the nations stop training for war.
Habakkuk 2:20: The same order to fall silent before God, given there to the whole earth after the prophet's complaint and here to the raging nations at verse 10.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַחֲסֶה (machaseh), Greek: καταφυγή, Aramaic: מחסיא
translationNotes.note: Shelter/place of protection (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַרְפּוּ (harpu); Greek: σχολάσατε
translationNotes.note: Cease/let go; stop striving (v. 10).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַל־עֲלָמוֹת (al-alamot)
translationNotes.note: Alamot is the plural of almah, a young woman. The direction appears here and once in the record of the ark's procession, where the harps are set 'according to Alamoth' while the lyres take Sheminith, 'the eighth' (1 Chronicles 15:20-21). The pairing of the two terms points to registers, high against low. Whether the high register means women's voices, boys' voices, or an instrument tuned up is not stated.

translationNotes.term: There is a river whose streams delight the city of God
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נָהָר פְּלָגָיו (nahar pelagav)
translationNotes.note: Jerusalem has no river. Its water came from the Gihon spring in the Kidron valley outside the wall, which is why a siege was survivable only if the supply could be brought inside. Hezekiah cut a tunnel about 1,750 feet through solid rock to carry the Gihon into the city ahead of Sennacherib's attack (2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:30), and an inscription found inside that tunnel in 1880 describes the two digging crews meeting in the middle.

stories.keyTakeaway: Amid upheaval and war, the psalm declares God present as refuge, commanding stillness and announcing His exaltation.

headings.text: God Is Our Refuge and Strength

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. Of the sons of Korah. According to Alamoth. A song.

stories.title: 👏 Psalms 47
summaryBullets: Clap your hands, all you peoples; shout unto God with a voice of triumph. (47:1).
How awesome is the LORD Most High, the great King over all the earth! (47:2).
He subdues nations beneath us, and peoples under our feet. (47:3).
He chooses our inheritance for us, the pride of Jacob, whom He loves. Selah (47:4).
God has ascended amid shouts of joy, the LORD with the sound of the horn. (47:5).
Sing praises to God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises! (47:6).
For God is King of all the earth; sing to Him a psalm of praise. (47:7).
God reigns over the nations; God is seated on His holy throne. (47:8).
The nobles of the nations have assembled as the people of the God of Abraham; for the shields of the earth belong to God; He is highly exalted. (47:9).
crossRefs: Psalm 93:1: The same acclamation with the same consequence. The LORD reigns and is robed in majesty, so the world is firmly established and cannot be moved.
Psalm 2:8: The inheritance of verse 4 handed over to the King. Ask Me, and I will make the nations Your inheritance and the ends of the earth Your possession.
1 Chronicles 16:31: The line sung when the ark was brought into Jerusalem, telling the nations that the LORD reigns, which is the shout this psalm calls for at verses 1 and 2.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֶלְיוֹן (ʿElyon), Greek: ὕψιστος, Aramaic: עילאה
translationNotes.note: Title emphasizing supreme sovereignty (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שׁוֹפָר (shofar) - חֲצֹצְרָה (chatsotserah)
translationNotes.note: Two instruments the English word 'trumpet' covers over. The shofar is a ram's horn, unpitched and loud, used for signals, alarms, and the great assemblies; anyone could sound one. The chatsotserah is a straight trumpet of hammered silver, and there were exactly two of them, made on God's instruction and blown only by the priests to summon the assembly and to sound over the offerings (Numbers 10:1-10). Verse 5 names the ram's horn.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָלָה (alah)
translationNotes.note: The verb is the ordinary one for going up, and the scene it fits is the ark going up to Zion: David and all Israel brought it up 'with shouting and with the sound of the shofar' (2 Samuel 6:15). Verse 5 names those same two things in the same order. Everything approaching Jerusalem is described as going up, because the city sits on the ridge at about 2,500 feet.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָגִנֵּי־אֶרֶץ (maginnei-erets)
translationNotes.note: The shields are men. Rulers are called the shield of their people because defending them was the job, and Psalm 89:18 uses the word the same way of the king. Verse 9 has the nobles of the nations assembling with the people of the God of Abraham, so the line is saying the protectors of the nations belong to God, not that weapons do.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm summons global praise because the LORD reigns as King over all nations.

headings.text: Clap Your Hands, All You Peoples

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of the sons of Korah.

stories.title: 🏙️ Psalms 48
summaryBullets: Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised in the city of our God, His holy mountain. (48:1).
Beautiful in loftiness, the joy of all the earth, like the peaks of Zaphon is Mount Zion, the city of the great King. (48:2).
God is in her citadels; He has shown Himself to be a fortress. (48:3).
For behold, the kings assembled; they all advanced together. (48:4).
They saw and were astounded; they fled in terror. (48:5).
Trembling seized them there, anguish like a woman in labor. (48:6).
With a wind from the east You wrecked the ships of Tarshish. (48:7).
As we have heard, so we have seen in the city of the LORD of Hosts, in the city of our God: God will establish her forever. Selah (48:8).
Within Your temple, O God, we contemplate Your loving devotion. (48:9).
Your name, O God, like Your praise, reaches to the ends of the earth; Your right hand is full of righteousness. (48:10).
Mount Zion is glad, the daughters of Judah rejoice, on account of Your judgments. (48:11).
March around Zion, encircle her, count her towers, (48:12).
consider her ramparts, tour her citadels, that you may tell the next generation. (48:13).
For this God is our God forever and ever; He will be our guide even till death. (48:14).
crossRefs: Psalm 46:4-7: The same city with the same guarantee. God is within her so she will not be moved, and the LORD of Hosts is her fortress.
Isaiah 33:20-22: Zion described as a tent whose pegs are never pulled up and whose cords never break, with the LORD as Judge and lawgiver and King, which is the permanence claimed at verse 8.
Psalm 122:3-5: What the pilgrim of verses 12 and 13 actually walked into. A city built up and united, the tribes going up to it, and the thrones of judgment of the house of David standing there.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֵיל / אַרְמְנוֹת (cheil / armonot); Greek: τεῖχος / παλάτια
translationNotes.note: Defensive wallworks and strong buildings (v. 13).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צָפוֹן (tsafon)
translationNotes.note: The word is the ordinary Hebrew for north, and it is also the name of a specific mountain on the Syrian coast north of Ugarit. English versions divide: some print 'the heights of the north,' others keep the name Zaphon. Either way the line is a comparison of height and grandeur, and it is pointed, because Zion is not a tall mountain. It stands about 2,500 feet up, lower than the ridge east of it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֳנִיּוֹת תַּרְשִׁישׁ (oniyyot Tarshish)
translationNotes.note: The phrase names a class of vessel, the largest deep-water merchant ship of the age, rather than ships from one port. Solomon's fleet of them returned once every three years carrying gold, silver, ivory, apes and peacocks (1 Kings 10:22), and Jonah boarded one at Joppa bound for Tarshish (Jonah 1:3). Verse 7 has the east wind destroying the biggest thing that floated.

translationNotes.term: Count her towers, consider her ramparts
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִגְדָּל (migdal) - חֵיל (chel) - אַרְמוֹן (armon)
translationNotes.note: Three parts of a fortified city named in order. Towers stood at intervals along the wall so defenders could shoot along its face; the chel is the outer rampart or the sloped bank at the wall's foot that kept siege engines off it; the armon is the fortified great house inside. Verses 12 and 13 are a walking inspection of real defences. A stretch of Jerusalem's wall about twenty-three feet thick, built in Hezekiah's time, was uncovered in the Jewish Quarter by Nahman Avigad in 1970.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm celebrates Zion’s security under the LORD and calls eyewitness remembrance for future generations.
stories.superscription: A song. A Psalm of the sons of Korah.

stories.title: 💬 Psalms 49
summaryBullets: Hear this, all you peoples; listen, all inhabitants of the world, (49:1).
both low and high, rich and poor alike. (49:2).
My mouth will impart wisdom, and the meditation of my heart will bring understanding. (49:3).
I will incline my ear to a proverb; I will express my riddle with the harp: (49:4).
Why should I fear in times of trouble, when wicked usurpers surround me? (49:5).
They trust in their wealth and boast in their great riches. (49:6).
No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God. (49:7).
For the redemption of his soul is costly, and never can payment suffice, (49:8).
that he should live on forever and not see decay. (49:9).
For it is clear that wise men die, and the foolish and the senseless both perish and leave their wealth to others. (49:10).
Their graves are their eternal homes — their dwellings for endless generations — even though their lands were their namesakes. (49:11).
But a man, despite his wealth, cannot endure; he is like the beasts that perish. (49:12).
This is the fate of the foolish and their followers who endorse their sayings. Selah (49:13).
Like sheep they are destined for Sheol. Death will be their shepherd. The upright will rule them in the morning, and their form will decay in Sheol, far from their lofty abode. (49:14).
But God will redeem my life from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself. Selah (49:15).
Do not be afraid when a man grows rich, when the splendor of his house increases. (49:16).
For when he dies, he will carry nothing away; his abundance will not follow him down. (49:17).
Though in his lifetime he blesses his soul — and men praise you when you prosper — (49:18).
he will join the generation of his fathers, who will never see the light of day. (49:19).
A man who has riches without understanding is like the beasts that perish. (49:20).
crossRefs: Luke 12:15-21: Jesus tells the parable this psalm argues for. A rich man tears down his barns to build bigger ones, God calls him a fool that night, and the question left over is who will own what he piled up.
Ecclesiastes 5:13-15: The same observation from the other wisdom book. A man comes from his mother's womb naked and departs the same way, taking nothing from his labor in his hands.
Matthew 16:26: The question of verses 7 and 8 put by Jesus. What can a man give in exchange for his soul, when gaining the whole world does not cover the price.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פָּדָה (padah) / כֹּפֶר (kofer, ransom price); Greek: λυτρόομαι / λύτρον
translationNotes.note: Deliverance by payment/substitution (vv. 7-8, 15).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
translationNotes.note: The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָשָׁל (mashal) - חִידָה (chidah)
translationNotes.note: A mashal is a comparison, a saying that sets one thing against another; a chidah is a puzzle put deliberately, meant to be worked out. Samson posed a chidah at his wedding feast and staked thirty garments on it (Judges 14:12-14), and the queen of Sheba came to test Solomon with them (1 Kings 10:1). Verse 4 announces the psalm as that kind of set problem, and it is sung to the lyre.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קָרְאוּ בִשְׁמוֹתָם (qare'u vishmotam)
translationNotes.note: Putting your own name on land was how a man made himself permanent. Absalom, having no son to keep his name alive, set up a pillar for himself in the King's Valley and named it after himself (2 Samuel 18:18), and Nobah renamed a captured town after himself in Numbers 32:42. Verse 11 sets that practice against the one piece of ground the rich man actually keeps, which is his grave.

stories.keyTakeaway: Wealth cannot redeem from death; the psalm warns against trusting riches and states God ransoms from Sheol.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of the sons of Korah.

stories.title: 🔥 Psalms 50
summaryBullets: The Mighty One, God the LORD, speaks and summons the earth from where the sun rises to where it sets. (50:1).
From Zion, perfect in beauty, God shines forth. (50:2).
Our God approaches and will not be silent! Consuming fire precedes Him, and a tempest rages around Him. (50:3).
He summons the heavens above, and the earth, that He may judge His people: (50:4).
“Gather to Me My saints, who made a covenant with Me by sacrifice.” (50:5).
And the heavens proclaim His righteousness, for God Himself is Judge. Selah (50:6).
“Hear, O My people, and I will speak, O Israel, and I will testify against you: I am God, your God. (50:7).
I do not rebuke you for your sacrifices, and your burnt offerings are ever before Me. (50:8).
I have no need for a bull from your stall or goats from your pens, (50:9).
for every beast of the forest is Mine — the cattle on a thousand hills. (50:10).
I know every bird in the mountains, and the creatures of the field are Mine. (50:11).
If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is Mine, and the fullness thereof. (50:12).
Do I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? (50:13).
Sacrifice a thank offering to God, and fulfill your vows to the Most High. (50:14).
Call upon Me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you will honor Me.” (50:15).
To the wicked, however, God says, “What right have you to recite My statutes and to bear My covenant on your lips? (50:16).
For you hate My instruction and cast My words behind you. (50:17).
When you see a thief, you befriend him, and throw in your lot with adulterers. (50:18).
You unleash your mouth for evil and harness your tongue to deceit. (50:19).
You sit and malign your brother; you slander your own mother’s son. (50:20).
You have done these things, and I kept silent; you thought I was just like you. But now I rebuke you and accuse you to your face. (50:21).
Now consider this, you who forget God, lest I tear you to pieces, with no one to rescue you: (50:22).
He who sacrifices a thank offering honors Me, and to him who rightly orders his way, I will show the salvation of God.” (50:23).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 15:22: Samuel says to Saul what God says here at verses 8 through 13. Obedience counts for more than burnt offerings and attentiveness for more than the fat of rams.

Isaiah 1:11-17: The same charge pressed harder. God says He is full of burnt offerings and cannot endure iniquity in a solemn assembly, and He tells the worshippers to wash, seek justice, and plead the widow's case.
Hebrews 13:15: The thank offering of verses 14 and 23 carried forward. A sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name, offered continually through Jesus.

translationNotes.term: The Mighty One, God the LORD
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵל אֱלֹהִים יְהוָה (El Elohim YHWH); Greek: ὁ Θεὸς θεῶν κύριος
translationNotes.note: Stacked divine titles emphasizing authority (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זֶבַח תּוֹדָה (zevach todah); Greek: θυσία αἰνέσεως
translationNotes.note: Praise/thank-offering as the fitting response (vv. 14, 23).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אָסָף (Asaf)
translationNotes.note: Asaph was a Levite of the line of Gershon whom David appointed to lead the music before the ark, where he sounded the bronze cymbals (1 Chronicles 6:39; 15:16-19; 16:4-7). Twelve psalms carry his name: 50 and 73 through 83. His descendants kept the office for centuries; the sons of Asaph are counted among the returning exiles at 128 men (Ezra 2:41).

translationNotes.term: Who made a covenant with Me by sacrifice
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֹּרְתֵי בְרִיתִי עֲלֵי־זָבַח (koretei veriti alei-zavach)
translationNotes.note: Hebrew does not make a covenant, it cuts one, and the phrase is literal. Animals were cut in half and the parties passed between the pieces, as Abram saw done in Genesis 15:9-18 and as Jeremiah 34:18-19 describes with a calf. At Sinai Moses threw half the blood on the altar and half on the people (Exodus 24:5-8). Verse 5 identifies the assembled as the people bound by that procedure.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Mighty One shines from Zion, summoning heaven and earth as He judges His people: He needs no bulls, for every beast of the forest is His, and He asks for thank offerings, fulfilled vows, and calling on Him in the day of trouble. He then rebukes the wicked who recite His statutes while befriending thieves and slandering their own kin, warning those who forget God and promising His salvation to the one who orders his way rightly.
stories.superscription: A Psalm of Asaph.

stories.title: 🫧 Psalms 51
summaryBullets: Have mercy on me, O God, according to Your loving devotion; according to Your great compassion, blot out my transgressions. (51:1).
Wash me clean of my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin. (51:2).
For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me. (51:3).
Against You, You only, have I sinned and done what is evil in Your sight, so that You may be proved right when You speak and blameless when You judge. (51:4).
Surely I was brought forth in iniquity; I was sinful when my mother conceived me. (51:5).
Surely You desire truth in the inmost being; You teach me wisdom in the inmost place. (51:6).
Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean; wash me, and I will be whiter than snow. (51:7).
Let me hear joy and gladness; let the bones You have crushed rejoice. (51:8).
Hide Your face from my sins and blot out all my iniquities. (51:9).
Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. (51:10).
Cast me not away from Your presence; take not Your Holy Spirit from me. (51:11).
Restore to me the joy of Your salvation, and sustain me with a willing spirit. (51:12).
Then I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners will return to You. (51:13).
Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, the God of my salvation, and my tongue will sing of Your righteousness. (51:14).
O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare Your praise. (51:15).
For You do not delight in sacrifice, or I would bring it; You take no pleasure in burnt offerings. (51:16).
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise. (51:17).
In Your good pleasure, cause Zion to prosper; build up the walls of Jerusalem. (51:18).
Then You will delight in righteous sacrifices, in whole burnt offerings; then bulls will be offered on Your altar. (51:19).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 12:13: The moment the heading names. Nathan has just said, You are that man, David answers that he has sinned against the LORD, and Nathan tells him the LORD has taken his sin away.
Exodus 12:22: The hyssop of verse 7 in its original use. A cluster of it was dipped in the blood of the Passover lamb and brushed on the doorframe so the destroyer would pass over that house.
Psalm 32:1-5: The other side of this prayer. Blessed is the man whose sin is covered, and David tells there what keeping silent cost him before he finally confessed.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּרָא (bara), Greek (LXX): κτίζω (ktizō), Aramaic: ברא (bara)
translationNotes.note: Bring into being; request for a clean heart (v. 10).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵזוֹב (ezov); Greek: ὕσσωπος (hussopos)
translationNotes.note: A small, fragrant herb (Origanum syriacum / Syrian oregano), growing in rocky soil. Bunches of hyssop were used to apply Passover blood to the doorposts (Exodus 12:22), in leper-cleansing rituals (Leviticus 14:6), and held up to Jesus on the cross with a wine-soaked sponge (John 19:29).

translationNotes.term: When Nathan the prophet came to him
translationNotes.note: The account is 2 Samuel 11-12. Nathan brought the charge as a legal case about a rich man who took a poor man's one ewe lamb, and David passed sentence on himself, ruling fourfold restitution under Exodus 22:1 before Nathan told him he was the man (2 Samuel 12:1-7). Verse 14 asks for deliverance from bloodguilt, which points at Uriah the Hittite, killed by David's written order (2 Samuel 11:14-17).

In the Hebrew Bible a superscription is counted as part of the psalm, so this heading takes up verses 1 and 2 and every following verse number runs two higher than in English: the famous 'Create in me a clean heart' stands at verse 10 in English and verse 12 in Hebrew. Wherever a psalm has a one-line heading the offset is one. This is why a Hebrew text and an English one can cite the same words with different numbers.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm is a confession asking for cleansing, a new heart, and restored joy, ending with sacrifices offered after contrition.

headings.text: Create in Me a Clean Heart, O God

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. When Nathan the prophet came to him after his adultery with Bathsheba.

stories.title: 🌿 Psalms 52
summaryBullets: Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? The loving devotion of God endures all day long. (52:1).
Your tongue devises destruction like a sharpened razor, O worker of deceit. (52:2).
You love evil more than good, falsehood more than speaking truth. Selah (52:3).
You love every word that devours, O deceitful tongue. (52:4).
Surely God will bring you down to everlasting ruin; He will snatch you up and tear you away from your tent; He will uproot you from the land of the living. Selah (52:5).
The righteous will see and fear; they will mock the evildoer, saying, (52:6).
“Look at the man who did not make God his refuge, but trusted in the abundance of his wealth and strengthened himself by destruction.” (52:7).
But I am like an olive tree flourishing in the house of God; I trust in the loving devotion of God forever and ever. (52:8).
I will praise You forever, because You have done it. I will wait on Your name — for it is good — in the presence of Your saints. (52:9).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 22:9-19: What the heading is pointing at. Doeg reports David's visit to Ahimelech, and when Saul's own guards refuse the order, Doeg kills eighty-five priests himself and puts the town of Nob to the sword.
James 3:5-8: The tongue of verses 2 through 4 measured. A small part of the body that sets a whole forest ablaze, restless and full of deadly poison, and no man can tame it.
Jeremiah 11:16: The olive tree of verse 8 turned against Israel. The LORD once called her a flourishing olive tree, then with a mighty roar set it on fire and consumed its branches.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גִּבּוֹר (gibbor), Greek (LXX): δυνατός, Aramaic: גבורא
translationNotes.note: Strongman title used ironically (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תַּעַר מֻלָּט (taʿar mullat); Greek: ξυρὸν ἀκονητόν
translationNotes.note: Image for injurious speech (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דֹּאֵג (Do'eg)
translationNotes.note: Doeg was Saul's chief herdsman, and he was at the sanctuary at Nob, detained before the LORD, on the day the priest Ahimelech gave David bread and Goliath's sword (1 Samuel 21:7). He reported it, and when Saul's own guards refused the order, Doeg killed eighty-five priests who wore the linen ephod and then put the whole town of Nob to the sword (1 Samuel 22:9-19).

translationNotes.term: An olive tree flourishing in the house of God
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זַיִת רַעֲנָן (zayit ra'anan)
translationNotes.note: The olive is the longest-lived tree in the country. It takes years to bear, then bears for centuries, and it will send up new shoots from the stump after the trunk is cut. Its oil lit the sanctuary lamps, and the law required pure oil from beaten olives for that purpose (Exodus 27:20). Verse 8 sets that against a man torn up by the roots in verse 5.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm denounces a destructive tongue and contrasts it with trust like a green olive tree in God’s house.

headings.text: Why Do You Boast of Evil?

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Maskil of David. After Doeg the Edomite went to Saul and told him, “David has gone to the house of Ahimelech.”

stories.title: 🚫 Psalms 53
summaryBullets: The fool says in his heart, “There is no God.” They are corrupt; their ways are vile. There is no one who does good. (53:1).
God looks down from heaven upon the sons of men to see if any understand, if any seek God. (53:2).
All have turned away, they have together become corrupt; there is no one who does good, not even one. (53:3).
Will the workers of iniquity never learn? They devour my people like bread; they refuse to call upon God. (53:4).
There they are, overwhelmed with dread, where there was nothing to fear. For God has scattered the bones of those who besieged you. You put them to shame, for God has despised them. (53:5).
Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion! When God restores His captive people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad! (53:6).
crossRefs: Romans 3:10-12: Paul quotes verses 1 through 3 to open his case that no one is righteous, no one understands, and no one seeks God, not even one.
Psalm 14:1-3: The same psalm in a nearly identical form. That one says the LORD looks down from heaven where this one says God, and the divine name is changed the same way throughout.
Isaiah 59:7-8: The same picture in full. Feet swift to shed innocent blood, ruin and destruction in their wake, and the way of peace never known.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נָבָל (naval), Greek (LXX): ἄφρων, Aramaic: נבל
translationNotes.note: Moral-spiritual insensibility (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שׁוּב שְׁבוּת (shuv shevut); Greek: ἐπιστρέψει αἰχμαλωσίαν
translationNotes.note: Idiom for reversing captivity/circumstances (v. 6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַל־מָחֲלַת (al-machalat)
translationNotes.note: The term heads this psalm and, in a longer form, Psalm 88. It has been connected to chalah, to be sick, to machol, a dance, and to chalil, a pipe, and none of those can be established from the text. It is a musical direction of some kind whose meaning did not survive. Saying more than that would be guesswork.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פָּחֲדוּ פָחַד (pachadu phachad)
translationNotes.note: Verse 5 reads, word for word, 'there they dreaded a dread where there was no dread.' Hebrew intensifies a verb by putting its own noun beside it, and no English version can repeat the word three times and still read as English. The line describes panic with nothing in front of it, which is what the rest of the verse then explains.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm states universal corruption and ends with a call for salvation from Zion.

headings.text: The Fool Says There Is No God

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. According to Mahalath. A Maskil of David.

stories.title: 🛡️ Psalms 54
summaryBullets: Save me, O God, by Your name, and vindicate me by Your might! (54:1).
Hear my prayer, O God; listen to the words of my mouth. (54:2).
For strangers rise up against me, and ruthless men seek my life — men with no regard for God. Selah (54:3).
Surely God is my helper; the Lord is the sustainer of my soul. (54:4).
He will reward my enemies with evil. In Your faithfulness, destroy them. (54:5).
Freely I will sacrifice to You; I will praise Your name, O LORD, for it is good. (54:6).
For He has delivered me from every trouble, and my eyes have looked in triumph on my foes. (54:7).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 23:19; 26:1: The occasion the heading names, and the Ziphites did it twice. Both times they went up to Saul at Gibeah to report that David was hiding on the hill of Hachilah.
Proverbs 18:10: What verse 1 is reaching for when it asks to be saved by God's name. The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous run into it and are safe.
Psalm 116:17: The freewill offering promised at verse 6 described elsewhere. A sacrifice of thanksgiving offered while calling on the name of the LORD.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֵׁם (shem), Greek: ὄνομα, Aramaic: שׁום
translationNotes.note: Invoked as authority/aid (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְדָבָה (nedavah), Greek: προαίρεσις (sense), Aramaic: נדבתא
translationNotes.note: Voluntary sacrifice (v. 6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זִיפִים (Zifim)
translationNotes.note: Ziph sat in the Judean hill country a few miles southeast of Hebron, which made its people David's own tribesmen. They went up to Saul at Gibeah and offered to hand David over, then did it again on a second occasion (1 Samuel 23:19-24; 26:1). Verse 3 calls them strangers, and the point of the word is that they were not.

Thirteen psalms carry a heading tying them to a specific episode in David's life: 3, 7, 18, 34, 51, 52, 54, 56, 57, 59, 60, 63 and 142. Seven of those cluster here in Psalms 51 through 63, and most of them point back to the years he spent running from Saul in 1 Samuel 19 through 27. The headings are part of the received Hebrew text, not editorial additions in the English.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm petitions for rescue by God’s name, affirms God as helper, and vows freewill sacrifice and thanks.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Maskil of David. When the Ziphites went to Saul and said, “Is David not hiding among us?”

stories.title: 🕊️ Psalms 55
summaryBullets: Listen to my prayer, O God, and do not ignore my plea. (55:1).
Attend to me and answer me. I am restless in my complaint, and distraught (55:2).
at the voice of the enemy, at the pressure of the wicked. For they bring down disaster upon me and resent me in their anger. (55:3).
My heart pounds within me, and the terrors of death assail me. (55:4).
Fear and trembling grip me, and horror has overwhelmed me. (55:5).
I said, “Oh, that I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and find rest. (55:6).
How far away I would flee! In the wilderness I would remain. Selah (55:7).
I would hurry to my shelter, far from this raging tempest.” (55:8).
O Lord, confuse and confound their speech, for I see violence and strife in the city. (55:9).
Day and night they encircle the walls, while malice and trouble lie within. (55:10).
Destruction is within; oppression and deceit never leave the streets. (55:11).
For it is not an enemy who insults me; that I could endure. It is not a foe who rises against me; from him I could hide. (55:12).
But it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend. (55:13).
We shared sweet fellowship together; we walked with the crowd into the house of God. (55:14).
Let death seize them by surprise; let them go down to Sheol alive, for evil is with them in their homes. (55:15).
But I call to God, and the LORD saves me. (55:16).
Morning, noon, and night, I cry out in distress, and He hears my voice. (55:17).
He redeems my soul in peace from the battle waged against me, even though many oppose me. (55:18).
God will hear and humiliate them — the One enthroned for the ages — Selah because they do not change and they have no fear of God. (55:19).
My companion attacks his friends; he violates his covenant. (55:20).
His speech is smooth as butter, but war is in his heart. His words are softer than oil, yet they are swords unsheathed. (55:21).
Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you; He will never let the righteous be shaken. (55:22).
But You, O God, will bring them down to the Pit of destruction; men of bloodshed and deceit will not live out half their days. But I will trust in You. (55:23).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 15:12: The kind of betrayal verses 12 through 14 describe. Absalom sends for Ahithophel, David's own counselor, and the conspiracy gains strength from the moment he joins it.
John 13:18: Jesus names the same wound at the last meal, saying Scripture must be fulfilled about the one who shared His bread lifting up his heel against Him.
1 Peter 5:7: The command at verse 22 restated for the church. Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְהָבְךָ (yehavkha), Greek (LXX): μέριμνά σου, Aramaic: יהבך
translationNotes.note: Load/what is given; cast upon the LORD (v. 22).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אִישׁ שְׁלוֹמִי / אַלּוּף (ish shelomi / alluf); Greek: ὁ ἑταῖρός μου
translationNotes.note: Trusted associate turned betrayer (vv. 13-14).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
translationNotes.note: The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֶלָה (selah) - Greek (LXX): διάψαλμα (diapsalma)
translationNotes.note: The word occurs seventy-one times in the Psalms, spread across thirty-nine of them, and three more times in Habakkuk 3, which is itself a psalm with musical directions. It always stands at a break in the sense, never inside a clause. The root probably means to lift up, whether voices or instruments, and the Greek translators rendered it with a word for an instrumental interlude. This psalm carries it at verses 7 and 19.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm laments treachery by a companion, describes city violence, and urges casting one’s burden on the LORD.

headings.text: Cast Your Burden upon the Lord

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Maskil of David.

stories.title: 🧪 Psalms 56
summaryBullets: Be merciful to me, O God, for men are hounding me; all day they press their attack. (56:1).
My enemies pursue me all day long, for many proudly assail me. (56:2).
When I am afraid, I put my trust in You. (56:3).
In God, whose word I praise — in God I trust. I will not be afraid. What can man do to me? (56:4).
All day long they twist my words; all their thoughts are on my demise. (56:5).
They conspire, they lurk, they watch my steps while they wait to take my life. (56:6).
In spite of such sin, will they escape? In Your anger, O God, cast down the nations. (56:7).
You have taken account of my wanderings. Put my tears in Your bottle — are they not in Your book? (56:8).
Then my enemies will retreat on the day I cry for help. By this I will know that God is on my side. (56:9).
In God, whose word I praise, in the LORD, whose word I praise, (56:10).
in God I trust; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me? (56:11).
Your vows are upon me, O God; I will render thank offerings to You. (56:12).
For You have delivered my soul from death, and my feet from stumbling, that I may walk before God in the light of life. (56:13).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 21:10-15: The occasion the heading names. David fled to Achish king of Gath, heard the servants there quoting the song about his ten thousands, then feigned madness at the gate until Achish drove him out.
Psalm 118:6: The same sentence this psalm says twice, at verses 4 and 11. The LORD is on my side, so what can man do to me.
Revelation 5:8: What becomes of the tears and prayers of verse 8. Golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints, held before the Lamb by the elders.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּשָׂר (basar), Greek: σάρξ, Aramaic: בשרא
translationNotes.note: Human mortality/weakness (v. 4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֹאד (noʾd), Greek: ἀσκός, Aramaic: נאדא
translationNotes.note: Skin bottle for liquids; image for preserving tears (v. 8).

translationNotes.term: To the tune of A Dove on Distant Oaks
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יוֹנַת אֵלֶם רְחֹקִים (yonat elem rechoqim)
translationNotes.note: A melody title. The middle word can be read as 'silence' or as 'terebinths,' which is why English versions give either 'a silent dove far away' or 'a dove on distant oaks.' The tune is lost and the title cannot be resolved from the words alone. What the heading does establish is that the psalm was sung to something the first singers already knew.

translationNotes.term: When the Philistines seized him in Gath
translationNotes.note: The episode is 1 Samuel 21:10-15. David, running from Saul, went to Achish king of Gath, was recognised by the king's men as the man the songs credited with ten thousands, and got out by feigning madness, scratching at the doors of the gate and letting saliva run into his beard. Psalm 34 carries a heading pointing to the same event, so two psalms in the book attach to one bad week.

stories.keyTakeaway: Amid constant attack, the psalmist declares trust in God, mentions tears kept in a bottle, and vows thanks after deliverance.

headings.text: Be Merciful to Me, O God

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. To the tune of “A Dove on Distant Oaks.” A Miktam of David, when the Philistines seized him in Gath.

stories.title: 🪽 Psalms 57
summaryBullets: Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy, for in You my soul takes refuge. In the shadow of Your wings I will take shelter until the danger has passed. (57:1).
I cry out to God Most High, to God who fulfills His purpose for me. (57:2).
He reaches down from heaven and saves me; He rebukes those who trample me. Selah God sends forth His loving devotion and His truth. (57:3).
My soul is among the lions; I lie down with ravenous beasts— with men whose teeth are spears and arrows, whose tongues are sharp swords. (57:4).
Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your glory cover all the earth. (57:5).
They spread a net for my feet; my soul was despondent. They dug a pit before me, but they themselves have fallen into it! Selah (57:6).
My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast. I will sing and make music. (57:7).
Awake, my glory! Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awaken the dawn. (57:8).
I will praise You, O Lord, among the nations; I will sing Your praises among the peoples. (57:9).
For Your loving devotion reaches to the heavens, and Your faithfulness to the clouds. (57:10).
Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your glory cover all the earth. (57:11).
crossRefs: Psalm 17:8: The same shelter asked for in the same words, hidden in the shadow of God's wings, which is how this psalm opens at verse 1.
Psalm 108:1-5: Verses 7 through 11 here turn up there almost unchanged, joined to the second half of a different psalm to make a new one.
Ruth 2:12: Boaz blesses a Moabite widow for taking refuge under the LORD's wings, the same image used of a foreigner who came to Israel for shelter.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּצֵל כְּנָפֶיךָ (betzel kenafekha), Greek: ἐν σκέπῃ τῶν πτερύγων σου, Aramaic: בְּטִל צִפְּרַפָּךְ
translationNotes.note: Image of protective cover (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נָכוֹן (nakhon), Greek: ἑτοίμη, Aramaic: מתקן
translationNotes.note: Fixed/firm disposition for praise (v. 7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַל־תַּשְׁחֵת (al-tashcheth)
translationNotes.note: This tune title heads four psalms: 57, 58, 59 and 75. The same two words are Moses' plea at Horeb, 'do not destroy Your people' (Deuteronomy 9:26), and they turn up in Isaiah 65:8 as a line sung over a cluster of grapes with juice still in it, 'do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it.' A vintage song by that name would explain how the phrase became a melody everyone could be pointed to.

translationNotes.term: When he fled from Saul into the cave
translationNotes.note: The record gives two caves and the heading does not say which. David hid in the cave of Adullam in the Judean foothills, where four hundred men in trouble gathered to him (1 Samuel 22:1-2), and later in a cave among the crags at En-gedi above the Dead Sea, where he cut the corner off Saul's robe instead of killing him (1 Samuel 24:1-7). Psalm 142 carries the same heading.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm seeks refuge under God’s wings, describes traps set by men, and calls for God’s exaltation and worldwide praise.

headings.text: In You My Soul Takes Refuge

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. To the tune of “Do Not Destroy.” A Miktam of David, when he fled from Saul into the cave.

stories.title: 🦷 Psalms 58
summaryBullets: Do you indeed speak justly, O rulers? Do you judge uprightly, O sons of men? (58:1).
No, in your hearts you devise injustice; with your hands you mete out violence on the earth. (58:2).
The wicked are estranged from the womb; the liars go astray from birth. (58:3).
Their venom is like the venom of a snake, like a cobra that shuts its ears, (58:4).
refusing to hear the tune of the charmer who skillfully weaves his spell. (58:5).
O God, shatter their teeth in their mouths; O LORD, tear out the fangs of the lions. (58:6).
May they vanish like water that runs off; when they draw the bow, may their arrows be blunted. (58:7).
Like a slug that dissolves in its slime, like a woman’s stillborn child, may they never see the sun. (58:8).
Before your pots can feel the burning thorns— whether green or dry— He will sweep them away. (58:9).
The righteous will rejoice when they see they are avenged; they will wash their feet in the blood of the wicked. (58:10).
Then men will say, “There is surely a reward for the righteous! There is surely a God who judges the earth!” (58:11).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 16:18-20: The standard the rulers of verses 1 and 2 are being measured against. Judges appointed in every town, no partiality, no bribes, and justice pursued for its own sake.
Isaiah 59:14-15: The same collapse reported by a prophet. Justice turned away, truth stumbling in the public square, and whoever turns from evil becoming prey.
Psalm 68:23: The same battlefield picture as verse 10, a foot dipped in the blood of enemies, which is what an army walked through after a rout.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵלֶם/אֵלִם (ʾelem/ʾelim; textual issue), Greek (LXX): συνεκροτήσατε ἀληθῆ, Aramaic: דיינין
translationNotes.note: Uncertain reading; likely addresses human judges (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פֶּתֶן (pethen), Greek: ἀσπίς, Aramaic: פתנא
translationNotes.note: Venomous snake used as metaphor (v. 4).

translationNotes.term: A cobra that shuts its ears
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פֶּתֶן חֵרֵשׁ (pethen cheresh)
translationNotes.note: Snake handling was a working trade in Egypt and the Near East, and Scripture treats it as ordinary: Jeremiah 8:17 threatens vipers that cannot be charmed, and Ecclesiastes 10:11 notes that a snake which bites before it is charmed leaves the charmer nothing. Verses 4 and 5 describe a snake that has stopped its own ears against the man whose whole skill depends on being heard.

translationNotes.term: Before your pots can feel the burning thorns
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אָטָד (atad)
translationNotes.note: Thorn brush was the cheap fuel of a poor kitchen. It catches at once, roars, and is gone before the pot above it warms through. Ecclesiastes 7:6 uses the same picture for the laughter of a fool, 'like the crackling of thorns under the pot.' Verse 9 says the wicked will be gone faster than a fire of brushwood can cook a meal.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm charges rulers with injustice and petitions graphic judgment, concluding that God judges on earth.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. To the tune of “Do Not Destroy.” A Miktam of David.

stories.title: 🐕 Psalms 59
summaryBullets: Deliver me from my enemies, O my God; protect me from those who rise against me. (59:1).
Deliver me from workers of iniquity, and save me from men of bloodshed. (59:2).
See how they lie in wait for me. Fierce men conspire against me for no transgression or sin of my own, O LORD. (59:3).
For no fault of my own, they move swiftly to attack me. Arise to help me, and take notice. (59:4).
O LORD God of Hosts, the God of Israel, rouse Yourself to punish all the nations; show no mercy to the wicked traitors. Selah (59:5).
They return in the evening, snarling like dogs and prowling around the city. (59:6).
See what they spew from their mouths— sharp words from their lips: “For who can hear us?” (59:7).
But You, O LORD, laugh at them; You scoff at all the nations. (59:8).
I will keep watch for You, O my strength, because You, O God, are my fortress. (59:9).
My God of loving devotion will come to meet me; God will let me stare down my foes. (59:10).
Do not kill them, or my people will forget. Scatter them by Your power, and bring them down, O Lord, our shield. (59:11).
By the sins of their mouths and the words of their lips, let them be trapped in their pride, in the curses and lies they utter. (59:12).
Consume them in wrath; consume them till they are no more, so it may be known to the ends of the earth that God rules over Jacob. Selah (59:13).
They return in the evening, snarling like dogs and prowling around the city. (59:14).
They scavenge for food, and growl if they are not satisfied. (59:15).
But I will sing of Your strength and proclaim Your loving devotion in the morning. For You are my fortress, my refuge in times of trouble. (59:16).
To You, O my strength, I sing praises, for You, O God, are my fortress, my God of loving devotion. (59:17).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 19:11: The night the heading names. Saul sends messengers to watch David's house and kill him in the morning, and Michal warns him to run for his life that night.
Psalm 2:4: The laughter of verse 8, where the LORD scoffs at the nations, first heard as the One enthroned in heaven laughing at kings plotting against His Anointed.
Psalm 18:2: The fortress David calls God four times in this psalm, spelled out there at length as rock and fortress and deliverer and shield and stronghold.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַנְשֵׁי דָמִים (anshei damim), Greek: ἄνδρες αἱμάτων, Aramaic: גברי דמיא
translationNotes.note: Bloodguilty men (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִשְׂגָּב (misgav), Greek: καταφυγή/ὑπερασπιστής, Aramaic: משגבָא
translationNotes.note: High, secure place of defense (vv. 9, 16, 17).

translationNotes.term: When Saul sent men to watch David's house
translationNotes.note: The account is 1 Samuel 19:11-17. Saul posted men around the house overnight with orders to kill David in the morning. Michal, Saul's daughter and David's wife, let him down through a window, then laid the household idol in the bed with goat hair at its head and told the messengers he was ill. Verses 6 and 14 describe the watchers circling the town at nightfall.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֶּלֶב (kelev)
translationNotes.note: Dogs in Israel were not household animals. They ran half-wild in packs on the edges of towns, living on refuse and on the dead, which is why the worst threat that could be made against a body was that dogs would eat it: Jeroboam's house (1 Kings 14:11), Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel (1 Kings 21:23), Ahab's blood licked up at the pool of Samaria (1 Kings 22:38). Verses 6, 14 and 15 use them as scavengers working the streets at night.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm pleads for rescue from murderous watchers and contrasts their nightly prowling with morning praise for God the fortress.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. To the tune of “Do Not Destroy.” A Miktam of David, when Saul sent men to watch David’s house in order to kill him.

stories.title: 🏴 Psalms 60
summaryBullets: You have rejected us, O God; You have broken us; You have been angry; restore us! (60:1).
You have shaken the land and torn it open. Heal its fractures, for it is quaking. (60:2).
You have shown Your people hardship; we are staggered from the wine You made us drink. (60:3).
You have raised a banner for those who fear You, that they may flee the bow. Selah (60:4).
Respond and save us with Your right hand, that Your beloved may be delivered. (60:5).
God has spoken from His sanctuary: “I will triumph! I will parcel out Shechem and apportion the Valley of Succoth. (60:6).
Gilead is Mine, and Manasseh is Mine; Ephraim is My helmet, Judah is My scepter. (60:7).
Moab is My washbasin; upon Edom I toss My sandal; over Philistia I shout in triumph.” (60:8).
Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom? (60:9).
Have You not rejected us, O God? Will You no longer march out, O God, with our armies? (60:10).
Give us aid against the enemy, for the help of man is worthless. (60:11).
With God we will perform with valor, and He will trample our enemies. (60:12).
crossRefs: Psalm 108:6-13: Verses 5 through 12 here turn up there word for word behind a different opening, so the same oracle about Shechem and Moab and Edom is sung twice in the book.

2 Samuel 8:1-14: The campaigns the heading is tied to, in the order the history gives them. David beats Hadadezer king of Zobah and the Arameans of Damascus, then strikes down Edomites in the Valley of Salt and garrisons Edom.
Numbers 34:1-12: The boundaries God set for the land, which is the map the oracle at verses 6 through 8 is claiming back piece by piece.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַל־אֱדוֹם אַשְׁלִיךְ נַעֲלִי (ʿal Edom ashlich naʿali); Greek: ἐπ᾽ Ἰδουμαίαν βαλῶ τὸ ὑπόδημά μου
translationNotes.note: Idiomatic sign of dominion/subjection (v. 8).

translationNotes.term: Vain is the salvation of man
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁוְא תְּשׁוּעַת אָדָם (shav teshuaʿat adam); Greek: μάταιος ἡ σωτηρία ἀνθρώπου
translationNotes.note: Human deliverance is futile without God (v. 11).

translationNotes.term: Aram-naharaim, Aram-zobah, and the Valley of Salt
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲרַם נַהֲרַיִם (Aram Naharayim) - אֲרַם צוֹבָה (Aram Tsovah)
translationNotes.note: Three places on two fronts. Aram-naharaim means 'Aram of the two rivers,' the country of upper Mesopotamia; Aram-zobah was the Aramean kingdom north of Damascus whose king Hadadezer David fought (2 Samuel 8:3). The Valley of Salt lies at the other end of the map, south of the Dead Sea toward Edom. The campaign is recorded in 2 Samuel 8:3-14 and 1 Chronicles 18:3-13.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סִיר רַחְצִי (sir rachtsi)
translationNotes.note: The basin is the one kept by the door for washing the dust off a traveller's feet, and handling it was the lowest work in a household; Abigail offered to do it for David's servants (1 Samuel 25:41), and Jesus took the job at the last meal (John 13:5). Verse 8 puts Moab in the role of the basin and Edom in the role of the spot where the master drops his sandal. It is a picture of a man coming home, not of a battle.

stories.keyTakeaway: After describing national rejection and shaking, the psalm records God’s territorial claims and asks for help, declaring human deliverance vain and victory with God.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. To the tune of “The Lily of the Covenant.” A Miktam of David for instruction. When he fought Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah, and Joab returned and struck down 12,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt.

stories.title: 🪨 Psalms 61
summaryBullets: Hear my cry, O God; attend to my prayer. (61:1).
From the ends of the earth I call out to You whenever my heart is faint. Lead me to the rock that is higher than I. (61:2).
For You have been my refuge, a tower of strength against the enemy. (61:3).
Let me dwell in Your tent forever and take refuge in the shelter of Your wings. Selah (61:4).
For You have heard my vows, O God; You have given me the inheritance reserved for those who fear Your name. (61:5).
Increase the days of the king’s life; may his years span many generations. (61:6).
May he sit enthroned in God’s presence forever; appoint Your loving devotion and Your faithfulness to guard him. (61:7).
Then I will ever sing praise to Your name and fulfill my vows day by day. (61:8).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 7:13-16: The promise behind the request at verses 6 and 7 that the king sit enthroned forever. God told David his house and his kingdom would be established forever before Him.
Proverbs 18:10: The tower of verse 3 named outright. The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous run into it and are safe.
Psalm 91:4: The shelter verse 4 asks to live under, pictured in close-up as feathers spread over a man, with God's faithfulness as his shield and rampart.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צוּר (tsur) / מִגְדַּל־עֹז (migdal-ʿoz), Greek: πέτρα / πύργος ἰσχυρός, Aramaic: טוּר / מגדלא דּעוּז
translationNotes.note: Images of security and protection (vv. 2-3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כָּנָף (kanaf), Greek: πτέρυγες, Aramaic: כנפין
translationNotes.note: Sheltering cover (v. 4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זֶרֶת (zeret)
translationNotes.note: The distance between thumb-tip and little-finger-tip with the fingers spread; half a cubit, about 9 inches (23 cm). The breastpiece of the high priest was a span square (Exodus 28:16).

translationNotes.term: From the ends of the earth
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִקְצֵה הָאָרֶץ (miqtseh ha'arets)
translationNotes.note: Erets means land as often as it means earth, so the phrase can mean the far edge of the country rather than the far side of the world. Read that way the line places the speaker at the border, at the maximum distance from the sanctuary he is asking to be brought back to in verse 4. Psalm 42:6 does the same thing by naming Hermon and the Jordan headwaters.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm petitions God for refuge and for long life for the king, with vows of continual praise.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. Of David.

stories.title: 🕊️ Psalms 62
summaryBullets: In God alone my soul finds rest; my salvation comes from Him. (62:1).
He alone is my rock and my salvation. He is my fortress; I will never be shaken. (62:2).
How long will you threaten a man? Will all of you throw him down like a leaning wall or a tottering fence? (62:3).
They fully intend to cast him down from his lofty perch; they delight in lies; with their mouths they bless, but inwardly they curse. Selah (62:4).
Rest in God alone, O my soul, for my hope comes from Him. (62:5).
He alone is my rock and my salvation; He is my fortress; I will not be shaken. (62:6).
My salvation and my honor rest on God, my strong rock; my refuge is in God. (62:7).
Trust in Him at all times, O people; pour out your hearts before Him. God is our refuge. Selah (62:8).
Lowborn men are but a vapor; the exalted are but a lie. Weighed on the scale, they go up; together they are but a vapor. (62:9).
Place no trust in extortion or false hope in stolen goods. If your riches increase, do not set your heart upon them. (62:10).
God has spoken once; I have heard this twice: that power belongs to God, (62:11).
and loving devotion to You, O Lord. For You will repay each man according to his deeds. (62:12).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 9:23-24: The same securities stripped away that verses 9 and 10 weigh and find empty. Let no man boast in wisdom or strength or riches, but only in knowing the LORD.
Proverbs 11:28: The warning of verse 10 in proverb form. He who trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will thrive like foliage.
Romans 2:6: Paul quotes the closing line of this psalm, that God will repay each one according to his deeds, as the standard He judges Jew and Greek by alike.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַךְ (ʾakh), Greek (LXX): πλὴν / μόνον, Aramaic: בַּר מִן
translationNotes.note: Refrain particle emphasizing exclusivity (vv. 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דּוּמִיָּה (dumiyyah), Greek: σιγή, Aramaic: שתוקא
translationNotes.note: Stillness/quiet trust (v. 1).

translationNotes.term: A leaning wall or a tottering fence
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גָּדֵר (gader)
translationNotes.note: Field walls were built of stones stacked dry, without mortar, cleared off the ground they enclosed. They bulge, then they go over, and a vineyard wall left unrepaired was the standard picture of a holding gone to ruin (Isaiah 5:5; Proverbs 24:30-31). Numbers 22:24 has Balaam's donkey pinned in a lane between two of them. Verse 3 describes a man about to be pushed over like one.

translationNotes.term: Weighed on the scale, they go up
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֹאזְנַיִם (mozenayim)
translationNotes.note: The balance was two pans on a beam, with cut stone weights kept in a pouch, and honest ones were a matter of law: correct scales and correct stones, no second set in the bag (Leviticus 19:35-36; Deuteronomy 25:13-15). A pan that rises is the empty one. Verse 9 puts high and low men together in that pan and has it float, which is the same verdict written on the wall for Belshazzar (Daniel 5:27).

stories.keyTakeaway: Exclusive trust is placed in God rather than in people, force, or wealth; God repays each according to his work.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. According to Jeduthun. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🌵 Psalms 63
summaryBullets: O God, You are my God. Earnestly I seek You; my soul thirsts for You. My body yearns for You in a dry and weary land without water. (63:1).
So I have seen You in the sanctuary and beheld Your power and glory. (63:2).
Because Your loving devotion is better than life, my lips will glorify You. (63:3).
So I will bless You as long as I live; in Your name I will lift my hands. (63:4).
My soul is satisfied as with the richest of foods; with joyful lips my mouth will praise You. (63:5).
When I remember You on my bed, I think of You through the watches of the night. (63:6).
For You are my help; I will sing for joy in the shadow of Your wings. (63:7).
My soul clings to You; Your right hand upholds me. (63:8).
But those who seek my life to destroy it will go into the depths of the earth. (63:9).
They will fall to the power of the sword; they will become a portion for foxes. (63:10).
But the king will rejoice in God; all who swear by Him will exult, for the mouths of liars will be shut. (63:11).
crossRefs: Psalm 42:1-2: The same thirst from a different singer. A deer panting for streams of water and a soul thirsting for the living God, which here is a body yearning in a land with no water in it.
Deuteronomy 10:20: The clinging of verse 8 given as a command. Fear the LORD your God, serve Him, hold fast to Him, and take your oaths in His name.
Psalm 36:8: The satisfaction of verse 5 described from the other side. They feast on the abundance of God's house and He gives them drink from His river of delights.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דָּבַק (davaq), Greek: κολλάομαι, Aramaic: דבק
translationNotes.note: Adhere/hold fast (v. 8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (ḥesed), Greek: ἔλεος, Aramaic: חסדא
translationNotes.note: Covenant loyalty (v. 3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִדְבַּר יְהוּדָה (midbar Yehudah)
translationNotes.note: The strip of country east of the Jerusalem ridge, falling about 3,900 feet in some fifteen miles to the Dead Sea. It lies in the rain shadow, so it is bare chalk and limestone with no permanent water off the few springs. David crossed it twice, running from Saul toward En-gedi (1 Samuel 23:14; 24:1) and again from Absalom (2 Samuel 15:23, 28; 16:14). Verse 1 says 'a dry and weary land without water' as a plain description.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַשְׁמֻרוֹת (ashmurot)
translationNotes.note: The night was divided into shifts for the men standing guard. The Old Testament reckons three: Exodus 14:24 names the morning watch, Judges 7:19 has Gideon attack at the start of the middle watch, and Lamentations 2:19 speaks of the beginning of the watches. By the New Testament the Roman count of four is in use, which Mark 13:35 lists as evening, midnight, cockcrow and dawn. Verse 6 means the sleepless stretches of a marked-out night.

stories.keyTakeaway: In wilderness longing, the psalmist declares God’s love better than life, clings to God, and states the downfall of those seeking his life.
stories.superscription: A Psalm of David, when he was in the Wilderness of Judah.

stories.title: 🏹 Psalms 64
summaryBullets: Hear, O God, my voice of complaint; preserve my life from dread of the enemy. (64:1).
Hide me from the scheming of the wicked, from the mob of workers of iniquity, (64:2).
who sharpen their tongues like swords and aim their bitter words like arrows, (64:3).
ambushing the innocent in seclusion, shooting suddenly, without fear. (64:4).
They hold fast to their evil purpose; they speak of hiding their snares. “Who will see them?” they say. (64:5).
They devise injustice and say, “We have perfected a secret plan.” For the inner man and the heart are mysterious. (64:6).
But God will shoot them with arrows; suddenly they will be wounded. (64:7).
They will be made to stumble, their own tongues turned against them. All who see will shake their heads. (64:8).
Then all mankind will fear and proclaim the work of God; so they will ponder what He has done. (64:9).
Let the righteous rejoice in the LORD and take refuge in Him; let all the upright in heart exult. (64:10).
crossRefs: Psalm 7:15-16: The same reversal as verses 7 and 8. The man digs a hole, falls into the pit he hollowed out himself, and his violence lands back on his own head.
James 3:5-8: The tongue treated as the weapon verses 3 and 4 make it. A small part of the body that sets a forest ablaze, restless and full of deadly poison, and no man can tame it.
Proverbs 26:27: The proverb behind verse 8, where the schemers are tripped by their own tongues. He who digs a pit falls into it, and he who rolls a stone has it roll back on him.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לָשׁוֹן (lashon) / חִצִּים (ḥitsim), Greek: γλῶσσα / ἄρθρα/βελεμνά, Aramaic: לישן / חיצין
translationNotes.note: Speech as weapon imagery (vv. 3-4).

translationNotes.term: Aim their bitter words like arrows
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דָּרַךְ קֶשֶׁת (darakh qeshet)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew verb is 'to tread.' A war bow was too stiff to bend by hand, so an archer braced it against his foot to string it and to draw it, and Hebrew says a man treads his bow rather than bends it (also Psalms 7:12; 11:2; 37:14). Verse 3 has them treading a bitter word onto the string, which is a slower and more deliberate act than the English 'aim' suggests.

translationNotes.term: The mob of workers of iniquity
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סוֹד (sod)
translationNotes.note: Sod is a closed circle of people and the confidential business they conduct; the one word covers both the council and its secret. Jacob refuses to enter Simeon and Levi's sod (Genesis 49:6), Jeremiah asks who has stood in the sod of the LORD (Jeremiah 23:18), and Psalm 55:14 uses it of close friendship. Verse 2 is not a crowd; it is a small group meeting in private.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נוּד (nud)
translationNotes.note: Wagging the head was a public jeer, done so the target could see it. Passers-by do it at ruined Jerusalem (Lamentations 2:15), mockers do it at the sufferer of Psalm 22:7, and the crowd at the cross does it in Matthew 27:39. In verse 8 the gesture switches sides and lands on the men who had been making it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Secret slander and ambush are reversed when God strikes and makes the wicked fall by their own words.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🌾 Psalms 65
summaryBullets: Praise awaits You, O God, in Zion; to You our vows will be fulfilled. (65:1).
O You who listen to prayer, all people will come to You. (65:2).
When iniquities prevail against me, You atone for our transgressions. (65:3).
Blessed is the one You choose and bring near to dwell in Your courts! We are filled with the goodness of Your house, the holiness of Your temple. (65:4).
With awesome deeds of righteousness You answer us, O God of our salvation, the hope of all the ends of the earth and of the farthest seas. (65:5).
You formed the mountains by Your power, having girded Yourself with might. (65:6).
You stilled the roaring of the seas, the pounding of their waves, and the tumult of the nations. (65:7).
Those who live far away fear Your wonders; You make the dawn and sunset shout for joy. (65:8).
You attend to the earth and water it; with abundance You enrich it. The streams of God are full of water, for You prepare our grain by providing for the earth. (65:9).
You soak its furrows and level its ridges; You soften it with showers and bless its growth. (65:10).
You crown the year with Your bounty, and Your paths overflow with plenty. (65:11).
The pastures of the wilderness overflow; the hills are robed with joy. (65:12).
The pastures are clothed with flocks, and the valleys are decked with grain. They shout in triumph; indeed, they sing. (65:13).
crossRefs: Leviticus 16:30: The atonement of verse 3 fixed to a day on the calendar. On that day atonement is made for the people so they are clean from all their sins before the LORD.
Psalm 104:13-15: The same rainfall traced all the way to the table. God waters the mountains, brings food out of the earth, and gives wine and oil and bread to men.
Isaiah 55:10-12: Rain and snow that never return without watering the earth, followed by hills bursting into song, which is the shouting harvest at verses 12 and 13 here.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּפֶּר (kipper), Greek (LXX): ἐξιλάσκομαι, Aramaic: כפר
translationNotes.note: Make propitiation/cover sin (v. 3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תַּעְטְרֶנָּה (taʿtrennah), Greek: ἐστεφάνωσας, Aramaic: כללת שתא
translationNotes.note: Figurative for loading the year with goodness (v. 11).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לְךָ דֻמִיָּה תְהִלָּה (lekha dumiyyah tehillah)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew reads 'to You silence is praise.' Dumiyyah is the same word for stillness used at Psalm 62:1. English versions cannot keep the paradox and so print 'praise awaits You,' 'praise is due,' or 'praise is silent before You,' each of which is a decision about how the two nouns relate. The original simply sets silence and praise side by side.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יוֹרֶה (yoreh) - מַלְקוֹשׁ (malqosh)
translationNotes.note: Two rains decide the harvest in this country and Hebrew names them separately. The yoreh, the early rain, comes in October and November and softens ground baked hard through the dry season so it can be plowed and sown. The malqosh, the latter rain, falls in March and April and fills out the grain before it is cut. Deuteronomy 11:14 promises both by name, and verses 9 through 13 describe the year that follows when they come.

stories.keyTakeaway: God is praised as the atoning hearer of prayer, ruler of creation, and provider of an abundant harvest.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. A song.

stories.title: 📣 Psalms 66
summaryBullets: Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth! (66:1).
Sing the glory of His name; make His praise glorious. (66:2).
Say to God, “How awesome are Your deeds! So great is Your power that Your enemies cower before You. (66:3).
All the earth bows down to You; they sing praise to You; they sing praise to Your name.” Selah (66:4).
Come and see the works of God; how awesome are His deeds toward mankind. (66:5).
He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the waters on foot; there we rejoiced in Him. (66:6).
He rules forever by His power; His eyes watch the nations. Do not let the rebellious exalt themselves. Selah (66:7).
Bless our God, O peoples; let the sound of His praise be heard. (66:8).
He preserves our lives and keeps our feet from slipping. (66:9).
For You , O God, have tested us; You have refined us like silver. (66:10).
You led us into the net; You laid burdens on our backs. (66:11).
You let men ride over our heads; we went through fire and water, but You brought us into abundance. (66:12).
I will enter Your house with burnt offerings; I will fulfill my vows to You — (66:13).
the vows that my lips promised and my mouth spoke in my distress. (66:14).
I will offer You fatlings as burnt offerings, with the fragrant smoke of rams; I will offer bulls and goats. Selah (66:15).
Come and listen, all you who fear God, and I will declare what He has done for me. (66:16).
I cried out to Him with my mouth and praised Him with my tongue. (66:17).
If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened. (66:18).
But God has surely heard; He has attended to the sound of my prayer. (66:19).
Blessed be God, who has not rejected my prayer or withheld from me His loving devotion! (66:20).
crossRefs: Exodus 14:21-22: The crossing verse 6 is remembering. A strong east wind drove the sea back all night and Israel walked through on dry ground with walls of water to the right and left.

Joshua 3:14-17: The second crossing on dry ground. The Jordan was in flood, the water backed up as far as the city of Adam, and the priests carrying the ark stood in the riverbed until the nation was over.
Malachi 3:3: The refining of verse 10 at work. God sits as a refiner and purifier of silver over the sons of Levi until they present offerings in righteousness.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צָרַף (tsaraf), Greek: δοκιμάζω/χωνεύω, Aramaic: צרף
translationNotes.note: Smelting image for testing (v. 10).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רְוָיָה (revayah), Greek: πλησμονή, Aramaic: רוויה
translationNotes.note: Overflowing place (v. 12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֶדֶר (neder)
translationNotes.note: A vow was a promise to give God something specific if He acted, and once spoken it was enforceable. Deuteronomy 23:21-23 forbids delaying payment and points out that staying silent would have cost nothing, and Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 says the same. The offering itself was a peace offering, eaten by the worshipper and his household at the sanctuary and finished within two days (Leviticus 7:16). Verses 13 to 15 describe a man arriving to settle the account.

translationNotes.term: He turned the sea into dry land
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יָם (yam) - נָהָר (nahar)
translationNotes.note: Verse 6 names two crossings in one line, sea and river. The sea is the Red Sea, where the east wind drove the water back overnight and Israel went across on dry ground (Exodus 14:21-22). The river is the Jordan at flood stage, which stopped and stood in a heap while the nation passed over opposite Jericho (Joshua 3:14-17). The generation that saw the second was not the one that saw the first.

stories.keyTakeaway: All peoples are called to see God’s deeds, as the psalm recounts deliverance through testing and affirms answered prayer.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A song. A Psalm.

stories.title: 🌍 Psalms 67
summaryBullets: May God be gracious to us and bless us, and cause His face to shine upon us, Selah (67:1).
that Your ways may be known on earth, Your salvation among all nations. (67:2).
Let the peoples praise You, O God; let all the peoples praise You. (67:3).
Let the nations be glad and sing for joy, for You judge the peoples justly and lead the nations of the earth. Selah (67:4).
Let the peoples praise You, O God; let all the peoples praise You. (67:5).
The earth has yielded its harvest; God, our God, blesses us. (67:6).
God blesses us, that all the ends of the earth shall fear Him. (67:7).
crossRefs: Numbers 6:24-26: The blessing verse 1 is quoting almost word for word. May the LORD bless you and keep you and cause His face to shine upon you, spoken over Israel by Aaron.
Genesis 12:3: The reason the blessing runs outward at verse 2. God told Abram that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him.
Revelation 7:9-10: The scene verses 3 and 5 are calling for. A multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, crying salvation to God and to the Lamb.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יָאֵר פָּנָיו (yaʾer panav), Greek: φωτίσαι τὸ πρόσωπον, Aramaic: נהיר אפוהי
translationNotes.note: Favor expressed as radiant face (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֵישָׁרִים (meysharim), Greek: εὐθύτης, Aramaic: מישרין
translationNotes.note: Upright justice (v. 4).

translationNotes.term: May God be gracious to us and bless us
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְבָרֶכְךָ יְהוָה וְיִשְׁמְרֶךָ (yevarekhekha YHWH veyishmerekha)
translationNotes.note: Verse 1 is the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 turned from 'you' into 'us' so a congregation can say it back. Aaron and his sons pronounced it over Israel, and the wording of the second line, that the LORD make His face shine on you and be gracious to you, is what the psalm opens with. Two small silver scrolls found in a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem in 1979, dated to about the seventh century BC, carry that blessing.

translationNotes.term: The earth has yielded its harvest
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְבוּלָהּ (yevulah)
translationNotes.note: The harvest in Israel runs on a fixed calendar and the appointed feasts are pinned to it. The sheaf of firstfruits was waved at the start of the barley cutting, the Feast of Weeks came seven weeks later at the wheat harvest, and the Feast of Ingathering closed the year when the grain, wine and oil were in (Leviticus 23:10-16, 39; Exodus 23:16). Verse 6 speaks from the end of that cycle, with the crop already in.
