stories.keyTakeaway: A prayer for God’s blessing so that all nations know, rejoice, and praise Him as the earth yields its harvest.

headings.text: May God Cause His Face to Shine upon Us

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Psalm. A song.

stories.title: 🛡️ Psalms 68
summaryBullets: God arises. His enemies are scattered, and those who hate Him flee His presence. (68:1).
As smoke is blown away, You will drive them out; as wax melts before the fire, the wicked will perish in the presence of God. (68:2).
But the righteous will be glad and rejoice before God; they will celebrate with joy. (68:3).
Sing to God! Sing praises to His name. Exalt Him who rides on the clouds— His name is the LORD— and rejoice before Him. (68:4).
A father of the fatherless and a defender of widows is God in His holy habitation. (68:5).
God settles the lonely in families; He leads the prisoners out to prosperity, but the rebellious dwell in a sun-scorched land. (68:6).
O God, when You went out before Your people, when You marched through the wasteland, Selah (68:7).
the earth shook and the heavens poured down rain before God, the One on Sinai, before God, the God of Israel. (68:8).
You sent abundant rain, O God; You refreshed Your weary inheritance. (68:9).
Your flock settled therein; O God, from Your bounty You provided for the poor. (68:10).
The Lord gives the command; a great company of women proclaim it: (68:11).
“Kings and their armies flee in haste; she who waits at home divides the plunder. (68:12).
Though you lie down among the sheepfolds, the wings of the dove are covered with silver, and her feathers with shimmering gold.” (68:13).
When the Almighty scattered the kings in the land, it was like the snow falling on Zalmon. (68:14).
A mountain of God is Mount Bashan; a mountain of many peaks is Mount Bashan. (68:15).
Why do you gaze in envy, O mountains of many peaks? This is the mountain God chose for His dwelling, where the LORD will surely dwell forever. (68:16).
The chariots of God are tens of thousands — thousands of thousands are they; the Lord is in His sanctuary as He was at Sinai. (68:17).
You have ascended on high; You have led captives away. You have received gifts from men, even from the rebellious, that the LORD God may dwell there. (68:18).
Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears our burden, the God of our salvation. Selah (68:19).
Our God is a God of deliverance; the Lord GOD is our rescuer from death. (68:20).
Surely God will crush the heads of His enemies, the hairy crowns of those who persist in guilty ways. (68:21).
The Lord said, “I will retrieve them from Bashan, I will bring them up from the depths of the sea, (68:22).
that your foot may be dipped in the blood of your foes— the tongues of your dogs in the same.” (68:23).
They have seen Your procession, O God — the march of my God and King into the sanctuary. (68:24).
The singers lead the way, the musicians follow after, among the maidens playing tambourines. (68:25).
Bless God in the great congregation; bless the LORD from the fountain of Israel. (68:26).
There is Benjamin, the youngest, ruling them, the princes of Judah in their company, the princes of Zebulun and of Naphtali. (68:27).
Summon Your power, O God; show Your strength, O God, which You have exerted on our behalf. (68:28).
Because of Your temple at Jerusalem kings will bring You gifts. (68:29).
Rebuke the beast in the reeds, the herd of bulls among the calves of the nations, until it submits, bringing bars of silver. Scatter the nations who delight in war. (68:30).
Envoys will arrive from Egypt; Cush will stretch out her hands to God. (68:31).
Sing to God, O kingdoms of the earth; sing praises to the Lord— Selah (68:32).
to Him who rides upon the highest heavens of old; behold, His mighty voice resounds. (68:33).
Ascribe the power to God, whose majesty is over Israel, whose strength is in the skies. (68:34).
O God, You are awesome in Your sanctuary; the God of Israel Himself gives strength and power to His people. Blessed be God! (68:35).
crossRefs: Numbers 10:35: The exact words Moses spoke whenever the ark set out, which is how this psalm opens. Rise up, O LORD, may Your enemies be scattered.
Ephesians 4:8: Paul quotes verse 18 about ascending on high and leading captives away, and takes the gifts as what the risen Christ hands down to the church.
Deuteronomy 33:2-5: The march from Sinai that verse 17 recalls. The LORD came from Sinai with myriads of holy ones and became King when the tribes of Israel gathered.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָלִיתָ לַמָּרוֹם (ʿalita la-marom), Greek (LXX): ἀνέβης εἰς ὕψος, Aramaic: סליקת למרום
translationNotes.note: Victory ascent with captives and gifts (v. 18).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲבִי יְתוֹמִים (ʾavi yetomim), Greek: πατὴρ ὀρφανῶν, Aramaic: אבא דיתומין
translationNotes.note: Title stressing care for vulnerable (v. 5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּיָהּ שְׁמוֹ (beYah shemo)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew of verse 4 uses Yah, the short form of the divine name, not the full four letters. It stands alone in the song at the sea, 'Yah is my strength and my song' (Exodus 15:2), and in Isaiah 12:2, and it is the second half of hallelu-Yah, 'praise Yah,' the word English keeps untranslated as hallelujah. English versions print LORD in both cases, so the difference between the long form and the short one does not survive.

translationNotes.term: The singers lead the way, the musicians follow
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁרִים (sharim) - נֹגְנִים (nogenim) - תֹּף (toph)
translationNotes.note: Verse 25 gives the marching order of a temple procession: voices in front, players of strings behind, and between them young women beating the toph, the hand drum. Nehemiah 12:31-42 describes the practice in full, with two great choirs set on the wall going opposite ways round the city and meeting at the house of God, each with a named list of players. The drum was consistently a woman's instrument (Exodus 15:20; Judges 11:34).

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm recounts God’s victorious march and care for the vulnerable, His enthronement in Zion, and a call for all kingdoms to praise Him.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. A song.

stories.title: 🌊 Psalms 69
summaryBullets: Save me, O God, for the waters are up to my neck. (69:1).
I have sunk into the miry depths, where there is no footing; I have drifted into deep waters, where the flood engulfs me. (69:2).
I am weary from my crying; my throat is parched. My eyes fail, looking for my God. (69:3).
Those who hate me without cause outnumber the hairs of my head; many are those who would destroy me — my enemies for no reason. Though I did not steal, I must repay. (69:4).
You know my folly, O God, and my guilt is not hidden from You. (69:5).
May those who hope in You not be ashamed through me, O Lord GOD of Hosts; may those who seek You not be dishonored through me, O God of Israel. (69:6).
For I have endured scorn for Your sake, and shame has covered my face. (69:7).
I have become a stranger to my brothers and a foreigner to my mother’s sons, (69:8).
because zeal for Your house has consumed me, and the insults of those who insult You have fallen on me. (69:9).
I wept and fasted, but it brought me reproach. (69:10).
I made sackcloth my clothing, and I was sport to them. (69:11).
Those who sit at the gate mock me, and I am the song of drunkards. (69:12).
But my prayer to You, O LORD, is for a time of favor. In Your abundant loving devotion, O God, answer me with Your sure salvation. (69:13).
Rescue me from the mire and do not let me sink; deliver me from my foes and out of the deep waters. (69:14).
Do not let the floods engulf me or the depths swallow me up; let not the Pit close its mouth over me. (69:15).
Answer me, O LORD, for Your loving devotion is good; turn to me in keeping with Your great compassion. (69:16).
Hide not Your face from Your servant, for I am in distress. Answer me quickly! (69:17).
Draw near to my soul and redeem me; ransom me because of my foes. (69:18).
You know my reproach, my shame and disgrace. All my adversaries are before You. (69:19).
Insults have broken my heart, and I am in despair. I looked for sympathy, but there was none, for comforters, but I found no one. (69:20).
They poisoned my food with gall and gave me vinegar to quench my thirst. (69:21).
May their table become a snare; may it be a retribution and a trap. (69:22).
May their eyes be darkened so they cannot see, and their backs be bent forever. (69:23).
Pour out Your wrath upon them, and let Your burning anger overtake them. (69:24).
May their place be deserted; let there be no one to dwell in their tents. (69:25).
For they persecute the one You struck and recount the pain of those You wounded. (69:26).
Add iniquity to their iniquity; let them not share in Your righteousness. (69:27).
May they be blotted out of the Book of Life and not listed with the righteous. (69:28).
But I am in pain and distress; let Your salvation protect me, O God. (69:29).
I will praise God’s name in song and exalt Him with thanksgiving. (69:30).
And this will please the LORD more than an ox, more than a bull with horns and hooves. (69:31).
The humble will see and rejoice. You who seek God, let your hearts be revived! (69:32).
For the LORD listens to the needy and does not despise His captive people. (69:33).
Let heaven and earth praise Him, the seas and everything that moves in them. (69:34).
For God will save Zion and rebuild the cities of Judah, that they may dwell there and possess it. (69:35).
The descendants of His servants will inherit it, and those who love His name will settle in it. (69:36).
crossRefs: John 2:17: After Jesus drives the traders out of the temple, the disciples remember verse 9 and read it as written about Him: zeal for Your house will consume Me.
John 19:28-29: The gall and vinegar of verse 21 on the day it happened. Jesus says He is thirsty and a sponge soaked in sour wine is lifted to His mouth on a stalk of hyssop.
Acts 1:20: Peter cites verse 25, may his place be deserted with no one to dwell in it, when the eleven decide to fill the position Judas left.
Romans 11:9-10: Paul quotes verses 22 and 23, the table that becomes a snare and eyes darkened so they cannot see, in his argument about Israel's hardening.
Romans 15:3: Paul quotes verse 9, the reproaches of those who reproach You fell on Me, to argue that Christ did not please Himself and that believers should carry the failings of the weak.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רֹאשׁ (rosh, ‘gall/poison’) / חֹמֶץ (chometz, ‘vinegar’), Greek: χολή / ὄξος, Aramaic: ראשא / חמאץ
translationNotes.note: Bitter/poisonous mixture and sour wine (v. 21).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶרְפָּה (ḥerpah), Greek: ὀνειδισμός, Aramaic: חרפתא
translationNotes.note: Disgrace/taunt recurring in the psalm (vv. 7, 9, 19-20).

A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂק (saq); Greek: σάκκος (sakkos)

translationNotes.note: Far more than an entrance; the public square where elders heard legal cases, contracts were witnessed, market business transacted, and news was exchanged. 'Sitting in the gate' (Genesis 19:1; Ruth 4:1-11; Proverbs 31:23) signals civic authority and active community life.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁעַר (sha'ar)

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm portrays overwhelming reproach and unjust suffering, petitions for judgment on enemies, and closes with praise and hope for Zion.

headings.text: The Waters Are up to My Neck

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. To the tune of “Lilies.” Of David.

stories.title: ⏩ Psalms 70
summaryBullets: Make haste, O God, to deliver me! Hurry, O LORD, to help me! (70:1).
May those who seek my life be ashamed and confounded; may those who wish me harm be repelled and humiliated. (70:2).
May those who say, “Aha, aha!” retreat because of their shame. (70:3).
May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You; may those who love Your salvation always say, “Let God be magnified!” (70:4).
But I am poor and needy; hurry to me, O God. You are my help and my deliverer; O LORD, do not delay. (70:5).
crossRefs: Psalm 40:13-17: These same five verses close a much longer psalm there, nearly word for word, where here they stand alone as a psalm of their own.
Psalm 35:4: The same petition in the same terms, that those who seek his life be disgraced and those who plan harm be driven back and confounded.
Philippians 4:4: The other half of verse 4, that all who seek God rejoice and be glad in Him, turned into a standing command. Rejoice in the Lord always.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חוּשָׁה (chushah), Greek: σπεῦσον, Aramaic: חוּש
translationNotes.note: Request for speedy help (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָנִי וְאֶבְיוֹן (ʿani ve-ʾevyon), Greek: πτωχὸς καὶ πένης, Aramaic: מסכן ועביוֹן
translationNotes.note: Self-description of destitution (v. 5).

This whole psalm stands already as Psalm 40:13-17, with small differences. The clearest is the divine name: where Psalm 40 has the LORD, this psalm mostly has God, the same swap that separates Psalm 14 from Psalm 53. Psalm 70 is placed here as a short standalone plea, with the opening line sharpened from 'be pleased to deliver me' to 'make haste.'

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֶאָח הֶאָח (he'ach he'ach)
translationNotes.note: Not a word but a noise, the sound of someone enjoying another man's ruin. Ezekiel puts it in the mouths of Ammon, Tyre and the nations gloating over Jerusalem's fall and the temple's desecration (Ezekiel 25:3; 26:2; 36:2). Job 39:25 uses the same syllables for a warhorse scenting battle. English keeps the sound because there is nothing to translate.

stories.keyTakeaway: A brief urgent plea for swift deliverance and for the shame of enemies, with a call for seekers of God to rejoice.

headings.text: Hurry, O Lord, to Help Me!

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. Of David. To bring remembrance.

stories.title: 🧓 Psalms 71
summaryBullets: In You, O LORD, I have taken refuge; let me never be put to shame. (71:1).
In Your justice, rescue and deliver me; incline Your ear and save me. (71:2).
Be my rock of refuge, where I can always go. Give the command to save me, for You are my rock and my fortress. (71:3).
Deliver me, O my God, from the hand of the wicked, from the grasp of the unjust and ruthless. (71:4).
For You are my hope, O Lord GOD, my confidence from my youth. (71:5).
I have leaned on You since birth; You pulled me from my mother’s womb. My praise is always for You. (71:6).
I have become a portent to many, but You are my strong refuge. (71:7).
My mouth is filled with Your praise and with Your splendor all day long. (71:8).
Do not discard me in my old age; do not forsake me when my strength fails. (71:9).
For my enemies speak against me, and those who lie in wait for my life conspire, (71:10).
saying, “God has forsaken him; pursue him and seize him, for there is no one to rescue him.” (71:11).
Be not far from me, O God. Hurry, O my God, to help me. (71:12).
May the accusers of my soul be ashamed and consumed; may those who seek my harm be covered with scorn and disgrace. (71:13).
But I will always hope and will praise You more and more. (71:14).
My mouth will declare Your righteousness and Your salvation all day long, though I cannot know their full measure. (71:15).
I will come in the strength of the Lord GOD; I will proclaim Your righteousness — Yours alone. (71:16).
O God, You have taught me from my youth, and to this day I proclaim Your marvelous deeds. (71:17).
Even when I am old and gray, do not forsake me, O God, until I proclaim Your power to the next generation, Your might to all who are to come. (71:18).
Your righteousness reaches to the heavens, O God, You who have done great things. Who, O God, is like You? (71:19).
Though You have shown me many troubles and misfortunes, You will revive me once again. Even from the depths of the earth You will bring me back up. (71:20).
You will increase my honor and comfort me once again. (71:21).
So I will praise You with the harp for Your faithfulness, O my God; I will sing praise to You with the lyre, O Holy One of Israel. (71:22).
When I sing praise to You my lips will shout for joy, along with my soul, which You have redeemed. (71:23).
My tongue will indeed proclaim Your righteousness all day long, for those who seek my harm are disgraced and confounded. (71:24).
crossRefs: Isaiah 46:4: The promise verse 9 is asking God to keep. Even to your old age I will be the same, and I will carry you and sustain you when you turn gray.
Psalm 22:9-10: The same claim on God reaching back to birth. You brought me from the womb and made me secure at my mother's breast, which is the confidence of verse 6 here.
2 Samuel 22:2-3: The rock and fortress of verse 3 stacked up in full. Rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, horn of salvation, stronghold, refuge, and Savior, all in two verses.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קְדוֹשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל (qedosh Yisraʾel), Greek: ὁ ἅγιος Ἰσραήλ, Aramaic: קדישא דישראל
translationNotes.note: Title for God used in praise (v. 22).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֵׂיבָה (seivah), Greek: πολιὰ, Aramaic: סֵיבַתָּא
translationNotes.note: Old age marker in the plea for continued help (v. 18).

Psalm 71 carries no superscription in Hebrew, which is unusual this far into the book; the psalms around it are all labelled. The Greek version supplies one that the Hebrew does not have, 'Of David, of the sons of Jonadab and the first taken captive.' Sons of Jonadab is a reference to the Rechabites of Jeremiah 35. Where the Hebrew is silent the Greek heading is the translators' addition, not part of the psalm.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מוֹפֵת (mofet)
translationNotes.note: A mofet is a sign, and specifically one people point at. Isaiah walked stripped and barefoot for three years as a sign against Egypt (Isaiah 20:3), and Ezekiel was told outright that he himself was a sign to Israel (Ezekiel 12:6, 11; 24:24). Verse 7 says the speaker's life has become one, which is not a compliment; it means his troubles are being read by everybody as a message.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm asks God to sustain and deliver in old age and vows continual praise from youth to gray hairs.

stories.title: 👑 Psalms 72
summaryBullets: Endow the king with Your justice, O God, and the son of the king with Your righteousness. (72:1).
May he judge Your people with righteousness and Your afflicted with justice. (72:2).
May the mountains bring peace to the people, and the hills bring righteousness. (72:3).
May he vindicate the afflicted among the people; may he save the children of the needy and crush the oppressor. (72:4).
May they fear him as long as the sun shines, as long as the moon remains, through all generations. (72:5).
May he be like rain that falls on freshly cut grass, like spring showers that water the earth. (72:6).
May the righteous flourish in his days and prosperity abound until the moon is no more. (72:7).
May he rule from sea to sea, and from the Euphrates to the ends of the earth. (72:8).
May the nomads bow before him, and his enemies lick the dust. (72:9).
May the kings of Tarshish and distant shores bring tribute; may the kings of Sheba and Seba offer gifts. (72:10).
May all kings bow down to him and all nations serve him. (72:11).
For he will deliver the needy who cry out and the afflicted who have no helper. (72:12).
He will take pity on the poor and needy and save the lives of the oppressed. (72:13).
He will redeem them from oppression and violence, for their blood is precious in his sight. (72:14).
Long may he live! May gold from Sheba be given him. May people ever pray for him; may they bless him all day long. (72:15).
May there be an abundance of grain in the land; may it sway atop the hills. May its fruit trees flourish like the forests of Lebanon, the people of its cities like the grass of the field. (72:16).
May his name endure forever; may his name continue as long as the sun shines. In him may all nations be blessed; may they call him blessed. (72:17).
Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel, who alone does marvelous deeds. (72:18).
And blessed be His glorious name forever; may all the earth be filled with His glory. Amen and amen. (72:19).
Thus conclude the prayers of David son of Jesse. (72:20).
crossRefs: Zechariah 9:10: The same borders given to a coming king who breaks the bow of war. His dominion runs from sea to sea and from the Euphrates to the ends of the earth.
1 Kings 10:1-10: The tribute of verse 10 actually arriving. The queen of Sheba came to Jerusalem with camels bearing spices and gave Solomon a hundred and twenty talents of gold.
Genesis 22:18: The promise verse 17 is reaching for when it asks that all nations be blessed in the king. God swore to Abraham that through his offspring all nations of the earth would be blessed.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִיָּם עַד־יָם (mi-yam ʿad-yam), Greek: ἀπὸ θαλάσσης ἕως θαλάσσης, Aramaic: מן ימא ועד ימא
translationNotes.note: Extent formula for wide dominion (v. 8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁבָא (Sheva), Greek: Σαβά, Aramaic: שבא
translationNotes.note: Southern Arabian kingdom named among gift-bringers (v. 10).

translationNotes.term: Thus conclude the prayers of David
translationNotes.note: Verse 20 is a scribe's closing line on a collection, not part of the psalm, and verses 18 and 19 are the doxology that ends Book II of the Psalms. Psalms of David appear again later in the book, at 86, 101, 103, 108 through 110, 122, 138 through 145 and elsewhere, so the note closes one gathering rather than the whole. The five books of the Psalter each end this way.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִנְחָה (minchah)
translationNotes.note: The same word that names the grain offering also names political tribute, the payment a weaker king sends a stronger one to buy peace. Ehud carried the minchah to Eglon of Moab with a dagger strapped under his cloak (Judges 3:15-21), and Hoshea paid it to Shalmaneser until he stopped, which brought the Assyrian army (2 Kings 17:3-4). Verse 10 has foreign kings arriving in that posture, which is a statement about who is the vassal.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm petitions for a just, worldwide-reigning king who defends the poor and brings flourishing, concluding with a doxology.

headings.text: Endow the King with Your Justice

stories.superscription: Of Solomon.

stories.title: 👀 Psalms 73
summaryBullets: Surely God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart. (73:1).
But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled; my steps had nearly slipped. (73:2).
For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. (73:3).
They have no struggle in their death; their bodies are well-fed. (73:4).
They are free of the burdens others carry; they are not afflicted like other men. (73:5).
Therefore pride is their necklace; a garment of violence covers them. (73:6).
From their prosperity proceeds iniquity; the imaginations of their hearts run wild. (73:7).
They mock and speak with malice; with arrogance they threaten oppression. (73:8).
They set their mouths against the heavens, and their tongues strut across the earth. (73:9).
So their people return to this place and drink up waters in abundance. (73:10).
The wicked say, “How can God know? Does the Most High have knowledge?” (73:11).
Behold, these are the wicked — always carefree as they increase their wealth. (73:12).
Surely in vain I have kept my heart pure; in innocence I have washed my hands. (73:13).
For I am afflicted all day long and punished every morning. (73:14).
If I had said, “I will speak this way,” then I would have betrayed Your children. (73:15).
When I tried to understand all this, it was troublesome in my sight (73:16).
until I entered God’s sanctuary; then I discerned their end. (73:17).
Surely You set them on slick ground; You cast them down into ruin. (73:18).
How suddenly they are laid waste, completely swept away by terrors! (73:19).
Like one waking from a dream, so You, O Lord, awaken and despise their form. (73:20).
When my heart was grieved and I was pierced within, (73:21).
I was senseless and ignorant; I was a brute beast before You. (73:22).
Yet I am always with You; You hold my right hand. (73:23).
You guide me with Your counsel, and later receive me in glory. (73:24).
Whom have I in heaven but You? And on earth I desire no one besides You. (73:25).
My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever. (73:26).
Those far from You will surely perish; You destroy all who are unfaithful to You. (73:27).
But as for me, it is good to draw near to God. I have made the Lord GOD my refuge, that I may proclaim all Your works. (73:28).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 12:1-2: A prophet raising the same complaint. Why does the way of the wicked prosper and why do the faithless live at ease, when God Himself planted them and they took root.
Psalm 16:5: The word Asaph finally lands on at verse 26. The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup, and He has made my lot secure.
Psalm 37:35-38: The same conclusion reached without the crisis. A ruthless man flourishes like a well-rooted native tree, then passes away and cannot be found however hard you look.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִקְדָּשׁ (mikdash), Greek: ἅγιον, Aramaic: מקדשא
translationNotes.note: Holy place where understanding is gained (v. 17).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֵלֶק (cheleq), Greek: μερὶς, Aramaic: מְנָתָא
translationNotes.note: Share/inheritance; used for the LORD as one’s lasting share (v. 26).

Psalm 73 opens the third of the five books the Psalms are divided into, running from 73 to 89 and closing with the doxology at 89:52. Eleven of its first eleven psalms are Asaph's: 73 through 83 all carry his name, the largest unbroken block by one author in the book, with Psalm 50 standing apart in Book II. The books are marked in the Hebrew manuscripts, not imposed by translators.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לָקַח (laqach)
translationNotes.note: The verb in verse 24 is the plain word for taking something, and it is the word used of Enoch, who 'was not, for God took him' (Genesis 5:24), and of Elijah, taken up in the whirlwind while Elisha watched (2 Kings 2:9-11). Psalm 49:15 uses it the same way. English 'receive' is gentler than the Hebrew, which is the verb for picking a thing up and carrying it off.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm moves from envy at the ease of the wicked to recognition of their end and declares God as lasting portion and refuge.

headings.text: BOOK III Surely God Is Good to Israel

stories.superscription: A Psalm of Asaph.

stories.title: 🏚️ Psalms 74
summaryBullets: Why have You rejected us forever, O God? Why does Your anger smolder against the sheep of Your pasture? (74:1).
Remember Your congregation, which You purchased long ago and redeemed as the tribe of Your inheritance — Mount Zion, where You dwell. (74:2).
Turn Your steps to the everlasting ruins, to everything in the sanctuary the enemy has destroyed. (74:3).
Your foes have roared within Your meeting place; they have unfurled their banners as signs, (74:4).
like men wielding axes in a thicket of trees (74:5).
and smashing all the carvings with hatchets and picks. (74:6).
They have burned Your sanctuary to the ground; they have defiled the dwelling place of Your Name. (74:7).
They said in their hearts, “We will crush them completely.” They burned down every place where God met us in the land. (74:8).
There are no signs for us to see. There is no longer any prophet. And none of us knows how long this will last. (74:9).
How long, O God, will the enemy taunt You? Will the foe revile Your name forever? (74:10).
Why do You withdraw Your strong right hand? Stretch it out to destroy them! (74:11).
Yet God is my King from ancient times, working salvation on the earth. (74:12).
You divided the sea by Your strength; You smashed the heads of the dragons of the sea; (74:13).
You crushed the heads of Leviathan; You fed him to the creatures of the desert. (74:14).
You broke open the fountain and the flood; You dried up the ever-flowing rivers. (74:15).
The day is Yours, and also the night; You established the moon and the sun. (74:16).
You set all the boundaries of the earth; You made the summer and winter. (74:17).
Remember how the enemy has mocked You, O LORD, how a foolish people has spurned Your name. (74:18).
Do not deliver the soul of Your dove to beasts; do not forget the lives of Your afflicted forever. (74:19).
Consider Your covenant, for haunts of violence fill the dark places of the land. (74:20).
Do not let the oppressed retreat in shame; may the poor and needy praise Your name. (74:21).
Rise up, O God; defend Your cause! Remember how the fool mocks You all day long. (74:22).
Do not disregard the clamor of Your adversaries, the uproar of Your enemies that ascends continually. (74:23).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 25:9: The burning of verse 7 as the history records it. Nebuzaradan, captain of the Babylonian guard, burned down the house of the LORD, the palace, and every significant building in Jerusalem.
Job 41:1-34: The Leviathan whose heads God crushes at verse 14, described at length as a creature no man can hook, harpoon, leash, or bargain over with merchants.
Genesis 8:22: The fixed order verses 16 and 17 are appealing to. As long as the earth endures, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter will never cease.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תַּנִּינִים (tannînîm); Greek (LXX): δράκοντες (drakontes)
translationNotes.note: Generic sea monsters defeated by God in Psalm 74:13; often rendered 'dragons' (KJV) or 'sea creatures' (modern translations).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִקְדָּשׁ (mikdash), Greek: ἁγίασμα, Aramaic: מקדשא
translationNotes.note: Holy dwelling vandalized and burned (vv. 3, 7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לִוְיָתָן (livyatan)
translationNotes.note: A great water creature. Job 41 gives the longest account of it in Scripture: scales shut against each other like a shield wall, a ring of teeth, and no weapon that touches it, since the sword glances off, arrows do not turn it, and a club counts as straw (Job 41:15-29). Isaiah 27:1 calls it the fleeing serpent in the sea. Verse 14 says its heads were crushed and it was given as food to the creatures of the desert, which is what happens to a carcass left in the open.

translationNotes.term: They have burned Your sanctuary to the ground
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַקַּרְדֻּמּוֹת (maqqardummot, axes)
translationNotes.note: The inside of the temple was cedar over stone, carved through with gourds, palm trees, cherubim and open flowers, and overlaid with gold (1 Kings 6:18, 29-32). Verses 5 and 6 describe men going at that carved work with axes and hammers as if clearing timber. Nebuzaradan, captain of Nebuchadnezzar's guard, burned the house of the LORD, the palace and every great house in Jerusalem in the nineteenth year of that king's reign (2 Kings 25:8-10; Jeremiah 52:12-13).

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm laments the burning and defiling of the sanctuary and appeals to God’s ancient power over sea and seasons to act.

headings.text: Why Have You Rejected Us Forever?

stories.superscription: A Maskil of Asaph.

stories.title: 🏆 Psalms 75
summaryBullets: We give thanks to You, O God; we give thanks, for Your Name is near. The people declare Your wondrous works. (75:1).
“When I choose a time, I will judge fairly. (75:2).
When the earth and all its dwellers quake, it is I who bear up its pillars. Selah (75:3).
I say to the proud, ‘Do not boast,’ and to the wicked, ‘Do not lift up your horn. (75:4).
Do not lift up your horn against heaven or speak with an outstretched neck.’” (75:5).
For exaltation comes neither from east nor west, nor out of the desert, (75:6).
but it is God who judges; He brings down one and exalts another. (75:7).
For a cup is in the hand of the LORD, full of foaming wine mixed with spices. He pours from His cup, and all the wicked of the earth drink it down to the dregs. (75:8).
But I will proclaim Him forever; I will sing praise to the God of Jacob. (75:9).
“All the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous will be exalted.” (75:10).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 2:7-8: Hannah sings the same claim that verse 7 makes. The LORD humbles and exalts, raising the poor from the dust and the needy from the ash heap to seat them among princes.
Isaiah 51:17: The cup of verse 8 put into Jerusalem's hand. She has drunk the cup of the LORD's fury and drained the goblet that makes men stagger down to the dregs.
Job 9:6: The pillars of verse 3 seen from the other direction. God shakes the earth from its place so that its own foundations tremble.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קֶרֶן (qeren), Greek: κέρας, Aramaic: קרנא
translationNotes.note: Symbol of strength/status (vv. 4-5, 10).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כּוֹס (kos), Greek: ποτήριον, Aramaic: כסא
translationNotes.note: Cup of mixed wine as judgment (v. 8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֶסֶךְ (mesekh) - שְׁמָרִים (shemarim)
translationNotes.note: Mixed wine is not watered wine; the mixture was spice or herbs stirred into it to make it stronger, which is what Wisdom prepares in Proverbs 9:2 and what Isaiah 5:22 condemns men for being expert at. The shemarim are the lees, the sediment that settles at the bottom of the jar during fermentation and is normally left behind. Verse 8 has the wicked drinking the jar out and swallowing the sludge as well.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צַוָּאר עָתָק (tsavvar atak)
translationNotes.note: The image comes from the farmyard. An ox that will not take the yoke sets its neck against it, which is where the whole family of stiff-necked language starts (Exodus 32:9; Deuteronomy 10:16; 2 Kings 17:14). Verse 5 pairs it with lifting the horn, so both halves of the warning are drawn from the same animal: the horn it fights with and the neck it braces.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm declares God’s set time to judge, His steadying of the earth, and His humbling and exalting of people.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster: To the tune of “Do Not Destroy.” A Psalm of Asaph. A song.

stories.title: 🏹 Psalms 76
summaryBullets: God is known in Judah; His name is great in Israel. (76:1).
His tent is in Salem, His dwelling place in Zion. (76:2).
There He shattered the flaming arrows, the shield and sword and weapons of war. Selah (76:3).
You are resplendent with light, more majestic than mountains filled with game. (76:4).
The valiant lie plundered; they sleep their last sleep. No men of might could lift a hand. (76:5).
At Your rebuke, O God of Jacob, both horse and rider lie stunned. (76:6).
You alone are to be feared. When You are angry, who can stand before You? (76:7).
From heaven You pronounced judgment, and the earth feared and was still (76:8).
when God rose up to judge, to save all the lowly of the earth. Selah (76:9).
Even the wrath of man shall praise You; with the survivors of wrath You will clothe Yourself. (76:10).
Make and fulfill your vows to the LORD your God; let all the neighboring lands bring tribute to Him who is to be feared. (76:11).
He breaks the spirits of princes; He is feared by the kings of the earth. (76:12).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 19:35: In one night the angel of the LORD struck down one hundred eighty-five thousand men in the Assyrian camp, and Jerusalem woke to a lifted siege and a field of bodies. That is the rescue at Zion this psalm sings about.

Psalm 46:9: God ends war by destroying the equipment, breaking the bow, shattering the spear, burning the shields. Verse 3 here fixes that same act to a place, Zion, where the flaming arrows and the shield and the sword were broken.

Ecclesiastes 5:4: The rule standing behind the psalm's closing charge to make and fulfill your vows. Delay in paying what you promised God is what marks a fool, and the instruction is blunt, fulfill your vow.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁלֵם (Salem), Greek: Σαλήμ, Aramaic: שלם
translationNotes.note: Poetic name for Jerusalem (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יִבְצֹר רוּחַ (yivtzor ruach); Greek: ἀφαιροῦται πνεῦμα
translationNotes.note: To break the pride/resolve of princes (v. 12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אָסָף (Asaph)
translationNotes.note: A Levite David appointed to lead the music before the ark, sounding the cymbals (1 Chronicles 16:4-5). His sons were set apart to prophesy with lyres, harps, and cymbals under the king's direction (1 Chronicles 25:1-2). Psalm 50 and Psalms 73 through 83 carry his name, and 128 of his descendants came back from Babylon as temple singers (Ezra 2:41).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בִּנְגִינוֹת (bin-neginot)
translationNotes.note: A performance direction, not part of the poem. Neginot are stringed instruments, so this psalm was set for lyre and harp rather than horn or percussion. The word beside it, lamnatseach, 'for the choirmaster,' hands a psalm to the director of the temple music; it heads 55 psalms and closes Habakkuk 3:19.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רִשְׁפֵי־קָשֶׁת (rishphei-qashet)
translationNotes.note: Literally 'the fire-shafts of the bow.' Resheph is a flame or a live coal; archers bound pitch-soaked tow behind the head and lit it to set roofs, gates, and siege works burning. Verse 3 names the full kit of an Iron Age army in one breath: incendiary arrows, shield, sword, battle.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm celebrates God’s defeat of attackers near Zion and calls for vows, stating He is feared by earth’s kings.

headings.text: God’s Name Is Great in Israel

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Psalm of Asaph. A song.

stories.title: 🌩️ Psalms 77
summaryBullets: I cried out to God; I cried aloud to God to hear me. (77:1).
In the day of trouble I sought the Lord; through the night my outstretched hands did not grow weary; my soul refused to be comforted. (77:2).
I remembered You, O God, and I groaned; I mused and my spirit grew faint. Selah (77:3).
You have kept my eyes from closing; I am too troubled to speak. (77:4).
I considered the days of old, the years long in the past. (77:5).
At night I remembered my song; in my heart I mused, and my spirit pondered: (77:6).
“Will the Lord spurn us forever and never show His favor again? (77:7).
Is His loving devotion gone forever? Has His promise failed for all time? (77:8).
Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has His anger shut off His compassion?” Selah (77:9).
So I said, “I am grieved that the right hand of the Most High has changed.” (77:10).
I will remember the works of the LORD; yes, I will remember Your wonders of old. (77:11).
I will reflect on all You have done and ponder Your mighty deeds. (77:12).
Your way, O God, is holy. What god is so great as our God? (77:13).
You are the God who works wonders; You display Your strength among the peoples. (77:14).
With power You redeemed Your people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph. Selah (77:15).
The waters saw You, O God; the waters saw You and swirled; even the depths were shaken. (77:16).
The clouds poured down water; the skies resounded with thunder; Your arrows flashed back and forth. (77:17).
Your thunder resounded in the whirlwind; the lightning lit up the world; the earth trembled and quaked. (77:18).
Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters, but Your footprints were not to be found. (77:19).
You led Your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron. (77:20).
crossRefs: Exodus 14:21-31: The night the sea opened, Israel walked through on dry ground between walls of water, and the pursuing army drowned behind them. That is the crossing the psalm reaches for when it says God's path led through the sea and left no footprints.

Habakkuk 3:3-15: A prophet's storm-hymn of God on the march, mountains crumbling, the deep lifting its hands, horses trampling the sea. It moves the way this psalm moves, from a shaken man's questions to the thunder of the exodus.

Psalm 78:52: The same picture compressed into one line, God bringing His people out like sheep and guiding them like a flock in the wilderness, which is exactly where this psalm stops, with the flock led by the hand of Moses and Aaron.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זָכַר (zakhar) / הָגָה (hagah), Greek: μιμνήσκομαι / μελετάω, Aramaic: דכר / יהגי
translationNotes.note: Verbs for recalling and pondering God’s works (vv. 11-12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֶלָה (selah); Greek: διάψαλμα
translationNotes.note: Musical/reflective pause used in the psalm (vv. 3, 9, 15).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְדוּתוּן (Yeduthun)
translationNotes.note: One of the three men David set over the temple music, with Asaph and Heman, whose sons prophesied with the lyre in thanksgiving and praise (1 Chronicles 25:1-3). He is called the king's seer at 2 Chronicles 35:15. Three psalms name him in the heading: 39, 62, and 77. The parallel list at 1 Chronicles 15:17-19 calls the third chief musician Ethan.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּיָּם דַּרְכֶּךָ (bayyam darkekha)
translationNotes.note: Verses 16 through 20 recount one event: the sea driven back by an east wind all night so Israel walked through on dry ground, and the water returning on Pharaoh's chariots (Exodus 14:21-28). 'Your footprints were not to be found' is exact; the water closed and left no track. Verse 20 names the two men who led that walk, Moses and Aaron.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm moves from distress to remembrance, recounting storm theophany and the sea path by which God led His people.

headings.text: In the Day of Trouble I Sought the Lord

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. According to Jeduthun. A Psalm of Asaph.

stories.title: 📜 Psalms 78
summaryBullets: Give ear, O my people, to my instruction; listen to the words of my mouth. (78:1).
I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the beginning, (78:2).
that we have heard and known and our fathers have relayed to us. (78:3).
We will not hide them from their children but will declare to the next generation the praises of the LORD and His might and the wonders He has performed. (78:4).
For He established a testimony in Jacob and appointed a law in Israel, which He commanded our fathers to teach to their children, (78:5).
that the coming generation would know them— even children yet to be born— to arise and tell their own children (78:6).
that they should put their confidence in God, not forgetting His works, but keeping His commandments. (78:7).
Then they will not be like their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation, whose heart was not loyal, whose spirit was not faithful to God. (78:8).
The archers of Ephraim turned back on the day of battle. (78:9).
They failed to keep God’s covenant and refused to live by His law. (78:10).
They forgot what He had done, the wonders He had shown them. (78:11).
He worked wonders before their fathers in the land of Egypt, in the region of Zoan. (78:12).
He split the sea and brought them through; He set the waters upright like a wall. (78:13).
He led them with a cloud by day and with a light of fire all night. (78:14).
He split the rocks in the wilderness and gave them drink as abundant as the seas. (78:15).
He brought streams from the stone and made water flow down like rivers. (78:16).
But they continued to sin against Him, rebelling in the desert against the Most High. (78:17).
They willfully tested God by demanding the food they craved. (78:18).
They spoke against God, saying, “Can God really prepare a table in the wilderness? (78:19).
When He struck the rock, water gushed out and torrents raged. But can He also give bread or supply His people with meat?” (78:20).
Therefore the LORD heard and was filled with wrath; so a fire was kindled against Jacob, and His anger flared against Israel, (78:21).
because they did not believe God or rely on His salvation. (78:22).
Yet He commanded the clouds above and opened the doors of the heavens. (78:23).
He rained down manna for them to eat; He gave them grain from heaven. (78:24).
Man ate the bread of angels; He sent them food in abundance. (78:25).
He stirred the east wind from the heavens and drove the south wind by His might. (78:26).
He rained meat on them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea. (78:27).
He felled them in the midst of their camp, all around their dwellings. (78:28).
So they ate and were well filled, for He gave them what they craved. (78:29).
Yet before they had filled their desire, with the food still in their mouths, (78:30).
God’s anger flared against them, and He put to death their strongest and subdued the young men of Israel. (78:31).
In spite of all this, they kept on sinning; despite His wonderful works, they did not believe. (78:32).
So He ended their days in futility, and their years in sudden terror. (78:33).
When He slew them, they would seek Him; they repented and searched for God. (78:34).
And they remembered that God was their Rock, that God Most High was their Redeemer. (78:35).
But they deceived Him with their mouths, and lied to Him with their tongues. (78:36).
Their hearts were disloyal to Him, and they were unfaithful to His covenant. (78:37).
And yet He was compassionate; He forgave their iniquity and did not destroy them. He often restrained His anger and did not unleash His full wrath. (78:38).
He remembered that they were but flesh, a passing breeze that does not return. (78:39).
How often they disobeyed Him in the wilderness and grieved Him in the desert! (78:40).
Again and again they tested God and provoked the Holy One of Israel. (78:41).
They did not remember His power — the day He redeemed them from the adversary, (78:42).
when He performed His signs in Egypt and His wonders in the fields of Zoan. (78:43).
He turned their rivers to blood, and from their streams they could not drink. (78:44).
He sent swarms of flies that devoured them, and frogs that devastated them. (78:45).
He gave their crops to the grasshopper, the fruit of their labor to the locust. (78:46).
He killed their vines with hailstones and their sycamore-figs with sleet. (78:47).
He abandoned their cattle to the hail and their livestock to bolts of lightning. (78:48).
He unleashed His fury against them, wrath, indignation, and calamity— a band of destroying angels. (78:49).
He cleared a path for His anger; He did not spare them from death but delivered their lives to the plague. (78:50).
He struck all the firstborn of Egypt, the virility in the tents of Ham. (78:51).
He led out His people like sheep and guided them like a flock in the wilderness. (78:52).
He led them safely, so they did not fear, but the sea engulfed their enemies. (78:53).
He brought them to His holy land, to the mountain His right hand had acquired. (78:54).
He drove out nations before them and apportioned their inheritance; He settled the tribes of Israel in their tents. (78:55).
But they tested and disobeyed God Most High, for they did not keep His decrees. (78:56).
They turned back and were faithless like their fathers, twisted like a faulty bow. (78:57).
They enraged Him with their high places and provoked His jealousy with their idols. (78:58).
On hearing it, God was furious and rejected Israel completely. (78:59).
He abandoned the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tent He had pitched among men. (78:60).
He delivered His strength to captivity, and His splendor to the hand of the adversary. (78:61).
He surrendered His people to the sword because He was enraged by His heritage. (78:62).
Fire consumed His young men, and their maidens were left without wedding songs. (78:63).
His priests fell by the sword, but their widows could not lament. (78:64).
Then the Lord awoke as from sleep, like a mighty warrior overcome by wine. (78:65).
He beat back His foes; He put them to everlasting shame. (78:66).
He rejected the tent of Joseph and refused the tribe of Ephraim. (78:67).
But He chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which He loved. (78:68).
He built His sanctuary like the heights, like the earth He has established forever. (78:69).
He chose David His servant and took him from the sheepfolds; (78:70).
from tending the ewes He brought him to be shepherd of His people Jacob, of Israel His inheritance. (78:71).
So David shepherded them with integrity of heart and guided them with skillful hands. (78:72).
crossRefs: Exodus 16:13-15: Quail covering the camp at evening, thin flakes like frost on the ground at morning, and Israel asking what it was because they had no name for it. The psalm retells this as bread of angels, then as the meal that turned to judgment.

1 Samuel 4:10-11: Israel routed, the ark of God captured, and Eli's two sons killed in a single day. That defeat is what the psalm means when it says God abandoned the tabernacle at Shiloh and handed His strength over to captivity.

2 Samuel 5:1-3: The tribes come to David at Hebron and cut a covenant with him, saying he was the one who led Israel out and brought them back. The psalm ends on that choice, David taken from the sheepfolds to shepherd Jacob.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָשָׁל (mashal), Greek: παραβολή, Aramaic: מתלא
translationNotes.note: Instructional saying used to teach (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵדוּת (ʿedut), Greek: μαρτύριον, Aramaic: סהדותא
translationNotes.note: Witness/ordinance set in Jacob (v. 5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צֹעַן (Tso'an) - Greek: Τάνις (Tanis)
translationNotes.note: The Egyptian city in the northeast Delta known to the Greeks as Tanis. Numbers 13:22 dates its founding seven years after Hebron. Putting the plagues 'in the fields of Zoan' (78:12, 43) places them in the Delta, the district where Israel was settled in Goshen and where Pharaoh's court sat, not in Upper Egypt hundreds of miles south.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֶחֶם אַבִּירִים (lechem abbirim)
translationNotes.note: Literally 'bread of the mighty ones'; the Greek Old Testament renders it 'bread of angels.' The food itself is the manna of Exodus 16: thin flakes like frost on the ground, gathered at an omer a head each day, tasting like wafers made with honey. An omer is a tenth of an ephah (Exodus 16:36), roughly two quarts.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁלֹה (Shiloh)
translationNotes.note: The tabernacle stood at Shiloh, about twenty miles north of Jerusalem, from Joshua 18:1 until the Philistines took the ark in Eli's day and his two sons died in the battle (1 Samuel 4:10-11). Verse 60 records its abandonment; Jeremiah 7:12-14 tells Judah to go and look at what was left of it. Israel Finkelstein's excavations at Khirbet Seilun in 1981-1984 found a heavy destruction layer there dated to about 1050 BC.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm instructs by recounting Israel’s repeated rebellion and God’s works, ending with the choice of Zion and David.

headings.text: I Will Open My Mouth in Parables

stories.superscription: A Maskil of Asaph.

stories.title: 🗡️ Psalms 79
summaryBullets: The nations, O God, have invaded Your inheritance; they have defiled Your holy temple and reduced Jerusalem to rubble. (79:1).
They have given the corpses of Your servants as food to the birds of the air, the flesh of Your saints to the beasts of the earth. (79:2).
They have poured out their blood like water all around Jerusalem, and there is no one to bury the dead. (79:3).
We have become a reproach to our neighbors, a scorn and derision to those around us. (79:4).
How long, O LORD? Will You be angry forever? Will Your jealousy burn like fire? (79:5).
Pour out Your wrath on the nations that do not acknowledge You, on the kingdoms that refuse to call on Your name, (79:6).
for they have devoured Jacob and devastated his homeland. (79:7).
Do not hold past sins against us; let Your compassion come quickly, for we are brought low. (79:8).
Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of Your name; deliver us and atone for our sins, for the sake of Your name. (79:9).
Why should the nations ask, “Where is their God?” Before our eyes, make known among the nations Your vengeance for the bloodshed of Your servants. (79:10).
May the groans of the captives reach You; by the strength of Your arm preserve those condemned to death. (79:11).
Pay back into the laps of our neighbors sevenfold the reproach they hurled at You, O Lord. (79:12).
Then we Your people, the sheep of Your pasture, will thank You forever; from generation to generation we will declare Your praise. (79:13).
crossRefs: Lamentations 2:21: Young and old lying together in the dust of the streets, fallen by the sword when Jerusalem was taken. The psalm reports the same streets, blood poured out like water with no one left alive to bury the dead.

2 Kings 25:8-10: The record of the day itself. Nebuzaradan burned the house of the LORD, the palace and every significant house, and the Chaldean army pulled down the walls, which is the ruin the psalm carries into prayer.

Deuteronomy 32:43: The Song of Moses closes with God avenging the blood of His children and repaying those who hate Him. That is the promise the psalm holds Him to when it asks who will avenge His servants' outpoured blood.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: טָמֵא (tame), Greek: μιαίνω, Aramaic: טמא
translationNotes.note: Render unclean/profane (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁבְעָתַיִם אֶל־חֵיקָם (shivʿatayim el-ḥeikam); Greek: ἑπταπλασίως εἰς τὸν κόλπον αὐτῶν
translationNotes.note: Full repayment pressed back (v. 12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לְעִיִּים (le'iyyim)
translationNotes.note: Iyyim are heaps of ruin. The event is dated: in the fifth month of Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year, 587 BC, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard burned the temple, the palace, and every great house, and the army broke down the walls of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25:8-10). The psalm is a prayer said over the wreckage.

translationNotes.term: No one to bury the dead
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְאֵין קוֹבֵר (ve'ein qover)
translationNotes.note: Burial was a binding duty, and a body was not to be left out overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22-23). Corpses left for the birds and the beasts is the standard curse for a broken covenant (Deuteronomy 28:26) and the horror Jeremiah 8:1-2 describes. Verse 2 is not scene-setting; it names the worst thing the invaders could do after the killing.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm laments desecration and mass death in Jerusalem and asks for wrath on the nations and swift compassion.
stories.superscription: A Psalm of Asaph.

stories.title: 🍇 Psalms 80
summaryBullets: Hear us, O Shepherd of Israel, who leads Joseph like a flock; You who sit enthroned between the cherubim, shine forth (80:1).
before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. Rally Your mighty power and come to save us. (80:2).
Restore us, O God, and cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved. (80:3).
O LORD God of Hosts, how long will Your anger smolder against the prayers of Your people? (80:4).
You fed them with the bread of tears and made them drink the full measure of their tears. (80:5).
You make us contend with our neighbors; our enemies mock us. (80:6).
Restore us, O God of Hosts, and cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved. (80:7).
You uprooted a vine from Egypt; You drove out the nations and transplanted it. (80:8).
You cleared the ground for it, and it took root and filled the land. (80:9).
The mountains were covered by its shade, and the mighty cedars with its branches. (80:10).
It sent out its branches to the Sea, and its shoots toward the River. (80:11).
Why have You broken down its walls, so that all who pass by pick its fruit? (80:12).
The boar from the forest ravages it, and the creatures of the field feed upon it. (80:13).
Return, O God of Hosts, we pray! Look down from heaven and see! Attend to this vine— (80:14).
the root Your right hand has planted, the son You have raised up for Yourself. (80:15).
Your vine has been cut down and burned; they perish at the rebuke of Your countenance. (80:16).
Let Your hand be upon the man at Your right hand, on the son of man You have raised up for Yourself. (80:17).
Then we will not turn away from You; revive us, and we will call on Your name. (80:18).
Restore us, O LORD God of Hosts; cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved. (80:19).
crossRefs: Numbers 6:25: The priestly blessing spoken over Israel asks the LORD to make His face shine on you and be gracious to you. The psalm turns that blessing into its refrain and its plea, sung three times, restore us and cause Your face to shine.

Exodus 25:18-22: Two cherubim of hammered gold at the ends of the mercy seat, wings spread, with God promising to meet and speak from the space between them. That is the throne the psalm addresses as God enthroned between the cherubim.

Isaiah 5:1-7: A song about a vineyard planted on a fertile hill, then stripped of its hedge and trampled, with the vineyard named plainly as the house of Israel. The psalm runs that same figure, a vine carried out of Egypt whose walls are now broken down.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רֹעֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל (roʿeh Yisraʾel), Greek: ποιμὴν Ἰσραήλ, Aramaic: רָעָא דישראל
translationNotes.note: Title addressing God as leader of the flock (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הָאֵר פָּנֶיךָ (haʾer panekha), Greek: ἐπίφανον τὸ πρόσωπόν σου, Aramaic: נהֵיר אפיך
translationNotes.note: Prayer refrain for favor and rescue (vv. 3, 7, 19).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶל־שֹׁשַׁנִּים עֵדוּת (el-shoshannim edut)
translationNotes.note: A tune name in the heading: sing this to 'Lilies,' a melody the temple singers already knew. Related rubrics head Psalm 45 and Psalm 69 ('Lilies') and Psalm 60 ('Lily of the Testimony'). The melodies are lost; only their titles survive.

translationNotes.term: You uprooted a vine from Egypt
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֶּפֶן מִמִּצְרַיִם תַּסִּיעַ (gephen mimmitsrayim tassia)
translationNotes.note: Verses 8 through 16 run the whole history of Israel as one planting: cleared ground, root taken, growth to the Sea in the west and the River, the Euphrates, in the east. A hill-country vineyard was terraced and walled with stone against animals and thieves (Isaiah 5:1-5), so 'broken down its walls' means the owner has stopped defending it and the boar can walk in.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm pleads for God to shine His face and restore His vine, using repeated refrain and vineyard imagery.

headings.text: Hear Us, O Shepherd of Israel

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. To the tune of “The Lilies of the Covenant.” A Psalm of Asaph.

stories.title: 📯 Psalms 81
summaryBullets: Sing for joy to God our strength; make a joyful noise to the God of Jacob. (81:1).
Lift up a song, strike the tambourine, play the sweet-sounding harp and lyre. (81:2).
Sound the ram’s horn at the New Moon, and at the full moon on the day of our Feast. (81:3).
For this is a statute for Israel, an ordinance of the God of Jacob. (81:4).
He ordained it as a testimony for Joseph when he went out over the land of Egypt, where I heard an unfamiliar language: (81:5).
“I relieved his shoulder of the burden; his hands were freed from the basket. (81:6).
You called out in distress, and I rescued you; I answered you from the cloud of thunder; I tested you at the waters of Meribah. Selah (81:7).
Hear, O My people, and I will warn you: O Israel, if only you would listen to Me! (81:8).
There must be no strange god among you, nor shall you bow to a foreign god. (81:9).
I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of Egypt. Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it. (81:10).
But My people would not listen to Me, and Israel would not obey Me. (81:11).
So I gave them up to their stubborn hearts to follow their own devices. (81:12).
If only My people would listen to Me, if Israel would follow My ways, (81:13).
how soon I would subdue their enemies and turn My hand against their foes! (81:14).
Those who hate the LORD would feign obedience, and their doom would last forever. (81:15).
But I would feed you the finest wheat; with honey from the rock I would satisfy you.” (81:16).
crossRefs: Leviticus 23:24: The appointed day in the seventh month, a day of rest marked by a blast of trumpets and a sacred assembly. That is the statute the psalm invokes when it orders the ram's horn sounded at the New Moon for the day of the Feast.

Exodus 17:7: Moses names the place Massah and Meribah because Israel quarreled there and tested the LORD, asking whether He was among them. God recalls that quarrel in the psalm as the moment He answered out of the thundercloud.

Deuteronomy 32:13: The Song of Moses has God feeding Israel honey from the rock and oil from the flinty crag. The psalm ends on that same offer, finest wheat and honey from the rock, held out to a people who would not listen.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שׁוֹפָר (shofar), Greek (LXX): σάλπιγξ (salpinx), Aramaic: שופרא (shofra)
translationNotes.note: Ram’s horn sounded at appointed times (v. 3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְרִיבָה (Merivah), Greek: λοιδορία/ἀντιλογία (sense), Aramaic: מריבתא
translationNotes.note: “Quarreling/strife”; site of Israel’s contention over water (v. 7).

translationNotes.term: The New Moon and the full moon
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּחֹדֶשׁ / בַּכֵּסֶה (ba-chodesh / ba-keseh)
translationNotes.note: Israel's months began at the new moon, marked with trumpet blasts over the offerings (Numbers 10:10; 28:11-15). The seventh month opens with a horn blast on its first day (Leviticus 23:24) and its feast of booths begins at the full moon, the fifteenth (Leviticus 23:34); Passover week likewise begins on a fifteenth (Leviticus 23:5-6). Verse 3 names both moon markers because the feast runs from the one to the other.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַל־הַגִּתִּית (al-haggittit)
translationNotes.note: A heading term whose sense is not recoverable. It is built on gat, a winepress, which would suit a vintage melody, and it is also the adjective for Gath. It appears on three psalms only: 8, 81, and 84. What is certain is that it directs the performance rather than saying anything about the poem.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דּוּד (dud)
translationNotes.note: The carrying basket of Egyptian forced labour, hauled on the shoulder with mud and bricks in it (Exodus 1:14; 5:7-19). Tomb paintings at Thebes, among them the tomb of the vizier Rekhmire from the fifteenth century BC, show foreign workers mixing mud, striking bricks from moulds, and carrying them in exactly such baskets under an overseer with a stick.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm commands festival praise, recalls rescue and testing at Meribah, and records God’s offer of provision if Israel would listen.

headings.text: Sing for Joy to God Our Strength

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. According to Gittith. Of Asaph.

stories.title: ⚖️ Psalms 82
summaryBullets: God presides in the divine assembly; He renders judgment among the gods: (82:1).
“How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked? Selah (82:2).
Defend the cause of the weak and fatherless; uphold the rights of the afflicted and oppressed. (82:3).
Rescue the weak and needy; save them from the hand of the wicked. (82:4).
They do not know or understand; they wander in the darkness; all the foundations of the earth are shaken. (82:5).
I have said, ‘You are gods; you are all sons of the Most High.’ (82:6).
But like mortals you will die, and like rulers you will fall.” (82:7).
Arise, O God, judge the earth, for all the nations are Your inheritance. (82:8).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 10:18: The law says God Himself executes justice for the fatherless and the widow and loves the foreigner, feeding and clothing him. The psalm charges the judges of the divine assembly with abandoning the exact duty He performs.

Isaiah 3:13-15: The LORD rises to contend and stands to judge, and the accused are the elders and leaders of His own people, who have devoured the vineyard and ground the faces of the poor. Same courtroom, same defendants.

John 10:34: Jesus quotes verse 6 of this psalm, 'I have said you are gods,' when the crowd picks up stones to kill Him for blasphemy. He argues from it that if the word of God could address men that way, their charge against Him collapses.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֱלֹהִים (ʾelohim), Greek (LXX): θεοί/θεός, Aramaic: אלהין (elahin)
translationNotes.note: Term can denote God, gods, or human authorities depending on context (vv. 1, 6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲדַת־אֵל (ʿadat-ʾEl), Greek: συναγωγὴ θεῶν (LXX sense), Aramaic: כנשתא דאל
translationNotes.note: Assembly where God judges (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תִּשְׂאוּ־פָנִים (tis'u-panim)
translationNotes.note: Literally 'lift the face.' A litigant bowed before the judge, and the judge who raised his face had recognised him before hearing a word of the case. The Torah forbids it twice over: 'Do not show partiality in judging' (Deuteronomy 1:17) and 'Do not pervert justice or show partiality, and do not accept a bribe' (Deuteronomy 16:19).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דַּל, יָתוֹם, עָנִי, אֶבְיוֹן (dal, yatom, ani, evyon)
translationNotes.note: Four Hebrew words in verses 3 and 4 that English levels into 'weak, fatherless, afflicted, needy': the low, the orphan, the bowed down, the destitute. These are legal categories with rights attached, including the corners of the field and the dropped gleanings (Leviticus 19:9-10), the third-year tithe (Deuteronomy 14:28-29), and a public curse on anyone who twists their case (Deuteronomy 27:19).

stories.keyTakeaway: In the divine assembly God charges the gods with judging unjustly, commands them to defend the weak, the fatherless, and the oppressed, and declares that they will die like mortals; the psalm ends with a call for God to arise and judge the earth, since all the nations are His inheritance.

headings.text: God Presides in the Divine Assembly

stories.superscription: A Psalm of Asaph.

stories.title: 🛡️ Psalms 83
summaryBullets: O God, be not silent; be not speechless; be not still, O God. (83:1).
See how Your enemies rage, how Your foes have reared their heads. (83:2).
With cunning they scheme against Your people and conspire against those You cherish, (83:3).
saying, “Come, let us erase them as a nation; may the name of Israel be remembered no more.” (83:4).
For with one mind they plot together; they form an alliance against You— (83:5).
the tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites, of Moab and the Hagrites, (83:6).
of Gebal, Ammon, and Amalek, of Philistia with the people of Tyre. (83:7).
Even Assyria has joined them, lending strength to the sons of Lot. Selah (83:8).
Do to them as You did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the River Kishon, (83:9).
who perished at Endor and became like dung on the ground. (83:10).
Make their nobles like Oreb and Zeeb, and all their princes like Zebah and Zalmunna, (83:11).
who said, “Let us possess for ourselves the pastures of God.” (83:12).
Make them like tumbleweed, O my God, like chaff before the wind. (83:13).
As fire consumes a forest, as a flame sets the mountains ablaze, (83:14).
so pursue them with Your tempest, and terrify them with Your storm. (83:15).
Cover their faces with shame, that they may seek Your name, O LORD. (83:16).
May they be ever ashamed and terrified; may they perish in disgrace. (83:17).
May they know that You alone, whose name is the LORD, are Most High over all the earth. (83:18).
crossRefs: Judges 5:19-21: Deborah's war song, kings of Canaan fighting at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo, the stars fighting from their courses, and the Kishon sweeping the army away. That torrent is the defeat the psalm asks God to repeat.

Judges 7:24-25: Ephraim seizes the fords and captures the two princes of Midian, killing Oreb at the rock and Zeeb at the winepress that now carry their names. Gideon's pursuit ran on until the two Midianite kings named beside them fell as well.

Joshua 11:1-5: Jabin king of Hazor summons every northern king into one army as numerous as the sand on the seashore and encamps at the waters of Merom. The psalm lists an alliance of the same shape, ten peoples with one plan.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גַּלְגַּל (galgal), Greek (LXX): τροχός, Aramaic: גלגלא
translationNotes.note: Wind-driven debris imagery (v. 13).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֶלְיוֹן (ʿElyon), Greek: ὕψιστος, Aramaic: עלויא
translationNotes.note: Title asserting supremacy over all the earth (v. 18).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גְּבָל (Geval) - Hebrew: הַגְרִים (Hagrim)
translationNotes.note: Verses 6 through 8 draw a ring around Israel: Edom south of the Dead Sea, Moab east of it, Ammon north of Moab, the Ishmaelites and Hagrites in the eastern desert (1 Chronicles 5:10, 19), Amalek in the Negev, Philistia on the southern coast, Tyre on the northern coast, and Assyria far to the northeast. Gebal is the Phoenician port the Greeks called Byblos, named at Joshua 13:5 and Ezekiel 27:9.

translationNotes.term: Oreb and Zeeb, Zebah and Zalmunna
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֹרֵב, זְאֵב, זֶבַח, צַלְמֻנָּע
translationNotes.note: Four Midianite commanders from Gideon's campaign. Oreb was killed at the rock that took his name and Zeeb at the winepress of Zeeb (Judges 7:25); the two kings, Zebah and Zalmunna, were run down across the Jordan and executed (Judges 8:10-21). Sisera and Jabin fell earlier, when the Kishon flooded and swept away the chariots (Judges 4:15-16; 5:21).

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm lists allied nations plotting to erase Israel and petitions defeat like historic battles so that God’s name is known.
stories.superscription: A song. A Psalm of Asaph.

stories.title: 🏟️ Psalms 84
summaryBullets: How lovely is Your dwelling place, O LORD of Hosts! (84:1).
My soul longs, even faints, for the courts of the LORD; my heart and my flesh cry out for the living God. (84:2).
Even the sparrow has found a home, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she places her young near Your altars, O LORD of Hosts, my King and my God. (84:3).
How blessed are those who dwell in Your house! They are ever praising You. Selah (84:4).
Blessed are those whose strength is in You, whose hearts are set on pilgrimage. (84:5).
As they pass through the Valley of Baca, they make it a place of springs; even the autumn rain covers it with pools. (84:6).
They go from strength to strength, until each appears before God in Zion. (84:7).
O LORD God of Hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, O God of Jacob. Selah (84:8).
Take notice of our shield, O God, and look with favor on the face of Your anointed. (84:9).
For better is one day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of the wicked. (84:10).
For the LORD God is a sun and a shield; the LORD gives grace and glory; He withholds no good thing from those who walk with integrity. (84:11).
O LORD of Hosts, how blessed is the man who trusts in You! (84:12).
crossRefs: Psalm 27:4: David asks God for one thing only, to dwell in His house all his days and gaze on His beauty. This psalm makes the same request from the road, weighing one day in those courts against a thousand anywhere else.

Isaiah 2:2-3: Peoples calling to each other, come, let us go up to the mountain of the house of the LORD. That is the journey this psalm is sung on, hearts set on pilgrimage, going from strength to strength until each one appears before God in Zion.

1 Kings 8:10-13: At the dedication the cloud fills the house so the priests cannot stand to minister, and Solomon says he has built an exalted place for God to dwell in forever. That is the dwelling place the psalm opens by calling lovely.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵמֶק הַבָּכָא (ʿemeq ha-Baka), Greek: κοιλὰς τοῦ κλαυθμῶνος (LXX sense), Aramaic: עמקא דבכא
translationNotes.note: Uncertain place name; associated with “weeping” or balsam trees (v. 6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הִסְתֹּפֵף (histofef, ‘stand at the threshold’); Greek: παραστῆναι ἐπὶ θυρῶν
translationNotes.note: Lowly post at the threshold preferred to dwelling in tents of wickedness (v. 10).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּנֵי־קֹרַח (bnei Qorach)
translationNotes.note: Descendants of the Korah who led the revolt against Moses and Aaron and went down alive into the ground (Numbers 16:31-33). Numbers 26:11 records that the sons of Korah did not die. Their line served as temple gatekeepers and singers (1 Chronicles 9:19; 26:1-19), and eleven psalms carry their name: 42, 44 through 49, 84, 85, 87, and 88.

translationNotes.term: Whose hearts are set on pilgrimage
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְסִלּוֹת בִּלְבָבָם (mesillot bilvavam)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew says the highways are in their hearts. Every male was to appear before the LORD three times a year, at Unleavened Bread, at Weeks, and at Booths (Exodus 23:17; Deuteronomy 16:16), which meant a walk of days from anywhere in the country. 'They go from strength to strength' describes the stages of that walk, and verse 7 ends it where the road ends, before God in Zion.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm longs for God’s courts, notes blessing for those dwelling and journeying to Zion, and declares one day there better than a thousand.

headings.text: Better Is One Day in Your Courts

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. According to Gittith. A Psalm of the sons of Korah.

stories.title: 🕊️ Psalms 85
summaryBullets: You showed favor to Your land, O LORD; You restored Jacob from captivity. (85:1).
You forgave the iniquity of Your people; You covered all their sin. Selah (85:2).
You withheld all Your fury; You turned from Your burning anger. (85:3).
Restore us, O God of our salvation, and put away Your displeasure toward us. (85:4).
Will You be angry with us forever? Will You draw out Your anger to all generations? (85:5).
Will You not revive us again, that Your people may rejoice in You? (85:6).
Show us Your loving devotion, O LORD, and grant us Your salvation. (85:7).
I will listen to what God the LORD will say; for He will surely speak peace to His people and His saints; He will not let them return to folly. (85:8).
Surely His salvation is near to those who fear Him, that His glory may dwell in our land. (85:9).
Loving devotion and faithfulness have joined together; righteousness and peace have kissed. (85:10).
Faithfulness sprouts from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven. (85:11).
The LORD will indeed provide what is good, and our land will yield its increase. (85:12).
Righteousness will go before Him to prepare the way for His steps. (85:13).
crossRefs: Psalm 126:1-4: Another prayer built on a restoration already granted, asking God to do it once more, restore our captives like streams in the Negev. This psalm is built the same way, You restored Jacob, now restore us again.

Hosea 2:19-20: God betroths Israel to Himself in righteousness and justice, in loving devotion and compassion and faithfulness. The psalm gathers that vocabulary and makes the words meet, love and faithfulness joined, righteousness and peace kissing.

Leviticus 26:4: The covenant blessing promises rain in season, land that yields its produce and trees that bear fruit, for a people who keep God's statutes. The psalm's last lines claim it, the LORD will give what is good and our land will yield its increase.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שׁוּב שְׁבוּת (shuv shevut), Greek: ἐπιστρέψει τὴν αἰχμαλωσίαν, Aramaic: ישיב שבותא
translationNotes.note: Idiom for reversing captivity/circumstances (vv. 1, 4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (ḥesed) / אֱמֶת (ʾemet), Greek: ἔλεος / ἀλήθεια, Aramaic: חסדא / קושטא
translationNotes.note: Covenant loyalty and reliability (v. 10).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צֶדֶק וְשָׁלוֹם נָשָׁקוּ (tsedeq ve-shalom nashaqu)
translationNotes.note: Four covenant words are paired off in verse 10: hesed with emet, tsedeq with shalom. The kiss is the greeting between kinsmen who meet after a long parting, as when Esau ran to Jacob and kissed him (Genesis 33:4), or Aaron met Moses at the mountain of God (Exodus 4:27). The picture is a reunion, not a sentiment.

translationNotes.term: Our land will yield its increase
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְבוּלָהּ (yevulah)
translationNotes.note: Yevul is the produce a field actually gives up at harvest. Leviticus 26:4 promises rain in its season and a land that yields its increase, and Deuteronomy 11:14-17 ties the early and the latter rains directly to covenant faithfulness. On rain-fed hill-country terraces with no river to draw on, verse 12 is a statement about survival.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm recalls past restoration, asks for renewal, and describes righteousness and peace meeting as the land yields its increase.

headings.text: You Showed Favor to Your Land

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of the sons of Korah.

stories.title: 🙏 Psalms 86
summaryBullets: Incline Your ear, O LORD, and answer me, for I am poor and needy. (86:1).
Preserve my soul, for I am godly. You are my God; save Your servant who trusts in You. (86:2).
Be merciful to me, O Lord, for I call to You all day long. (86:3).
Bring joy to Your servant, for to You, O Lord, I lift up my soul. (86:4).
For You, O Lord, are kind and forgiving, rich in loving devotion to all who call on You. (86:5).
Hear my prayer, O LORD, and attend to my plea for mercy. (86:6).
In the day of my distress I call on You, because You answer me. (86:7).
O Lord, there is none like You among the gods, nor any works like Yours. (86:8).
All the nations You have made will come and bow before You, O Lord, and they will glorify Your name. (86:9).
For You are great and perform wonders; You alone are God. (86:10).
Teach me Your way, O LORD, that I may walk in Your truth. Give me an undivided heart, that I may fear Your name. (86:11).
I will praise You, O Lord my God, with all my heart; I will glorify Your name forever. (86:12).
For great is Your loving devotion to me; You have delivered me from the depths of Sheol. (86:13).
The arrogant rise against me, O God; a band of ruthless men seeks my life; they have no regard for You. (86:14).
But You, O Lord, are a compassionate and gracious God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness. (86:15).
Turn to me and have mercy; grant Your strength to Your servant; save the son of Your maidservant. (86:16).
Show me a sign of Your goodness, that my enemies may see and be ashamed; for You, O LORD, have helped me and comforted me. (86:17).
crossRefs: Exodus 34:6-7: God proclaims His own name as He passes before Moses on the mountain, compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness. The psalm quotes that self-description back to Him as the ground of its plea.
Psalm 27:11: The identical petition, teach me Your way, O LORD. There it asks for a level path because of enemies; here it goes on to ask for an undivided heart, one that will not split its loyalty.

Isaiah 60:3: Nations coming to your light and kings to the brightness of your dawn. The psalm states it as settled fact in the middle of a personal prayer, all the nations You have made will come and bow before You.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יַחֵד לְבָבִי (yaḥed levavi), Greek (LXX): ἑνώσον τὴν καρδίαν μου, Aramaic: חבר לבי
