translationNotes.note: Request for undivided inner focus (v. 11).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אוֹת לְטוֹבָה (ʾot le-tovah), Greek: σημεῖον εἰς ἀγαθόν, Aramaic: אתא לטבותא
translationNotes.note: Visible token of favor (v. 17).

The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
Hebrew: בֶּן־אֲמָתֶךָ (ben-amatekha)
translationNotes.note: Not a flourish of humility but a legal status. A servant born in the household, as against one bought at the market, belonged to it permanently and had the master's protection by right (Exodus 21:4; Genesis 14:14). Psalm 116:16 uses the same phrase. The plea in verse 16 is being made on the ground of that standing.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm pleads for preservation and instruction, quotes God’s merciful character, and asks for a sign of favor.
stories.superscription: A prayer of David.

stories.title: 🏙️ Psalms 87
summaryBullets: He has founded His city on the holy mountains. (87:1).
The LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob. (87:2).
Glorious things are ascribed to you, O city of God. Selah (87:3).
“I will mention Rahab and Babylon among those who know Me — along with Philistia, Tyre, and Cush — when I say, ‘This one was born in Zion.’” (87:4).
And it will be said of Zion: “This one and that one were born in her, and the Most High Himself will establish her.” (87:5).
The LORD will record in the register of the peoples: “This one was born in Zion.” Selah (87:6).
Singers and pipers will proclaim, “All my springs of joy are in You.” (87:7).
crossRefs: Isaiah 2:2-3: Many peoples streaming up to the mountain of the house of the LORD to be taught His ways. The psalm goes further than pilgrimage and enrolls them as natives, born in Zion rather than merely visiting her.

Psalm 48:1-3: Zion praised as the city of the great King, beautiful in loftiness, the joy of all the earth, with God shown to be a fortress within her citadels. This psalm takes up that praise and adds a birth register to it.

Isaiah 56:6-7: Foreigners who bind themselves to the LORD are brought to His holy mountain, and His house is named a house of prayer for all peoples. The psalm names those peoples outright, Rahab and Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Cush.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רַהַב (Rahav), Greek (LXX): Ῥαάβ, Aramaic: רהב
translationNotes.note: Poetic epithet for Egypt (v. 4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַעְיָן (maʿyan), Greek: πηγαί, Aramaic: מעינין
translationNotes.note: Sources of life/joy located in Zion (v. 7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יִסְפֹּר בִּכְתוֹב עַמִּים (yispor bikhtov ammim)
translationNotes.note: Towns kept written enrolment lists of citizens by birth. Ezra 2:59-63 records families struck from the priestly roll because they could not produce their registration, and Nehemiah 7:5 describes the book of the genealogy of those who came up first. Isaiah 4:3 speaks of everyone recorded for life in Jerusalem. Verse 6 pictures God keeping that ledger Himself.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כּוּשׁ (Kush) - Greek: Αἰθιοπία (Aithiopia)
translationNotes.note: The Nile kingdom upstream of Egypt, Nubia, in what is now northern Sudan; the Greek label Aithiopia is why older English Bibles print 'Ethiopia,' which is not the modern country of that name. Cush ruled Egypt outright as the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, and Tirhakah, whom 2 Kings 19:9 calls king of Cush, is the pharaoh Taharqa, who reigned 690-664 BC.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm speaks of Zion’s special status as the city God loves, with peoples enrolled as born there.

headings.text: The Lord Loves the Gates of Zion

stories.superscription: A Psalm of the sons of Korah. A song.

stories.title: 🌑 Psalms 88
summaryBullets: O LORD, the God of my salvation, day and night I cry out before You. (88:1).
May my prayer come before You; incline Your ear to my cry. (88:2).
For my soul is full of troubles, and my life draws near to Sheol. (88:3).
I am counted among those descending to the Pit. I am like a man without strength. (88:4).
I am forsaken among the dead, like the slain who lie in the grave, whom You remember no more, who are cut off from Your care. (88:5).
You have laid me in the lowest Pit, in the darkest of the depths. (88:6).
Your wrath weighs heavily upon me; all Your waves have submerged me. Selah (88:7).
You have removed my friends from me; You have made me repulsive to them; I am confined and cannot escape. (88:8).
My eyes grow dim with grief. I call to You daily, O LORD; I spread out my hands to You. (88:9).
Do You work wonders for the dead? Do departed spirits rise up to praise You? Selah (88:10).
Can Your loving devotion be proclaimed in the grave, Your faithfulness in Abaddon? (88:11).
Will Your wonders be known in the darkness, or Your righteousness in the land of oblivion? (88:12).
But to You, O LORD, I cry for help; in the morning my prayer comes before You. (88:13).
Why, O LORD, do You reject me? Why do You hide Your face from me? (88:14).
From my youth I was afflicted and near death. I have borne Your terrors; I am in despair. (88:15).
Your wrath has swept over me; Your terrors have destroyed me. (88:16).
All day long they engulf me like water; they enclose me on every side. (88:17).
You have removed my beloved and my friend; darkness is my closest companion. (88:18).
crossRefs: Psalm 6:5: The argument that death ends praise, since there is no mention of God in death and no one to praise Him from Sheol. This psalm presses it hardest, asking whether His wonders are known in the darkness or His righteousness in the land of oblivion.

Job 17:13-16: A man who has already spread his bed in darkness and called corruption his father and the worm his mother, then asks where his hope is. The psalm ends in that same place and never climbs back out of it.

Lamentations 3:7-9: Walled in so he cannot escape, weighed down with chains, his prayer shut out even as he cries for help. The psalm says the same thing about itself, confined with no way out and eyes grown dim with grief.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בּוֹר (bor), Greek: λάκκος, Aramaic: ברא
translationNotes.note: Grave/abyss imagery (vv. 4, 6).

The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
Hebrew: הֵימָן הָאֶזְרָחִי (Heman ha-Ezrachi)
translationNotes.note: The third of David's chief musicians beside Asaph and Jeduthun, a Kohathite Levite (1 Chronicles 6:33), appointed to sound the bronze cymbals when the ark came up (1 Chronicles 15:17-19). He is called the king's seer, and 1 Chronicles 25:5 records that God gave him fourteen sons and three daughters. This is the only psalm in his name.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַל־מָחֲלַת לְעַנּוֹת (al-machalat le'annot)
translationNotes.note: A performance rubric of uncertain sense. Machalath also heads Psalm 53 and may name a tune or an instrument; leannot is built on a root that carries both singing in response and being brought low. What is clear is that it directs how the piece was sung, and the piece it fronts is the one lament in the Psalter that ends in the dark with no turn.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲבַדּוֹן (Avaddon)
translationNotes.note: 'Destruction,' used as a name for the place of the dead. It stands beside Sheol at Proverbs 15:11 and Job 26:6, and beside Death itself at Job 28:22. Verse 11 asks whether God's covenant love gets reported there. Revelation 9:11 gives Abaddon as the name of the angel of the abyss, with Apollyon as its Greek.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm is an unrelieved lament describing nearness to death, isolation, and darkness while continuing to cry to God.
stories.superscription: A song. A Psalm of the sons of Korah. For the choirmaster. According to Mahalath Leannoth. A Maskil of Heman the Ezrahite.

stories.title: 🌟 Psalms 89
summaryBullets: I will sing of the loving devotion of the LORD forever; with my mouth I will proclaim Your faithfulness to all generations. (89:1).
For I have said, “Loving devotion is built up forever; in the heavens You establish Your faithfulness.” (89:2).
You said, “I have made a covenant with My chosen one, I have sworn to David My servant: (89:3).
‘I will establish your offspring forever and build up your throne for all generations.’” Selah (89:4).
The heavens praise Your wonders, O LORD — Your faithfulness as well — in the assembly of the holy ones. (89:5).
For who in the skies can compare with the LORD? Who among the heavenly beings is like the LORD? (89:6).
In the council of the holy ones, God is greatly feared, and awesome above all who surround Him. (89:7).
O LORD God of Hosts, who is like You? O mighty LORD, Your faithfulness surrounds You. (89:8).
You rule the raging sea; when its waves mount up, You still them. (89:9).
You crushed Rahab like a carcass; You scattered Your enemies with Your mighty arm. (89:10).
The heavens are Yours, and also the earth. The earth and its fullness You founded. (89:11).
North and south You created; Tabor and Hermon shout for joy at Your name. (89:12).
Mighty is Your arm; strong is Your hand. Your right hand is exalted. (89:13).
Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne; loving devotion and faithfulness go before You. (89:14).
Blessed are those who know the joyful sound, who walk, O LORD, in the light of Your presence. (89:15).
They rejoice in Your name all day long, and in Your righteousness they exult. (89:16).
For You are the glory of their strength, and by Your favor our horn is exalted. (89:17).
Surely our shield belongs to the LORD, and our king to the Holy One of Israel. (89:18).
You once spoke in a vision; to Your godly ones You said, “I have bestowed help on a warrior; I have exalted one chosen from the people. (89:19).
I have found My servant David; with My sacred oil I have anointed him. (89:20).
My hand will sustain him; surely My arm will strengthen him. (89:21).
No enemy will exact tribute; no wicked man will oppress him. (89:22).
I will crush his foes before him and strike down those who hate him. (89:23).
My faithfulness and loving devotion will be with him, and through My name his horn will be exalted. (89:24).
I will set his hand over the sea, and his right hand upon the rivers. (89:25).
He will call to Me, ‘You are my Father, my God, the Rock of my salvation.’ (89:26).
I will indeed appoint him as My firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth. (89:27).
I will forever preserve My loving devotion for him, and My covenant with him will stand fast. (89:28).
I will establish his line forever, his throne as long as the heavens endure. (89:29).
If his sons forsake My law and do not walk in My judgments, (89:30).
if they violate My statutes and fail to keep My commandments, (89:31).
I will attend to their transgression with the rod, and to their iniquity with stripes. (89:32).
But I will not withdraw My loving devotion from him, nor ever betray My faithfulness. (89:33).
I will not violate My covenant or alter the utterance of My lips. (89:34).
Once and for all I have sworn by My holiness — I will not lie to David — (89:35).
his offspring shall endure forever, and his throne before Me like the sun, (89:36).
like the moon, established forever, a faithful witness in the sky.” Selah (89:37).
Now, however, You have spurned and rejected him; You are enraged by Your anointed one. (89:38).
You have renounced the covenant with Your servant and sullied his crown in the dust. (89:39).
You have broken down all his walls; You have reduced his strongholds to rubble. (89:40).
All who pass by plunder him; he has become a reproach to his neighbors. (89:41).
You have exalted the right hand of his foes; You have made all his enemies rejoice. (89:42).
You have bent the edge of his sword and have not sustained him in battle. (89:43).
You have ended his splendor and cast his throne to the ground. (89:44).
You have cut short the days of his youth; You have covered him with shame. Selah (89:45).
How long, O LORD? Will You hide Yourself forever? Will Your wrath keep burning like fire? (89:46).
Remember the briefness of my lifespan! For what futility You have created all men! (89:47).
What man can live and never see death? Can he deliver his soul from the power of Sheol? Selah (89:48).
Where, O Lord, is Your loving devotion of old, which You faithfully swore to David? (89:49).
Remember, O Lord, the reproach of Your servants, which I bear in my heart from so many people — (89:50).
how Your enemies have taunted, O LORD, and have mocked every step of Your anointed one! (89:51).
Blessed be the LORD forever! Amen and amen. (89:52).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 7:12-16: The promise itself, delivered through Nathan, that David's throne will stand forever, his sons disciplined for wrongdoing but never stripped of loving devotion the way Saul was. The psalm quotes those terms, then asks why they now look broken.

Job 26:12: The same claim in nearly the same words, that by His power He stirred the sea and by His understanding He shattered Rahab. The psalm uses it as evidence, arguing that the God who crushed the sea can be trusted to keep an oath.

Psalm 97:2: The line this psalm shares word for word, righteousness and justice as the foundation of God's throne. Here it stands immediately before the covenant with David, so the human throne is set on that same footing.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּרִית (berit), Greek (LXX): διαθήκη (diathēkē), Aramaic: קיימא (qayyama)
translationNotes.note: Formal sworn commitment (vv. 3-4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רָהַב (Rahav), Greek: Ῥαάβ, Aramaic: רהב
translationNotes.note: Poetic name for a proud sea/chaos or Egypt (v. 10).

The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
Hebrew: אֵיתָן הָאֶזְרָחִי (Ethan ha-Ezrachi)
translationNotes.note: The measure of human wisdom in his own generation: 1 Kings 4:31 says Solomon was wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and than Heman, Calcol, and Darda. 1 Chronicles 15:17-19 sets an Ethan with Heman and Asaph over the music, sounding bronze cymbals before the ark. This is the only psalm bearing his name.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תְּרוּעָה (teruah)
translationNotes.note: Teruah is a specific noise: the blast or the war shout. It is the horn signal that breaks camp (Numbers 10:5-6), the shout that brought down Jericho (Joshua 6:5, 20), and the name of the first day of the seventh month, a memorial of teruah (Leviticus 23:24). Verse 15 blesses the people who know that sound, meaning the people who know what it is summoning them to.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm rehearses God’s sworn covenant with David, praises His power, and then laments present rejection and broken defenses.

headings.text: I Will Sing of His Love Forever

stories.superscription: A Maskil of Ethan the Ezrahite.

stories.title: ⏳ Psalms 90
summaryBullets: Lord, You have been our dwelling place through all generations. (90:1).
Before the mountains were born or You brought forth the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting You are God. (90:2).
You return man to dust, saying, “Return, O sons of mortals.” (90:3).
For in Your sight a thousand years are but a day that passes, or a watch of the night. (90:4).
You sweep them away in their sleep; they are like the new grass of the morning— (90:5).
in the morning it springs up new, but by evening it fades and withers. (90:6).
For we are consumed by Your anger and terrified by Your wrath. (90:7).
You have set our iniquities before You, our secret sins in the light of Your presence. (90:8).
For all our days decline in Your fury; we finish our years with a sigh. (90:9).
The length of our days is seventy years — or eighty if we are strong — yet their pride is but labor and sorrow, for they quickly pass, and we fly away. (90:10).
Who knows the power of Your anger? Your wrath matches the fear You are due. (90:11).
So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom. (90:12).
Return, O LORD! How long will it be? Have compassion on Your servants. (90:13).
Satisfy us in the morning with Your loving devotion, that we may sing for joy and be glad all our days. (90:14).
Make us glad for as many days as You have afflicted us, for as many years as we have seen evil. (90:15).
May Your work be shown to Your servants, and Your splendor to their children. (90:16).
May the favor of the Lord our God rest upon us; establish for us the work of our hands— yes, establish the work of our hands! (90:17).
crossRefs: Genesis 3:19: The sentence passed in Eden, you are dust and to dust you will return. The psalm of Moses turns that sentence into arithmetic, seventy years or eighty with strength, and then we fly away.

Psalm 39:4-5: David asks to be shown his end and the measure of his days, and calls a whole lifetime no more than a handbreadth before God. This psalm makes the same request at its turning point, teach us to number our days.
2 Peter 3:8: Peter takes up this psalm's measure of time, a day with the Lord like a thousand years and a thousand years like a day, to answer people who mock God for being slow to keep His promise.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תָּשֵׁב אֱנוֹשׁ עַד־דַּכָּא (tashev enosh ʿad-dakkāʾ, ‘crushed/dust’), Greek (LXX): ἀπόστρεψον… εἰς ταπείνωσιν, Aramaic: תשיב אנש עד דכא
translationNotes.note: Expression for mortality (v. 3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כּוֹנֵן (konen), Greek: κατευθῦνον/στήριξον, Aramaic: קַיֵּם
translationNotes.note: Make firm/confirm the work of our hands (v. 17).

Old Testament Hebrew time-keeping used three night watches (Lamentations 2:19). Roman-era New Testament texts use four watches, evening, midnight, cockcrow, and dawn (Mark 13:35), each about three hours long. The 'fourth watch' is roughly 3 a.m. to 6 a.m.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַשְׁמֻרָה (ashmurah); Greek: φυλακή (phylake)

translationNotes.term: A prayer of Moses the man of God
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תְּפִלָּה לְמֹשֶׁה אִישׁ־הָאֱלֹהִים (tefillah le-Mosheh ish ha-Elohim)
translationNotes.note: The only psalm headed with Moses' name, and the oldest heading in the book. 'Man of God' is a fixed title, used of Moses at Deuteronomy 33:1 and Joshua 14:6, and later of Samuel (1 Samuel 9:6), Elijah (1 Kings 17:18), and Elisha (2 Kings 4:9). Psalms 90 through 106 make up Book IV of the Psalter.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁבְעִים שָׁנָה (shiv'im shanah)
translationNotes.note: A measurement, not a promise. The figure sits against the ages recorded around Moses: he died at 120 with his eyes undimmed (Deuteronomy 34:7), Aaron at 123 (Numbers 33:39), Joshua at 110 (Joshua 24:29). Verse 12 draws the practical conclusion, to number the days rather than assume them.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm contrasts God’s eternity with human brevity, asks to number days wisely, and prays for compassion and established work.

headings.text: BOOK IV From Everlasting to Everlasting

stories.superscription: A prayer of Moses the man of God.

stories.title: 🛡️ Psalms 91
summaryBullets: He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty. (91:1).
I will say to the LORD, “You are my refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust.” (91:2).
Surely He will deliver you from the snare of the fowler, and from the deadly plague. (91:3).
He will cover you with His feathers; under His wings you will find refuge; His faithfulness is a shield and rampart. (91:4).
You will not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow that flies by day, (91:5).
nor the pestilence that stalks in the darkness, nor the calamity that destroys at noon. (91:6).
Though a thousand may fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand, no harm will come near you. (91:7).
You will only see it with your eyes and witness the punishment of the wicked. (91:8).
Because you have made the LORD your dwelling— my refuge, the Most High— (91:9).
no evil will befall you, no plague will approach your tent. (91:10).
For He will command His angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways. (91:11).
They will lift you up in their hands, so that you will not strike your foot against a stone. (91:12).
You will tread on the lion and cobra; you will trample the young lion and serpent. (91:13).
“Because he loves Me, I will deliver him; because he knows My name, I will protect him. (91:14).
When he calls out to Me, I will answer him; I will be with him in trouble. I will deliver him and honor him. (91:15).
With long life I will satisfy him and show him My salvation.” (91:16).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 32:11: The Song of Moses pictures God as an eagle stirring up its nest, hovering over the young, spreading its wings to catch them and carrying them on its pinions. The psalm compresses that to feathers and wings, cover and refuge.
Psalm 34:7: The angel of the LORD encamping around those who fear Him and delivering them, one guard for one man. This psalm makes it a standing order given to angels, to guard you in all your ways.

Matthew 4:6: The devil sets Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple and quotes verses 11 and 12 of this psalm back at Him, telling Him to jump because angels are commanded to catch Him. Jesus answers from the law, do not put the Lord your God to the test.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֶלְיוֹן (ʿElyon) / שַׁדַּי (Shaddai), Greek (LXX): Ὕψιστος / παντοκράτωρ, Aramaic: עליא / שַדַּי
translationNotes.note: Divine titles paired in v. 1.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַחְסֶה (maḥseh) / מְצוּדָה (metsudah), Greek: καταφυγή / ὀχύρωμα, Aramaic: מחסה / מצודתא
translationNotes.note: Places of protection (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דֶּבֶר (dever), Greek: λοιμός, Aramaic: דברא
translationNotes.note: Deadly plague (vv. 3, 6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פַּח יָקוּשׁ (pach yaqush)
translationNotes.note: A bird trap: a net that clapped shut or a baited stick that sprang, laid on the ground and covered over. Amos 3:5 asks whether a snare springs up when it has taken nothing. The image in verse 3 is not a danger you can face down but one built to be invisible until it closes.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶלֶף / רְבָבָה (eleph / revavah)
translationNotes.note: Israel's fighting men were organised in thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens with a commander over each (Exodus 18:21, 25; Deuteronomy 1:15). 'Thousand' and 'ten thousand' is the standard step up in Hebrew verse, as in the song about Saul and David at 1 Samuel 18:7. Verse 7 pictures a battle line collapsing on both sides of a man still standing.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm states protection, angelic guarding, and deliverance for the one who dwells in the Most High’s shelter.

headings.text: You Are My Refuge and My Fortress

stories.title: 🎶 Psalms 92
summaryBullets: It is good to praise the LORD, and to sing praises to Your name, O Most High, (92:1).
to proclaim Your loving devotion in the morning and Your faithfulness at night (92:2).
with the ten-stringed harp and the melody of the lyre. (92:3).
For You, O LORD, have made me glad by Your deeds; I sing for joy at the works of Your hands. (92:4).
How great are Your works, O LORD, how deep are Your thoughts! (92:5).
A senseless man does not know, and a fool does not understand, (92:6).
that though the wicked sprout like grass, and all evildoers flourish, they will be forever destroyed. (92:7).
But You, O LORD, are exalted forever! (92:8).
For surely Your enemies, O LORD, surely Your enemies will perish; all evildoers will be scattered. (92:9).
But You have exalted my horn like that of a wild ox; with fine oil I have been anointed. (92:10).
My eyes see the downfall of my enemies; my ears hear the wailing of my wicked foes. (92:11).
The righteous will flourish like a palm tree, and grow like a cedar in Lebanon. (92:12).
Planted in the house of the LORD, they will flourish in the courts of our God. (92:13).
In old age they will still bear fruit; healthy and green they will remain, (92:14).
to proclaim, “The LORD is upright; He is my Rock, and in Him there is no unrighteousness.” (92:15).
crossRefs: Psalm 1:3-4: The same pair of images, a tree planted by streams that yields fruit and does not wither, set against chaff the wind drives off. This psalm keeps the pair but changes the plants, evildoers sprouting like grass, the righteous growing like a palm.

1 Kings 6:15-18: Solomon lined the temple interior with cedar from floor to ceiling, carved with gourds and open flowers, until not a stone could be seen. That is the wood behind the psalm's righteous man, grown like a cedar and planted in the house of the LORD.

Leviticus 23:3: The Sabbath heads the list of the LORD's appointed times, six days of work and a seventh of complete rest and sacred assembly. This is the only psalm whose title assigns it to that day, sung on the day no work was done.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (ḥesed) / אֱמֶת (ʾemet), Greek: ἔλεος / ἀλήθεια, Aramaic: חסדא / קושטא
translationNotes.note: Paired covenant terms (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תָּרִים כְּרֶאֵם קַרְנִי (tarim k’rem qarni), Greek: ὑψωθήσεται τὸ κέρας μου, Aramaic: תרום קרני
translationNotes.note: Symbol of strength/status (v. 10).

The seventh day, set apart by God's command (Exodus 20:8-11). All work ceased from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday. By Jesus' day, rabbinical tradition had elaborated 39 categories of forbidden labor; many of Jesus' healings deliberately challenged those additional rules without violating the Torah command itself.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁבָּת (shabbat); Greek: σάββατον (sabbaton)

translationNotes.term: A song for the Sabbath day
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁיר לְיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת (shir le-yom ha-shabbat)
translationNotes.note: The heading assigns the psalm to a day of the week. The Mishnah, in tractate Tamid 7:4, records the psalm the Levites sang over the daily offering in the temple: Psalm 24 on the first day, 48 on the second, 82 on the third, 94 on the fourth, 81 on the fifth, 93 on the sixth, and this one on the Sabbath.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תָּמָר / אֶרֶז (tamar / erez)
translationNotes.note: Two long-lived trees from opposite country. The date palm stands in desert heat around springs and keeps bearing fruit for decades; the cedar of Lebanon grows on cold mountain slopes and stands for centuries. Solomon panelled the temple in cedar and carved palm trees on its walls and doors (1 Kings 6:29-32), so the worshipper hearing verse 12 was standing inside both images.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm for the Sabbath contrasts perishing wicked with flourishing righteous and affirms the LORD’s uprightness.
stories.superscription: A Psalm. A song for the Sabbath day.

stories.title: 👑 Psalms 93
summaryBullets: The LORD reigns! He is robed in majesty; the LORD has clothed and armed Himself with strength. The world indeed is firmly established; it cannot be moved. (93:1).
Your throne was established long ago; You are from all eternity. (93:2).
The floodwaters have risen, O LORD; the rivers have raised their voice; the seas lift up their pounding waves. (93:3).
Above the roar of many waters— the mighty breakers of the sea— the LORD on high is majestic. (93:4).
Your testimonies are fully confirmed; holiness adorns Your house, O LORD, for all the days to come. (93:5).
crossRefs: Psalm 29:10: The LORD enthroned over the flood and enthroned as King forever. This psalm builds its whole argument on that one claim, floodwaters lifting their voice while a throne established long ago does not move.

Psalm 96:10: The same sentence sent out as an announcement rather than sung in the courts, the LORD reigns and the world is firmly established so it cannot be moved. There it is what the nations are told; here it is what the singer sees.

1 Chronicles 16:29: David's charge on the day the ark came to Jerusalem, to worship the LORD in the splendor of His holiness. The psalm ends on that word, holiness adorning God's house for all the days to come.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָלַךְ (malakh), Greek: ἐβασίλευσεν, Aramaic: מלך
translationNotes.note: Royal assertion “The LORD has become king” (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵדֹתֶיךָ (ʿedotekha), Greek: μαρτύριά σου, Aramaic: סהדותך
translationNotes.note: Divine statutes/witnesses (v. 5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לָבֵשׁ / הִתְאַזָּר (lavesh / hit'azzar)
translationNotes.note: Two clothing verbs. To gird was to hitch the long robe up into the belt so a man could run or fight, as Elijah did before he outran Ahab's chariot (1 Kings 18:46). Verse 1 dresses the LORD as a king arming Himself, and the sentence that follows says the world stands firm because of it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְהָרוֹת (neharot)
translationNotes.note: A nahar is a river or a wadi torrent. In the Judean hills a dry stone channel can run head-high within an hour of a winter storm and take away anything in it. Verse 4 adds the breakers of the Mediterranean. Between them, verses 3 and 4 name the loudest and least manageable forces a Judean ever met, and set the LORD above both.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm declares the LORD’s everlasting reign and greater power than the surging floods, with firm testimonies and holy house.

stories.title: ⚒️ Psalms 94
summaryBullets: O LORD, God of vengeance, O God of vengeance, shine forth. (94:1).
Rise up, O Judge of the earth; render a reward to the proud. (94:2).
How long will the wicked, O LORD, how long will the wicked exult? (94:3).
They pour out arrogant words; all workers of iniquity boast. (94:4).
They crush Your people, O LORD; they oppress Your heritage. (94:5).
They kill the widow and the foreigner; they murder the fatherless. (94:6).
They say, “The LORD does not see; the God of Jacob pays no heed.” (94:7).
Take notice, O senseless among the people! O fools, when will you be wise? (94:8).
He who affixed the ear, can He not hear? He who formed the eye, can He not see? (94:9).
He who admonishes the nations, does He not discipline? He who teaches man, does He lack knowledge? (94:10).
The LORD knows the thoughts of man, that they are futile. (94:11).
Blessed is the man You discipline, O LORD, and teach from Your law, (94:12).
to grant him relief from days of trouble, until a pit is dug for the wicked. (94:13).
For the LORD will not forsake His people; He will never abandon His heritage. (94:14).
Surely judgment will again be righteous, and all the upright in heart will follow it. (94:15).
Who will rise up for me against the wicked? Who will stand for me against the workers of iniquity? (94:16).
Unless the LORD had been my helper, I would soon have dwelt in the abode of silence. (94:17).
If I say, “My foot is slipping,” Your loving devotion, O LORD, supports me. (94:18).
When anxiety overwhelms me, Your consolation delights my soul. (94:19).
Can a corrupt throne be Your ally — one devising mischief by decree? (94:20).
They band together against the righteous and condemn the innocent to death. (94:21).
But the LORD has been my stronghold, and my God is my rock of refuge. (94:22).
He will bring upon them their own iniquity and destroy them for their wickedness. The LORD our God will destroy them. (94:23).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 10:18: The law says God executes justice for the fatherless and the widow and loves the foreigner, feeding and clothing him. The psalm reports the exact reverse on the ground, widow and foreigner killed and the fatherless murdered.

Proverbs 20:12: Ears that hear and eyes that see, the LORD has made them both. The psalm turns that proverb into a question aimed at men who say God pays no heed, He who affixed the ear, can He not hear.

Nahum 1:2: A jealous and avenging God who takes vengeance on His foes and reserves wrath for His enemies. The psalm opens by calling on that same title twice in one breath, O God of vengeance, shine forth.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְקָמוֹת (neqamot), Greek: ἐκδικήσεις, Aramaic: נקמתא
translationNotes.note: Lawful retribution claimed by God (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִשְׂגָּב (misgav), Greek: καταφυγή, Aramaic: מבגא
translationNotes.note: High refuge (v. 22).

translationNotes.term: The widow, the foreigner, the fatherless
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַלְמָנָה, גֵּר, יָתוֹם (almanah, ger, yatom)
translationNotes.note: The three classes with no clan to take their side, named together throughout the law. They hold specific rights: the corners of the field and the dropped grain (Leviticus 19:9-10), the forgotten sheaf and the second pass over the olive and the vine (Deuteronomy 24:19-21), and the tithe of the third year (Deuteronomy 14:28-29). Killing them, in verse 6, is the extreme end of a crime the law already treats as capital contempt.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דּוּמָה (dumah)
translationNotes.note: Dumah means silence, used here as a name for the grave. The same idea runs through Psalm 115:17, 'It is not the dead who praise the LORD, nor any who descend into silence.' Verse 17 says the psalmist would already be living there if the LORD had not helped.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm appeals to the judge of the earth against murderous injustice and states that the LORD sees, disciplines, consoles, and repays.

headings.text: The Lord Will Not Forget His People

stories.title: 🎺 Psalms 95
summaryBullets: Come, let us sing for joy to the LORD; let us shout to the Rock of our salvation! (95:1).
Let us enter His presence with thanksgiving; let us make a joyful noise to Him in song. (95:2).
For the LORD is a great God, a great King above all gods. (95:3).
In His hand are the depths of the earth, and the mountain peaks belong to Him. (95:4).
The sea is His, for He made it, and His hands formed the dry land. (95:5).
O come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the LORD our Maker. (95:6).
For He is our God, and we are the people of His pasture, the sheep under His care. Today, if you hear His voice, (95:7).
do not harden your hearts as you did at Meribah, in the day at Massah in the wilderness, (95:8).
where your fathers tested and tried Me, though they had seen My work. (95:9).
For forty years I was angry with that generation, and I said, “They are a people whose hearts go astray, and they have not known My ways.” (95:10).
So I swore on oath in My anger, “They shall never enter My rest.” (95:11).
crossRefs: Exodus 17:7: Moses names the place Massah and Meribah, testing and quarreling, after Israel demanded water and asked whether the LORD was among them. The psalm hands that place name to the congregation as a warning about today.

Numbers 14:22-23: The oath itself. After the spies' report God swears that not one of the men who saw His signs and tested Him ten times will see the land He promised their fathers. The psalm ends on that sentence, they shall never enter My rest.

Hebrews 3:7-11: The letter to the Hebrews quotes this psalm's closing verses in full, attributes them to the Holy Spirit, and builds two chapters of argument on the single word Today, warning its readers not to repeat the wilderness generation's refusal.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַל־תַּקְשׁוּ לְבַבְכֶם (ʾal-taqshu levavkhem), Greek: μὴ σκληρύνητε τὰς καρδίας, Aramaic: לא תקשון לבכון
translationNotes.note: Refusal to heed (v. 8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁחָה (shachah)
translationNotes.note: To bow down or prostrate oneself in humility. Used for reverence toward God (Genesis 22:5; Exodus 4:31; Psalm 95:6; Isaiah 66:23) but also for kings or angels. Very physical and posture-centered.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְנוּחָה (menuḥah), Greek: κατάπαυσις, Aramaic: נחותא
translationNotes.note: State/place of settling (v. 11).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְרִיבָה / מַסָּה (Merivah / Massah)
translationNotes.note: Two names given to one place at Rephidim, where Israel demanded water and asked whether the LORD was among them or not. Meribah means quarrelling, Massah means testing, and Moses named the site with both words (Exodus 17:1-7). A second Meribah is named later at Kadesh (Numbers 20:13). English keeps the names and drops their meanings, so verse 8 reads as geography when it is an accusation.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַרְבָּעִים שָׁנָה (arba'im shanah)
translationNotes.note: A sentence with a fixed term. Numbers 14:33-34 sets the wilderness years at one for each of the forty days the twelve spies were in the land, until the generation that refused to enter had died in the desert. Verse 11 quotes the oath from that day: they shall never enter My rest.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm summons joyful worship of the Maker and warns against hardening the heart as in the wilderness testing.

stories.title: 🌍 Psalms 96
summaryBullets: Sing to the LORD a new song; sing to the LORD, all the earth. (96:1).
Sing to the LORD, bless His name; proclaim His salvation day after day. (96:2).
Declare His glory among the nations, His wonders among all peoples. (96:3).
For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; He is to be feared above all gods. (96:4).
For all the gods of the nations are idols, but it is the LORD who made the heavens. (96:5).
Splendor and majesty are before Him; strength and beauty fill His sanctuary. (96:6).
Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the nations, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength. (96:7).
Ascribe to the LORD the glory due His name; bring an offering and enter His courts. (96:8).
Worship the LORD in the splendor of His holiness; tremble before Him, all the earth. (96:9).
Declare among the nations: “The LORD reigns!” The world is firmly established; it cannot be moved; He will judge the peoples with equity. (96:10).
Let the heavens be glad and the earth rejoice; let the sea resound, and all that fills it. (96:11).
Let the fields exult, and all that is in them. Then all the trees of the forest will sing for joy (96:12).
before the LORD, for He is coming— He is coming to judge the earth. He will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in His faithfulness. (96:13).
crossRefs: 1 Chronicles 16:23-33: Nearly this whole psalm stands there as the song David handed to Asaph on the day the ark came into Jerusalem, from sing to the LORD all the earth down to the trees of the forest singing before Him.

Psalm 93:1: The same declaration this psalm orders carried to the nations, the LORD reigns and the world is firmly established so it cannot be moved. There it is worship; here it is a message given to messengers.

Acts 17:24: Paul tells the Athenians that the God who made the world and everything in it is Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples built by hands. The psalm makes the same case, the gods of the peoples are idols and the LORD made the heavens.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֱלִילִים (ʾelilim, ‘nothings’), Greek: εἴδωλα, Aramaic: אלילין
translationNotes.note: Contrast with the Maker (v. 5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּהַדְרַת־קֹדֶשׁ (behadrat-qodesh), Greek: ἁγιωσύνη/εὐπρέπεια, Aramaic: הדרתא דקודשא
translationNotes.note: Worship attire/beauty (v. 9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁיר חָדָשׁ (shir chadash)
translationNotes.note: The call is for a song matched to a fresh act of rescue, not for a new tune to old words. It turns up at Psalm 33:3, 40:3, 96:1, 98:1, 144:9, and 149:1, and at Isaiah 42:10, always tied to something God has just done.

Almost all of Psalm 96 stands in 1 Chronicles 16:23-33 as part of the song David handed to Asaph and his brothers on the day the ark came into Jerusalem. The verses around it there are drawn from Psalm 105:1-15 and Psalm 106:1, 47-48. The Psalter and Chronicles are preserving the same temple liturgy.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm calls all nations and creation to praise because the LORD reigns and is coming to judge with righteousness.

headings.text: Sing to the Lord, All the Earth

stories.title: ⚡ Psalms 97
summaryBullets: The LORD reigns, let the earth rejoice; let the distant shores be glad. (97:1).
Clouds and darkness surround Him; righteousness and justice are His throne’s foundation. (97:2).
Fire goes before Him and consumes His foes on every side. (97:3).
His lightning illuminates the world; the earth sees and trembles. (97:4).
The mountains melt like wax at the presence of the LORD, before the Lord of all the earth. (97:5).
The heavens proclaim His righteousness; all the peoples see His glory. (97:6).
All worshipers of images are put to shame — those who boast in idols. Worship Him, all you gods! (97:7).
Zion hears and rejoices, and the towns of Judah exult because of Your judgments, O LORD. (97:8).
For You, O LORD, are Most High over all the earth; You are exalted far above all gods. (97:9).
Hate evil, O you who love the LORD! He preserves the souls of His saints; He delivers them from the hand of the wicked. (97:10).
Light shines on the righteous, gladness on the upright in heart. (97:11).
Rejoice in the LORD, you righteous ones, and praise His holy name. (97:12).
crossRefs: Exodus 19:16-18: Thunder and lightning, a thick cloud, a long blast of the ram's horn, and Sinai wrapped in smoke like a furnace because the LORD came down on it in fire. The psalm reuses that scene, fire going ahead of Him and mountains melting like wax.

Psalm 89:14: The identical line, righteousness and justice as the foundation of God's throne, used there to argue against the collapse of David's house. Here it sits inside cloud and darkness, so what surrounds the throne hides what holds it up.

Habakkuk 3:3-6: A prophet's vision of God on the march, glory covering the heavens, plague going before Him, the ancient mountains crumbling when He looks. The psalm describes the same arrival with the same equipment.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָרָפֶל (ʿaraphel), Greek: γνόφος, Aramaic: ערפלא
translationNotes.note: Storm-theophany term (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זֵכֶר קָדְשׁוֹ (zekher qodsho), Greek: τὸ μνημόσυνον τῆς ἁγιωσύνης αὐτοῦ, Aramaic: דכירא דקודשיה
translationNotes.note: Name set apart (v. 12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אִיִּים (iyyim)
translationNotes.note: Coastlands and islands. In Hebrew the word marks the far western rim of the known world, the Mediterranean coasts and islands that Phoenician shipping reached (Isaiah 41:5; 42:4; Jeremiah 2:10). Verse 1 is calling in the places furthest from Zion.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֱלֹהִים (elohim) - Greek: ἄγγελοι (angeloi)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew word in verse 7 is elohim, which the same psalm has just used of the LORD Himself in verse 1. The Greek Old Testament translates it here as angeloi, angels. Psalm 82:1 and 82:6 raise the same question of range for the word.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm depicts the LORD’s reign with storm imagery, exposes idols, and notes joy for Zion and light for the righteous.

stories.title: 🎺 Psalms 98
summaryBullets: Sing to the LORD a new song, for He has done wonders; His right hand and holy arm have gained Him the victory. (98:1).
The LORD has proclaimed His salvation and revealed His righteousness to the nations. (98:2).
He has remembered His love and faithfulness to the house of Israel; all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God. (98:3).
Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth; break forth — let your cry ring out, and sing praises! (98:4).
Sing praises to the LORD with the lyre, in melodious song with the harp. (98:5).
With trumpets and the blast of the ram’s horn shout for joy before the LORD, the King. (98:6).
Let the sea resound, and all that fills it, the world, and all who dwell in it. (98:7).
Let the rivers clap their hands, let the mountains sing together for joy (98:8).
before the LORD, for He comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness and the peoples with equity. (98:9).
crossRefs: Isaiah 52:10: The LORD bares His holy arm in the sight of all the nations so that the ends of the earth see the salvation of our God. The psalm opens with that arm and closes the thought with the same ends of the earth having seen it.

Psalm 96:11-13: The companion psalm ends the same way, heavens glad and sea resounding because God is coming to judge the earth with righteousness. This one adds the rivers clapping their hands and the mountains singing together.
Luke 1:54-55: Mary's song lands where this psalm's third verse does, God helping His servant Israel because He remembered the mercy He had promised the fathers.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זְרוֹעַ קָדְשׁוֹ (zeroaʿ qodsho), Greek: βραχίων ἅγιός, Aramaic: דרועא קדישא
translationNotes.note: Powerful action attributed to God (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הָרִיעוּ (hariʿu), Greek: ἀλαλάξατε, Aramaic: הריעו
translationNotes.note: Shout of praise (vv. 4, 6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲצֹצְרוֹת / שׁוֹפָר (chatsotserot / shofar)
translationNotes.note: Two different instruments that English often prints with one word. The chatsotserot are the pair of hammered silver trumpets Moses was told to make, blown by the priests to summon the assembly, to break camp, and over the offerings at feasts and new moons (Numbers 10:1-10). The shofar is a ram's horn, sounded for alarm, for the jubilee (Leviticus 25:9), and at a king's accession (2 Samuel 15:10). Verse 6 calls for both at once.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּנּוֹר / נֵבֶל (kinnor / nevel)
translationNotes.note: The kinnor is the small hand-held lyre, the instrument David played to Saul (1 Samuel 16:23) and the one hung on the poplars in Psalm 137:2. The nevel is the bigger, deeper-toned stringed instrument, sometimes made with ten strings (Psalm 33:2; 144:9). English versions swap the labels 'harp' and 'lyre' between the two, so the pairing in verse 5 matters more than which word a given Bible uses.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm summons loud praise from people and creation because the LORD’s salvation is revealed and He is coming to judge.

headings.text: Sing to the Lord a New Song

stories.superscription: A Psalm.

stories.title: 🕯️ Psalms 99
summaryBullets: The LORD reigns; let the nations tremble! He is enthroned above the cherubim; let the earth quake! (99:1).
Great is the LORD in Zion; He is exalted above all the peoples. (99:2).
Let them praise Your great and awesome name — He is holy! (99:3).
The mighty King loves justice. You have established equity; You have exercised justice and righteousness in Jacob. (99:4).
Exalt the LORD our God, and worship at His footstool; He is holy! (99:5).
Moses and Aaron were among His priests; Samuel was among those who called on His name. They called to the LORD and He answered. (99:6).
He spoke to them from the pillar of cloud; they kept His decrees and the statutes He gave them. (99:7).
O LORD our God, You answered them. You were a forgiving God to them, yet an avenger of their misdeeds. (99:8).
Exalt the LORD our God and worship at His holy mountain, for the LORD our God is holy. (99:9).
crossRefs: Exodus 25:22: God tells Moses He will meet him above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim over the ark of the Testimony, and speak with him from there. That is the seat the psalm means by enthroned above the cherubim.

1 Samuel 7:9: Samuel offers a nursing lamb as a whole burnt offering, cries out to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answers him. The psalm names him beside Moses and Aaron as one who called and was answered.
Leviticus 19:2: Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy, spoken to the whole congregation of Israel. The psalm turns that into a refrain shouted three times, and the third one ends the poem.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כְּרֻבִים (keruvim), Greek: χερουβίμ, Aramaic: כרובין
translationNotes.note: Winged throne guardians over the ark (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קָדוֹשׁ (qadosh), Greek: ἅγιος, Aramaic: קדיש
translationNotes.note: Set apart; refrain in vv. 3, 5, 9.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֲדֹם רַגְלָיו (hadom raglav)
translationNotes.note: David calls the ark of the covenant the footstool of our God (1 Chronicles 28:2), and Lamentations 2:1 mourns that He did not remember His footstool in the day of His anger. Thrones in the region came with a matching footstool; the one recovered from Tutankhamun's tomb is carved with bound foreign captives underfoot. To worship at the footstool, in verse 5, is to come to the ark.

translationNotes.term: Moses and Aaron among His priests
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֹּהֲנָיו (kohanav)
translationNotes.note: Aaron was the first high priest (Exodus 28:1) and Moses performed the priestly acts himself at the tabernacle's consecration, before the line was handed over (Leviticus 8:14-30). Samuel, added in the same verse, grew up serving at Shiloh under Eli and was a Levite by descent through Kohath (1 Chronicles 6:33-38), though 1 Samuel 1:1 places his family in the hill country of Ephraim.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm proclaims the LORD’s holy reign from between the cherubim, recalls responses to Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, and repeats that He is holy.

stories.title: 🎉 Psalms 100
summaryBullets: Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth. (100:1).
Serve the LORD with gladness; come into His presence with joyful songs. (100:2).
Know that the LORD is God. It is He who made us, and we are His; we are His people, and the sheep of His pasture. (100:3).
Enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise; give thanks to Him and bless His name. (100:4).
For the LORD is good, and His loving devotion endures forever; His faithfulness continues to all generations. (100:5).
crossRefs: Psalm 95:6-7: The same call to kneel before the LORD our Maker because we are the people of His pasture and the sheep under His care. That psalm follows the line with a warning about hardened hearts, this one follows it with thanksgiving.

Psalm 118:19: Open to me the gates of righteousness, that I may enter and give thanks, spoken by one man arriving. This psalm gives the same instruction to a whole congregation, enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise.

Exodus 34:6: God proclaims His own name to Moses, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness. The psalm's last verse is that proclamation in miniature, the LORD is good, His loving devotion endures forever, His faithfulness to all generations.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְלֹא אֲנַחְנוּ (ve-loʾ anaḥnu, alt. qere: וְלוֹ אֲנַחְנוּ ‘and His are we’), Greek: καὶ οὐχ ἡμεῖς, Aramaic: ודיליה אנחנא
translationNotes.note: Textual note on reading in v. 3 (ketiv/qere).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (ḥesed) / אֱמוּנָה (ʾemunah), Greek: ἔλεος / ἀλήθεια/πιστότης, Aramaic: חסדא / הימנותא
translationNotes.note: Enduring attributes in v. 5.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִזְמוֹר לְתוֹדָה (mizmor le-todah)
translationNotes.note: Todah is both the thank offering and the song sung over it. Leviticus 7:12-15 sets out that offering: unleavened cakes and wafers mixed with oil, well-kneaded loaves of leavened bread, and meat that had to be eaten the same day with nothing left until morning. This psalm is the liturgy for walking that offering into the courts.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁעָרָיו / חֲצֵרֹתָיו (she'arav / chatserotav)
translationNotes.note: The temple was graded space. Solomon built a great court for the people and an inner court for the priests (1 Kings 6:36; 7:12), and past that stood the holy place and the most holy place, which no worshipper entered. 'Enter His gates' names how far a pilgrim went, and verse 4 treats that as the whole point of the trip.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm summons all the earth to glad service and grateful entry to God’s courts, stating His enduring love and faithfulness.
stories.superscription: A Psalm of thanksgiving.

stories.title: 🏛️ Psalms 101
summaryBullets: I will sing of Your loving devotion and justice; to You, O LORD, I will sing praises. (101:1).
I will ponder the way that is blameless — when will You come to me? I will walk in my house with integrity of heart. (101:2).
I will set no worthless thing before my eyes. I hate the work of those who fall away; it shall not cling to me. (101:3).
A perverse heart shall depart from me; I will know nothing of evil. (101:4).
Whoever slanders his neighbor in secret, I will put to silence; the one with haughty eyes and a proud heart, I will not endure. (101:5).
My eyes favor the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with me; he who walks in the way of integrity shall minister to me. (101:6).
No one who practices deceit shall dwell in my house; no one who tells lies shall stand in my presence. (101:7).
Every morning I will remove all the wicked of the land, that I may cut off every evildoer from the city of the LORD. (101:8).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 8:15: The one-line verdict on David's reign, that he administered justice and righteousness for all his people. This psalm is the policy behind that verdict, written in the first person as a set of rules for his own conduct.

Psalm 15:1-5: The question of who may dwell on God's holy mountain, answered entirely by conduct, no slander, no harm to a neighbor, no bribe taken against the innocent. This psalm applies the same test to everyone who serves inside the king's house.

Deuteronomy 13:5: The law's phrase for cutting corruption out of Israel, you must purge the evil from among you. The psalm makes that judicial duty the daily work of the throne, every morning removing the wicked of the land.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (ḥesed) / מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat), Greek: ἔλεος / κρίσις, Aramaic: חסדא / דינא
translationNotes.note: Key virtues the singer promises to celebrate (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דֶּרֶךְ תָּמִים (derekh tamim), Greek: ὁδὸς ἀμώμητος, Aramaic: אורח תמים
translationNotes.note: A whole, unimpaired manner of life (vv. 2, 6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּיתִי (beiti)
translationNotes.note: Bayit means the building and the household inside it, which for a king meant his court: the officers, scribes, and dependants who ate at his table and ran the kingdom (2 Samuel 9:7-13; 1 Kings 4:1-6). Verses 5 through 7 are hiring policy. The slanderer and the liar are not being kept out of a home; they are being kept out of government.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לַבְּקָרִים (labbeqarim)
translationNotes.note: Court sat at first light, before the heat, at the city gate. Absalom rose early and stood beside the gate to catch petitioners on their way in (2 Samuel 15:2), and Jeremiah 21:12 orders the house of David to administer justice every morning. Verse 8 describes the king's daily docket, not a mood on waking.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm states a commitment to personal and administrative integrity and to removing deceit and evil from the city.

headings.text: I Will Set No Worthless Thing before My Eyes

stories.superscription: A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🕯️ Psalms 102
summaryBullets: Hear my prayer, O LORD; let my cry for help come before You. (102:1).
Do not hide Your face from me in my day of distress. Incline Your ear to me; answer me quickly when I call. (102:2).
For my days vanish like smoke, and my bones burn like glowing embers. (102:3).
My heart is afflicted, and withered like grass; I even forget to eat my bread. (102:4).
Through my loud groaning my skin hangs on my bones. (102:5).
I am like a desert owl, like an owl among the ruins. (102:6).
I lie awake; I am like a lone bird on a housetop. (102:7).
All day long my enemies taunt me; they ridicule me and curse me. (102:8).
For I have eaten ashes like bread and mixed my drink with tears (102:9).
because of Your indignation and wrath, for You have picked me up and cast me aside. (102:10).
My days are like lengthening shadows, and I wither away like grass. (102:11).
But You, O LORD, sit enthroned forever; Your renown endures to all generations. (102:12).
You will rise up and have compassion on Zion, for it is time to show her favor — the appointed time has come. (102:13).
For Your servants delight in her stones and take pity on her dust. (102:14).
So the nations will fear the name of the LORD, and all the kings of the earth will fear Your glory. (102:15).
For the LORD will rebuild Zion; He has appeared in His glory. (102:16).
He will turn toward the prayer of the destitute; He will not despise their prayer. (102:17).
Let this be written for the generation to come, so that a people not yet created may praise the LORD. (102:18).
For He looked down from the heights of His sanctuary; the LORD gazed out from heaven to earth (102:19).
to hear a prisoner’s groaning, to release those condemned to death, (102:20).
that they may proclaim the name of the LORD in Zion and praise Him in Jerusalem, (102:21).
when peoples and kingdoms assemble to serve the LORD. (102:22).
He has broken my strength on the way; He has cut short my days. (102:23).
I say: “O my God, do not take me in the midst of my days! Your years go on through all generations. (102:24).
In the beginning You laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands. (102:25).
They will perish, but You remain; they will all wear out like a garment. Like clothing You will change them, and they will be passed on. (102:26).
But You remain the same, and Your years will never end. (102:27).
The children of Your servants will dwell securely, and their descendants will be established before You.” (102:28).
crossRefs: Hebrews 1:10-12: The letter to the Hebrews quotes this psalm's closing lines and addresses them to the Son, arguing that the One who laid the foundations of the earth outlasts the heavens He made, which wear out like a garment and get rolled up like a robe.

Lamentations 5:19: You, O LORD, reign forever, Your throne enduring from generation to generation, said standing in the ruins of Jerusalem. The psalm makes the same turn at its midpoint, from a man withering like grass to a God enthroned forever.

Isaiah 61:1: Good news to the poor and liberty to the captives, the errand of the Anointed. The psalm gives God the same errand, looking down from heaven to hear a prisoner's groaning and release those condemned to death.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָנִי (ʿani), Greek: πτωχός, Aramaic: עני
translationNotes.note: Sufferer who cries out (title; vv. 1-2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מוֹעֵד (moʿed), Greek: καιρός, Aramaic: זמן
translationNotes.note: Fixed time for God’s favor on Zion (v. 13).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קָאַת / כּוֹס (qa'at / kos)
translationNotes.note: Two birds from the unclean list of Leviticus 11:17-18. Which species each name marks is not certain; English versions print pelican, desert owl, or little owl for them. What the verse fixes is the habitat: waste ground and collapsed buildings, where nothing else lives. Isaiah 34:11 puts the same birds in a ruined city.

translationNotes.term: I have eaten ashes like bread
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵפֶר כַּלֶּחֶם (epher kallechem)
translationNotes.note: Mourners sat down in ashes and put dust on their heads: Tamar in 2 Samuel 13:19, Job scraping himself in the ash heap (Job 2:8), Mordecai in sackcloth and ashes (Esther 4:1). Verse 9 says the mourning has gone on so long that the ash pile is where he eats and his own tears are what he drinks.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm records personal wasting away, a promise of favor to Zion, and the unchanging years of the Creator.
stories.superscription: A prayer of one who is afflicted, when he grows faint and pours out his lament before the LORD.

stories.title: 🌤️ Psalms 103
summaryBullets: Bless the LORD, O my soul; all that is within me, bless His holy name. (103:1).
Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds — (103:2).
He who forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases, (103:3).
who redeems your life from the Pit and crowns you with loving devotion and compassion, (103:4).
who satisfies you with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s. (103:5).
The LORD executes righteousness and justice for all the oppressed. (103:6).
He made known His ways to Moses, His deeds to the people of Israel. (103:7).
The LORD is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. (103:8).
He will not always accuse us, nor harbor His anger forever. (103:9).
He has not dealt with us according to our sins or repaid us according to our iniquities. (103:10).
For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is His loving devotion for those who fear Him. (103:11).
As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us. (103:12).
As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him. (103:13).
For He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust. (103:14).
As for man, his days are like grass— he blooms like a flower of the field; (103:15).
when the wind passes over, it vanishes, and its place remembers it no more. (103:16).
But from everlasting to everlasting the loving devotion of the LORD extends to those who fear Him, and His righteousness to their children’s children — (103:17).
to those who keep His covenant and remember to obey His precepts. (103:18).
The LORD has established His throne in heaven, and His kingdom rules over all. (103:19).
Bless the LORD, all His angels mighty in strength who carry out His word, who hearken to the voice of His command. (103:20).
Bless the LORD, all His hosts, you servants who do His will. (103:21).
Bless the LORD, all His works in all places of His dominion. Bless the LORD, O my soul! (103:22).
crossRefs: Exodus 34:6-7: God proclaims His own name as He passes before Moses on the mountain, compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. Verse 8 of the psalm repeats that formula almost word for word.

Psalm 90:5-6: Human life as grass that springs up new in the morning and fades by evening. This psalm keeps the image and finishes it, the wind passes over the flower and its place remembers it no more.
Micah 7:19: God casting all our sins into the depths of the sea. The psalm measures the same removal by a different distance, as far as the east is from the west, which is a gap that never closes.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּרַךְ (barakh), Greek: εὐλογεῖν, Aramaic: ברך
translationNotes.note: Speak well of/praise (vv. 1-2, 20-22).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רַחֲמִים (raḥamim), Greek: οἰκτιρμοί, Aramaic: רחמין
translationNotes.note: Pity/mercy shown to the weak (v. 4, 13).

translationNotes.term: As far as the east is from the west
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִזְרָח / מַעֲרָב (mizrach / ma'arav)
translationNotes.note: Hebrew names the north and the south with places, tsafon and negev, so those directions have edges. East and west are named from the sun: mizrach is where it rises, ma'arav where it goes in. That axis has no landmark and no end, which is the pair verse 12 chooses to measure the removal of transgressions.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֶשֶׁר (nesher)
translationNotes.note: Nesher covers the great soaring birds of the region, the eagle and the griffon vulture alike; Micah 1:16 uses the same word for a bald head, which fits the vulture. The comparison in verse 5 is the annual moult, when worn feathers drop and the bird comes back into full plumage and flight. Isaiah 40:31 uses the same picture for renewed strength.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm lists God’s benefits, recalls His revealed character, contrasts human frailty with enduring love, and calls all to bless Him.

headings.text: Bless the Lord, O My Soul

stories.superscription: Of David.

stories.title: 🌿 Psalms 104
summaryBullets: Bless the LORD, O my soul! O LORD my God, You are very great; You are clothed with splendor and majesty. (104:1).
He wraps Himself in light as with a garment; He stretches out the heavens like a tent, (104:2).
laying the beams of His chambers in the waters above, making the clouds His chariot, walking on the wings of the wind. (104:3).
He makes the winds His messengers, flames of fire His servants. (104:4).
He set the earth on its foundations, never to be moved. (104:5).
You covered it with the deep like a garment; the waters stood above the mountains. (104:6).
At Your rebuke the waters fled; at the sound of Your thunder they hurried away — (104:7).
the mountains rose and the valleys sank to the place You assigned for them — (104:8).
You set a boundary they cannot cross, that they may never again cover the earth. (104:9).
He sends forth springs in the valleys; they flow between the mountains. (104:10).
They give drink to every beast of the field; the wild donkeys quench their thirst. (104:11).
The birds of the air nest beside the springs; they sing among the branches. (104:12).
He waters the mountains from His chambers; the earth is satisfied by the fruit of His works. (104:13).
He makes the grass grow for the livestock and provides crops for man to cultivate, bringing forth food from the earth: (104:14).
wine that gladdens the heart of man, oil that makes his face to shine, and bread that sustains his heart. (104:15).
The trees of the LORD have their fill, the cedars of Lebanon that He planted, (104:16).
where the birds build their nests; the stork makes her home in the cypresses. (104:17).
The high mountains are for the wild goats, the cliffs a refuge for the rock badgers. (104:18).
He made the moon to mark the seasons; the sun knows when to set. (104:19).
You bring darkness, and it becomes night, when all the beasts of the forest prowl. (104:20).
The young lions roar for their prey and seek their food from God. (104:21).
The sun rises, and they withdraw; they lie down in their dens. (104:22).
Man goes forth to his work and to his labor until evening. (104:23).
How many are Your works, O LORD! In wisdom You have made them all; the earth is full of Your creatures. (104:24).
Here is the sea, vast and wide, teeming with creatures beyond number, living things both great and small. (104:25).
There the ships pass, and Leviathan, which You formed to frolic there. (104:26).
All creatures look to You to give them their food in due season. (104:27).
When You give it to them, they gather it up; when You open Your hand, they are satisfied with good things. (104:28).
When You hide Your face, they are terrified; when You take away their breath, they die and return to dust. (104:29).
When You send Your Spirit, they are created, and You renew the face of the earth. (104:30).
May the glory of the LORD endure forever; may the LORD rejoice in His works. (104:31).
He looks on the earth, and it trembles; He touches the mountains, and they smolder. (104:32).
I will sing to the LORD all my life; I will sing praise to my God while I have my being. (104:33).
May my meditation be pleasing to Him, for I rejoice in the LORD. (104:34).
May sinners vanish from the earth and the wicked be no more. Bless the LORD, O my soul. Hallelujah! (104:35).
crossRefs: Genesis 1:14-18: Lights set in the expanse to mark signs and seasons, the greater ruling the day and the lesser ruling the night. The psalm follows the creation order and reaches the same pair, the moon marking seasons and the sun knowing when to set.

Job 38:1-39:30: God answers Job out of the whirlwind with questions about the doors of the sea, the storehouses of snow, the wild donkey, the young lions in their dens and the eagle's nest. The psalm walks the same ground as praise instead of interrogation.

Psalm 148:7-12: A roll call of everything summoned to praise, sea creatures and lightning, mountains and cedars, wild animals and kings. That psalm commands what this one describes, a creation that eats from God's open hand and dies when He withdraws its breath.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רוּחַ (ruaḥ), Greek: πνεῦμα, Aramaic: רוחא
translationNotes.note: Life-giving breath sent forth to create/renew (v. 30).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לִוְיָתָן (livyatan)
translationNotes.note: A sea creature named at Job 41, Psalm 74:14, Psalm 104:26, and Isaiah 27:1. Job 41 describes it at length: rows of shields for scales, teeth ringed with terror, a breath that kindles coals, and no weapon of the period that can hold it, so no man puts a hook in its nose. Most English Bibles leave the word untranslated because no living animal answers the whole description. Here in verse 26 it is simply one of God's creatures, at play in the sea He made.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁפַנִּים (shefannim)
translationNotes.note: The rock hyrax, an animal about the size of a rabbit that lives in colonies in cliff crevices and sunbathes on the rocks. It is not a badger and not a rodent. Leviticus 11:5 lists it among the unclean, and Proverbs 30:26 names it as one of the small things that are exceedingly wise, because it makes its home in the crags.

translationNotes.term: The moon to mark the seasons
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מוֹעֲדִים (mo'adim)
translationNotes.note: Mo'adim are the appointed times, the word Leviticus 23 uses for the feasts. Verse 19 is calendar language: the moon is the clock that fixes Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month, Booths on the fifteenth of the seventh, and the offerings at every new moon (Numbers 28:11-14). Genesis 1:14 gives the lights the same job on the fourth day.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm praises the Creator’s order and provision in heavens, earth, and sea, including creatures’ cycles and Leviathan in the deep.

headings.text: How Many Are Your Works, O Lord!

stories.title: 🧭 Psalms 105
summaryBullets: Give thanks to the LORD, call upon His name; make known His deeds among the nations. (105:1).
Sing to Him, sing praises to Him; tell of all His wonders. (105:2).
Glory in His holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice. (105:3).
Seek out the LORD and His strength; seek His face always. (105:4).
Remember the wonders He has done, His marvels, and the judgments He has pronounced, (105:5).
O offspring of His servant Abraham, O sons of Jacob, His chosen ones. (105:6).
He is the LORD our God; His judgments carry throughout the earth. (105:7).
He remembers His covenant forever, the word He ordained for a thousand generations— (105:8).
the covenant He made with Abraham, and the oath He swore to Isaac. (105:9).
He confirmed it to Jacob as a decree, to Israel as an everlasting covenant: (105:10).
“I will give you the land of Canaan as the portion of your inheritance.” (105:11).
When they were few in number, few indeed, and strangers in the land, (105:12).
they wandered from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another. (105:13).
He let no man oppress them; He rebuked kings on their behalf: (105:14).
“Do not touch My anointed ones! Do no harm to My prophets!” (105:15).
He called down famine on the land and cut off all their supplies of food. (105:16).
He sent a man before them— Joseph, sold as a slave. (105:17).
They bruised his feet with shackles and placed his neck in irons, (105:18).
until his prediction came true and the word of the LORD proved him right. (105:19).
The king sent and released him; the ruler of peoples set him free. (105:20).
He made him master of his household, ruler over all his substance, (105:21).
to instruct his princes as he pleased and teach his elders wisdom. (105:22).
Then Israel entered Egypt; Jacob dwelt in the land of Ham. (105:23).
And the LORD made His people very fruitful, more numerous than their foes, (105:24).
whose hearts He turned to hate His people, to conspire against His servants. (105:25).
He sent Moses His servant, and Aaron, whom He had chosen. (105:26).
They performed His miraculous signs among them, and wonders in the land of Ham. (105:27).
He sent darkness, and it became dark— yet they defied His words. (105:28).
He turned their waters to blood and caused their fish to die. (105:29).
Their land teemed with frogs, even in their royal chambers. (105:30).
He spoke, and insects swarmed— gnats throughout their country. (105:31).
He gave them hail for rain, with lightning throughout their land. (105:32).
He struck their vines and fig trees and shattered the trees of their country. (105:33).
He spoke, and the locusts came— young locusts without number. (105:34).
They devoured every plant in their land and consumed the produce of their soil. (105:35).
Then He struck all the firstborn in their land, the firstfruits of all their vigor. (105:36).
He brought Israel out with silver and gold, and none among His tribes stumbled. (105:37).
Egypt was glad when they departed, for the dread of Israel had fallen on them. (105:38).
He spread a cloud as a covering and a fire to light up the night. (105:39).
They asked, and He brought quail and satisfied them with the bread of heaven. (105:40).
He opened a rock, and water gushed out; it flowed like a river in the desert. (105:41).
For He remembered His holy promise to Abraham His servant. (105:42).
He brought forth His people with rejoicing, His chosen with shouts of joy. (105:43).
He gave them the lands of the nations, that they might inherit the fruit of others’ labor, (105:44).
that they might keep His statutes and obey His laws. Hallelujah! (105:45).
crossRefs: Genesis 15:18: The covenant God cut with Abram, granting his descendants the land from the river of Egypt to the great river. The psalm calls that oath the word God ordained for a thousand generations and never forgot.

Genesis 41:39-44: Pharaoh puts his signet ring on Joseph's finger, dresses him in fine linen and a gold chain, and sets him in the second chariot with men calling out ahead of him. The psalm compresses all of it into master of his household.

Exodus 10:21-23: Three days of darkness thick enough that no one could see anyone else or leave his place, while Israel had light where they lived. The psalm's retelling of the plagues opens with this one rather than with the water turned to blood.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּרִית (berit), Greek: διαθήκη, Aramaic: קיימא (qayyama)
translationNotes.note: Formal pledge to the patriarchs (vv. 8-11).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְשִׁיחָי (meshiḥai), Greek: χριστοί, Aramaic: משיחי
translationNotes.note: Refers to patriarchs/prophets under God’s protection (v. 15).

The first portion of each harvest offered to God before the rest could be eaten (Exodus 23:19; Leviticus 23:9-14). Paul calls the resurrected Christ 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep' (1 Corinthians 15:20); the guarantee that the full resurrection harvest will follow.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בִּכּוּרִים (bikkurim)
Hebrew: אֶרֶץ־חָם (erets Cham)
translationNotes.note: Egypt, named for Ham the son of Noah, whose son Mizraim is the ordinary Hebrew word for Egypt (Genesis 10:6). The psalm uses the ancestor's name for the country in verses 23 and 27, and Psalm 78:51 and 106:22 do the same.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּרְזֶל (barzel)
translationNotes.note: Verse 18 says literally that iron came into his soul, with fetters on the feet and a collar at the neck. The events are Genesis 39:20 through 41:14: Joseph was seventeen when his brothers sold him (Genesis 37:2) and thirty when he stood before Pharaoh (Genesis 41:46), so the shackles cover most of thirteen years.

This psalm recounts seven blows and opens with darkness (105:28-36); Psalm 78:44-51 recounts a different selection in a different order. Neither is trying to give the sequence. The full ten stand in Exodus 7 through 12, ending with the death of the firstborn, which both psalms keep last.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm recounts covenant promises and God’s acts through Joseph, the plagues, and the exodus, ending with provision in the land.

stories.title: 🔁 Psalms 106
summaryBullets: Hallelujah! Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever. (106:1).
Who can describe the mighty acts of the LORD or fully proclaim His praise? (106:2).
Blessed are those who uphold justice, who practice righteousness at all times. (106:3).
Remember me, O LORD, in Your favor to Your people; visit me with Your salvation, (106:4).
that I may see the prosperity of Your chosen ones, and rejoice in the gladness of Your nation, and give glory with Your inheritance. (106:5).
We have sinned like our fathers; we have done wrong and acted wickedly. (106:6).
Our fathers in Egypt did not grasp Your wonders or remember Your abundant kindness; but they rebelled by the sea, there at the Red Sea. (106:7).
Yet He saved them for the sake of His name, to make His power known. (106:8).
He rebuked the Red Sea, and it dried up; He led them through the depths as through a desert. (106:9).
He saved them from the hand that hated them; He redeemed them from the hand of the enemy. (106:10).
The waters covered their foes; not one of them remained. (106:11).
Then they believed His promises and sang His praise. (106:12).
Yet they soon forgot His works and failed to wait for His counsel. (106:13).
They craved intensely in the wilderness and tested God in the desert. (106:14).
So He granted their request, but sent a wasting disease upon them. (106:15).
In the camp they envied Moses, as well as Aaron, the holy one of the LORD. (106:16).
The earth opened up and swallowed Dathan; it covered the assembly of Abiram. (106:17).
Then fire blazed through their company; flames consumed the wicked. (106:18).
At Horeb they made a calf and worshiped a molten image. (106:19).
They exchanged their Glory for the image of a grass-eating ox. (106:20).
They forgot God their Savior, who did great things in Egypt, (106:21).
wondrous works in the land of Ham, and awesome deeds by the Red Sea. (106:22).
So He said He would destroy them— had not Moses His chosen one stood before Him in the breach to divert His wrath from destroying them. (106:23).
They despised the pleasant land; they did not believe His promise. (106:24).
They grumbled in their tents and did not listen to the voice of the LORD. (106:25).
So He raised His hand and swore to cast them down in the wilderness, (106:26).
to disperse their offspring among the nations and scatter them throughout the lands. (106:27).
They yoked themselves to Baal of Peor and ate sacrifices offered to lifeless gods. (106:28).
So they provoked the LORD to anger with their deeds, and a plague broke out among them. (106:29).
But Phinehas stood and intervened, and the plague was restrained. (106:30).
It was credited to him as righteousness for endless generations to come. (106:31).
At the waters of Meribah they angered the LORD, and trouble came to Moses because of them. (106:32).
For they rebelled against His Spirit, and Moses spoke rashly with his lips. (106:33).
They did not destroy the peoples as the LORD had commanded them, (106:34).
but they mingled with the nations and adopted their customs. (106:35).
They worshiped their idols, which became a snare to them. (106:36).
They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons. (106:37).
They shed innocent blood— the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the idols of Canaan, and the land was polluted with blood. (106:38).
They defiled themselves by their actions and prostituted themselves by their deeds. (106:39).
