So the anger of the LORD burned against His people, and He abhorred His own inheritance. (106:40).
He delivered them into the hand of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them. (106:41).
Their enemies oppressed them and subdued them under their hand. (106:42).
Many times He rescued them, but they were bent on rebellion and sank down in their iniquity. (106:43).
Nevertheless He heard their cry; He took note of their distress. (106:44).
And He remembered His covenant with them, and relented by the abundance of His loving devotion. (106:45).
He made them objects of compassion to all who held them captive. (106:46).
Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from the nations, that we may give thanks to Your holy name, that we may glory in Your praise. (106:47).
Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. Let all the people say, “Amen!” Hallelujah! (106:48).
crossRefs: Numbers 16:31-35: The ground splits and swallows Dathan and Abiram alive with their households, then fire from the LORD consumes the men who were offering incense. The psalm names both halves of that judgment in two consecutive lines.

Exodus 32:4-6: Aaron casts the gold into a molten calf, builds an altar, calls a feast to the LORD, and the people eat and drink and get up to revel. The psalm files the whole episode as trading their Glory for the image of a grass-eating ox.

Numbers 25:7-13: Phinehas takes a spear and drives it through the Israelite and the Midianite woman, the plague stops, and God grants him a covenant of permanent priesthood. The psalm says the act was credited to him as righteousness.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּעַל פְּעוֹר (Baʿal Peʿor), Greek: Βάαλ Φεγώρ, Aramaic: בעל פעורא
translationNotes.note: Local deity associated with the Moabite incident (v. 28).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וַתֵּחָשֶׁב לוֹ לִצְדָקָה (vatteḥashev lo litzdaqah), Greek: ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην, Aramaic: אתחשב ליה לצדקתא
translationNotes.note: Evaluation of Phinehas’ deed (v. 31).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דָּתָן / אֲבִירָם (Dathan / Aviram)
translationNotes.note: Numbers 16 records two deaths in one day: the ground split and swallowed Dathan and Abiram with their households and goods, and fire from the LORD consumed the 250 men who had come with censers. Verses 17 and 18 keep those two events in that order. Korah himself is named at Numbers 16:32, though verse 11 of Numbers 26 records that his sons did not die.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵגֶל (egel)
translationNotes.note: The image at Horeb was a young bull, not a nursery calf: Aaron took the gold earrings, cast it, and built an altar (Exodus 32:1-6). The bull stood for strength and fertility across Egypt and Canaan; the Apis bull was kept and worshipped at Memphis. Verse 20 makes the trade explicit by naming what the animal does, which is eat grass.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֵׁדִים (shedim)
translationNotes.note: Verses 37 and 38 name child sacrifice, forbidden on pain of death (Leviticus 18:21; 20:2-5). It was carried out at Topheth in the Valley of Ben Hinnom until Josiah defiled the site so no one could pass a son or daughter through the fire there (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31). Excavation of the tophet at Carthage, the Phoenician colony, has turned up thousands of urns holding the burned bones of infants.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm catalogs repeated sins; at the sea, Horeb, Baal Peor, and Meribah; along with rescues and a closing plea for gathering.

headings.text: Give Thanks to the Lord, for He Is Good

stories.title: 🧭 Psalms 107
summaryBullets: Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever. (107:1).
Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom He has redeemed from the hand of the enemy (107:2).
and gathered from the lands, from east and west, from north and south. (107:3).
Some wandered in desert wastelands, finding no path to a city in which to dwell. (107:4).
They were hungry and thirsty; their soul fainted within them. (107:5).
Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He delivered them from their distress. (107:6).
He led them on a straight path to reach a city where they could live. (107:7).
Let them give thanks to the LORD for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men. (107:8).
For He satisfies the thirsty and fills the hungry with good things. (107:9).
Some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, prisoners in affliction and chains, (107:10).
because they rebelled against the words of God and despised the counsel of the Most High. (107:11).
He humbled their hearts with hard labor; they stumbled, and there was no one to help. (107:12).
Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He saved them from their distress. (107:13).
He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death and broke away their chains. (107:14).
Let them give thanks to the LORD for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men. (107:15).
For He has broken down the gates of bronze and cut through the bars of iron. (107:16).
Fools, in their rebellious ways, and through their iniquities, suffered affliction. (107:17).
They loathed all food and drew near to the gates of death. (107:18).
Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He saved them from their distress. (107:19).
He sent forth His word and healed them; He rescued them from the Pit. (107:20).
Let them give thanks to the LORD for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men. (107:21).
Let them offer sacrifices of thanksgiving and declare His works with rejoicing. (107:22).
Others went out to sea in ships, conducting trade on the mighty waters. (107:23).
They saw the works of the LORD, and His wonders in the deep. (107:24).
For He spoke and raised a tempest that lifted the waves of the sea. (107:25).
They mounted up to the heavens, then sunk to the depths; their courage melted in their anguish. (107:26).
They reeled and staggered like drunkards, and all their skill was useless. (107:27).
Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He brought them out of their distress. (107:28).
He calmed the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed. (107:29).
They rejoiced in the silence, and He guided them to the harbor they desired. (107:30).
Let them give thanks to the LORD for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men. (107:31).
Let them exalt Him in the assembly of the people and praise Him in the council of the elders. (107:32).
He turns rivers into deserts, springs of water into thirsty ground, (107:33).
and fruitful land into fields of salt, because of the wickedness of its dwellers. (107:34).
He turns a desert into pools of water and a dry land into flowing springs. (107:35).
He causes the hungry to settle there, that they may establish a city in which to dwell. (107:36).
They sow fields and plant vineyards that yield a fruitful harvest. (107:37).
He blesses them, and they multiply greatly; He does not let their herds diminish. (107:38).
When they are decreased and humbled by oppression, evil, and sorrow, (107:39).
He pours out contempt on the nobles and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland. (107:40).
But He lifts the needy from affliction and increases their families like flocks. (107:41).
The upright see and rejoice, and all iniquity shuts its mouth. (107:42).
Let him who is wise pay heed to these things and consider the loving devotion of the LORD. (107:43).
crossRefs: Psalm 106:1: The previous psalm opens with this same sentence, give thanks to the LORD for He is good, His loving devotion endures forever. The repetition marks the seam where the fourth book of the Psalter ends and the fifth begins.

Psalm 65:7: God stilling the roaring of the seas and the pounding of their waves. The psalm's fourth rescue is that stilling seen from a deck, sailors reeling like drunkards with all their skill useless until He calms the storm to a whisper.

Isaiah 43:5-6: God calling to the four directions to give up His scattered people and bring His sons and daughters from the ends of the earth. The psalm opens with that gathering already done, the redeemed brought in from east and west, from north and south.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גָּאַל (gaʾal), Greek: λυτρόω, Aramaic: פרק
translationNotes.note: Deliver by purchase/rescue (vv. 2, 20).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צַלְמָוֶת (tsalmavet), Greek: σκιὰ θανάτου, Aramaic: טולא דמותא
translationNotes.note: Deep darkness, death-shadow (vv. 10, 14).

translationNotes.term: Gates of bronze and bars of iron
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דַּלְתוֹת נְחֹשֶׁת / בְּרִיחֵי בַרְזֶל (daltot nechoshet / berichei varzel)
translationNotes.note: City gates were heavy timber sheathed in bronze and held by iron bars dropped into sockets in the jambs, the strongest point of a walled town and the last thing an attacker got through. Isaiah 45:2 promises the same two obstacles broken for Cyrus. Verse 16 is naming the hardest thing to break, not decorating a prison.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֳנִיּוֹת (oniyyot)
translationNotes.note: Israel was not a seafaring nation. It had no natural harbour on its coast, and its ventures depended on Phoenician crews: Solomon's fleet at Ezion-geber on the Red Sea sailed with sailors sent by Hiram of Tyre (1 Kings 9:26-28), and Jehoshaphat's ships broke up in port before they ever sailed (1 Kings 22:48). Verses 23 through 30 are written from the deck by people who found the sea genuinely terrifying.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm recounts four rescue scenes and changing fortunes, calling the redeemed to thank the LORD for steadfast love.

stories.title: 🎵 Psalms 108
summaryBullets: My heart is steadfast, O God; I will sing and make music with all my being. (108:1).
Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awaken the dawn. (108:2).
I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing Your praises among the peoples. (108:3).
For Your loving devotion extends beyond the heavens, and Your faithfulness reaches to the clouds. (108:4).
Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your glory cover all the earth. (108:5).
Respond and save us with Your right hand, that Your beloved may be delivered. (108:6).
God has spoken from His sanctuary: “I will triumph! I will parcel out Shechem and apportion the Valley of Succoth. (108:7).
Gilead is Mine, and Manasseh is Mine; Ephraim is My helmet, Judah is My scepter. (108:8).
Moab is My washbasin; upon Edom I toss My sandal; over Philistia I shout in triumph.” (108:9).
Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom? (108:10).
Have You not rejected us, O God? Will You no longer march out, O God, with our armies? (108:11).
Give us aid against the enemy, for the help of man is worthless. (108:12).
With God we will perform with valor, and He will trample our enemies. (108:13).
crossRefs: Psalm 57:7-11; Psalm 60:5-12: This psalm is those two passages joined end to end, the closing praise of the first and the whole battle oracle of the second, reused almost word for word as a single new song.

Numbers 34:1-12: God dictates the borders of Canaan to Moses one leg at a time, south through the Wilderness of Zin, west along the Great Sea, north to Lebo-hamath. The psalm quotes God claiming that same ground by name, Gilead is Mine, Manasseh is Mine.

Obadiah 1:1: An entire prophecy aimed at one nation, opening with an envoy sent among the nations saying rise up and let us go to battle against Edom. The psalm asks that question twice, who will lead me to Edom.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סִיר רַחְצִי (sir raḥtsi), Greek: λουτῆρ, Aramaic: דלופני
translationNotes.note: Moab depicted as a basin for washing (v. 9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַשְׁלִיךְ נַעֲלִי (ashlikh naʿali), Greek: βαλῶ τὸ ὑπόδημά μου, Aramaic: אשדי מסאני
translationNotes.note: Gesture of claim/subjugation over Edom (v. 9).

translationNotes.term: A psalm made of two psalms
translationNotes.note: Verses 1 through 5 are Psalm 57:7-11 and verses 6 through 13 are Psalm 60:5-12, almost word for word. The temple collection reused its own material: Psalm 70 stands again inside Psalm 40:13-17, and most of Psalm 96 appears at 1 Chronicles 16:23-33. What changes here is the joining, which puts the praise first and the war petition second.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָעוֹז רֹאשִׁי / מְחֹקְקִי (ma'oz roshi / mechoqeqi)
translationNotes.note: Verses 7 and 8 name the land by its parts, west of the Jordan and east: Shechem in the central hills, Succoth in the valley across the river, Gilead on the eastern tableland, Manasseh on both banks, Ephraim in the highlands, Judah in the south. 'Ephraim is My helmet' translates ma'oz roshi, the stronghold of my head, and 'Judah is My scepter' translates mechoqeqi, the ruler's staff of Genesis 49:10.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm blends praise with God’s territorial claim and asks for help against fortified enemies, declaring victory with God.
stories.superscription: A song. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🗣️ Psalms 109
summaryBullets: O God of my praise, be not silent. (109:1).
For wicked and deceitful mouths open against me; they speak against me with lying tongues. (109:2).
They surround me with hateful words and attack me without cause. (109:3).
In return for my love they accuse me, but I am a man of prayer. (109:4).
They repay me evil for good, and hatred for my love. (109:5).
Set over him a wicked man; let an accuser stand at his right hand. (109:6).
When he is tried, let him be found guilty, and may his prayer be regarded as sin. (109:7).
May his days be few; may another take his position. (109:8).
May his children be fatherless and his wife a widow. (109:9).
May his children wander as beggars, seeking sustenance far from their ruined homes. (109:10).
May the creditor seize all he owns, and strangers plunder the fruits of his labor. (109:11).
May there be no one to extend kindness to him, and no one to favor his fatherless children. (109:12).
May his descendants be cut off; may their name be blotted out from the next generation. (109:13).
May the iniquity of his fathers be remembered before the LORD, and the sin of his mother never be blotted out. (109:14).
May their sins always remain before the LORD, that He may cut off their memory from the earth. (109:15).
For he never thought to show kindness, but pursued the poor and needy and brokenhearted, even to their death. (109:16).
The cursing that he loved, may it fall on him; the blessing in which he refused to delight, may it be far from him. (109:17).
The cursing that he wore like a coat, may it soak into his body like water, and into his bones like oil. (109:18).
May it be like a robe wrapped about him, like a belt tied forever around him. (109:19).
May this be the LORD’s reward to my accusers, to those who speak evil against me. (109:20).
But You, O GOD, the Lord, deal kindly with me for the sake of Your name; deliver me by the goodness of Your loving devotion. (109:21).
For I am poor and needy; my heart is wounded within me. (109:22).
I am fading away like a lengthening shadow; I am shaken off like a locust. (109:23).
My knees are weak from fasting, and my body grows lean and gaunt. (109:24).
I am an object of scorn to my accusers; when they see me, they shake their heads. (109:25).
Help me, O LORD my God; save me according to Your loving devotion. (109:26).
Let them know that this is Your hand, that You, O LORD, have done it. (109:27).
Though they curse, You will bless. When they rise up, they will be put to shame, but Your servant will rejoice. (109:28).
May my accusers be clothed with disgrace; may they wear their shame like a robe. (109:29).
With my mouth I will thank the LORD profusely; I will praise Him in the presence of many. (109:30).
For He stands at the right hand of the needy one, to save him from the condemners of his soul. (109:31).
crossRefs: Acts 1:20: Peter stands up among the believers, says the Spirit spoke this through David concerning Judas, and quotes verse 8 of this psalm as the warrant for filling his place, may another take his position.

Zechariah 3:1: Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of the LORD with Satan at his right hand to accuse him. That is the exact courtroom position verse 6 of this psalm asks God to assign to the man being prayed against.

Psalm 35:7-8: The same prayer in a milder form, that the net a man hid without cause would catch him and the pit he dug would take him. This psalm carries the request much further, past the man to his children, his creditors and his name.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׂטָן (satan, ‘adversary/accuser’), Greek: κατήγωρ/διάβολος, Aramaic: סטן
translationNotes.note: Stands at the right hand to accuse (v. 6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קָלַל (qalal, ‘curse’) / בָּרַךְ (barakh, ‘bless’), Greek: καταρᾶσθαι / εὐλογεῖν, Aramaic: ליט / ברך
translationNotes.note: Contrasting speech acts central to the psalm (vv. 17-18, 28).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַל־יְמִינוֹ (al-yemino)
translationNotes.note: A courtroom position. The accuser stood at the right of the man on trial, which is exactly where the satan stands to accuse Joshua the high priest in Zechariah 3:1. The psalm ends by reversing the seating: verse 31 has the LORD standing at the right hand of the needy man, in the accuser's place, to save him from those who condemn him.

The request is specific and it is not softened anywhere in the psalm: a guilty verdict, a short life, the man's office given to someone else, his children fatherless and begging, his wife a widow, his creditors taking everything, his line ended and his name blotted out within a generation. The psalmist asks God to do all of it and does none of it himself; verse 4 says 'I am a man of prayer.' Acts 1:20 quotes verse 8 of the office Judas left empty.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm presents accusations and a series of curses against a treacherous accuser, ending with a plea and promise of thanks.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🪖 Psalms 110
summaryBullets: The LORD said to my Lord: “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.” (110:1).
The LORD extends Your mighty scepter from Zion: “Rule in the midst of Your enemies.” (110:2).
Your people shall be willing on Your day of battle. Arrayed in holy splendor, from the womb of the dawn, to You belongs the dew of Your youth. (110:3).
The LORD has sworn and will not change His mind: “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” (110:4).
The Lord is at Your right hand; He will crush kings in the day of His wrath. (110:5).
He will judge the nations, heaping up the dead; He will crush the leaders far and wide. (110:6).
He will drink from the brook by the road; therefore He will lift up His head. (110:7).
crossRefs: Genesis 14:18: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, comes out to Abram with bread and wine and blesses him, and Abram gives him a tenth of everything. He appears once in the whole Torah, and this psalm builds an order of priesthood on him.

Matthew 22:44: Jesus asks the Pharisees whose son the Christ is, they answer David's, and He quotes this psalm's opening line against them. If David calls Him Lord, the answer is incomplete, and no one dared question Him after that.
Hebrews 7:17: The letter to the Hebrews quotes verse 4 of this psalm to argue that Jesus holds a priesthood older than Levi's and confirmed by an oath, a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְהוָה (YHWH) / לַאדֹנִי (laʾdoni, ‘to my lord’), Greek: κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου, Aramaic: יי / למרִי
translationNotes.note: Two different terms in v. 1: the divine name and “my lord.”

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק (Malki-tsedeq), Greek: Μελχισεδέκ, Aramaic: מלכי צדק
translationNotes.note: Named priestly figure whose order is invoked (v. 4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֹּהֵן לְעוֹלָם (kohen le'olam)
translationNotes.note: Israel kept the two offices apart. Priests came from Aaron's line only, and when King Uzziah went into the temple to burn incense he was struck with leprosy on the spot and lived in isolation until he died (2 Chronicles 26:16-21). Melchizedek held both offices at once, king of Salem and priest of God Most High (Genesis 14:18), which is why verse 4 swears the king in under his order and not Aaron's.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: טַל יַלְדֻתֶיךָ (tal yaldutekha)
translationNotes.note: Verse 3 is the hardest line in the psalm and the ancient versions do not agree on it. The Hebrew runs roughly 'in holy splendour, from the womb of the dawn, yours is the dew of your youth.' The Greek Old Testament reads instead 'from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.' Translations that differ here are not guessing at the theology; they are working from different readings of the consonants.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm reports a decree of enthronement, a perpetual priesthood after Melchizedek, and victorious judgment over kings and nations.
stories.superscription: A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 📚 Psalms 111
summaryBullets: Hallelujah! I will give thanks to the LORD with all my heart in the council of the upright and in the assembly. (111:1).
Great are the works of the LORD; they are pondered by all who delight in them. (111:2).
Splendid and majestic is His work; His righteousness endures forever. (111:3).
He has caused His wonders to be remembered; the LORD is gracious and compassionate. (111:4).
He provides food for those who fear Him; He remembers His covenant forever. (111:5).
He has shown His people the power of His works by giving them the inheritance of the nations. (111:6).
The works of His hands are truth and justice; all His precepts are trustworthy. (111:7).
They are upheld forever and ever, enacted in truth and uprightness. (111:8).
He has sent redemption to His people; He has ordained His covenant forever; holy and awesome is His name. (111:9).
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom; all who follow His precepts gain rich understanding. His praise endures forever! (111:10).
crossRefs: Proverbs 9:10: Wisdom's own summary, the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding. This psalm ends on that sentence, so its alphabet finishes exactly where wisdom starts.
Exodus 34:6-7: God proclaiming His own name to Moses as gracious and compassionate. The psalm reuses that pair in the middle of its alphabet and ties it directly to the covenant He remembers forever.

Deuteronomy 7:9: The faithful God who keeps His covenant of loving devotion to a thousand generations of those who love Him. The psalm makes that permanence its subject, precepts upheld forever and a covenant ordained forever.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יִרְאַת יְהוָה (yirʾat YHWH), Greek (LXX): φόβος Κυρίου, Aramaic: דחלתא דיי
translationNotes.note: Reverent awe and submission; stated as the beginning of wisdom (v. 10).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פְּדוּת (pedut), Greek: λύτρωσις, Aramaic: פריקא
translationNotes.note: Ransom/deliverance sent to His people (v. 9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אָלֶף / תָּו (aleph / tav)
translationNotes.note: After the opening Hallelujah, this psalm runs 22 lines, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet in order: the first eight verses carry two lines each, the last two carry three. Psalm 112 is built to the same pattern, line for line, and answers it. Psalms 9 and 10, 25, 34, 37, 111, 112, 119, and 145 are all alphabetical, and none of it survives translation.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סוֹד / עֵדָה (sod / edah)
translationNotes.note: Two different words in verse 1. A sod is a small circle in close conversation, the group you tell things to (Psalm 25:14; Amos 3:7). An edah is the whole assembled congregation. The psalmist gives thanks in both settings, private and public, and English blurs them into 'council' and 'assembly.'

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm praises God’s enduring works and precepts and states that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.

stories.title: 🌱 Psalms 112
summaryBullets: Hallelujah! Blessed is the man who fears the LORD, who greatly delights in His commandments. (112:1).
His descendants will be mighty in the land; the generation of the upright will be blessed. (112:2).
Wealth and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever. (112:3).
Light dawns in the darkness for the upright — for the gracious, compassionate, and righteous. (112:4).
It is well with the man who is generous and lends freely, whose affairs are guided by justice. (112:5).
Surely he will never be shaken; the righteous man will be remembered forever. (112:6).
He does not fear bad news; his heart is steadfast, trusting in the LORD. (112:7).
His heart is assured; he does not fear, until he looks in triumph on his foes. (112:8).
He has scattered abroad his gifts to the poor; his righteousness endures forever; his horn will be lifted high in honor. (112:9).
The wicked man will see and be grieved; he will gnash his teeth and waste away; the desires of the wicked will perish. (112:10).
crossRefs: 2 Corinthians 9:9: Paul quotes verse 9 of this psalm while pressing the collection for the poor in Jerusalem, taking a line about a generous man and using it to argue that God supplies whatever the giver scatters.

Psalm 111:1-10: Its twin. Both run the Hebrew alphabet one letter to a line, both open with Hallelujah, and phrases the earlier psalm applies to God, gracious and compassionate, righteousness enduring forever, this one applies to the man who fears Him.

Proverbs 11:24-25: One man gives freely and gains more, another withholds and grows poor, and the generous soul prospers. The psalm says the same of the righteous man, he has scattered his gifts to the poor and his horn is lifted high in honor.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צַדִּיק (tsaddiq), Greek: δίκαιος, Aramaic: זכאי
translationNotes.note: Descriptor for the upright person in the psalm (vv. 4, 6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קֶרֶן (qeren), Greek: κέρας, Aramaic: קרנא
translationNotes.note: Symbol of strength/status; said to be exalted (v. 9).

This psalm runs the same 22-line alphabet as Psalm 111 and then repeats its phrases about the man who fears the LORD. Psalm 111:3 says of God 'His righteousness endures forever'; 112:3 says it of the man. Psalm 111:4 calls the LORD gracious and compassionate; 112:4 uses those words of the upright. The pair was built to be read together.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַלְוֶה (malveh)
translationNotes.note: Lending to a fellow Israelite carried no interest at all, on grain or on silver (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35-37; Deuteronomy 23:19-20), and every seventh year cancelled outstanding debts (Deuteronomy 15:1-2). Deuteronomy 15:9 names the obvious temptation, refusing a loan as the seventh year approaches. Verse 5 praises the man who lends anyway.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm describes the stable, generous life of the one who fears the LORD and contrasts it with the perishing desire of the wicked.

headings.text: The Blessed Fear of the Lord

stories.title: 🎺 Psalms 113
summaryBullets: Hallelujah! Give praise, O servants of the LORD; praise the name of the LORD. (113:1).
Blessed be the name of the LORD both now and forevermore. (113:2).
From where the sun rises to where it sets, the name of the LORD is praised. (113:3).
The LORD is exalted over all the nations, His glory above the heavens. (113:4).
Who is like the LORD our God, the One enthroned on high? (113:5).
He humbles Himself to behold the heavens and the earth. (113:6).
He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the dump (113:7).
to seat them with nobles, with the princes of His people. (113:8).
He settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother to her children. Hallelujah! (113:9).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 2:8: Hannah's song, raising the poor from the dust and the needy from the ash heap to seat them among princes. This psalm repeats her words closely and then adds her own case, the barren woman settled as a joyful mother.

Matthew 26:30: When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. The hymn at a Passover meal is the Hallel, the run of six praise psalms this one opens, so those are the words sung on the last night before the crucifixion.

Psalm 146:7-9: A later psalm working the same list, God feeding the hungry, freeing prisoners, lifting the bowed down, sustaining the fatherless and the widow. This one states the principle behind the list, the God enthroned on high stoops in order to raise.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַלְלוּ־יָהּ (Hallelu-Yah), Greek: Ἀλληλούϊα, Aramaic: הללויה
translationNotes.note: Call to praise appearing at start/end (vv. 1, 9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַשְׁפֹּת (ʾashpot), Greek: κοπρία, Aramaic: דּוּנְיָא/אַשְׁפָּתָא
translationNotes.note: Rubbish/ashes pile symbolizing low estate (v. 7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַלֵּל (Hallel)
translationNotes.note: Psalms 113 through 118 were sung together at Passover, Weeks, Booths, Dedication, and the new moon. The Mishnah, tractate Pesahim 10:5-7, sets the Passover order: the first part over the second cup before the meal, ending at Psalm 113 in the House of Shammai and at Psalm 114 in the House of Hillel, and the rest after the fourth cup. Matthew 26:30 and Mark 14:26 record that after the supper Jesus and the disciples sang a hymn and went out to the Mount of Olives.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲקֶרֶת הַבַּיִת (aqeret ha-bayit)
translationNotes.note: Verses 7 through 9 come almost word for word from Hannah's song after Samuel was born: the LORD raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap to seat them with princes (1 Samuel 2:8), and the barren has borne seven (1 Samuel 2:5). In a society where a woman's security ran through her sons, childlessness was destitution as well as grief.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm calls for universal praise of the Most High who stoops to raise the poor and seat them with princes.

stories.title: 🌊 Psalms 114
summaryBullets: When Israel departed from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of foreign tongue, (114:1).
Judah became God’s sanctuary, Israel His dominion. (114:2).
The sea observed and fled; the Jordan turned back; (114:3).
the mountains skipped like rams, the hills like lambs. (114:4).
Why was it, O sea, that you fled, O Jordan, that you turned back, (114:5).
O mountains, that you skipped like rams, O hills, like lambs? (114:6).
Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob, (114:7).
who turned the rock into a pool, the flint into a fountain of water! (114:8).
crossRefs: Exodus 14:21-22: The sea driven back all night by an east wind and Israel walking through on dry ground with walls of water on both sides. The psalm reports it from the water's point of view, the sea observed and fled.

Joshua 3:13-17: The Jordan at flood stage stops the moment the priests carrying the ark step into it, the water backing up as far as the city of Adam while the nation crosses dry. The psalm sets that beside the exodus, the sea fled and the Jordan turned back.

Exodus 17:6: God stands on the rock at Horeb, Moses strikes it, and water comes out for the people to drink. The psalm's closing line makes that its whole point, the One who turns rock into a pool and flint into a fountain.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִקְדָּשׁ (miqdash), Greek: ἁγίασμα, Aramaic: מקדשא
translationNotes.note: Judah is called His sanctuary (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יִסֹּב (yisov) / נָסוֹג (nasog), Greek: ἀνεστράφη, Aramaic: אתיהפך
translationNotes.note: Description of Jordan’s reversal (v. 3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַיָּם / הַיַּרְדֵּן (ha-yam / ha-Yarden)
translationNotes.note: Verse 3 puts the two water crossings side by side, forty years apart. The sea is the Red Sea driven back by an east wind (Exodus 14:21-22). The Jordan was in flood at harvest when the priests carrying the ark stepped in, and the water stood in a heap upstream at Adam near Zarethan while the nation crossed over near Jericho (Joshua 3:14-17).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹעֵז (lo'ez)
translationNotes.note: This word occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, here in verse 1. It marks speech you cannot make sense of. Israel had lived in Egypt for generations without the language ever becoming theirs, which is why Joseph used an interpreter with his brothers to keep his cover (Genesis 42:23).

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm recounts Israel’s departure from Egypt, the sea’s flight, the Jordan’s reversal, and water from rock at God’s presence.

stories.title: 🔊 Psalms 115
summaryBullets: Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to Your name be the glory, because of Your loving devotion, because of Your faithfulness. (115:1).
Why should the nations say, “Where is their God?” (115:2).
Our God is in heaven; He does as He pleases. (115:3).
Their idols are silver and gold, made by the hands of men. (115:4).
They have mouths, but cannot speak; they have eyes, but cannot see; (115:5).
they have ears, but cannot hear; they have noses, but cannot smell; (115:6).
they have hands, but cannot feel; they have feet, but cannot walk; they cannot even clear their throats. (115:7).
Those who make them become like them, as do all who trust in them. (115:8).
O Israel, trust in the LORD! He is their help and shield. (115:9).
O house of Aaron, trust in the LORD! He is their help and shield. (115:10).
You who fear the LORD, trust in the LORD! He is their help and shield. (115:11).
The LORD is mindful of us; He will bless us. He will bless the house of Israel; He will bless the house of Aaron; (115:12).
He will bless those who fear the LORD— small and great alike. (115:13).
May the LORD give you increase, both you and your children. (115:14).
May you be blessed by the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth. (115:15).
The highest heavens belong to the LORD, but the earth He has given to mankind. (115:16).
It is not the dead who praise the LORD, nor any who descend into silence. (115:17).
But it is we who will bless the LORD, both now and forevermore. Hallelujah! (115:18).
crossRefs: Psalm 135:15-18: The same indictment in nearly the same words, idols of silver and gold with mouths that cannot speak and eyes that cannot see, ending in the same verdict, those who make them become like them.

Deuteronomy 10:14: The heavens, even the highest heavens, and the earth and everything in it belong to the LORD. The psalm divides that estate, the highest heavens are His and the earth He has given to mankind.
Psalm 6:5: The plea that no one praises God from the grave. This psalm turns that into the reason the living must do it, the dead do not praise the LORD, so we will, both now and forevermore.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲצַבִּים (ʿatsabbim), Greek: εἴδωλα, Aramaic: צלמיא
translationNotes.note: Crafted images described as senseless (vv. 4-7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יִרְאֵי יְהוָה (yirʾei YHWH), Greek: οἱ φοβούμενοι τὸν Κύριον, Aramaic: דחלי יי
translationNotes.note: Third group addressed alongside Israel and Aaron (vv. 11-13).

The Greek Old Testament and the Latin Vulgate join Psalms 114 and 115 into one and then split Psalm 116 into two. Combined with an earlier join of Psalms 9 and 10, their numbering runs one behind the Hebrew from Psalm 11 to Psalm 113 and again from 117 to 146. The Hebrew Psalm 23 is Psalm 22 in an older Catholic Bible, and both are counting the same poem.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גָּרוֹן (garon)
translationNotes.note: Verses 5 through 7 walk down a body: mouth, eyes, ears, nose, hands, feet, and last the throat, which cannot even make a sound. The point is that the idol has every organ and uses none of them. Isaiah 44:14-20 follows the same craftsman from the tree he cuts, to the fire he cooks on, to the leftover block he bows to.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm rejects lifeless idols, urges all Israel to trust the LORD, and commits to bless His name forever.

headings.text: To Your Name Be the Glory

stories.title: 🍷 Psalms 116
summaryBullets: I love the LORD, for He has heard my voice — my appeal for mercy. (116:1).
Because He has inclined His ear to me, I will call on Him as long as I live. (116:2).
The ropes of death entangled me; the anguish of Sheol overcame me; I was confronted by trouble and sorrow. (116:3).
Then I called on the name of the LORD: “O LORD, deliver my soul!” (116:4).
The LORD is gracious and righteous; our God is full of compassion. (116:5).
The LORD preserves the simplehearted; I was helpless, and He saved me. (116:6).
Return to your rest, O my soul, for the LORD has been good to you. (116:7).
For You have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling. (116:8).
I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living. (116:9).
I believed, therefore I said, “I am greatly afflicted.” (116:10).
In my alarm I said, “All men are liars!” (116:11).
How can I repay the LORD for all His goodness to me? (116:12).
I will lift the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD. (116:13).
I will fulfill my vows to the LORD in the presence of all His people. (116:14).
Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of His saints. (116:15).
Truly, O LORD, I am Your servant; I am Your servant, the son of Your maidservant; You have broken my bonds. (116:16).
I will offer to You a sacrifice of thanksgiving and call on the name of the LORD. (116:17).
I will fulfill my vows to the LORD in the presence of all His people, (116:18).
in the courts of the LORD’s house, in your midst, O Jerusalem. Hallelujah! (116:19).
crossRefs: 2 Corinthians 4:13: Paul quotes verse 10 of this psalm, I believed and therefore I spoke, and applies it to preaching while being handed over to death. The psalm said it as a man freshly pulled out of death.

Jonah 2:9: A man swallowed by the sea promises to sacrifice with the voice of thanksgiving and pay what he vowed. The psalm carries that out step by step, lifting the cup of salvation and fulfilling its vows in front of all the people.

Psalm 56:13: The same sentence, You have delivered my soul from death and my feet from stumbling. This psalm inserts a third rescue between them, my eyes from tears, and then asks how any of it can be repaid.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כּוֹס יְשׁוּעוֹת (kos yeshuʿot), Greek: ποτήριον σωτηρίων, Aramaic: כס דפורקנין
translationNotes.note: Metaphor for thanksgiving and deliverance (v. 13).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יָקָר (yaqar), Greek: τίμιος, Aramaic: יקיר
translationNotes.note: Highly valued; of the death of His saints (v. 15).

The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
Hebrew: נְדָרַי (nedaray)
translationNotes.note: A vow made under pressure had to be paid, and paid publicly at the sanctuary: 'you must be careful to follow through on what your lips have promised' (Deuteronomy 23:21-23), with the offering eaten on the day it is brought (Leviticus 7:16). Verses 14 and 18 say in the presence of all His people, and verse 19 names the address, the courts of the LORD's house in Jerusalem. The psalm is the script for settling that debt.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm recounts deliverance from death, vows public thanks, and speaks of the precious death of His faithful ones.

headings.text: The Lord Has Heard My Voice

stories.title: 🌍 Psalms 117
summaryBullets: Praise the LORD, all you nations! Extol Him, all you peoples! (117:1).
For great is His loving devotion toward us, and the faithfulness of the LORD endures forever. Hallelujah! (117:2).
crossRefs: Romans 15:11: Paul chains together four Old Testament lines to prove that God always meant the Gentiles to praise Him alongside Israel, and this psalm supplies one of them, praise the Lord all you Gentiles.

Psalm 100:1: The same summons to the whole earth, make a joyful noise to the LORD, heading a full psalm of thanksgiving. Here it gets two verses, the shortest chapter in the Bible, carrying nothing but the summons and the reason for it.

Isaiah 49:6: God tells His Servant that restoring the tribes of Jacob is not enough, He will be made a light to the nations so salvation reaches the ends of the earth. The psalm assumes that reach and simply calls the nations in.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גּוֹיִם (goyim) / אֻמִּים (ʾummim), Greek: ἔθνη / λαοί, Aramaic: עממיא / עמין
translationNotes.note: All groups addressed to praise (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (ḥesed) / אֱמֶת (ʾemet), Greek: ἔλεος / ἀλήθεια, Aramaic: חסדא / קושטא
translationNotes.note: Grounds for universal praise (v. 2).

translationNotes.term: The shortest chapter in the Bible
translationNotes.note: Two verses, and sixteen words in the Hebrew. It is also the 595th chapter of the 1,189 in the Bible, which puts it exactly in the middle by count. Psalm 119, two chapters later, is the longest at 176 verses.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כָּל־גּוֹיִם (kol-goyim)
translationNotes.note: Paul quotes this verse at Romans 15:11 in a run of four texts about the nations praising God, alongside 2 Samuel 22:50, Deuteronomy 32:43, and Isaiah 11:10. In its own setting the psalm sits in the middle of the Hallel, sung at Passover, so this call to the goyim was part of Israel's own festival singing.

stories.keyTakeaway: The shortest psalm calls all nations to praise because of enduring steadfast love and faithfulness.

stories.title: 🚪 Psalms 118
summaryBullets: Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever. (118:1).
Let Israel say, “His loving devotion endures forever.” (118:2).
Let the house of Aaron say, “His loving devotion endures forever.” (118:3).
Let those who fear the LORD say, “His loving devotion endures forever.” (118:4).
In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered and set me free. (118:5).
The LORD is on my side; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me? (118:6).
The LORD is on my side; He is my helper. Therefore I will look in triumph on those who hate me. (118:7).
It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man. (118:8).
It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in princes. (118:9).
All the nations surrounded me, but in the name of the LORD I cut them off. (118:10).
They surrounded me on every side, but in the name of the LORD I cut them off. (118:11).
They swarmed around me like bees, but they were extinguished like burning thorns; in the name of the LORD I cut them off. (118:12).
I was pushed so hard I was falling, but the LORD helped me. (118:13).
The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation. (118:14).
Shouts of joy and salvation resound in the tents of the righteous: “The right hand of the LORD performs with valor! (118:15).
The right hand of the LORD is exalted! The right hand of the LORD performs with valor!” (118:16).
I will not die, but I will live and proclaim what the LORD has done. (118:17).
The LORD disciplined me severely, but He has not given me over to death. (118:18).
Open to me the gates of righteousness, that I may enter and give thanks to the LORD. (118:19).
This is the gate of the LORD; the righteous shall enter through it. (118:20).
I will give You thanks, for You have answered me, and You have become my salvation. (118:21).
The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. (118:22).
This is from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes. (118:23).
This is the day that the LORD has made; we will rejoice and be glad in it. (118:24).
O LORD, save us, we pray. We beseech You, O LORD, cause us to prosper! (118:25).
Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD. From the house of the LORD we bless you. (118:26).
The LORD is God; He has made His light to shine upon us. Bind the festal sacrifice with cords to the horns of the altar. (118:27).
You are my God, and I will give You thanks. You are my God, and I will exalt You. (118:28).
Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever. (118:29).
crossRefs: Matthew 21:9: The crowd at the entry into Jerusalem shouts Hosanna and Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord, which is verses 25 and 26 of this psalm, the greeting called out to a pilgrim arriving at the temple gate.

Psalm 146:3: Put not your trust in princes, in mortal man, who cannot save. This psalm says it as a comparison made twice over, better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man, better than to trust in princes.
Acts 4:11: Peter stands before the rulers and elders who condemned Jesus and turns verse 22 of this psalm on them by name, He is the stone you builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הוֹשִׁיעָה נָּא (hoshiʿah naʾ), Greek: ὡσαννά, Aramaic: הושענא
translationNotes.note: Liturgical plea for salvation (v. 25).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רֹאשׁ פִּנָּה (roʾsh pinnah), Greek: κεφαλὴ γωνίας, Aramaic: ריש קרנא
translationNotes.note: Cornerstone imagery (v. 22).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קַרְנוֹת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ (qarnot ha-mizbeach)
translationNotes.note: The altar had four raised projections, one at each corner, made of one piece with it and overlaid with bronze (Exodus 27:2). Blood from the sin offering was put on them (Leviticus 4:7), and a man in fear of his life grabbed them for asylum, as Adonijah and Joab both did (1 Kings 1:50-51; 2:28). Verse 27 is difficult in the Hebrew; it describes the festival victim brought up with cords to those horns.

Psalm 118 closes the Hallel, so these are the last words of the hymn sung after the Passover meal. Verse 22 on the rejected stone is quoted at Matthew 21:42, Mark 12:10, Luke 20:17, Acts 4:11, and 1 Peter 2:7. Verse 25, hoshiah na, is the shout at the entry into Jerusalem, and verse 26 the line that went with it (Matthew 21:9).

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm gives thanks for deliverance, urges refuge in the LORD, and proclaims the rejected stone as the cornerstone while entering the gate of righteousness.

headings.text: The Lord Is on My Side

stories.title: 📖 Psalms 119
summaryBullets: Blessed are those whose way is blameless, who walk in the Law of the LORD. (119:1).
Blessed are those who keep His testimonies and seek Him with all their heart. (119:2).
They do no iniquity; they walk in His ways. (119:3).
You have ordained Your precepts, that we should keep them diligently. (119:4).
Oh, that my ways were committed to keeping Your statutes! (119:5).
Then I would not be ashamed when I consider all Your commandments. (119:6).
I will praise You with an upright heart when I learn Your righteous judgments. (119:7).
I will keep Your statutes; do not utterly forsake me. (119:8).
How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to Your word. (119:9).
With all my heart I have sought You; do not let me stray from Your commandments. (119:10).
I have hidden Your word in my heart that I might not sin against You. (119:11).
Blessed are You, O LORD; teach me Your statutes. (119:12).
With my lips I proclaim all the judgments of Your mouth. (119:13).
I rejoice in the way of Your testimonies as much as in all riches. (119:14).
I will meditate on Your precepts and regard Your ways. (119:15).
I will delight in Your statutes; I will not forget Your word. (119:16).
Deal bountifully with Your servant, that I may live and keep Your word. (119:17).
Open my eyes that I may see wondrous things from Your law. (119:18).
I am a stranger on the earth; do not hide Your commandments from me. (119:19).
My soul is consumed with longing for Your judgments at all times. (119:20).
You rebuke the arrogant — the cursed who stray from Your commandments. (119:21).
Remove my scorn and contempt, for I have kept Your testimonies. (119:22).
Though rulers sit and slander me, Your servant meditates on Your statutes. (119:23).
Your testimonies are indeed my delight; they are my counselors. (119:24).
My soul cleaves to the dust; revive me according to Your word. (119:25).
I recounted my ways, and You answered me; teach me Your statutes. (119:26).
Make clear to me the way of Your precepts; then I will meditate on Your wonders. (119:27).
My soul melts with sorrow; strengthen me according to Your word. (119:28).
Remove me from the path of deceit and graciously grant me Your law. (119:29).
I have chosen the way of truth; I have set Your ordinances before me. (119:30).
I cling to Your testimonies, O LORD; let me not be put to shame. (119:31).
I run in the path of Your commandments, for You will enlarge my heart. (119:32).
Teach me, O LORD, the way of Your statutes, and I will keep them to the end. (119:33).
Give me understanding that I may obey Your law, and follow it with all my heart. (119:34).
Direct me in the path of Your commandments, for there I find delight. (119:35).
Turn my heart to Your testimonies and not to covetous gain. (119:36).
Turn my eyes away from worthless things; revive me with Your word. (119:37).
Establish Your word to Your servant, to produce reverence for You. (119:38).
Turn away the disgrace I dread, for Your judgments are good. (119:39).
How I long for Your precepts! Revive me in Your righteousness. (119:40).
May Your loving devotion come to me, O LORD, Your salvation, according to Your promise. (119:41).
Then I can answer him who taunts, for I trust in Your word. (119:42).
Never take Your word of truth from my mouth, for I hope in Your judgments. (119:43).
I will always obey Your law, forever and ever. (119:44).
And I will walk in freedom, for I have sought Your precepts. (119:45).
I will speak of Your testimonies before kings, and I will not be ashamed. (119:46).
I delight in Your commandments because I love them. (119:47).
I lift up my hands to Your commandments, which I love, and I meditate on Your statutes. (119:48).
Remember Your word to Your servant, upon which You have given me hope. (119:49).
This is my comfort in affliction, that Your promise has given me life. (119:50).
The arrogant utterly deride me, but I do not turn from Your law. (119:51).
I remember Your judgments of old, O LORD, and in them I find comfort. (119:52).
Rage has taken hold of me because of the wicked who reject Your law. (119:53).
Your statutes are songs to me in the house of my pilgrimage. (119:54).
In the night, O LORD, I remember Your name, that I may keep Your law. (119:55).
This is my practice, for I obey Your precepts. (119:56).
The LORD is my portion; I have promised to keep Your words. (119:57).
I have sought Your face with all my heart; be gracious to me according to Your promise. (119:58).
I considered my ways and turned my steps to Your testimonies. (119:59).
I hurried without hesitating to keep Your commandments. (119:60).
Though the ropes of the wicked bind me, I do not forget Your law. (119:61).
At midnight I rise to give You thanks for Your righteous judgments. (119:62).
I am a friend to all who fear You, and to those who keep Your precepts. (119:63).
The earth is filled with Your loving devotion, O LORD; teach me Your statutes. (119:64).
You are good to Your servant, O LORD, according to Your word. (119:65).
Teach me good judgment and knowledge, for I believe in Your commandments. (119:66).
Before I was afflicted, I went astray; but now I keep Your word. (119:67).
You are good, and You do what is good; teach me Your statutes. (119:68).
Though the arrogant have smeared me with lies, I keep Your precepts with all my heart. (119:69).
Their hearts are callous and insensitive, but I delight in Your law. (119:70).
It was good for me to be afflicted, that I might learn Your statutes. (119:71).
The law from Your mouth is more precious to me than thousands of pieces of gold and silver. (119:72).
Your hands have made me and fashioned me; give me understanding to learn Your commandments. (119:73).
May those who fear You see me and rejoice, for I have hoped in Your word. (119:74).
I know, O LORD, that Your judgments are righteous, and that in faithfulness You have afflicted me. (119:75).
May Your loving devotion comfort me, I pray, according to Your promise to Your servant. (119:76).
May Your compassion come to me, that I may live, for Your law is my delight. (119:77).
May the arrogant be put to shame for subverting me with a lie; I will meditate on Your precepts. (119:78).
May those who fear You turn to me, those who know Your testimonies. (119:79).
May my heart be blameless in Your statutes, that I may not be put to shame. (119:80).
My soul faints for Your salvation; I wait for Your word. (119:81).
My eyes fail, looking for Your promise; I ask, “When will You comfort me?” (119:82).
Though I am like a wineskin dried up by smoke, I do not forget Your statutes. (119:83).
How many days must Your servant wait? When will You execute judgment on my persecutors? (119:84).
The arrogant have dug pits for me in violation of Your law. (119:85).
All Your commandments are faithful; I am persecuted without cause— help me! (119:86).
They almost wiped me from the earth, but I have not forsaken Your precepts. (119:87).
Revive me according to Your loving devotion, that I may obey the testimony of Your mouth. (119:88).
Your word, O LORD, is everlasting; it is firmly fixed in the heavens. (119:89).
Your faithfulness continues through all generations; You established the earth, and it endures. (119:90).
Your ordinances stand to this day, for all things are servants to You. (119:91).
If Your law had not been my delight, then I would have perished in my affliction. (119:92).
I will never forget Your precepts, for by them You have revived me. (119:93).
I am Yours; save me, for I have sought Your precepts. (119:94).
The wicked wait to destroy me, but I will ponder Your testimonies. (119:95).
I have seen a limit to all perfection, but Your commandment is without limit. (119:96).
Oh, how I love Your law! All day long it is my meditation. (119:97).
Your commandments make me wiser than my enemies, for they are always with me. (119:98).
I have more insight than all my teachers, for Your testimonies are my meditation. (119:99).
I discern more than the elders, for I obey Your precepts. (119:100).
I have kept my feet from every evil path, that I may keep Your word. (119:101).
I have not departed from Your ordinances, for You Yourself have taught me. (119:102).
How sweet are Your words to my taste— sweeter than honey in my mouth! (119:103).
I gain understanding from Your precepts; therefore I hate every false way. (119:104).
Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path. (119:105).
I have sworn and confirmed that I will keep Your righteous judgments. (119:106).
I am severely afflicted, O LORD; revive me through Your word. (119:107).
Accept the freewill offerings of my mouth, O LORD, and teach me Your judgments. (119:108).
I constantly take my life in my hands, yet I do not forget Your law. (119:109).
The wicked have set a snare for me, but I have not strayed from Your precepts. (119:110).
Your testimonies are my heritage forever, for they are the joy of my heart. (119:111).
I have inclined my heart to perform Your statutes, even to the very end. (119:112).
The double-minded I despise, but Your law I love. (119:113).
You are my hiding place and my shield; I put my hope in Your word. (119:114).
Depart from me, you evildoers, that I may obey the commandments of my God. (119:115).
Sustain me as You promised, that I may live; let me not be ashamed of my hope. (119:116).
Uphold me, and I will be saved, that I may always regard Your statutes. (119:117).
You reject all who stray from Your statutes, for their deceitfulness is in vain. (119:118).
All the wicked on earth You discard like dross; therefore I love Your testimonies. (119:119).
My flesh trembles in awe of You; I stand in fear of Your judgments. (119:120).
I have done what is just and right; do not leave me to my oppressors. (119:121).
Ensure Your servant’s well-being; do not let the arrogant oppress me. (119:122).
My eyes fail, looking for Your salvation, and for Your righteous promise. (119:123).
Deal with Your servant according to Your loving devotion, and teach me Your statutes. (119:124).
I am Your servant; give me understanding, that I may know Your testimonies. (119:125).
It is time for the LORD to act, for they have broken Your law. (119:126).
Therefore I love Your commandments more than gold, even the purest gold. (119:127).
Therefore I admire all Your precepts and hate every false way. (119:128).
Wonderful are Your testimonies; therefore I obey them. (119:129).
The unfolding of Your words gives light; it informs the simple. (119:130).
I open my mouth and pant, longing for Your commandments. (119:131).
Turn to me and show me mercy, as You do to those who love Your name. (119:132).
Order my steps in Your word; let no sin rule over me. (119:133).
Redeem me from the oppression of man, that I may keep Your precepts. (119:134).
Make Your face shine upon Your servant, and teach me Your statutes. (119:135).
My eyes shed streams of tears because Your law is not obeyed. (119:136).
Righteous are You, O LORD, and upright are Your judgments. (119:137).
The testimonies You have laid down are righteous and altogether faithful. (119:138).
My zeal has consumed me because my foes forget Your words. (119:139).
Your promise is completely pure; therefore Your servant loves it. (119:140).
I am lowly and despised, but I do not forget Your precepts. (119:141).
Your righteousness is everlasting and Your law is true. (119:142).
Trouble and distress have found me, but Your commandments are my delight. (119:143).
Your testimonies are righteous forever. Give me understanding, that I may live. (119:144).
I call with all my heart; answer me, O LORD! I will obey Your statutes. (119:145).
I call to You; save me, that I may keep Your testimonies. (119:146).
I rise before dawn and cry for help; in Your word I have put my hope. (119:147).
My eyes anticipate the watches of night, that I may meditate on Your word. (119:148).
Hear my voice, O LORD, according to Your loving devotion; give me life according to Your justice. (119:149).
Those who follow after wickedness draw near; they are far from Your law. (119:150).
You are near, O LORD, and all Your commandments are true. (119:151).
Long ago I learned from Your testimonies that You have established them forever. (119:152).
Look upon my affliction and rescue me, for I have not forgotten Your law. (119:153).
Defend my cause and redeem me; revive me according to Your word. (119:154).
Salvation is far from the wicked because they do not seek Your statutes. (119:155).
Great are Your mercies, O LORD; revive me according to Your ordinances. (119:156).
Though my persecutors and foes are many, I have not turned from Your testimonies. (119:157).
I look on the faithless with loathing because they do not keep Your word. (119:158).
Consider how I love Your precepts, O LORD; give me life according to Your loving devotion. (119:159).
The entirety of Your word is truth, and all Your righteous judgments endure forever. (119:160).
Rulers persecute me without cause, but my heart fears only Your word. (119:161).
I rejoice in Your promise like one who finds great spoil. (119:162).
I hate and abhor falsehood, but Your law I love. (119:163).
Seven times a day I praise You for Your righteous judgments. (119:164).
Abundant peace belongs to those who love Your law; nothing can make them stumble. (119:165).
I wait for Your salvation, O LORD, and I carry out Your commandments. (119:166).
I obey Your testimonies and love them greatly. (119:167).
I obey Your precepts and Your testimonies, for all my ways are before You. (119:168).
May my cry come before You, O LORD; give me understanding according to Your word. (119:169).
May my plea come before You; rescue me according to Your promise. (119:170).
My lips pour forth praise, for You teach me Your statutes. (119:171).
My tongue sings of Your word, for all Your commandments are righteous. (119:172).
May Your hand be ready to help me, for I have chosen Your precepts. (119:173).
I long for Your salvation, O LORD, and Your law is my delight. (119:174).
Let me live to praise You; may Your judgments sustain me. (119:175).
I have strayed like a lost sheep; seek Your servant, for I have not forgotten Your commandments. (119:176).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 6:6-9: The command to keep these words on the heart, teach them to the children, and speak them sitting at home, walking on the road, lying down and getting up. This psalm is what that instruction sounds like when it is actually carried out.

Psalm 19:7-11: The short version of this psalm's entire subject, law and testimony and precepts and commandments and judgments stacked up in five verses, more precious than gold and sweeter than honey from the comb.

2 Timothy 3:16: Paul tells Timothy that all Scripture is God-breathed and useful for instruction, conviction, correction and training in righteousness. This psalm spends one hundred seventy-six verses on that usefulness, eight for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תּוֹרָה (torah), עֵדוֹת (edot), פִּקּוּדִים (piqqudim), חֻקִּים (chuqqim), מִצְוֹת (mitzvot), מִשְׁפָּטִים (mishpatim), דָּבָר (davar), אִמְרָה (imrah)
translationNotes.note: Eight words for God's instruction, cycled through all 176 verses, and English levels most of them into 'law' or 'word.' Torah is teaching or direction, from a root for pointing the way. Edot are testimonies, terms of a covenant put on record. Piqqudim are charges laid on someone in trust, like orders left with a steward. Chuqqim are things engraved, fixed statutes. Mitzvot are commands given by authority. Mishpatim are the verdicts a judge hands down, case law. Davar is a spoken word and imrah the saying or promise itself. Reading the psalm with the eight kept distinct is a different experience from reading it with one word repeated.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֵר לְרַגְלִי דְבָרֶךָ (ner le-ragli devarekha), Greek: λύχνος τοῖς ποσίν μου ὁ λόγος σου, Aramaic: ניר לרגלי מימרך
translationNotes.note: Metaphor for guidance (v. 105).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַשְׁרֵי (ʾashrei); Greek: μακάριοι (makarioi)
translationNotes.note: Opening word (vv. 1-2), denoting happiness from covenant faithfulness, not mere emotion.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּכָל־לֵב (be-khol lev)
translationNotes.note: Refers to undivided devotion and integrity, appearing several times (vv. 2, 10, 34, 58, 69, 145).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׂיחַ (siach)
translationNotes.note: Siach is not silent reflection. The verb means to go over a thing out loud, to rehearse or talk it through, and it is used of complaint as well as of study (1 Samuel 1:16 uses the noun for Hannah's outpouring). The psalmist uses it at verses 15, 23, 27, 48, 78, 97, 99, and 148, including at the night watches. Reading aloud was the normal way to read in the ancient world; Acts 8:30 has Philip hear the Ethiopian reading Isaiah from the road.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁעֲשֻׁעַי (shaʿashuʿai)
translationNotes.note: Often translated 'delight' (vv. 24, 77, 92, 143, 174); conveys joy, play, or pleasure in God’s law.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חַיֵּנִי (chayyeni); Greek: ζῳοποίησόν με (zōopoiēson me)
translationNotes.note: Repeated prayer (vv. 25, 37, 40, 88, 107, 149, 154, 156, 159) meaning 'give me life' or 'restore vitality'.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אָלֶף / תָּו (aleph / tav)
translationNotes.note: The longest chapter in the Bible is built as an alphabet. Twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet in order, eight verses each, and every one of the eight verses in a stanza begins with that letter: 22 times 8 is the psalm's 176 verses. The letter headings printed through this chapter mark where each stanza starts. Nothing of the pattern survives translation, which is why the psalm can read in English as if it simply goes on.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דֶּרֶךְ (derekh), נָתִיב (nativ), אֹרַח (orach)
translationNotes.note: Images of life-direction or conduct; often paired with 'keep,' 'walk,' or 'turn' in relation to God’s commands.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נַחֲלָה (nachalah) (v. 111)
translationNotes.note: Means 'inheritance' or 'portion'; the psalmist treats God’s statutes as his true possession.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm is an extended acrostic praising, pleading for, and committing to God’s word with many synonyms and repeated petitions.

headings.text: Your Word Is a Lamp to My Feet א ALEPH

stories.title: 🧭 Psalms 120
summaryBullets: In my distress I cried to the LORD, and He answered me. (120:1).
Deliver my soul, O LORD, from lying lips and a deceitful tongue. (120:2).
What will He do to you, and what will be added to you, O deceitful tongue? (120:3).
Sharp arrows will come from the warrior, with burning coals of the broom tree! (120:4).
Woe to me that I dwell in Meshech, that I live among the tents of Kedar! (120:5).
Too long have I dwelt among those who hate peace. (120:6).
I am in favor of peace; but when I speak, they want war. (120:7).
crossRefs: Psalm 134:1-3: The last of the fifteen Songs of Ascents, sung at the top of the climb by servants standing in the house of the LORD through the night. This is the first of them, sung by a man as far from Jerusalem as the collection ever gets.

Jeremiah 9:8: Tongues called deadly arrows that speak deception, a man wishing his neighbor peace aloud while setting a trap for him in his heart. The psalm uses both images, sharp arrows and men who answer talk of peace with war.

1 Peter 3:10: Peter quotes a psalm about keeping the tongue from evil and the lips from deceitful speech as the way to love life and see good days. Lying lips and a deceitful tongue are the exact trouble this song opens with.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁיר הַמַּעֲלוֹת (shir ha-maʿalot), Greek: ᾠδὴ τῶν ἀναβαθμῶν, Aramaic: שירתא דמעלות
translationNotes.note: Title for pilgrimage songs (Pss 120-134).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֶשֶׁךְ (Meshekh) / קֵדָר (Qedar), Greek: Μοσόχ / Κεδάρ, Aramaic: משך / קדר
translationNotes.note: Distant peoples evoked to depict exile-like sojourning (v. 5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַעֲלוֹת (ma'alot)
translationNotes.note: Ma'alot means steps or stairs; the collection is a set of songs for the walk up. The law required every male to appear before the LORD three times a year (Deuteronomy 16:16), and Scripture always uses 'go up' for the trip, whatever direction it came from: Elkanah went up yearly from Ramah (1 Samuel 1:3), and Jesus' family went up for Passover when He was twelve (Luke 2:41-42). Families travelled in company, which is how they lost track of Him for a day.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גַּחֲלֵי רְתָמִים (gachalei retamim)
translationNotes.note: The white broom is a desert shrub that Elijah slept under in the wilderness (1 Kings 19:4-5). Its wood makes the hottest and longest-burning charcoal available in that country, and desert dwellers still cut it for exactly that. Verse 4 pairs the sharpened arrows of a warrior with coals that will not go out; the point of both is that a slanderous tongue keeps burning long after it is used.

stories.keyTakeaway: The first Song of Ascents cries for deliverance from deceit and laments living among hostile peoples far from peace.

headings.text: In My Distress I Cried to the Lord

stories.superscription: A song of ascents.

stories.title: ⛰️ Psalms 121
summaryBullets: I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come? (121:1).
My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth. (121:2).
He will not allow your foot to slip; your Protector will not slumber. (121:3).
Behold, the Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep. (121:4).
The LORD is your keeper; the LORD is the shade on your right hand. (121:5).
The sun will not strike you by day, nor the moon by night. (121:6).
The LORD will guard you from all evil; He will preserve your soul. (121:7).
The LORD will watch over your coming and going, both now and forevermore. (121:8).
crossRefs: Numbers 6:24: The opening line of the blessing the priests were ordered to speak over Israel, may the LORD bless you and keep you. This song is that second verb worked out at length, the LORD is your keeper, guarding your going out and your coming in.

Isaiah 27:3: God speaking about His vineyard, I am its keeper, I water it continually, I guard it night and day so no one can disturb it. The psalm applies that round-the-clock watch to one traveler, a keeper who never slumbers.

Psalm 124:8: The same line closes another Song of Ascents, our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth. There it is the last word after a narrow escape, here it is the answer to the question the singer opens with.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שׁמר (shamar), Greek (LXX): φυλάσσω, Aramaic: נטר (natar)
translationNotes.note: Repeated verb meaning guard/preserve (vv. 3-8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צאתך ובואך (tsetekha u-voʾekha), Greek: τὴν ἔξοδόν σου καὶ τὴν εἴσοδόν σου, Aramaic: מפקך ועיילך
translationNotes.note: Merism for daily activities and movements (v. 8).

translationNotes.term: I lift up my eyes to the hills
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֶהָרִים (he-harim)
translationNotes.note: Jerusalem stands on the central ridge at about 2,500 feet above sea level, so every road to it climbs. A pilgrim coming from Jericho, which lies about 850 feet below sea level, gained more than 3,000 feet in roughly fifteen miles of bare hill country with no water and a name for bandits. That is the road in the parable of Luke 10:30, and the hills of verse 1 are the ones still to be crossed.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁמֵר (shomer)
translationNotes.note: These psalms climb by repeating a word from one line at the head of the next, like feet on stairs. Verses 1 and 2 hand off 'help,' then verses 3 through 5 repeat the keeper six times: He will not slumber, He who keeps Israel will not slumber, the LORD is your keeper. The same stepping runs through 122:2-3, 123:2, 124:1-2, 126:2-3, and 129:1-2.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm states that the LORD, Maker of heaven and earth, constantly keeps and guards His people in all their ways.

headings.text: I Lift Up My Eyes to the Hills

stories.superscription: A song of ascents.

stories.title: 🏙️ Psalms 122
summaryBullets: I was glad when they said to me, “Let us go to the house of the LORD.” (122:1).
Our feet are standing in your gates, O Jerusalem. (122:2).
Jerusalem is built up as a city united together, (122:3).
where the tribes go up, the tribes of the LORD, as a testimony for Israel, to give thanks to the name of the LORD. (122:4).
For there the thrones of judgment stand, the thrones of the house of David. (122:5).
Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: “May those who love you prosper. (122:6).
May there be peace within your walls, and prosperity inside your fortresses.” (122:7).
For the sake of my brothers and friends, I will say, “Peace be within you.” (122:8).
For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your prosperity. (122:9).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 16:16: The law requiring every man to appear before the LORD three times a year, at Unleavened Bread, at Weeks and at Tabernacles. That obligation is why the tribes go up in verse 4, and why a collection of pilgrim songs exists at all.

2 Samuel 8:15: David reigned over all Israel and administered justice and righteousness for all his people. The psalm points at the institution that did it, the thrones of judgment standing in Jerusalem, the thrones of the house of David.

Psalm 48:12-13: The instruction to march around Zion, count her towers and consider her ramparts so the next generation can be told. This psalm runs the same survey from inside the gates, a city built up and joined together.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁלוֹם (shalom) / שַׁלְוָה (shalvah), Greek: εἰρήνη / εὐθηνία, Aramaic: שלמא / שלוותא
translationNotes.note: Blessings requested for the city (vv. 6-7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית יְהוָה (beit YHWH), Greek: οἶκος Κυρίου, Aramaic: ביתא דיי
translationNotes.note: Temple designation (vv. 1, 9).

translationNotes.term: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁאֲלוּ שְׁלוֹם יְרוּשָׁלָיִם (sha'alu shelom Yerushalayim)
translationNotes.note: Verses 6 and 7 run a chain of sounds English cannot carry: sha'alu, shelom, Yerushalayim, yishlayu, shalvah, shalom. Four of the six turn on the same consonants as shalom, and the name of the city itself ends in them. The line is built out of its own subject.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּסְאוֹת לְמִשְׁפָּט (kis'ot le-mishpat)
translationNotes.note: The king was the final court of appeal, which is why the capital held the thrones. Solomon judged the two women disputing a child (1 Kings 3:16-28) and built a Hall of the Throne, a hall of judgment panelled in cedar, for hearing cases (1 Kings 7:7). Absalom stole the kingdom by intercepting men bringing their suits to that court (2 Samuel 15:2-6). Verse 5 lists it as one of the reasons to go up.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm rejoices in going to Jerusalem, notes its unity and judgment seats, and calls for prayers for its peace and security.

headings.text: Pray for the Peace of Jerusalem

stories.superscription: A song of ascents. Of David.

stories.title: 👀 Psalms 123
summaryBullets: I lift up my eyes to You, the One enthroned in heaven. (123:1).
As the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a maidservant look to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes are on the LORD our God until He shows us mercy. (123:2).
Have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy, for we have endured much contempt. (123:3).
We have endured much scorn from the arrogant, much contempt from the proud. (123:4).
crossRefs: Psalm 25:15: My eyes are always on the LORD, for He will free my feet from the mesh. This song opens the same way but names what forces the stare, contempt from the arrogant and nowhere else to look.

Isaiah 37:23: Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes in pride, against the Holy One of Israel. Those are the proud eyes this psalm answers, lifted in scorn while the singer lifts his in appeal.

Luke 18:13: A tax collector at the temple will not lift his eyes to heaven at all, but beats his breast and asks God for mercy. The psalm lifts its eyes and asks the same thing twice over, have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בּוּז (buz) / לַעַג (laʿag), Greek: καταφρόνησις / ἐμπαιγμός, Aramaic: בוזא / לעגא
translationNotes.note: Derision faced by the petitioner (vv. 3-4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חָנֵּנוּ (ḥannenu), Greek: ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς, Aramaic: רחם עלנא
translationNotes.note: Appeal for favor/mercy (vv. 2-3).

translationNotes.term: The eyes of servants look to the hand
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶל־יַד (el-yad)
translationNotes.note: Verse 2 is watching the hand, not the face. Household servants stood through a meal waiting for a gesture, since orders at table were given by hand and a servant who was not looking missed his. The psalm sets that posture as the picture of waiting on God: attention fixed, nothing done until the hand moves.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַשַּׁאֲנַנִּים (ha-sha'ananim)
translationNotes.note: Sha'anan means settled, undisturbed, with nothing pressing. It is the word Amos 6:1 uses against those at ease in Zion, stretched on ivory beds. Verse 4 identifies where the contempt is coming from: not enemies in arms but comfortable people with time on their hands.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm looks to the LORD for grace amid contempt and scorn from the proud.

headings.text: I Lift Up My Eyes to You

stories.superscription: A song of ascents.

stories.title: 🪤 Psalms 124
summaryBullets: If the LORD had not been on our side— let Israel now declare— (124:1).
if the LORD had not been on our side when men attacked us, (124:2).
when their anger flared against us, then they would have swallowed us alive, (124:3).
then the floods would have engulfed us, then the torrent would have overwhelmed us, (124:4).
then the raging waters would have swept us away. (124:5).
Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey to their teeth. (124:6).
We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowler; the net is torn, and we have slipped away. (124:7).
Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth. (124:8).
crossRefs: Psalm 121:2: The same sentence, our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, which this psalm holds back for its final line. There it answers a question at the start of a journey, here it is the verdict on a rescue already survived.

Exodus 14:28-30: The water flowing back over the chariots and horsemen until not one of Pharaoh's army survived, while Israel walked out on dry ground. The psalm reverses that picture, imagining the flood sweeping over Israel instead had God not been on their side.

Proverbs 6:5: Free yourself like a gazelle from the hunter and like a bird from the snare of the fowler, advice to a man who has pledged himself for a stranger's debt. The psalm reports the escape as finished, the net is torn and we have slipped away.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פַּח (paḥ), Greek: παγίς, Aramaic: פחא
translationNotes.note: Trap for birds; image of sudden capture (v. 7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֹשֵׂה שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ (ʿoseh shamayim vaʾarets), Greek: ποιήσας οὐρανὸν καὶ γῆν, Aramaic: דעבד שמיא וארעא
translationNotes.note: Title affirming power to help (v. 8).

translationNotes.term: The torrent would have swept over us
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נַחְלָה (nachlah)
translationNotes.note: A nachal is a wadi, a stone channel that is dry most of the year. Rain falling miles away fills it without warning and it runs deep and fast within minutes, which still kills hikers in the Judean wilderness. Verses 4 and 5 pile up water, torrent, and raging waters for something that arrives too fast to outrun.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יֹאמַר־נָא יִשְׂרָאֵל (yomar na Yisrael)
translationNotes.note: A cue line. One voice sings the first half and the assembly answers with the repeat, which is why verse 1 breaks off and verse 2 starts again from the top. The same call sets up the responses at Psalm 118:2-4 and Psalm 129:1. These were marching songs for a crowd, not solos.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm describes rescue from hostile men, overwhelming waters, and a broken snare, crediting the LORD, Maker of heaven and earth.

headings.text: Our Help Is in the Name of the Lord

stories.superscription: A song of ascents. Of David.

stories.title: 🏔️ Psalms 125
summaryBullets: Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion. It cannot be moved; it abides forever. (125:1).
As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds His people, both now and forevermore. (125:2).
For the scepter of the wicked will not rest upon the land allotted to the righteous, so that the righteous will not put forth their hands to injustice. (125:3).
Do good, O LORD, to those who are good, and to the upright in heart. (125:4).
But those who turn to crooked ways the LORD will banish with the evildoers. Peace be upon Israel. (125:5).
