crossRefs: Psalm 48:1-2: Mount Zion praised as the city of the great King, beautiful in loftiness and the joy of all the earth. This psalm uses that same mountain as a unit of measurement, those who trust in the LORD are like it and cannot be moved.

Isaiah 10:5: Assyria called the rod of God's anger, a staff He picks up to strike with and later breaks. The psalm sets the limit on that arrangement, the scepter of the wicked will not rest on the land allotted to the righteous.
Galatians 6:16: Paul ends his letter with peace and mercy on all who walk by this rule, even the Israel of God. That closing greeting is this psalm's last line, peace be upon Israel.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֵׁבֶט (shevet), Greek: ῥάβδος, Aramaic: שבטא
translationNotes.note: Rod of rule; here “scepter of wickedness” (v. 3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַקַלְקַלּוֹת (ʿaqalqalot), Greek: σκολιαί, Aramaic: עקלתון
translationNotes.note: Twisted paths contrasted with uprightness (v. 5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הָרִים סָבִיב לָהּ (harim saviv lah)
translationNotes.note: Literal topography. The Temple Mount sits at about 2,400 feet, and the Mount of Olives across the Kidron valley rises higher, near 2,700. Hills stand around the city on the east, south, and west, so a traveller sees the ring before he sees the city, and an army on those heights looks down into it. Verse 2 takes the arrangement as the picture of protection.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צִיּוֹן (Tsiyyon)
translationNotes.note: The name moves. It first belongs to the Jebusite stronghold David captured, 'the fortress of Zion, that is, the City of David' (2 Samuel 5:7), a narrow ridge south of the later temple platform. It then covers the temple hill (Psalm 132:13), and then the whole city and its people (Isaiah 40:9). Which one a verse means has to be read from its context.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm compares trusters to immovable Mount Zion, states surrounding protection, and contrasts the upright with those turning aside.
stories.superscription: A song of ascents.

stories.title: 🌾 Psalms 126
summaryBullets: When the LORD restored the captives of Zion, we were like dreamers. (126:1).
Then our mouths were filled with laughter, our tongues with shouts of joy. Then it was said among the nations, “The LORD has done great things for them.” (126:2).
The LORD has done great things for us; we are filled with joy. (126:3).
Restore our captives, O LORD, like streams in the Negev. (126:4).
Those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy. (126:5).
He who goes out weeping, bearing a trail of seed, will surely return with shouts of joy, carrying sheaves of grain. (126:6).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 30:18: God promises to restore the fortunes of Jacob's tents and rebuild the city on its own ruins. The psalm reports part of that already granted and asks for the remainder, restore our captives like streams in the Negev.

Isaiah 35:6-7: Water gushing in the wilderness, streams in the desert, parched ground turning into a pool. That is the picture behind the psalm's request, dry beds in the Negev filling within hours once the rains arrive.

Ezra 1:1-4: Cyrus of Persia issues the decree sending the exiles home to rebuild the house of the LORD in Jerusalem. The psalm is that homecoming remembered, mouths full of laughter and the nations saying the LORD has done great things for them.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שׁוּב שְׁבִית/שְׁבוּת (shuv shevit/shevut), Greek: ἐπιστρέφειν αἰχμαλωσίαν, Aramaic: להשיב שביתה
translationNotes.note: Idiom for turning captivity/condition (vv. 1, 4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲלֻמּוֹת (ʾalumot), Greek: δράγματα, Aramaic: עמריא
translationNotes.note: Bundles of harvested stalks (v. 6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כַּאֲפִיקִים בַּנֶּגֶב (ka-aphiqim ba-Negev)
translationNotes.note: The Negev is the dry south of the country, where the annual rainfall is a few inches and the stream beds hold nothing for most of the year. After the winter rains those same channels run hard for a few days and the desert greens. Verse 4 asks for that kind of turnaround: not gradual improvement, but a dry bed suddenly full.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֶשֶׁךְ הַזָּרַע (meshekh ha-zara)
translationNotes.note: Seed grain and food grain are the same grain. After a bad year, a farmer scattering seed was taking bread out of his household's mouth on the chance of a harvest four months off. Genesis 47:19-24 shows Egyptians trading themselves for seed in the famine. The tears in verses 5 and 6 are the cost of the sowing, and the sheaves are the answer to it.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm recalls a restoration of Zion and prays for renewed restoration, stating that sowing in tears ends with sheaves and joy.
stories.superscription: A song of ascents.

stories.title: 🏠 Psalms 127
summaryBullets: Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain; unless the LORD protects the city, its watchmen stand guard in vain. (127:1).
In vain you rise early and stay up late, toiling for bread to eat — for He gives sleep to His beloved. (127:2).
Children are indeed a heritage from the LORD, and the fruit of the womb is His reward. (127:3).
Like arrows in the hand of a warrior, so are children born in one’s youth. (127:4).
Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them. He will not be put to shame when he confronts the enemies at the gate. (127:5).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 6:6-9: The words commanded to be taught to children at home and on the road and written on the doorposts of the house. This psalm is about the same house and names who actually builds it, since without Him the builders labor for nothing.

Nehemiah 4:9: Nehemiah prays to God and posts a guard day and night while the wall goes up, doing both at once. The psalm explains why that is not a contradiction, unless the LORD protects the city the watchmen stand guard in vain.

Ruth 4:11: The elders at the gate bless Boaz and Ruth, asking that she be like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel. This psalm of Solomon opens on that same verb, and the children it goes on to describe are the building material.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְדִידוֹ (yedidō), Greek: ἀγαπητός, Aramaic: ידידא
translationNotes.note: Recipient of God’s gift of sleep (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נַחֲלָה (naḥalah) / שָׂכָר (sakar), Greek: κληρονομία / μισθός, Aramaic: ירותא / אגרא
translationNotes.note: Status and gift language for children (v. 3).

Far more than an entrance; the public square where elders heard legal cases, contracts were witnessed, market business transacted, and news was exchanged. 'Sitting in the gate' (Genesis 19:1; Ruth 4:1-11; Proverbs 31:23) signals civic authority and active community life.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁעַר (sha'ar)

translationNotes.term: Unless the LORD builds the house
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אִם־יְהוָה לֹא־יִבְנֶה בַיִת (im YHWH lo yivneh vayit)
translationNotes.note: Bayit means the building, the family living in it, and the dynasty descending from it. All three senses are in play in a psalm headed with Solomon's name: he built the temple and the palace, and 2 Samuel 7:11-13 turns on the same word when David offers to build God a house and God answers that He will build David one. Verse 3 then names what the house is actually made of, which is children.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm states the futility of toil without the LORD’s building and watching and calls children a heritage and reward.

headings.text: Children Are a Heritage from the Lord

stories.superscription: A song of ascents. Of Solomon.

stories.title: 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 Psalms 128
summaryBullets: Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in His ways! (128:1).
For when you eat the fruit of your labor, blessings and prosperity will be yours. (128:2).
Your wife will be like a fruitful vine flourishing within your house, your sons like olive shoots sitting around your table. (128:3).
In this way indeed shall blessing come to the man who fears the LORD. (128:4).
May the LORD bless you from Zion, that you may see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life, (128:5).
that you may see your children’s children. Peace be upon Israel! (128:6).
crossRefs: Psalm 112:1-3: The same opening line, blessed is the man who fears the LORD, followed there by wealth in the house and descendants mighty in the land. This psalm keeps the blessing domestic, the fruit of your own labor, a wife like a vine, sons around the table.
Psalm 52:8: David calls himself an olive tree flourishing in the house of God. This psalm moves that tree to the family table and makes it plural, sons like olive shoots set around it.

Proverbs 31:10-12: A wife of noble character whose husband trusts her completely and who brings him good all the days of her life. The psalm draws the same household from the husband's side, a man eating what his own hands earned.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זִיתִים (zitim), Greek: ἐλαῖαι, Aramaic: זיתין
translationNotes.note: New growth around an olive tree (v. 3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יִרְאַת יְהוָה (yirʾat YHWH), Greek: φόβος Κυρίου, Aramaic: דחלתא דיי
translationNotes.note: Reverent regard that frames the blessings (vv. 1, 4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְגִיעַ כַּפֶּיךָ (yegia kappekha)
translationNotes.note: Verse 2 reverses a specific curse. Deuteronomy 28:30-33 lists the covenant penalties: you will build a house and not live in it, plant a vineyard and not enjoy it, and a people you do not know will eat what your land produces. Eating what your own hands grew is not a modest wish; it is the sign that the curse is not running.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּנִים לְבָנֶיךָ (banim le-vanekha)
translationNotes.note: Living to see grandchildren marked a completed life, and it is recorded when it happens: Joseph saw the third generation of Ephraim's sons (Genesis 50:23), and Job saw four generations after his restoration (Job 42:16). With no written records for most families, an old man surrounded by descendants was the whole of a man's continuity.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm describes home, work, and family blessing for the one who fears the LORD, with wishes for Zion’s good and peace.

headings.text: The Blessed Fear of the Lord

stories.superscription: A song of ascents.

stories.title: 🌿 Psalms 129
summaryBullets: Many a time they have persecuted me from my youth— let Israel now declare— (129:1).
many a time they have persecuted me from my youth, but they have not prevailed against me. (129:2).
The plowmen plowed over my back; they made their furrows long. (129:3).
The LORD is righteous; He has cut me from the cords of the wicked. (129:4).
May all who hate Zion be turned back in shame. (129:5).
May they be like grass on the rooftops, which withers before it can grow, (129:6).
unable to fill the hands of the reaper, or the arms of the binder of sheaves. (129:7).
May none who pass by say to them, “The blessing of the LORD be on you; we bless you in the name of the LORD.” (129:8).
crossRefs: Isaiah 51:1-2: Israel told to look back to the rock it was cut from, to Abraham and Sarah, when the whole nation was one man. The psalm looks back the same distance but at the affliction, persecuted from my youth, and reports that it never prevailed.

2 Kings 19:26: Sennacherib's own taunt, that the peoples he conquered were like grass on the rooftops, scorched before it could grow. The psalm asks for exactly that image to fall on everyone who hates Zion.
Psalm 124:7: Another Song of Ascents on the same escape, the net torn and the bird gone. This one names the cutting instead, the LORD is righteous and He has cut me free from the cords of the wicked.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַעְלֻנוֹת (maʿlunot), Greek: αὔλακες, Aramaic: תלמי
translationNotes.note: Plow lines as a metaphor for deep wounds (v. 3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲצִיר גַּגּוֹת (ḥatsir gaggot), Greek: χόρτος ἐπὶ δωμάτων, Aramaic: חמרא על גגות
translationNotes.note: Shallow-soil growth that quickly withers (v. 6).

translationNotes.term: The blessing of the LORD be upon you
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בִּרְכַּת־יְהוָה אֲלֵיכֶם (birkat YHWH aleikhem)
translationNotes.note: This was the ordinary greeting called out to men working a harvest, and the reapers called an answer back. Ruth 2:4 records the exchange word for word: Boaz arrives and says 'The LORD be with you,' and the harvesters answer 'The LORD bless you.' Verse 8 says that of this crop nobody says it, which is a way of saying the field is cursed without using the word.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִנְּעוּרַי (minne'uray)
translationNotes.note: The speaker in verses 1 and 2 is the nation, and its youth is Egypt and the wilderness. Hosea 11:1 uses the same frame, 'when Israel was a child I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son,' and Jeremiah 2:2 recalls the devotion of Israel's youth in the desert. The claim in verse 2 is that the oppression never once finished the job.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm recalls long affliction without defeat, the LORD cutting cords, and wishes shame on Zion-haters like rooftop grass.
stories.superscription: A song of ascents.

stories.title: 🌊 Psalms 130
summaryBullets: Out of the depths I cry to You, O LORD! (130:1).
O Lord, hear my voice; let Your ears be attentive to my plea for mercy. (130:2).
If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand? (130:3).
But with You there is forgiveness, so that You may be feared. (130:4).
I wait for the LORD; my soul does wait, and in His word I put my hope. (130:5).
My soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning— more than watchmen wait for the morning. (130:6).
O Israel, put your hope in the LORD, for with the LORD is loving devotion, and with Him is redemption in abundance. (130:7).
And He will redeem Israel from all iniquity. (130:8).
crossRefs: Lamentations 3:55-57: A man calls on God's name out of the depths of the pit, is heard, and God draws near and tells him not to be afraid. The psalm opens from that same floor, out of the depths I cry to You.

Nehemiah 9:17: The Levites' public confession recalls a God who is forgiving, gracious and compassionate, and who did not abandon a people that refused to listen. The psalm makes that forgiveness the reason God is feared at all.
Psalm 121:4: The Protector of Israel who neither slumbers nor sleeps. This psalm puts the singer in the watchman's shift instead, waiting for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַעֲמַקִּים (maʿamaqim), Greek: βάθη, Aramaic: עמיקתא
translationNotes.note: Abyssal places; figurative for severe distress (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פָּדָה (padah) / גְּאֻלָּה (geʾullah), Greek: λυτρόω / ἀπολύτρωσις, Aramaic: פרק / פריקא
translationNotes.note: Deliver/rescue terms used in vv. 7-8.

Psalms 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, and 143 have been grouped as the seven penitential psalms in Western use since Cassiodorus listed them in his commentary in the sixth century. This one is known by its first words in Latin, De profundis, 'out of the depths.' Four of the seven fall in this half of the Psalter.

translationNotes.term: More than watchmen for the morning
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁמְרִים לַבֹּקֶר (shomrim la-boqer)
translationNotes.note: Sentries stood the night in shifts on the walls, and the Hebrew night ran in three watches (Judges 7:19; Lamentations 2:19). The last of them ended at first light, when attack became unlikely and the relief came up. Verse 6 says the phrase twice in a row, watchmen for the morning, watchmen for the morning, which is the psalm imitating the waiting.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm cries from the depths, states forgiveness with the LORD, urges waiting and hope, and declares redemption for Israel.
stories.superscription: A song of ascents.

stories.title: 🧸 Psalms 131
summaryBullets: My heart is not proud, O LORD, my eyes are not haughty. I do not aspire to great things or matters too lofty for me. (131:1).
Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul; like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me. (131:2).
O Israel, put your hope in the LORD, both now and forevermore. (131:3).
crossRefs: Proverbs 16:19: Better to be lowly in spirit among the humble than to divide the spoil with the proud. The psalm is that proverb spoken in the first person by a king, my heart is not proud and my eyes are not haughty.

Psalm 37:11: The meek will inherit the land and delight in abundant prosperity. This psalm shows what that meekness feels like from inside, a soul stilled and quieted like a weaned child with his mother.

Micah 6:8: What the LORD requires, to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God. The psalm takes the third of those and does nothing else with its three verses, refusing matters too lofty and going quiet.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גָּמוּל (gamul)
translationNotes.note: Child no longer nursing; image of settled rest (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נִפְלָאוֹת (niflaʾot)
translationNotes.note: Matters beyond one’s scope (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גָּמֻל (gamul)
translationNotes.note: Weaning came late, at two to three years old, and it was an occasion: Abraham held a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned (Genesis 21:8), and Hannah kept Samuel at home until he was weaned before taking him to Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:22-24). The picture in verse 2 is exact. The child is old enough to have stopped crying for the breast and still stays on the mother, wanting her rather than what she gives.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא־רָמוּ עֵינַי (lo ramu einai)
translationNotes.note: The lifted eye is the standard Hebrew figure for arrogance: haughty eyes head the list of things the LORD hates in Proverbs 6:17, and the king in Psalm 101:5 will not put up with them. In a collection of songs about going up, verse 1 has the pilgrim climbing with his eyes down.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm states humility, a quieted soul like a weaned child, and calls Israel to hope in the LORD.
stories.superscription: A song of ascents. Of David.

stories.title: 🛏️ Psalms 132
summaryBullets: O LORD, remember on behalf of David all the hardships he endured, (132:1).
how he swore an oath to the LORD, and vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob: (132:2).
“I will not enter my house or get into my bed, (132:3).
I will not give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids, (132:4).
until I find a place for the LORD, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob.” (132:5).
We heard that the ark was in Ephrathah; we found it in the fields of Jaar. (132:6).
Let us go to His dwelling place; let us worship at His footstool. (132:7).
Arise, O LORD, to Your resting place, You and the ark of Your strength. (132:8).
May Your priests be clothed with righteousness, and Your saints shout for joy. (132:9).
For the sake of Your servant David, do not reject Your anointed one. (132:10).
The LORD swore an oath to David, a promise He will not revoke: “One of your descendants I will place on your throne. (132:11).
If your sons keep My covenant and the testimony I will teach them, then their sons will also sit on your throne forever and ever.” (132:12).
For the LORD has chosen Zion; He has desired it for His home: (132:13).
“This is My resting place forever and ever; here I will dwell, for I have desired this home. (132:14).
I will bless her with abundant provisions; I will satisfy her poor with bread. (132:15).
I will clothe her priests with salvation, and her saints will sing out in joy. (132:16).
There I will make a horn grow for David; I have prepared a lamp for My anointed one. (132:17).
I will clothe his enemies with shame, but the crown upon him will gleam.” (132:18).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 6:12-19: David brings the ark up to the city, dancing before the LORD in a linen ephod with shouting and the ram's horn, and sets it in the tent he had pitched. The psalm relives that procession, let us go to His dwelling place.

2 Samuel 7:12-16: God's promise through Nathan that David's throne will be established forever. The psalm quotes it back as an oath the LORD will not revoke, then attaches the condition, if your sons keep My covenant.

1 Chronicles 15:1-3: David prepares a place in the City of David, pitches a tent for the ark, and rules that no one but the Levites may carry it. The psalm turns that preparation into a vow, no sleep until I find a place for the LORD.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָשִׁיחַ (mashiaḥ), Greek: χριστός (christos), Aramaic: משיחא (meshicha)
translationNotes.note: God’s appointed king (vv. 10, 17).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְנוּחָה (menuchah), Greek: κατάπαυσις, Aramaic: מנוחה
translationNotes.note: Declared of Zion and the ark’s dwelling (vv. 8, 14).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׂדֵי־יָעַר (sdei-ya'ar)
translationNotes.note: Jaar is Kiriath-jearim, where the ark sat for twenty years after the Philistines sent it back on a cart, kept in Abinadab's house on the hill (1 Samuel 6:21 through 7:2). Ephrathah in the same verse is Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19). Verse 6 is retracing David's search before he brought the ark up to Jerusalem in 2 Samuel 6.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֵר (ner)
translationNotes.note: The lamp is a standing promise to David's line, and the phrase recurs when the line nearly fails: God kept a lamp for David in Jerusalem for Solomon's son (1 Kings 11:36; 15:4) and for Jehoram (2 Kings 8:19). Verse 17 pairs it with making a horn sprout for David, horn being the animal image for strength that can still grow.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm recalls David’s vow, the ark, God’s oath to David, and His choice of Zion as His resting place with blessings and a sprouting horn.
stories.superscription: A song of ascents.

stories.title: 🫂 Psalms 133
summaryBullets: Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony! (133:1).
It is like fine oil on the head, running down on the beard, running down Aaron’s beard over the collar of his robes. (133:2).
It is like the dew of Hermon falling on the mountains of Zion. For there the LORD has bestowed the blessing of life forevermore. (133:3).
crossRefs: Exodus 29:7: The instruction for ordaining Aaron, take the anointing oil and pour it on his head. The psalm makes that pouring its measure of unity, oil running down the beard and over the collar of his robes.

Leviticus 8:12: Moses carrying the instruction out, pouring the anointing oil on Aaron's head to consecrate him. The psalm names Aaron directly, so the picture is a priest being set apart for God, not a pleasant gesture at a meal.

Deuteronomy 33:28: Moses blesses Israel with a land of grain and new wine where the heavens drip with dew and the nation dwells secure. The psalm joins those two, dew off Hermon settling on the mountains of Zion and brothers living together in one place.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יָחַד (yaḥad), Greek: ὁμονοία, Aramaic: יחד
translationNotes.note: Dwelling together in oneness (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֶׁמֶן הַטּוֹב (shemen ha-tov)
translationNotes.note: Consecrating oil flowing on Aaron (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֶׁמֶן הַמִּשְׁחָה (shemen ha-mishchah)
translationNotes.note: The anointing oil was a fixed formula: liquid myrrh, fragrant cinnamon, fragrant cane, cassia, and olive oil, blended by a perfumer (Exodus 30:22-25). Copying it for ordinary use, or putting it on an outsider, cut a man off from his people (Exodus 30:32-33). It was poured on Aaron's head at his ordination (Leviticus 8:12), and verse 2 follows it down the beard to the collar of his robes.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: טַל־חֶרְמוֹן (tal-Chermon)
translationNotes.note: Mount Hermon marks the northern limit of the land and rises to about 9,200 feet, snow-covered much of the year. Its heights collect heavy night dew, while Jerusalem sits some 120 miles south on a dry ridge. Verse 3 takes the moisture from the wettest high ground in the country and puts it on Zion, which is the point: the two are nowhere near each other.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm compares unity to Aaron’s anointing oil and Hermon’s dew and states that the LORD commands blessing there.

headings.text: How Pleasant to Live in Harmony!

stories.superscription: A song of ascents. Of David.

stories.title: 🌙 Psalms 134
summaryBullets: Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD who serve by night in the house of the LORD! (134:1).
Lift up your hands to the sanctuary and bless the LORD! (134:2).
May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion. (134:3).
crossRefs: 1 Chronicles 9:33: The Levite musicians lived in the temple chambers and were excused from every other duty because they were on call day and night. The psalm is addressed to exactly those men, servants of the LORD who stand in His house through the night.

Psalm 63:4: In Your name I will lift my hands, said by David out in the Wilderness of Judah with no sanctuary anywhere near him. This psalm gives the same gesture its proper address, lift up your hands to the sanctuary and bless the LORD.

Numbers 6:24-26: The blessing the priests were commanded to speak over Israel. The last of the Songs of Ascents reverses the direction and then restores it, the people bless the LORD and are sent home blessed from Zion.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׂאוּ יְדֵיכֶם (seʾu yedeikhem), Greek: αἴρατε τὰς χεῖρας, Aramaic: שאו ידיכון
translationNotes.note: Gesture of prayer/praise (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּרַךְ (barakh), Greek: εὐλογεῖν, Aramaic: ברך
translationNotes.note: Speak well of or invoke favor (vv. 1-3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּלֵּילוֹת (ba-leilot)
translationNotes.note: The temple was staffed around the clock. The singers were on duty day and night (1 Chronicles 9:33), and the gatekeepers spent the night around the house of God because they held the keys and opened it every morning (1 Chronicles 9:27). This last of the ascents is what the pilgrims called out to the men staying behind on the night shift, and verse 3 is the answer from inside.

translationNotes.term: The LORD bless you from Zion
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְבָרֶכְךָ יְהוָה מִצִּיּוֹן (yevarekhekha YHWH mi-Tsiyyon)
translationNotes.note: The opening words of the priestly blessing Aaron and his sons were given for Israel: 'The LORD bless you and keep you' (Numbers 6:24-26). Two rolled silver amulets found by Gabriel Barkay in 1979 in a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom, just outside Jerusalem, carry that blessing and date to around 600 BC, which makes them the oldest known copies of any text from the Hebrew Bible.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm calls night ministers to lift hands and bless the LORD and pronounces blessing from Zion’s Maker.

headings.text: Bless the Lord, All You Servants

stories.superscription: A song of ascents.

stories.title: 🎶 Psalms 135
summaryBullets: Hallelujah! Praise the name of the LORD. Give praise, O servants of the LORD, (135:1).
who stand in the house of the LORD, in the courts of the house of our God. (135:2).
Hallelujah, for the LORD is good; sing praises to His name, for it is lovely. (135:3).
For the LORD has chosen Jacob as His own, Israel as His treasured possession. (135:4).
For I know that the LORD is great; our Lord is above all gods. (135:5).
The LORD does all that pleases Him in the heavens and on the earth, in the seas and in all their depths. (135:6).
He causes the clouds to rise from the ends of the earth. He generates the lightning with the rain and brings forth the wind from His storehouses. (135:7).
He struck down the firstborn of Egypt, of both man and beast. (135:8).
He sent signs and wonders into your midst, O Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants. (135:9).
He struck down many nations and slaughtered mighty kings: (135:10).
Sihon king of the Amorites, Og king of Bashan, and all the kings of Canaan. (135:11).
He gave their land as an inheritance, as a heritage to His people Israel. (135:12).
Your name, O LORD, endures forever, Your renown, O LORD, through all generations. (135:13).
For the LORD will vindicate His people and will have compassion on His servants. (135:14).
The idols of the nations are silver and gold, made by the hands of men. (135:15).
They have mouths, but cannot speak; they have eyes, but cannot see; (135:16).
they have ears, but cannot hear; nor is there breath in their mouths. (135:17).
Those who make them become like them, as do all who trust in them. (135:18).
O house of Israel, bless the LORD; O house of Aaron, bless the LORD; (135:19).
O house of Levi, bless the LORD; you who fear the LORD, bless the LORD! (135:20).
Blessed be the LORD from Zion — He who dwells in Jerusalem. Hallelujah! (135:21).
crossRefs: Exodus 12:29: At midnight the LORD struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from Pharaoh's heir on the throne to the firstborn of the livestock. The psalm keeps both ends of that range in one line, of both man and beast.

Numbers 21:21-35: Sihon refuses Israel passage on the King's Highway and loses his kingdom, then Og of Bashan comes out to fight at Edrei and is wiped out with his sons. Those two names became the standing example of mighty kings slaughtered.

Psalm 115:4-8: The same mockery of idols in nearly the same words, silver and gold made by human hands, mouths that cannot speak and eyes that cannot see, closing on the same verdict about the people who make them.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סְגֻלָּה (segullah)
translationNotes.note: Israel called His special property (v. 4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַלְלוּ־יָהּ (Hallelu-Yah), Greek: Ἀλληλούϊα, Aramaic: הללויה
translationNotes.note: “Praise the LORD,” framing the psalm (vv. 1, 21).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אוֹצָרוֹת (otsarot), treasuries or storehouses
translationNotes.note: Psalm 135:7 pictures weather being issued from a store: clouds raised from the ends of the earth, lightning made to go with the rain, wind brought out of its treasuries. The same sentence appears almost word for word at Jeremiah 10:13 and 51:16, and Job 38:22 asks whether anyone has entered the storehouses of the snow and the hail. It is the settled Hebrew way of speaking about weather as something kept and released, not something that simply happens.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סִיחוֹן (Sichon) - עוֹג (Og)
translationNotes.note: Psalm 135:11 names two kings as shorthand for the whole conquest east of the Jordan, and every Israelite would have known why. Sihon ruled the Amorites from Heshbon and refused Israel passage; Og ruled Bashan in the north. Numbers 21:21-35 tells both defeats, and they became the standard example of what God had already done, repeated at Psalm 136:19-20, Deuteronomy 3:1-11, and Joshua 2:10, where Rahab says the news of them is what broke Jericho's nerve.

translationNotes.term: a psalm made of other psalms
translationNotes.note: Psalm 135:15-18 on the idols of the nations is almost identical to Psalm 115:4-8, shortened by a few lines. Verse 7 is shared with Jeremiah 10:13, and the closing blessings echo Psalm 134. Hebrew worship reused its own words deliberately; a congregation that already knew Psalm 115 would have recognized the lines as they were sung and heard the older psalm inside the newer one.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm praises the LORD for sovereign acts in creation and history, contrasts Him with lifeless idols, and calls all His households to bless Him.

headings.text: Give Praise, O Servants of the Lord

stories.title: 🔁 Psalms 136
summaryBullets: Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good. His loving devotion endures forever. (136:1).
Give thanks to the God of gods. His loving devotion endures forever. (136:2).
Give thanks to the Lord of lords. His loving devotion endures forever. (136:3).
He alone does great wonders. His loving devotion endures forever. (136:4).
By His insight He made the heavens. His loving devotion endures forever. (136:5).
He spread out the earth upon the waters. His loving devotion endures forever. (136:6).
He made the great lights — His loving devotion endures forever. (136:7).
the sun to rule the day, His loving devotion endures forever. (136:8).
the moon and stars to govern the night. His loving devotion endures forever. (136:9).
He struck down the firstborn of Egypt His loving devotion endures forever. (136:10).
and brought Israel out from among them His loving devotion endures forever. (136:11).
with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. His loving devotion endures forever. (136:12).
He divided the Red Sea in two His loving devotion endures forever. (136:13).
and led Israel through the midst, His loving devotion endures forever. (136:14).
but swept Pharaoh and his army into the Red Sea. His loving devotion endures forever. (136:15).
He led His people through the wilderness. His loving devotion endures forever. (136:16).
He struck down great kings His loving devotion endures forever. (136:17).
and slaughtered mighty kings— His loving devotion endures forever. (136:18).
Sihon king of the Amorites His loving devotion endures forever. (136:19).
and Og king of Bashan— His loving devotion endures forever. (136:20).
and He gave their land as an inheritance, His loving devotion endures forever. (136:21).
a heritage to His servant Israel. His loving devotion endures forever. (136:22).
He remembered us in our low estate His loving devotion endures forever. (136:23).
and freed us from our enemies. His loving devotion endures forever. (136:24).
He gives food to every creature. His loving devotion endures forever. (136:25).
Give thanks to the God of heaven! His loving devotion endures forever. (136:26).
crossRefs: Genesis 1:14-18: The lights made on the fourth day, the greater to rule the day and the lesser with the stars to rule the night. The psalm keeps that division exactly and hangs its refrain on each half, His loving devotion endures forever.

Exodus 14:21-28: The sea driven back by an east wind, Israel walking through the middle of it, and the water returning over Pharaoh's chariots and horsemen. The psalm breaks that single event into three lines and answers each one with the refrain.

Ezra 3:11: The returned exiles sing responsively at the foundation of the second temple, for He is good, His loving devotion to Israel endures forever. That is this psalm's refrain still in use, still sung antiphonally, generations later.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (ḥesed), Greek: ἔλεος, Aramaic: חסדא
translationNotes.note: Covenant loyalty repeated in every line.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הוֹדוּ (hodu), Greek: ἐξομολογεῖσθε, Aramaic: אודו
translationNotes.note: Call to public thanksgiving (vv. 1-3, 26).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (chesed), loyal covenant love
translationNotes.note: All twenty-six verses close with the same line, and that is a performance instruction as much as a poem. One voice sang the first half and the whole assembly answered with the refrain. Scripture records exactly this: at the dedication of Solomon's temple the people fell down and said the words together (2 Chronicles 7:3), at the founding of the second temple the singers sang responsively with them (Ezra 3:11), and Jehoshaphat sent singers ahead of his army chanting the same sentence (2 Chronicles 20:21).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַלֵּל הַגָּדוֹל (Hallel ha-Gadol)
translationNotes.note: Jewish tradition gives Psalm 136 its own name, the Great Hallel, distinct from the Hallel of Psalms 113 to 118, and sings it at Passover after the meal. The psalm's structure supports the name: it runs creation first (136:4-9), then the exodus (136:10-15), then the wilderness and the land (136:16-22), and each act of God gets the same answer from the people.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm recounts creation and exodus with the repeated refrain that His steadfast love endures forever.

stories.title: 🏞️ Psalms 137
summaryBullets: By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept when we remembered Zion. (137:1).
There on the willows we hung our harps, (137:2).
for there our captors requested a song; our tormentors demanded songs of joy: “Sing us a song of Zion.” (137:3).
How can we sing a song of the LORD in a foreign land? (137:4).
If I forget you, O Jerusalem, may my right hand cease to function. (137:5).
May my tongue cling to the roof of my mouth if I do not remember you, if I do not exalt Jerusalem as my greatest joy! (137:6).
Remember, O LORD, the sons of Edom on the day Jerusalem fell: “Destroy it,” they said, “tear it down to its foundations!” (137:7).
O Daughter of Babylon, doomed to destruction, blessed is he who repays you as you have done to us. (137:8).
Blessed is he who seizes your infants and dashes them against the rocks. (137:9).
crossRefs: Obadiah 1:10-14: The charge against Edom set out item by item, standing at the crossroads to cut down the fugitives, handing over survivors, and looting the city on the day of its disaster, which is what 137:7 asks the LORD to remember.
Deuteronomy 32:35: 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,' says the LORD, the claim the psalm defers to when it says 'Remember, O LORD' instead of saying what the singer will do.

Jeremiah 51:24: 'Before your very eyes I will repay Babylon and all the dwellers of Chaldea for all the evil they have done in Zion,' the sentence already passed on the city this psalm asks to see repaid.
Isaiah 13:16: A judgment oracle spoken over Babylon says its own infants will be dashed to pieces before its eyes, given long before Babylon ever took Jerusalem.
Lamentations 2:20-21: An eyewitness account of the same fall of Jerusalem, with women eating their own offspring and young and old lying dead in the streets, which is the day 137:7 is remembering.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּבֶל (Bavel), Greek: Βαβυλών, Aramaic: בבל
translationNotes.note: Place of exile in the lament (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נִפֵּץ אֶל־הַסֶּלַע (nipetz el-ha-selaʿ), Greek: προσκόψει πρὸς τὸν λίθον, Aramaic: נְפֵץ על טינרא
translationNotes.note: Explicit violent expression of retribution (v. 9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נַהֲרוֹת (naharot), rivers or canals
translationNotes.note: Babylonia was a flat alluvial plain, and its water was managed: the Euphrates and Tigris were tapped by a network of large irrigation canals, and the Hebrew word covers those as well as rivers. Deportees were settled along them and put to work. Ezekiel dates his visions among the exiles by the Kebar canal (Ezekiel 1:1), and Ezra 8:15 gathers the returning company at the river Ahava. The trees lining those banks, rendered willows or poplars, are the ones the harps were hung on.

translationNotes.term: sing us a song of Zion
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּנּוֹר (kinnor), the lyre
translationNotes.note: The demand in 137:3 is worse than mockery. The songs of Zion were temple music, sung by trained Levite singers at a sanctuary that now lay in ruins, and the captors want them performed as after-dinner entertainment. The instrument hung up in verse 2 is the kinnor, the small hand-held lyre that David played (1 Samuel 16:23) and the standard instrument of that music. Refusing to play it is refusing to turn the worship of a destroyed temple into a party trick.

translationNotes.term: the sons of Edom on that day
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֱדוֹם (Edom)
translationNotes.note: Psalm 137:7 asks God to remember Edom shouting for Jerusalem to be leveled. Obadiah 1:10-14 lays out the charge in detail: Edom stood at the crossroads and cut down the men escaping, handed over survivors, and looted the city on the day of its disaster. Edom was Esau's line and therefore a relative (Genesis 36:1), which is why the betrayal is put the way it is.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נִפֵּץ (nippets), to shatter
translationNotes.note: The last verse asks for something the ancient world actually did to a captured city, and Scripture reports it several times: Hazael of Aram would do it to Israel's children (2 Kings 8:12), it happened to Samaria (Hosea 13:16) and to Thebes when Assyria took it (Nahum 3:10), and Isaiah 13:16 says it will be done to Babylon. The psalm is asking for Babylon to receive what Babylon dealt out, in the words of a survivor who had watched it.

translationNotes.term: Who the psalm asks to act
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זְכֹר יְהוָה (zekhor YHWH) - אַשְׁרֵי (ashrei)
translationNotes.note: The psalm never says what the singer will do. 137:7 is a petition addressed to God, 'Remember, O LORD, the sons of Edom.' Verses 8 and 9 then open with ashrei, the same word that opens Psalm 1 as 'Blessed is the man', and pronounce that blessing on whoever repays Babylon what Babylon dealt out; no agent is named and no one is given an order. Deuteronomy 32:35 is where the law puts that repayment: 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay.'

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm laments in Babylon, vows remembrance of Jerusalem, calls for recompense on Edom and Babylon, and ends with a violent line about infants being dashed on rock.

stories.title: 🕍 Psalms 138
summaryBullets: I give You thanks with all my heart; before the gods I sing Your praises. (138:1).
I bow down toward Your holy temple and give thanks to Your name for Your loving devotion and Your faithfulness; You have exalted Your name and Your word above all else. (138:2).
On the day I called, You answered me; You emboldened me and strengthened my soul. (138:3).
All the kings of the earth will give You thanks, O LORD, when they hear the words of Your mouth. (138:4).
They will sing of the ways of the LORD, for the glory of the LORD is great. (138:5).
Though the LORD is on high, He attends to the lowly; but the proud He knows from afar. (138:6).
If I walk in the midst of trouble, You preserve me from the anger of my foes; You extend Your hand, and Your right hand saves me. (138:7).
The LORD will fulfill His purpose for me. O LORD, Your loving devotion endures forever — do not abandon the works of Your hands. (138:8).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 8:29-30: Solomon asks that God's eyes stay open toward the temple night and day and that He hear whenever Israel prays toward this place. The psalm does exactly that, bowing toward the holy temple to give thanks.

Psalm 113:6: The God enthroned on high who humbles Himself even to look at the heavens and the earth. This psalm states the same paradox in one line, though the LORD is on high, He attends to the lowly.

Psalm 57:2: David crying out to God Most High, who fulfills His purpose for me, from inside a cave. This psalm closes on that same phrase and then refuses to leave it alone, do not abandon the works of Your hands.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֵיכַל קָדְשֶׁךָ (heikhal qodshekha), Greek: ναὸς ἅγιος, Aramaic: היכלא דקודשא
translationNotes.note: Place toward which thanks is offered (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁפָל (shafal) / גָּבֹהַּ (gavohah), Greek: ταπεινός / ὑψηλός, Aramaic: משפיל / רם
translationNotes.note: Contrasting objects of divine regard (v. 6).

translationNotes.term: I bow down toward Your holy temple
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֵיכָל קֹדֶשׁ (heikhal qodesh), holy palace or temple
translationNotes.note: Praying while facing the temple was a settled practice, and Solomon asked for it at the dedication: when Your people are far off, or carried captive, and they pray toward this house, hear from heaven (1 Kings 8:44-48). Daniel keeps it under threat of death, going up to his roof chamber where the windows opened toward Jerusalem and kneeling three times a day (Daniel 6:10). Jonah 2:4 and 2:7 use the same orientation from inside the fish.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm thanks toward the holy temple, speaks of the LORD’s regard for the lowly, and asks Him to fulfill His purpose for the singer.
stories.superscription: Of David.

stories.title: 🕊️ Psalms 139
summaryBullets: O LORD, You have searched me and known me. (139:1).
You know when I sit and when I rise; You understand my thoughts from afar. (139:2).
You search out my path and my lying down; You are aware of all my ways. (139:3).
Even before a word is on my tongue, You know all about it, O LORD. (139:4).
You hem me in behind and before; You have laid Your hand upon me. (139:5).
Such knowledge is too wonderful for me, too lofty for me to attain. (139:6).
Where can I go to escape Your Spirit? Where can I flee from Your presence? (139:7).
If I ascend to the heavens, You are there; if I make my bed in Sheol, You are there. (139:8).
If I rise on the wings of the dawn, if I settle by the farthest sea, (139:9).
even there Your hand will guide me; Your right hand will hold me fast. (139:10).
If I say, “Surely the darkness will hide me, and the light become night around me”— (139:11).
even the darkness is not dark to You, but the night shines like the day, for darkness is as light to You. (139:12).
For You formed my inmost being; You knit me together in my mother’s womb. (139:13).
I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Marvelous are Your works, and I know this very well. (139:14).
My frame was not hidden from You when I was made in secret, when I was woven together in the depths of the earth. (139:15).
Your eyes saw my unformed body; all my days were written in Your book and ordained for me before one of them came to be. (139:16).
How precious to me are Your thoughts, O God, how vast is their sum! (139:17).
If I were to count them, they would outnumber the grains of sand; and when I awake, I am still with You. (139:18).
O God, that You would slay the wicked— away from me, you bloodthirsty men— (139:19).
who speak of You deceitfully; Your enemies take Your name in vain. (139:20).
Do I not hate those who hate You, O LORD, and detest those who rise against You? (139:21).
I hate them with perfect hatred; I count them as my enemies. (139:22).
Search me, O God, and know my heart; test me and know my concerns. (139:23).
See if there is any offensive way in me; lead me in the way everlasting. (139:24).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 1:5: Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, God's answer to a prophet who objected that he was too young. The psalm says the same of an ordinary man, knit together in secret and known before one of his days had come.

Amos 9:2-4: God tells Israel there is no hiding, dig down to Sheol and His hand takes them, climb to heaven and He pulls them down, hide at the bottom of the sea and He commands the serpent. The psalm walks that same route and takes it as comfort.

Job 10:11: You clothed me with skin and flesh and knit me together with bones and sinews, said by a man arguing that God assembled him only to break him. The psalm uses the identical weaving image to reach the opposite verdict, fearfully and wonderfully made.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סָכַךְ (sakhakh, “weave/cover”), Greek: κατεσκεύασάς με, Aramaic: סכך
translationNotes.note: Verb used for forming in the womb (v. 13).

The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)

translationNotes.term: the wings of the dawn and the farthest sea
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַחֲרִית יָם (acharit yam), the far end of the sea
translationNotes.note: Verse 9 names the two ends of the world as an Israelite measured it. The dawn comes up over the eastern desert; the sea is the Mediterranean, and its far side is the western limit past which nobody in Canaan went, the direction Jonah ran when he took ship for Tarshish (Jonah 1:3). Verse 8 has already given the vertical pair, the heavens above and Sheol below. Between them the four directions are covered, and the point of the list is that none of them is an exit.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֵפֶר (sefer), a scroll or written record
translationNotes.note: Ancient cities and armies kept written registers of who belonged, and Scripture uses that filing system as an image. Moses asks to be blotted out of the book God has written (Exodus 32:32), Psalm 69:28 asks that enemies be erased from the book of the living, Malachi 3:16 has a scroll of remembrance written before the LORD, and Revelation 20:12 has books opened at the judgment. Psalm 139:16 puts a man's days in that record before any of them happened.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm states God’s exhaustive knowledge and presence, His forming in the womb, a wish against the wicked, and a request to be searched and led.

headings.text: You Have Searched Me and Known Me

stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🛡️ Psalms 140
summaryBullets: Rescue me, O LORD, from evil men. Protect me from men of violence, (140:1).
who devise evil in their hearts and stir up war all day long. (140:2).
They sharpen their tongues like snakes; the venom of vipers is on their lips. Selah (140:3).
Guard me, O LORD, from the hands of the wicked. Keep me safe from men of violence who scheme to make me stumble. (140:4).
The proud hide a snare for me; the cords of their net are spread along the path, and lures are set out for me. Selah (140:5).
I say to the LORD, “You are my God.” Hear, O LORD, my cry for help. (140:6).
O GOD the Lord, the strength of my salvation, You shield my head in the day of battle. (140:7).
Grant not, O LORD, the desires of the wicked; do not promote their evil plans, lest they be exalted. Selah (140:8).
May the heads of those who surround me be covered in the trouble their lips have caused. (140:9).
May burning coals fall on them; may they be thrown into the fire, into the miry pits, never to rise again. (140:10).
May no slanderer be established in the land; may calamity hunt down the man of violence. (140:11).
I know that the LORD upholds justice for the poor and defends the cause of the needy. (140:12).
Surely the righteous will praise Your name; the upright will dwell in Your presence. (140:13).
crossRefs: Romans 3:13: Paul chains psalm lines together to prove that no one is righteous, and verse 3 of this psalm supplies one of them, the venom of vipers is on their lips.

Psalm 141:9: The neighboring psalm makes the same request in nearly the same words, keep me from the snares they have laid for me and from the lures of evildoers. Both are about traps set along a path the man has to walk anyway.

Proverbs 21:30: There is no wisdom, no understanding and no counsel that can prevail against the LORD. The psalm turns that into a petition, grant not the desires of the wicked and do not promote their plans.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַנְשֵׁי חָמָס (anshei ḥamas), Greek: ἄνδρες ἄνομοι/βίαιοι, Aramaic: גברין דחמסא
translationNotes.note: Men of wrong/violence (vv. 1-4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲמַת אַסְפִּיד (ḥamat aspid), Greek: ἰὸς ἀσπίδων, Aramaic: חמת אפידא
translationNotes.note: Image for deadly speech (v. 3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַכְשׁוּב (akhshuv), a venomous snake
translationNotes.note: Psalm 140:3 says they sharpen their tongues like a serpent and keep viper's venom under their lips. Paul quotes this exact line, along with Psalm 5:9 and 10:7, in the chain of Old Testament citations at Romans 3:13. The picture is deliberate: the harm is invisible until it is delivered, and the delivery is speech. James 3:8 keeps the same figure, calling the tongue full of deadly poison.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm asks for rescue from violent plotters with venomous speech and traps and affirms that the LORD upholds the afflicted.
stories.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🕯️ Psalms 141
summaryBullets: I call upon You, O LORD; come quickly to me. Hear my voice when I call to You. (141:1).
May my prayer be set before You like incense; my uplifted hands, like the evening offering. (141:2).
Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch at the door of my lips. (141:3).
Do not let my heart be drawn to any evil thing or take part in works of wickedness with men who do iniquity; let me not feast on their delicacies. (141:4).
Let the righteous man strike me; let his rebuke be an act of loving devotion. It is oil for my head; let me not refuse it. For my prayer is ever against the deeds of the wicked. (141:5).
When their rulers are thrown down from the cliffs, the people will listen to my words, for they are pleasant. (141:6).
As when one plows and breaks up the soil, so our bones have been scattered at the mouth of Sheol. (141:7).
But my eyes are fixed on You, O GOD the Lord. In You I seek refuge; do not leave my soul defenseless. (141:8).
Keep me from the snares they have laid for me, and from the lures of evildoers. (141:9).
Let the wicked fall into their own nets, while I pass by in safety. (141:10).
crossRefs: Exodus 30:7-8: Aaron burns fragrant incense on the golden altar every morning as he tends the lamps and again at twilight, perpetually. The psalm asks for prayer to be received like that incense and lifted hands like the evening offering.
Proverbs 13:3: He who guards his mouth protects his life, and the one who opens his lips invites his own ruin. The psalm asks God to do the guarding for him, keep watch at the door of my lips.

Revelation 5:8: The living creatures and the elders fall before the Lamb holding harps and golden bowls of incense, which John identifies as the prayers of the saints. This psalm made that connection first, let my prayer be set before You like incense.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קְטֹרֶת (qetoret), Greek: θυμίαμα, Aramaic: קטורתא
translationNotes.note: Perfumed smoke associated with prayer (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִנְחַת־עָרֶב (minḥat-ʿarev), Greek: θυσία ἑσπερινή, Aramaic: קרבנא דמערבָא
translationNotes.note: Grain/sacrifice presented toward evening (v. 2).

The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)

translationNotes.term: like incense, like the evening offering
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קְטֹרֶת (qetoret), incense - מִנְחַת עָרֶב (minchat arev), the evening grain offering
translationNotes.note: Verse 2 asks for prayer to be received the way two fixed daily acts were. Incense was burned on the gold altar every morning and every evening (Exodus 30:7-8), and a grain offering with a lamb went up at the same two hours (Exodus 29:38-41). Luke 1:9-10 shows how it looked: a priest chosen by lot goes in to burn the incense while the whole congregation prays outside at that hour. Revelation 5:8 and 8:3-4 make the connection directly, with the incense named as the prayers of the saints.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm asks the LORD to receive prayer like incense, guard the speaker’s mouth and heart, and protect from snares.
stories.superscription: A Psalm of David.

stories.title: 🕳️ Psalms 142
summaryBullets: I cry aloud to the LORD; I lift my voice to the LORD for mercy. (142:1).
I pour out my complaint before Him; I reveal my trouble to Him. (142:2).
Although my spirit grows faint within me, You know my way. Along the path I travel they have hidden a snare for me. (142:3).
Look to my right and see; no one attends to me. There is no refuge for me; no one cares for my soul. (142:4).
I cry to You, O LORD: “You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living.” (142:5).
Listen to my cry, for I am brought quite low. Rescue me from my pursuers, for they are too strong for me. (142:6).
Free my soul from prison, that I may praise Your name. The righteous will gather around me because of Your goodness to me. (142:7).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 22:1: David leaves Gath and takes refuge in the cave of Adullam, where his family comes down to him and about four hundred distressed and indebted men gather around him. This psalm's title puts it in a cave and insists that no one cared for his soul.
Psalm 57:1: The other psalm titled from a cave, sheltering in the shadow of God's wings until the danger has passed. Both call God a refuge from inside a hole in the rock.
Isaiah 61:1: The Anointed sent to proclaim liberty to the captives and release for the prisoners. The psalm ends on that word, free my soul from prison, that I may praise Your name.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַשְׂכִּיל (maskil), Greek: συνετός, Aramaic: משכילא
translationNotes.note: A literary/musical term in the psalm’s heading.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַסְגֵּר (masger), Greek: φυλακή, Aramaic: מסגרא
translationNotes.note: Confinement image used for distress (v. 7).

translationNotes.term: when he was in the cave
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְעָרָה (mearah), cave
translationNotes.note: The heading places this prayer in a cave during David's flight from Saul, and Psalm 57 carries the same setting. The Judean hills are limestone, riddled with caves large enough to hide a band of men: 1 Samuel 22:1-2 has David in the cave of Adullam in the western foothills, where four hundred debtors and desperate men gathered to him, and 1 Samuel 24:1-7 puts him deep in a cave at En-gedi above the Dead Sea when Saul walks in alone. Verse 4 says no one cares for his life, which is the position of a man with no legal standing and no town to shelter him.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm describes a cave prayer where traps and abandonment are noted, and asks for release to give thanks.

headings.text: I Lift My Voice to the Lord

stories.superscription: A Maskil of David, when he was in the cave. A prayer.

stories.title: 🌤️ Psalms 143
summaryBullets: O LORD, hear my prayer. In Your faithfulness, give ear to my plea; in Your righteousness, answer me. (143:1).
Do not bring Your servant into judgment, for no one alive is righteous before You. (143:2).
For the enemy has pursued my soul, crushing my life to the ground, making me dwell in darkness like those long since dead. (143:3).
My spirit grows faint within me; my heart is dismayed inside me. (143:4).
I remember the days of old; I meditate on all Your works; I consider the work of Your hands. (143:5).
I stretch out my hands to You; my soul thirsts for You like a parched land. Selah (143:6).
Answer me quickly, O LORD; my spirit fails. Do not hide Your face from me, or I will be like those who descend to the Pit. (143:7).
Let me hear Your loving devotion in the morning, for I have put my trust in You. Teach me the way I should walk, for to You I lift up my soul. (143:8).
Deliver me from my enemies, O LORD; I flee to You for refuge. (143:9).
Teach me to do Your will, for You are my God. May Your good Spirit lead me on level ground. (143:10).
For the sake of Your name, O LORD, revive me. In Your righteousness, bring my soul out of trouble. (143:11).
And in Your loving devotion, cut off my enemies. Destroy all who afflict me, for I am Your servant. (143:12).
crossRefs: Romans 3:20: Paul concludes that no one will be justified in God's sight by works of the law, since the law only makes a man aware of sin. Verse 2 of this psalm is that conclusion turned into a prayer, no one alive is righteous before You.

Psalm 23:3: He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name. This psalm asks for that guidance instead of reporting it, teach me the way I should walk, and keeps the same reason, for the sake of Your name.
Nehemiah 9:20: You gave Your good Spirit to instruct them, said of Israel in the wilderness. This psalm asks for the same rare thing by the same name, may Your good Spirit lead me on level ground.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רוּחֲךָ הַטּוֹבָה (ruḥekha ha-tovah), Greek: τὸ πνεῦμά σου τὸ ἀγαθόν, Aramaic: רוחך טבא
translationNotes.note: Requested to lead on level ground (v. 10).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶרֶץ מִישֹׁר (ʾerets miyshor), Greek: εὐθεῖα, Aramaic: מישרין
translationNotes.note: Figurative for a straight/right path (v. 10).

translationNotes.term: I stretch out my hands to You
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פֵּרַשְׂתִּי יָדַי (perasti yadai)
translationNotes.note: The normal posture for prayer was standing, with the head up and both hands spread open and lifted, not folded and bowed. Solomon prays that way at the temple dedication, standing before the altar and spreading out his hands toward heaven (1 Kings 8:22), Ezra does it at 9:5, and Paul still assumes it at 1 Timothy 2:8. Kneeling and lying face down were kept for grief or great urgency, as with Daniel 6:10 and Ezra 10:1.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm pleads for mercy, admits that no one living is righteous, and asks to be taught and led by the LORD’s good Spirit.

headings.text: I Stretch Out My Hands to You

stories.superscription: A Psalm of David.

stories.title: ⚔️ Psalms 144
summaryBullets: Blessed be the LORD, my Rock, who trains my hands for war, my fingers for battle. (144:1).
He is my steadfast love and my fortress, my stronghold and my deliverer. He is my shield, in whom I take refuge, who subdues peoples under me. (144:2).
O LORD, what is man, that You regard him, the son of man that You think of him? (144:3).
Man is like a breath; his days are like a passing shadow. (144:4).
Part Your heavens, O LORD, and come down; touch the mountains, that they may smoke. (144:5).
Flash forth Your lightning and scatter them; shoot Your arrows and rout them. (144:6).
Reach down from on high; set me free and rescue me from the deep waters, from the grasp of foreigners, (144:7).
whose mouths speak falsehood, whose right hands are deceitful. (144:8).
I will sing to You a new song, O God; on a harp of ten strings I will make music to You — (144:9).
to Him who gives victory to kings, who frees His servant David from the deadly sword. (144:10).
Set me free and rescue me from the grasp of foreigners, whose mouths speak falsehood, whose right hands are deceitful. (144:11).
Then our sons will be like plants nurtured in their youth, our daughters like corner pillars carved to adorn a palace. (144:12).
Our storehouses will be full, supplying all manner of produce; our flocks will bring forth thousands, tens of thousands in our fields. (144:13).
Our oxen will bear great loads. There will be no breach in the walls, no going into captivity, and no cry of lament in our streets. (144:14).
Blessed are the people of whom this is so; blessed are the people whose God is the LORD. (144:15).
crossRefs: Psalm 8:4: What is man that You are mindful of him, asked while looking up at the moon and the stars. This psalm asks it again inside a war song and answers harder, man is like a breath and his days are a passing shadow.

2 Samuel 22:17: David's victory song, He reached down from on high and took hold of me, He drew me out of deep waters. The psalm repeats the line and then names the waters, the grasp of foreigners whose mouths speak falsehood.

Psalm 33:16-17: No king is saved by his vast army and a horse is a vain hope for salvation. This psalm is a king's prayer built on that, asking God to part the heavens and come down rather than trusting the trained hands it opens with.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֵבֶל עָשׂוֹר (nevel ʿasor), Greek: ψαλτήριον δεκάχορδον, Aramaic: נבל עשרא
translationNotes.note: Instrument named in the praise (v. 9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זָוִיּוֹת מְחֻטָּבוֹת (zaviyyot meḥuttavot), Greek: γωνίαι λαξευταί, Aramaic: זיות מחטבין
translationNotes.note: Sculpted supports imagery for daughters (v. 12).

translationNotes.term: what a good year looked like
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְזָוִים (mezavim), storehouses or granaries
translationNotes.note: Verses 12-14 spell out prosperity in the concrete terms of an agricultural town: sons growing straight like well-tended plants, daughters like the carved corner pillars of a palace, granaries full of every kind of produce, flocks multiplying by the thousand in the fields, oxen strong enough to carry heavy loads, no breach in the city wall, nobody being marched off into captivity, and no wailing in the streets. Every item names a thing that could be taken away, which is why the list ends with the wall and the silence in the streets.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm credits the LORD with battle training and deliverance, and pictures communal plenty and safety.

headings.text: Blessed Be the Lord, My Rock

stories.superscription: Of David.

stories.title: 👑 Psalms 145
summaryBullets: I will exalt You, my God and King; I will bless Your name forever and ever. (145:1).
Every day I will bless You, and I will praise Your name forever and ever. (145:2).
Great is the LORD and greatly to be praised; His greatness is unsearchable. (145:3).
One generation will commend Your works to the next, and will proclaim Your mighty acts— (145:4).
the glorious splendor of Your majesty. And I will meditate on Your wondrous works. (145:5).
They will proclaim the power of Your awesome deeds, and I will declare Your greatness. (145:6).
They will extol the fame of Your abundant goodness and sing joyfully of Your righteousness. (145:7).
The LORD is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion. (145:8).
The LORD is good to all; His compassion rests on all He has made. (145:9).
All You have made will give You thanks, O LORD, and Your saints will bless You. (145:10).
They will tell of the glory of Your kingdom and speak of Your might, (145:11).
to make known to men Your mighty acts and the glorious splendor of Your kingdom. (145:12).
Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and Your dominion endures through all generations. The LORD is faithful in all His words and kind in all His actions. (145:13).
The LORD upholds all who fall and lifts up all who are bowed down. (145:14).
The eyes of all look to You, and You give them their food in season. (145:15).
You open Your hand and satisfy the desire of every living thing. (145:16).
The LORD is righteous in all His ways and kind in all His deeds. (145:17).
The LORD is near to all who call on Him, to all who call out to Him in truth. (145:18).
He fulfills the desires of those who fear Him; He hears their cry and saves them. (145:19).
The LORD preserves all who love Him, but all the wicked He will destroy. (145:20).
My mouth will declare the praise of the LORD; let every creature bless His holy name forever and ever. (145:21).
crossRefs: Exodus 34:6: God proclaims His own name to Moses, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. The psalm repeats that formula and then widens it past Israel, the LORD is good to all and His compassion rests on all He has made.

Psalm 104:27-28: Every creature looking to God for food in due season and satisfied when He opens His hand. This psalm reuses the image and makes it evidence for the kingdom it is describing, You open Your hand and satisfy the desire of every living thing.

Daniel 4:3: Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, of all people, declaring that God's kingdom is an eternal kingdom and His dominion endures through all generations. The psalm says it in nearly the same words and describes how that king governs.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תְּהִלָּה (tehillah), Greek: αἴνεσις, Aramaic: תשבחְתָא
translationNotes.note: Title word for praise/hymn (superscription).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַלְכוּת (malkhut), Greek: βασιλεία, Aramaic: מלכותא
translationNotes.note: Reign/dominion emphasized (v. 13).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נ (nun), the fourteenth letter
translationNotes.note: Psalm 145 runs the Hebrew alphabet, one letter to each verse, and in the standard Hebrew text one letter is absent: nothing begins with nun. The Psalms scroll from Qumran Cave 11, copied in the first century AD, carries the line, and so do the Greek and Syriac Old Testaments: faithful is the LORD in all His words and gracious in all His deeds. That is why some English Bibles print it inside verse 13 and others number it 13b.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תְּהִלָּה (tehillah), praise, the word behind the Hebrew name of the book
translationNotes.note: Eight psalms use the alphabet as their frame, at 9 and 10 together, 25, 34, 37, 111, 112, 119, and 145. It is not decoration. Running A to Z is a claim to have covered the subject completely, and it is also a memory aid for a congregation learning by ear rather than reading. Psalm 145 is the only psalm whose heading calls it a tehillah, a praise, which is the singular of the Hebrew title of the whole book.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm is an acrostic that declares the LORD’s greatness, mercy, provision, and everlasting kingdom.

headings.text: I Will Exalt You, My God and King

stories.superscription: A Psalm of praise. Of David.

stories.title: 🕊️ Psalms 146
summaryBullets: Hallelujah! Praise the LORD, O my soul. (146:1).
I will praise the LORD all my life; I will sing praises to my God while I have my being. (146:2).
Put not your trust in princes, in mortal man, who cannot save. (146:3).
When his spirit departs, he returns to the ground; on that very day his plans perish. (146:4).
Blessed is he whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the LORD his God, (146:5).
the Maker of heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them. He remains faithful forever. (146:6).
He executes justice for the oppressed and gives food to the hungry. The LORD sets the prisoners free, (146:7).
the LORD opens the eyes of the blind, the LORD lifts those who are weighed down, the LORD loves the righteous. (146:8).
The LORD protects foreigners; He sustains the fatherless and the widow, but the ways of the wicked He frustrates. (146:9).
The LORD reigns forever, your God, O Zion, for all generations. Hallelujah! (146:10).
crossRefs: Psalm 118:8-9: Better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man, better than to trust in princes. This psalm supplies the reason in one line, when a man's spirit departs he returns to the ground and on that very day his plans perish.

Isaiah 61:1: The Anointed sent with good news for the poor and liberty for the captives. The psalm lists those same acts as things the LORD does Himself, justice for the oppressed, food for the hungry, prisoners set free.

Exodus 22:21-24: The law forbidding the mistreatment of a foreign resident, a widow or an orphan, with God promising to hear them if they cry out and to answer with the sword. The psalm names those same three as the people He protects and sustains.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְדִיבִים (nedivim), Greek: ἄρχοντες, Aramaic: נדיבין
translationNotes.note: High officials contrasted with the LORD (v. 3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֵּר (ger), Greek: προσήλυτος/ξένος, Aramaic: גרא
translationNotes.note: Resident foreigner under protection (v. 9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַלְלוּ יָהּ (halelu Yah), praise Yah
translationNotes.note: Psalms 146 through 150 each open and close with Hallelujah, and together they form the ending of the whole book. The Psalter is arranged in five books, and each of the first four ends with a short blessing that is not part of the psalm it is attached to: 41:13, 72:18-19, 89:52, and 106:48. Book Five has no single closing line of that kind. These five psalms do the job instead.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְדִיבִים (nedivim), nobles or generous ones
translationNotes.note: The word means the highborn, the men with power to grant favors, and in an ancient city getting a patron among them was the ordinary way an ordinary person got anything done. Verse 4 gives the reason not to lean on that: his breath goes out, he goes back to the ground, and on that same day his plans die with him. Psalm 118:9 makes the same judgment, that it is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in princes, and Isaiah 2:22 puts it as a command to stop.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm warns against trusting princes and lists the LORD’s care for oppressed, hungry, prisoners, blind, bowed, sojourners, orphans, and widows.

headings.text: Praise the Lord, O My Soul

stories.title: ❄️ Psalms 147
summaryBullets: Hallelujah! How good it is to sing praises to our God, how pleasant and lovely to praise Him! (147:1).
The LORD builds up Jerusalem; He gathers the exiles of Israel. (147:2).
He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. (147:3).
He determines the number of the stars; He calls them each by name. (147:4).
Great is our Lord, and mighty in power; His understanding has no limit. (147:5).
The LORD sustains the humble, but casts the wicked to the ground. (147:6).
Sing to the LORD with thanksgiving; make music on the harp to our God, (147:7).
who covers the sky with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth, who makes grass to grow on the hills. (147:8).
He provides food for the animals, and for the young ravens when they call. (147:9).
He does not delight in the strength of the horse; He takes no pleasure in the legs of a man. (147:10).
The LORD is pleased with those who fear Him, who hope in His loving devotion. (147:11).
Exalt the LORD, O Jerusalem; praise your God, O Zion! (147:12).
For He strengthens the bars of your gates and blesses the children within you. (147:13).
He makes peace at your borders; He fills you with the finest wheat. (147:14).
He sends forth His command to the earth; His word runs swiftly. (147:15).
He spreads the snow like wool; He scatters the frost like ashes; (147:16).
He casts forth His hail like pebbles. Who can withstand His icy blast? (147:17).
He sends forth His word and melts them; He unleashes His winds, and the waters flow. (147:18).
He declares His word to Jacob, His statutes and judgments to Israel. (147:19).
He has done this for no other nation; they do not know His judgments. Hallelujah! (147:20).
crossRefs: Isaiah 40:26: God leading out the starry host by number and calling each one by name, offered as an argument to exiles who thought He had lost track of them. The psalm repeats that claim and sets it directly beside healing the brokenhearted.

Nehemiah 7:1: The wall rebuilt, the doors set in place, and gatekeepers and singers and Levites appointed. That is the Jerusalem the psalm has in view, gates whose bars God strengthens and exiles He has gathered back inside them.

Job 37:6: Elihu describing God speaking to the snow and telling it to fall on the earth. The psalm uses the same weather as evidence of the same authority, snow spread like wool and frost scattered like ashes.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נִדְחֵי (nidḥei), Greek: ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι, Aramaic: נדחיא
translationNotes.note: Those driven away, now gathered (v. 2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נִשְׁבְּרֵי־לֵב (nishbere-lev), Greek: συντετριμμένοι τῇ καρδίᾳ, Aramaic: מדכי לבא
translationNotes.note: Those crushed in spirit (v. 3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֶּפוֹר (kefor), frost - קֶרַח (qerach), ice
translationNotes.note: Verses 16-18 describe weather a reader in a cold country may skim past, but in Jerusalem snow is rare and memorable, and the psalm treats it as a display of power: laid down like fleece, frost scattered like ash, hail thrown down like gravel, and then the word sent to melt it and the wind made to blow so the water runs. 2 Samuel 23:20 dates one of Benaiah's feats by the day it snowed. Job 38:22-30 asks the same set of questions about where snow, hail, and ice are kept.

translationNotes.term: not the strength of the horse
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סוּס (sus), horse
translationNotes.note: In the ancient Near East the horse was a weapons system, not transport: it pulled the war chariot, and a nation's strength was counted in chariotry. That is what verse 10 is refusing to be impressed by, along with the legs of a man, meaning infantry. Deuteronomy 17:16 forbids a king of Israel to stockpile horses, Psalm 20:7 sets chariots and horses against the name of the LORD, and Isaiah 31:1 attacks reliance on Egyptian cavalry by name.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm praises the LORD who rebuilds Jerusalem, heals the brokenhearted, governs stars and weather, and uniquely gives His word to Israel.

headings.text: It Is Good to Sing Praises

stories.title: 🌞 Psalms 148
summaryBullets: Hallelujah! Praise the LORD from the heavens; praise Him in the highest places. (148:1).
Praise Him, all His angels; praise Him, all His heavenly hosts. (148:2).
Praise Him, O sun and moon; praise Him, all you shining stars. (148:3).
Praise Him, O highest heavens, and you waters above the skies. (148:4).
Let them praise the name of the LORD, for He gave the command and they were created. (148:5).
He established them forever and ever; He issued a decree that will never pass away. (148:6).
Praise the LORD from the earth, all great sea creatures and ocean depths, (148:7).
lightning and hail, snow and clouds, powerful wind fulfilling His word, (148:8).
mountains and all hills, fruit trees and all cedars, (148:9).
wild animals and all cattle, crawling creatures and flying birds, (148:10).
kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all rulers of the earth, (148:11).
young men and maidens, old and young together. (148:12).
Let them praise the name of the LORD, for His name alone is exalted; His splendor is above the earth and the heavens. (148:13).
He has raised up a horn for His people, the praise of all His saints, of Israel, a people near to Him. Hallelujah! (148:14).
crossRefs: Genesis 1:6-8: The expanse made on the second day to separate the waters below from the waters above it. The psalm calls those upper waters by name and orders them to praise, O highest heavens, and you waters above the skies.

Job 38:22: God asks Job whether he has ever entered the storehouses of snow or observed the storehouses of hail. The psalm summons the contents of those storehouses into the choir, lightning and hail, snow and clouds, and wind that does what it is told.

Luke 1:69: Zechariah says God has raised up a horn of salvation in the house of His servant David. The psalm ends on that same phrase, He has raised up a horn for His people, the horn being the animal image for a king's strength.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תַּנִּינִם (tanninim), Greek: κῆτοι, Aramaic: תנינין
translationNotes.note: Large sea beings included in praise (v. 7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קֶרֶן (qeren), Greek: κέρας, Aramaic: קרנא
translationNotes.note: Symbol of strength/raised status (v. 14).

translationNotes.term: the order of the roll call
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִן־הַשָּׁמַיִם (min ha-shamayim), from the heavens
translationNotes.note: The psalm summons creation in a deliberate order, top down. First the heavens: angels, hosts, sun, moon, stars, and the waters above (148:1-6). Then the earth from its depths upward: sea creatures, the weather, mountains and hills, fruit trees and cedars, wild animals, livestock, creeping things, and birds (148:7-10). Then people, and here the order is reversed so that kings and princes come first and young men, women, old men, and children come last (148:11-12). Genesis 1 runs the same sequence.

translationNotes.term: He has raised up a horn
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קֶרֶן (qeren), horn
translationNotes.note: The image is taken straight from the animal: a bull or ram carries its strength on its head, and a horn lowered is a weapon. So raising up a horn means putting strength in the field, and cutting off a horn means breaking it (Jeremiah 48:25). Hannah's song uses it twice (1 Samuel 2:1, 2:10), Psalm 92:10 has the horn exalted like that of a wild ox, and Zechariah takes it up at Luke 1:69, a horn of salvation raised in the house of David.
