stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm summons heaven, earth, creatures, and all peoples to praise the LORD, noting a raised horn for His people.

headings.text: Praise the Lord from the Heavens

stories.title: 🥁 Psalms 149
summaryBullets: Hallelujah! Sing to the LORD a new song — His praise in the assembly of the godly. (149:1).
Let Israel rejoice in their Maker; let the children of Zion rejoice in their King. (149:2).
Let them praise His name with dancing, and make music to Him with tambourine and harp. (149:3).
For the LORD takes pleasure in His people; He adorns the afflicted with salvation. (149:4).
Let the saints exult in glory; let them shout for joy upon their beds. (149:5).
May the high praises of God be in their mouths, and a double-edged sword in their hands, (149:6).
to inflict vengeance on the nations and punishment on the peoples, (149:7).
to bind their kings with chains and their nobles with shackles of iron, (149:8).
to execute the judgment written against them. This honor is for all His saints. Hallelujah! (149:9).
crossRefs: 2 Chronicles 20:21: Jehoshaphat appoints singers to go out ahead of the army praising the splendor of His holiness, so the singing goes first and the fighting follows. The psalm puts those two things in the same hands, high praises of God and a sword.

Deuteronomy 32:41: God sharpening His flashing sword and grasping it in judgment to take vengeance on His adversaries. The psalm hands that vengeance to His people as an assignment, executing the judgment already written against the nations.

Hebrews 4:12: The word of God described as living and active and sharper than any double-edged sword. The psalm arms the saints with the same two things at once, praise in the mouth and a double-edged sword in the hand.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲסִידִים (ḥasidim), Greek: ὅσιοι, Aramaic: חסידיא
translationNotes.note: The pious/loyal assembly (vv. 1, 5, 9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶרֶב פִּיפִיּוֹת (ḥerev pifiyyot), Greek: ῥομφαία δίστομος, Aramaic: סייפא דתרין פיות
translationNotes.note: Weapon image in the psalm (v. 6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָחוֹל (machol), a ring dance - תֹּף (tof), hand drum
translationNotes.note: The dance in view is a circling or whirling group dance, and it goes with the tof, a small hand-held frame drum with a skin head, played mostly by women. Miriam leads the women out with drums and dancing after the sea (Exodus 15:20), the women meet Saul and David the same way (1 Samuel 18:6), Jephthah's daughter comes out to him with drums and dancing (Judges 11:34), and David dances before the ark (2 Samuel 6:14). Psalm 150:4 pairs the two again.

translationNotes.term: a double-edged sword in their hands
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶרֶב פִּיפִיּוֹת (cherev pifiyot), a sword of two mouths
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew calls a blade's edge its mouth, so a two-edged sword is literally a sword of two mouths, which is what puts it in the same line as praises in the mouth at 149:6. Verse 8 continues with the standard treatment of a defeated ruler, bound with chains and iron shackles; 2 Kings 25:7 has Zedekiah blinded and taken to Babylon in bronze shackles, and 2 Chronicles 33:11 has Manasseh taken with a hook in his nose and bound in bronze shackles. Hebrews 4:12 and Revelation 1:16 keep the same two-edged sword as an image.

stories.keyTakeaway: Israel sings a new song in the assembly of the godly, rejoicing in their Maker and King with dancing and music, for the LORD takes pleasure in His people and adorns the afflicted with salvation; with high praises in their mouths and a double-edged sword in their hands, the saints inflict vengeance on the nations, bind their kings with chains, and execute the judgment written, an honor for all His saints.

headings.text: Sing to the Lord a New Song

stories.title: 🎺 Psalms 150
summaryBullets: Hallelujah! Praise God in His sanctuary. Praise Him in His mighty heavens. (150:1).
Praise Him for His mighty acts; praise Him for His excellent greatness. (150:2).
Praise Him with the sound of the horn; praise Him with the harp and lyre. (150:3).
Praise Him with tambourine and dancing; praise Him with strings and flute. (150:4).
Praise Him with clashing cymbals; praise Him with resounding cymbals. (150:5).
Let everything that has breath praise the LORD! Hallelujah! (150:6).
crossRefs: Psalm 98:4-6: A shorter version of the same instrument list, lyre and harp, trumpets and the blast of the ram's horn, shouted before the LORD the King. This psalm runs the list to the end and adds strings, flute, and two kinds of cymbal.

2 Samuel 6:14-15: David dancing with all his might in a linen ephod while all Israel brought the ark up with shouting and the sound of the ram's horn. The psalm asks for that again by name, praise Him with tambourine and dancing.

Revelation 5:13: John hears every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea giving praise together. That is this psalm's last line carried all the way out, let everything that has breath praise the LORD.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִקְדָּשׁ (miqdash) / רָקִיעַ (raqiaʿ), Greek: ἁγίασμα / στερέωμα, Aramaic: מקדשא / רקיעא
translationNotes.note: Locations named for praise (v. 1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְשָׁמָה (neshamah), Greek: πνοή, Aramaic: נשמתא
translationNotes.note: All breathing creatures called to praise (v. 6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שׁוֹפָר (shofar) - נֵבֶל (nevel) - כִּנּוֹר (kinnor) - עוּגָב (ugav) - צִלְצְלִים (tsiltselim)
translationNotes.note: Verses 3-5 list the temple orchestra by name. The shofar is a ram's horn, not a musical instrument at all in the modern sense but a signal, used to call an assembly or open a year. The kinnor is the small lyre played by hand, the nevel the larger deeper harp. The tof is the frame drum. Minnim means strings and ugav is a wind instrument, usually rendered pipe or flute. The tsiltselim are cymbals, and the psalm names two kinds, the clashing and the resounding, which points to a small pair struck together and a large pair swung.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לְוִיִּם (Leviim), Levites
translationNotes.note: Temple music was a staffed profession, not a volunteer effort. 1 Chronicles 23:5 has David assign four thousand Levites to praise the LORD with instruments he had made for the purpose, and 1 Chronicles 25:7 counts two hundred and eighty-eight of them as trained and skilled in song, organized in twenty-four rotating courses under Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun. Those three names appear in the headings of psalms across the book. Verse 6 then hands the last line to everything that breathes.

stories.keyTakeaway: The psalm calls for praise everywhere, for God’s deeds and greatness, with a full range of instruments, ending with ‘Let everything that has breath praise the LORD.’

headings.text: Let Everything That Has Breath Praise the Lord

intro:
Psalms is a collection of 150 sacred songs composed by multiple authors across roughly a thousand years, from approximately 1410 BC to 430 BC. The largest single contributor was King David (c. 1040-970 BC), to whom 73 psalms are attributed in their Hebrew superscriptions (the Greek Septuagint attributes additional psalms to David, raising the count to 85 in that tradition). Other named authors include Asaph the Levite (12 psalms: 50, 73-83), the sons of Korah (11 psalms: 42, 44-49, 84-85, 87-88), Solomon (2 psalms: 72, 127), Moses (Psalm 90, the oldest in the collection), Heman the Ezrahite (Psalm 88), and Ethan the Ezrahite (Psalm 89). About forty-nine psalms are anonymous in the Hebrew text, several of which Jewish tradition assigns to Ezra. The final compilation of the Psalter is traditionally credited to Ezra around 450-430 BC during the post-exilic period, when the collection was gathered, organized, and standardized for second-temple worship.

David was born in Bethlehem, the youngest son of Jesse of the tribe of Judah, a shepherd in his youth who was anointed by the prophet Samuel and later became king of Judah at Hebron and then of a united Israel from Jerusalem. He composed psalms across his entire life: as a shepherd-boy in the hills around Bethlehem, as a court musician in Saul's household (1 Samuel 16:23), as a fugitive in the wilderness of Judah, as king celebrating victories or grieving losses, and as a father near the end of his reign. Asaph was a Levite musician of the clan of Gershon, appointed by David as one of three chief musicians at the tabernacle in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 6:39; 16:5); the "sons of Asaph" continued his musical guild for generations. The sons of Korah were Levite descendants of Korah whose ancestor led the rebellion recorded in Numbers 16; his sons survived (Numbers 26:11), and their descendants served as temple gatekeepers and musicians (1 Chronicles 9:19). Heman and Ethan the Ezrahites are named in 1 Kings 4:31 as wisdom figures comparable to Solomon. Moses composed Psalm 90 during the wilderness wandering between the Exodus (c. 1446 BC) and his death (c. 1406 BC), making it the oldest psalm in the collection.

Psalms is the nineteenth book of the Christian Old Testament. The Hebrew name Tehillim means "Praises" (singular Tehillah). The English title "Psalms" comes from the Greek Septuagint Psalmoi (3rd century BC), meaning "songs accompanied by stringed instruments" (related to psallein, "to pluck"); the Septuagint also called the book the Psalter. The collection is divided into five books (Psalms 1-41, 42-72, 73-89, 90-106, 107-150), each ending with a doxology. Psalms is the most heavily represented book of the Hebrew Bible among the Dead Sea Scrolls, with fragments from 36 separate scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD); the largest, 11QPs-a (the "Great Psalms Scroll"), contains 41 psalms plus some non-canonical compositions and dates to the 1st century AD.
